interventions.use_case: Embedding GPT-4 into an existing college algebra intelligent tutoring system to diagnose student errors and generate individualized corrective hints from transaction data and problem context
LLM-generated personalized corrective feedback for math tutor steps, including error diagnosis, hint authoring, and automated helpfulness evaluation

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 diagnosed student math errors with 87.8% accuracy overall on n=1,144 incorrect tutor transactions after prompt refinement, with near-perfect recognition of correct answers (99%) but weaker performance on wrong-field errors and multi-error responses. The paper reports accuracy by error type rather than learning gains; it evaluates whether LLMs can reliably identify and support algebraic problem-solving steps in an ITS context.
finding.measure: Error diagnosis accuracy on incorrect student responses in College Algebra tutors
finding.study_size: n=1,144 incorrect transactions (from 6,926 total tutor transactions)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues GPT-4 could reduce human tutor-author workload by scaling feedback creation and automating diagnosis/helpfulness evaluation, but it does not report a direct time-savings effect size. In the feedback analysis, 66% of hints were targeted, 22.3% were general, 7.1% gave the answer, and 4.8% were incorrect, suggesting promising but imperfect automation for authoring corrective hints.
finding.measure: Distribution of feedback quality categories; automated evaluation pass rate
finding.study_size: n=1,144 incorrect transactions for feedback generation; automated helpfulness evaluation not separately sample-sized

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in middle school mathematics, especially when real classrooms cannot always provide well-matched peers, sustained participation, or enough teacher orchestration. The authors ask whether large language models can be used not just as tutors, but as simulated student peers that participate in math discussions in ways that resemble authentic classroom collaboration.

To explore this, they built MathVC, an LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom in which one student interacts with multiple virtual classmates. The system uses a meta-planning controller to move conversations through CPS stages such as shared understanding, team organization, planning, execution, and validation, and a persona-simulation stack that encodes a task schema and error-injected persona schemas based on teacher-specified or curated misconceptions. The system also controls next-speaker selection and prompts responses to be short and colloquial.

The evaluation involved 14 U.S. middle school students in grades 6–8 who solved mathematics problems with two virtual peers: one limited-skill persona and one advanced-skill persona. Data came from chat logs, exit surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Students generally reported constructive interaction, shared understanding, engagement, motivation, and confidence gains. They especially valued the human-like fallibility of the peers, immediate scaffolding, and diverse perspectives, though some noted that the peers could sound too formal or adult-like. Overall, the paper argues that LLM-based peer simulation can support collaborative mathematical problem-solving, but authenticity depends on both conversational procedure and persona realism.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/user-study evaluation with 14 middle school participants, using interviews, logs, and descriptive survey data. It is methodologically useful but lacks experimental control, randomization, and inferential achievement outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests a promising, positive engagement and collaboration impact, but the evidence is descriptive and based on a small sample with no measured learning gains or effect sizes. The practical impact appears interesting but remains unclear for broader generalization.

interventions.use_case: LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom for middle school mathematics collaborative problem solving, where ChatGPT/GPT-4o generates virtual peer dialogue, stage-aware prompts, dialogue acts, and error-injected peer reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: In a 14-student middle school evaluation, MathVC was used for collaborative math problem solving on grade-level tasks, and participants reported that they were able to reach shared solutions and work effectively on the problems (exit survey mean=4.43/5 for shared understanding/solution; mean=4.21/5 for understanding and working effectively). The paper does not report pre/post achievement gains or effect sizes, so the evidence is based on descriptive survey and qualitative interaction data rather than measured test-score improvement.
finding.measure: Collaborative mathematical problem-solving success, self-reported understanding of the math problem, and exit survey ratings about shared solution attainment

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased engagement, motivation, persistence, and confidence while working with the virtual peers. Qualitative interviews described reduced cognitive burden, friendly competition, immediate feedback, and supportive scaffolding as mechanisms that helped sustain effort, but no standardized pre/post measure or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes, engagement/motivation perceptions, and exit survey responses

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively focused on collaboration, planning, and metacognitive reflection in mathematical CPS. Participants rated themselves highly on planning their steps and understanding how actions contributed to solving the problem (mean=4.36/5), and the system was explicitly designed to scaffold shared understanding, role organization, execution, and validation through stage-based dialogue.
finding.measure: Exit survey items on planning/role contribution and qualitative evidence of collaborative dialogue and metacognitive reflection

paper_profiles.title: Research on the Pathway of AI Technology Empowering the Development of Core Competencies in Middle School Mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Educational Theory and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how AI technology can support the development of core mathematical competencies in middle school mathematics, especially under conditions where traditional class-based instruction struggles to provide personalized guidance, timely feedback, and visualization of abstract thinking. The author frames the problem as a mismatch between broad, uniform teaching and the precise, differentiated cultivation of competencies such as abstraction, reasoning, modeling, intuitive imagination, operation, and data analysis.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper proposes a conceptual pathway for AI-enabled mathematics teaching. It describes five functional roles of AI in education—intelligent diagnosis, personalized recommendation, interactive feedback, visualization of thinking, and automated processing—and maps them onto the six middle-school mathematics competency dimensions. Examples include using VR/AR to support abstraction, dynamic geometry and 3D modeling to strengthen intuition and imagination, stepwise reasoning support and error diagnosis to improve logical reasoning and calculation, and data visualization and scenario simulation to support modeling and data analysis.

The paper focuses on middle school mathematics in the Chinese education context and argues that AI can make instruction more personalized, visual, and precise. It also identifies implementation challenges such as over-instrumentalization, limited teacher AI competence, uneven resource quality, and student foundation constraints. The conclusion recommends competency-oriented design, teacher training, student AI literacy development, and higher-quality resource construction, but it does not present outcome data from a specific classroom study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper rather than an empirical evaluation. It does not report a research design, sample, comparison condition, or outcome data, so it provides no basis for causal or correlational evidence grading beyond grey-literature style analysis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical impacts are reported. The paper discusses potential instructional pathways and implementation challenges, but it does not measure learning gains, engagement, or efficiency effects.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual use of ChatGPT-like generative AI as an intelligent interaction tool to support middle school mathematics learning through question answering, prompt-based guidance, personalized feedback, and thinking scaffolds for abstraction, reasoning, modeling, visualization, and data analysis.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT scaffolding in supporting metacognition for limit concepts in guided inquiry mathematics learning
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how ChatGPT-mediated scaffolding can support students’ metacognitive development while learning limit concepts in calculus through a guided inquiry approach. The paper is motivated by the challenge that students often struggle with planning, monitoring, and evaluating their problem-solving in abstract mathematics, and by the question of whether generative AI can serve as a metacognitive partner rather than merely a tool for getting answers. The authors focus on systematic integration of ChatGPT within inquiry-based mathematics learning and on the scaffolding patterns that emerge during student-AI interactions.

The intervention was implemented with 75 undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in Calculus I at Universitas Jambi, Indonesia. Over four weeks and six 120-minute sessions, students worked through guided inquiry activities on limit concepts with support from ChatGPT and instructor guidance. Two experienced mathematics lecturers, both of whom received specialized training in integrating ChatGPT into guided inquiry, facilitated the activities. Data sources included pre/post metacognitive assessments, a limit concept test, screen recordings of 180 hours of ChatGPT interactions, reflective journals, and interviews.

The study finds that ChatGPT-supported guided inquiry was associated with significant gains in metacognitive skills, especially monitoring and evaluation, as well as improved conceptual understanding of limits. The analysis identifies six scaffolding patterns: prior knowledge activation, guided exploration, structured analysis, critical evaluation, independent application, and metacognitive reflection. These patterns suggest that ChatGPT can help students connect everyday examples to formal mathematics, generate and test hypotheses, analyze representations, and reflect on their reasoning. However, the paper also notes that a substantial minority of students passively accepted AI-generated answers, indicating that learning outcomes depend heavily on structured prompts, teacher mediation, and explicit instruction in critical questioning. The authors conclude that ChatGPT is most effective when embedded in a carefully designed guided inquiry framework that preserves student agency and supports reflective mathematical thinking.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed convergent mixed-methods study, but it is not a randomized controlled trial and relies on a single-group pre-post design with qualitative coding. The evidence is informative but limited by the absence of a comparison group and potential selection/implementation effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are modest-to-large for metacognition and positive for limit learning, with effect sizes around d=0.78-0.88 and a mean learning gain of 0.82. The study is on a specific undergraduate mathematics population rather than a broad K-12 group, so the broader impact is promising but not definitive.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-mediated scaffolding in guided inquiry mathematics learning for limit concepts, using dialogic prompts, iterative feedback, and reflective questioning to support metacognition and problem solving.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed significant gains in understanding limit concepts after the four-week ChatGPT-supported guided inquiry intervention (n=75). The paper reports a mean improvement of 0.82 (p < .001) on the Limit Concept Assessment, with stronger performance especially in conceptual and procedural limit tasks.
finding.measure: Limit Concept Assessment (LCA), 20-item test of procedural and conceptual understanding of limits

finding.finding_summary: Metacognitive skills improved significantly over the intervention, with the largest gains in monitoring (d = 0.85), followed by evaluation (d = 0.82) and planning (d = 0.78). Across 180 hours of interaction data, students shifted from procedural queries toward more investigative and reflective questioning, indicating stronger self-regulated problem solving.
finding.measure: Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI) and coded ChatGPT-student interaction patterns
finding.effect_size: d=0.85 (monitoring), d=0.82 (evaluation), d=0.78 (planning); overall d=0.85 reported for metacognitive skills

paper_profiles.title: LLAMA LIMA: A Living Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Generative AI on Learning Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents LLAMA LIMA, a living meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies on generative AI interventions for mathematics learning. The authors focus on a rapidly changing evidence base around tools such as ChatGPT, arguing that conventional reviews quickly become outdated as model capabilities and educational uses evolve. Their central question is whether generative AI-based instructional interventions improve mathematics learning outcomes and, more broadly, which study, learner, context, and implementation factors may shape those effects.

The intervention studied is not a single program but a synthesis of many generative-AI-based implementations, including uses of AI as a mathematics expert, tutor/feedback system, instructor, collaborative-learning facilitator, and teacher-support tool. Across the included studies, generative AI was used in a range of mathematics topics and learning arrangements, with interventions delivered in classroom, online, and other instructional settings. The meta-analysis included 21 studies and 38 effect sizes, with participants spanning primary, lower-secondary, upper-secondary, bachelor’s-level, adult, and unspecified K-12 populations.

The pooled result suggests a small positive overall effect on mathematics learning (g = 0.42), but with substantial heterogeneity and wide credible intervals. The authors conclude that generative AI may support mathematics learning, but the current evidence is too limited and variable to support strong generalizations. They emphasize that effectiveness likely depends on instructional design, learner characteristics, contextual fit, and how the AI is implemented, and they frame the work as an ongoing living synthesis rather than a final verdict.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a living meta-analysis following PRISMA-LSR, synthesizing 21 experimental/quasi-experimental studies with Bayesian multilevel modeling. Although the evidence base is still limited and heterogeneous, the methodology is strong and directly relevant.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on mathematics outcomes is medium in size (g=0.42), exceeding the 0.20 threshold. However, the authors emphasize substantial uncertainty and heterogeneity, so the impact is promising but not yet fully stable.

interventions.use_case: Living meta-analysis of generative AI/LLM-based interventions for mathematics learning, including ChatGPT-style tutors, chatbots, AI assistants, and related conversational tools used for assessment, feedback, instruction, and support in K-12 and higher education mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Across 21 studies and 38 effect sizes (total n=4,071), generative AI–based interventions for mathematics learning showed a positive pooled effect on mathematics outcomes, with Hedges' g=0.42 and a 95% credible interval of [0.13, 0.72]. The authors note substantial heterogeneity (between-study SD=0.28; within-study SD=0.71), indicating effects vary meaningfully by implementation and context.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes / mathematics performance

paper_profiles.title: Struggle First, Prompt Later: How Task Complexity Shapes Learning with GenAI-Assisted Pretesting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether pretesting before using generative AI can improve learning, and whether the benefits depend on how the pretesting is implemented and on task complexity. The authors focus on a core instructional problem in AI-supported learning: students may rely on ChatGPT or similar tools too quickly, reducing productive struggle and weakening retention. The paper tests whether requiring learners to attempt a problem before consulting ChatGPT leads to better learning than immediate access to the AI.

Across three randomized experiments, the study compares different pretesting approaches. Study 1 compares a pretest condition, where participants first attempt a problem and then use ChatGPT, with a no-pretest condition, where participants access ChatGPT immediately. Study 2 compares fixed prewritten pretest questions with AI-assisted adaptive pretesting that generates follow-up questions based on student responses. Study 3 examines whether these effects differ for a more complex, iterative, exploratory task and adds motivation measures from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory. In all studies, students worked with ChatGPT to complete statistics-related cybersecurity tasks and then completed objective posttests.

The participants were undergraduate information sciences students at a large public research university in Pennsylvania, United States. The tasks were embedded in an intermediate-level statistics course and covered one-way and two-way chi-square analysis in Studies 1 and 2, and regression/model selection in Study 3. The interventions were delivered during regular course sessions over the course of the same week in Studies 1 and 2, and a similar short classroom-based schedule in Study 3.

The main conclusion is that pretesting before ChatGPT use can improve learning, but the value of AI-adaptive scaffolding depends on task structure. In the more structured chi-square task, adaptive AI-assisted pretesting did not outperform fixed pretesting. In the more complex model-selection task, adaptive pretesting improved both final test performance and interest/enjoyment. The authors conclude that pretesting helps preserve productive struggle in AI-supported learning, and that AI is most useful when it dynamically supports open-ended, higher-order tasks rather than routine computational ones.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a multi-study randomized experimental paper with clear group assignment, comparative conditions, and quantitative outcome measures, which supports strong causal inference. However, it is a single preprint/early-stage study in one course context with some methodological concerns and no peer-reviewed publication status indicated here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gains are large in Study 1 (d=1.543) and meaningful in Study 3, indicating substantial impact when pretesting is combined with ChatGPT in complex tasks. The intervention appears especially effective for higher-order reasoning and transfer, which suggests strong potential relevance for education settings.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT is used as the information-retrieval and coaching tool inside pretesting tasks: students first attempt a problem, then query ChatGPT for step-by-step explanations, clarification, and additional prompts. In Study 2 and Study 3, an AI Coach dynamically generates follow-up pretest questions tailored to student responses.

finding.finding_summary: In Study 1, pretesting before using ChatGPT improved performance on a 11-item multiple-choice transfer test about two-way chi-square analysis. The pretest group scored significantly higher than the no-pretest group (M=91.85, SD=9.52 vs. M=78.59, SD=7.62), t(58)=5.979, p<.001, Cohen's d=1.543.
finding.measure: Final multiple-choice transfer test on chi-square concepts

finding.finding_summary: In Study 2, fixed pretesting and AI-assisted pretesting produced similar final test performance after students used ChatGPT for a two-way chi-square task. Final scores did not differ significantly between groups (Fixed Pretesting M=85.71, SD=8.49; AI-Assisted Pretesting M=83.56, SD=10.44), t(76)=1.002, p=0.319.
finding.measure: Final multiple-choice test on chi-square learning and transfer

finding.finding_summary: In Study 3, AI-assisted pretesting outperformed fixed pretesting on a regression/model-selection task that required iterative reasoning and decision-making. Final test scores were higher for the AI-assisted group (M=76.87, SD=10.72) than the fixed-pretesting group (M=69.65, SD=17.03), F(1,85)=5.839, p=0.018, partial η²=0.064.
finding.measure: Final multiple-choice test on regression concepts, model selection, multicollinearity, and transfer

finding.finding_summary: Study 3 found that AI-assisted pretesting increased learners' interest and enjoyment relative to fixed pretesting. The difference was statistically significant, F(1,85)=4.417, p=0.039, partial η²=0.049, with the AI-assisted group reporting higher interest-enjoyment (M=33.35, SD=7.0) than the control group (M=29.08, SD=11.8).
finding.measure: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscale: interest-enjoyment

finding.finding_summary: Study 3 did not find significant differences between AI-assisted and fixed pretesting on tension-pressure, perceived choice, perceived competence, or perceived value. Although means trended in a favorable direction for AI-assisted pretesting, these motivational outcomes were not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales: tension-pressure, perceived choice, perceived competence, perceived value

paper_profiles.title: Exploring elementary pre-service teachers’ instrumental genesis in designing AI chatbots
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary pre-service teachers design AI chatbots for mathematics instruction and how their design decisions reveal instrumental genesis, meaning the reciprocal shaping between the designer and the digital artifact. The study asks what instructional functions teachers assign to chatbots, what design considerations they embed in prompts, and what constraints or failures they encounter when trying to make the chatbot behave as intended.

The intervention was a four-week chatbot-design project embedded in an advanced mathematics education course at a South Korean university of education. Eleven elementary pre-service teachers first received a lecture on generative AI and prompt engineering techniques, then used the Wrtn generative AI platform with GPT-4 to build chatbots for grade 5–6 number-and-operations content. They submitted lesson plans, prompts, chatbot links, and reflective reports; the analysis focused on the initial design artifacts and reflections.

Findings show that teachers designed chatbots for four main instructional functions: problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual understanding, and real-life application. Their prompts commonly incorporated scaffolding, affective support, bounded autonomy tied to the curriculum, and gamification. The study concludes that pre-service teachers can move beyond simple tool use to deliberate instructional design with AI, but they often struggle with curriculum non-compliance, limited diversity in chatbot outputs, incomplete scaffolding, and unpredictable responses outside the prompt scope. The author argues that teacher education should emphasize reflective prompt design, curriculum alignment, and adaptive mediation of AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study with thematic analysis of 11 pre-service teachers’ chatbot designs and reflections. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not test learning outcomes or use a causal design, so it meets limited credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful instructional design implications for AI-supported mathematics learning, but it reports no student outcome effects and no classroom implementation results. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service teachers designed ChatGPT-like generative AI chatbots in Wrtn for elementary mathematics instruction in the number and operations domain, using prompt engineering to make the chatbot act as a problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual-understanding, or application-support instrument.
Gamified chatbot lesson designs with storylines, target scores, secret codes, and level-based challenges to motivate elementary students while solving arithmetic tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The study qualitatively found that pre-service teachers designed chatbots to support mathematical numeracy through problem-solving, problem-posing, conceptual understanding, and real-life application. However, the paper did not evaluate student learning gains; it instead documents intended instructional functions and design constraints in 11 chatbot designs, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of chatbot prompts and reflective reports for intended mathematics-learning functions

finding.finding_summary: Participants intentionally built affective support into most chatbot designs, aiming to increase student motivation through friendly, polite, and encouraging responses. The study reports these as design intentions only and does not measure student engagement or motivation outcomes, so no quantitative effect estimate is available.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of prompts for affective support and gamification features

finding.finding_summary: The chatbots were deliberately designed to promote scaffolding, bounded autonomy, and learning-by-teaching, all of which are intended to support metacognitive and critical-thinking processes. The paper provides qualitative evidence of these intended mechanisms but no direct assessment of durable-skill outcomes in students.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of prompt design and reflective reports for scaffolding, bounded autonomy, and learning-by-teaching mechanisms

paper_profiles.title: Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how knowledge-building during learning-by-teaching relates to middle school students’ learning outcomes in algebra. The central question is whether students’ elaborated responses to a teachable agent’s follow-up questions predict gains in conceptual knowledge and procedural skill, and whether those gains are explained by prior knowledge or by the dialogic process itself.

The intervention is an online learning-by-teaching environment, APLUS, in which students tutor a virtual agent, SimStudent, to solve algebraic equations. The key instructional feature is ExpectAdapt, an LLM-based questioning framework that generates adaptive follow-up questions after students respond to static focal questions such as why a solution step should or should not be performed. The prompts use role prompting, few-shot demonstrations, extra context, and domain-specific mathematical assertions to elicit more elaborated, knowledge-building responses.

The study involved 23 middle school students in grades 6–8 from across the United States in a hybrid format over up to five days. Students completed pretests and posttests measuring procedural skill and conceptual knowledge, and their dialogue responses were classified as knowledge-building or knowledge-telling. Results showed that a higher proportion of knowledge-building responses was associated with higher post-test performance in both domains. Prior knowledge did not significantly predict knowledge-building overall, and low-prior students who produced more knowledge-building responses performed as well as high-prior peers on post-tests. The authors conclude that adaptive follow-up questioning can scaffold knowledge-building and may help narrow performance gaps, though the evidence is correlational rather than causal.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/path-analysis study with a small sample (n=23), no random assignment, and outcome analyses based on pre-post change plus associations between dialogue behavior and post-test scores. It provides useful evidence on mechanisms, but internal validity is limited relative to an RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows meaningful learning gains and moderate mechanistic effects, but the evidence is from a small single-group sample and the reported path coefficients are modest. The practical impact is promising but still unclear for broader K-12 implementation without stronger causal evidence.

interventions.use_case: LLM-driven teachable-agent questioning framework (ExpectAdapt) embedded in a learning-by-teaching algebra environment to generate adaptive follow-up questions, classify tutor responses, and elicit knowledge-building dialogue from middle school students.
SimStudent/APLUS teachable-agent tutoring environment for algebra equation solving with step-by-step guided problem solving, quizzes, and metacognitive scaffolds.

finding.finding_summary: Middle school students (n=23) showed significant pre-to-post gains in both conceptual and procedural mathematics tests after interacting with the teachable-agent system. Mean conceptual test performance increased from 0.78±0.18 to 0.90±0.13 (paired t(22)=-4.47, p<0.001), and procedural skill increased from 0.70±0.33 to 0.81±0.27 (t(22)=-2.68, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Conceptual Knowledge Test (CKT) and Procedural Skill Test (PST) on algebra equation solving
finding.std_deviation: CKT pre/post SDs=0.18/0.13; PST pre/post SDs=0.33/0.27

finding.finding_summary: The proportion of knowledge-building responses to adaptive follow-up questions (%KBR) was a significant independent predictor of post-test outcomes. Path analysis showed %KBR predicted conceptual post-test performance (β=.138, p<0.05), and the authors report the association with procedural post-test scores as positive as well, indicating that elaborative reasoning during dialogue supported learning beyond prior performance.
finding.measure: Percentage of knowledge-building responses (%KBR) during tutor-tutee dialogue; post-test conceptual and procedural scores
finding.effect_size: β=.138 for conceptual post-test; other path coefficients not fully reported in text

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appears to support engagement in productive teaching dialogue and sustained participation, especially for low-prior students, but this was not the primary outcome and was measured indirectly through interaction behavior rather than validated affective scales. The paper suggests adaptive questioning helped students persist in explanation-building and respond more deeply over time.
finding.measure: Dialogue participation/engagement inferred from adaptive follow-up question responses and %KBR

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students perceive different AI roles during mathematical modelling and whether those preferences vary by learner characteristics. The authors focus on a gap in the literature: while AI and large language models are increasingly used in mathematics education, there is limited evidence about which kinds of AI support are most useful for the iterative, open-ended process of modelling.

The study compares five AI personas: Tutor, Teaching Assistant, Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student. Each role was implemented with GPT-based models and role-specific system prompts that constrained responses to short outputs. The experiment used a within-subjects, counterbalanced randomized controlled design in which participants completed a baseline modelling task without AI and then five short modelling tasks online with each AI role. Before the tasks, participants completed surveys measuring design thinking, computational thinking, and mathematical modelling self-efficacy; after each task they rated their experience and at the end they ranked the roles.

The participants were 26 university students in Hong Kong SAR and China who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, so their mathematical background was comparable to typical high school graduates. The tasks were simplified to a high-school level and framed around the modelling cycle, with explanations of situation model, real model, and mathematical model provided at the start. The authors found that students strongly preferred competent, supportive roles over the Struggling Student role. Tutor was generally most preferred, followed by Excellent Student, Peer, and TA, though differences among these four constructive roles were not significant. The Struggling Student role was consistently rated lowest for preference, confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction.

The study also found that design thinking and computational thinking were positively associated with mathematical modelling self-efficacy, especially design thinking. However, these baseline competencies largely did not predict AI role preferences, except that students with higher design thinking slightly preferred the TA role more than those with lower design thinking. The main conclusion is that students value competent, process-supportive AI personas in modelling tasks, and that AI scaffolding should emphasize guidance, clarity, and encouragement rather than low-quality or misleading peer-like support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized, counterbalanced within-subjects study, but the main analyses are preference and perception outcomes rather than direct learning gains, and the sample is very small (n=26). It provides useful formative evidence on AI role design, but not high-credibility causal evidence of achievement impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear learner preference and experience differences across AI roles, but it does not demonstrate achievement gains or quantify educational impact with a learning effect size. The practical implication is useful for design, yet the observed impact on learning outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: GPT-based role-playing AI used in mathematical modelling tasks as a tutor, teaching assistant, peer student, struggling student, or excellent student; responses were constrained to 100-150 characters and delivered through chat during stepwise modelling problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure learning gains directly; instead, it evaluates how students prefer different AI roles during mathematical modelling. Across n=26, students preferred the Tutor role most (mean rank=2.35) and the Struggling Student role least (mean rank=4.42), with a significant Friedman test effect, χ2(4, N=26)=28.83, p<.001. This indicates that competent, process-oriented AI support is favored in mathematics modelling contexts, but the study provides no direct achievement effect size.
finding.measure: AI role preference rankings during mathematical modelling tasks; task confidence and perceived helpfulness/ease of interaction

finding.finding_summary: AI role significantly affected task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction, all with n=26 and Friedman tests p<.001. The Struggling Student role was consistently worst (task confidence M=1.88, helpfulness M=1.92, ease of interaction M=1.81), while competent roles were rated similarly and more positively, suggesting that emotionally supportive and clear AI personas improve learner experience even though no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction ratings

finding.finding_summary: Baseline design thinking and computational thinking were positively associated with mathematical modelling self-efficacy, supporting the paper’s argument that these durable skills matter for modelling. PLS-SEM showed DT strongly predicted MMSE (β=0.730, p<.001) and CT also predicted MMSE (β=0.300, p<.001), with R2=0.808 for the model.
finding.measure: Correlations and PLS-SEM paths among design thinking, computational thinking, and mathematical modelling self-efficacy

paper_profiles.title: Reflection-Satisfaction Tradeoff: Investigating Impact of Reflection on Student Engagement with AI-Generated Programming Hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how reflection prompts interact with AI-generated programming hints in an online introductory programming course, with a particular focus on the tradeoff between students’ satisfaction with AI support and the quality of their reflective responses. The authors ask whether prompting students to reflect before or after receiving an AI hint, whether aligning prompts with different self-regulated learning (SRL) phases, and whether using directed versus open reflection prompts changes hint-seeking behavior, reflective depth, and problem-solving outcomes.

The intervention was implemented in two randomized controlled trials using a custom JupyterLab-based support system that delivered GPT-4-generated hints on demand. Trial 1 compared before-hint reflection, after-hint reflection, and control conditions, and varied the SRL phase targeted by each prompt (planning, monitoring, evaluation). Trial 2 compared open versus directed prompts and also incorporated students’ reflections into the hint-generation prompt. The study was conducted in two offerings of the same online introductory data science programming course at the University of Michigan, with students working on Python programming assignments.

The main finding was a consistent inverse relationship between the quality of students’ reflections and their satisfaction with the AI-generated hints: more structured reflection conditions tended to produce deeper reflections but lower hint satisfaction. Before-hint prompts, planning-focused prompts, and directed prompts generally elicited higher-quality reflections than their counterparts, but these conditions were often rated as less satisfying. Immediate performance differences were small or not statistically significant. The authors conclude that educational AI should not be optimized only for user satisfaction; instead, it should be designed to encourage effortful engagement and self-regulated learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled field experiment with two trials in an authentic course setting, which provides relatively strong causal evidence. However, the sample sizes are modest, some analyses are descriptive due to low participation, and the paper focuses on short-term outcomes rather than long-term learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows meaningful changes in reflection quality and engagement, but not in immediate performance outcomes. The overall impact is therefore modest and somewhat mixed, with stronger effects on metacognitive engagement than on academic achievement.

interventions.use_case: AI-generated programming hints in a JupyterLab course environment, with GPT-4 producing personalized debugging/help hints from buggy code and execution feedback; the study adds reflection prompts around hint requests and also incorporates student reflections into hint generation in Trial 2.

finding.finding_summary: The study found a clear reflection-quality tradeoff: before-hint, planning, and directed prompts produced higher-quality reflections, but students reported lower satisfaction with the AI-generated hints. Immediate problem-solving performance did not differ significantly across conditions (e.g., immediate success rates ranged from 18.8% to 23.1% in Trial 1 and 17.6% to 26.3% across SRL-phase prompts), suggesting the scaffolds changed the depth of processing more than short-term task success.
finding.measure: Reflection quality coding; hint satisfaction ratings; immediate success rate on the next submission after a hint request
finding.study_size: n=33 Trial 1 students; n=64 Trial 2 students

finding.finding_summary: Reflection prompts changed students' engagement with AI support: before-hint reflection increased participation and produced more non-empty reflections (83.3% of students wrote at least one non-empty reflection vs. 53.8% in after-hint), but hint satisfaction was lower (54.0% before-hint vs. 61.0% control). The intervention appears to increase effortful engagement and self-regulation, while reducing perceived convenience or satisfaction with the AI hints.
finding.measure: Hint satisfaction ratings; participation rate in reflection; number of non-empty reflections

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been conceptualized, what forms it takes in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors note that the term scaffolding has been used inconsistently across educational research, often as a broad synonym for support, and they aim to clarify the construct by synthesizing the literature.

The review analyzes 66 English-language SSCI-listed articles published between 1998 and 2009 in primary and secondary education. The paper distinguishes three key characteristics of scaffolding: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility. It also proposes a framework separating scaffolding means (feeding back, hints, instructing, explaining, modeling, questioning) from scaffolding intentions (direction maintenance, cognitive structuring, reduction of degrees of freedom, recruitment, and contingency management/frustration control). Most included studies were descriptive and concentrated on literacy, though math and science studies were also present.

Across the reviewed studies, scaffolding was most often examined in face-to-face classroom interactions, sometimes in one-to-one tutoring and sometimes in whole-class or small-group settings. The review concludes that scaffolding appears effective in the limited body of experimental and quasi-experimental research, especially for metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, but that the field is hindered by measurement problems and the lack of a shared operationalization. The authors call for better instruments, stronger fidelity checks, and more research in naturalistic classroom settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review of scaffolding research, not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention. It synthesizes prior studies but does not itself use a controlled or observational design to estimate effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact estimate is reported in this paper, and it does not evaluate a technology or intervention relevant to the requested ChatGPT-in-middle-school-math topic. The article is useful conceptually for scaffolding, but it provides no measurable impact for this taxonomy.

paper_profiles.title: Digital Technologies In The Early Primary School Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter surveys research on digital technologies in early primary mathematics, focusing on how different technologies change teaching and learning rather than on a single intervention effect. It asks what affordances, interaction types, and pedagogical constraints of digital tools matter for mathematics learning in the early grades, and it draws together findings from prior studies to compare design choices across tools.

The chapter reviews a wide range of digital technologies, including virtual manipulatives, desktop software, touchscreen and multitouch applications, dynamic geometry environments, and programming tools. It discusses how these tools support number sense, geometry, and programming-related mathematical activity through different interaction modes such as conversing, manipulating, navigating, and through instructional structures ranging from instructive to constructive environments. Particular attention is given to how feedback, direct manipulation, symbolic representation, bodily engagement, and teacher mediation shape learning.

The paper is not a single empirical study but a synthesis of prior work, mostly on early primary learners, with some examples extending to older elementary and middle school geometry research for theoretical continuity. The main conclusion is that digital technologies can support mathematics learning in early grades when their design affordances are aligned with the mathematical goal and when teachers interpret, orchestrate, and mediate student interaction. The chapter emphasizes that different tools support different kinds of mathematical activity, and that implementation details such as feedback, task structure, and opportunities for teacher-student interaction strongly affect learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a chapter/review synthesizing prior studies rather than reporting a new controlled study. It is peer-reviewed scholarly synthesis with clear conceptual structure, but the evidence base is largely qualitative, descriptive, or drawn from small studies with mixed designs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter argues that digital technologies can shape early mathematics learning, but it does not provide a single estimate of effect or strong causal evidence. Reported impacts are generally modest and highly dependent on tool design, teacher mediation, and task structure.

interventions.use_case: chapter-length review of computer-based mathematics software, virtual manipulatives, touchscreen applications, and programming tools used in early primary mathematics learning

reviews game-like and simulation-like digital tools for number sense and geometry, including adaptive number games (e.g., Number Race), fraction estimation games, and touchscreen task environments with game mechanics
reviews programmable robotic toys (e.g., Bee-bot, Probot, Lego NXT) used to support preschool and primary mathematics problem solving, mapping, and measurement

paper_profiles.title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how collaborative design of curriculum and learning materials can function as professional development for teachers. The authors argue that many teacher design activities are grounded in situated learning and cultural-historical activity theory, and that key features of productive teacher learning include situatedness, agency, and the cyclical nature of learning and educational change.

Rather than testing a single intervention in one setting, the paper synthesizes three case descriptions from different contexts: an online participatory professional development model for secondary English teachers in the United States; teacher design teams working on curriculum reform in Ethiopia, Ghana, and Tanzania; and the Remote Networked School initiative in Quebec, Canada. Across these cases, teachers collaboratively designed, adapted, enacted, and revised curricular materials, often with support from researchers, facilitators, or domain experts, and in some cases with technology-mediated collaboration.

The main conclusion is that collaborative design can support teacher learning when it is authentic to teachers’ work, well scaffolded, and organized as an iterative cycle of design, implementation, reflection, and revision. The paper emphasizes that teachers learn not only through exposure to new ideas but also through active participation in designing materials for their own contexts, negotiating shared problems, and observing the effects of their designs in practice. It also highlights that successful implementation depends on supportive partnerships, access to expertise, and alignment with local needs and constraints.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conceptual/theoretical synthesis with three qualitative case descriptions of collaborative design as professional development, not an experimental evaluation of a technology intervention. The paper uses design-based research and case evidence, but it does not report causal impact estimates for a specific AI or instructional technology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear educational relevance for understanding collaborative curriculum design and teacher learning, but it does not demonstrate measurable student or system impact from a technology intervention. Any implications are indirect and theoretical rather than quantified.

paper_profiles.title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an adaptive mathematics tutoring system, Wayang Outpost (later MathSpring), can improve learning by addressing three interacting dimensions of student experience: cognition, metacognition, and affect. The authors ask how intelligent tutoring systems can personalize content, support problem-solving strategies, and respond to students’ emotions and self-regulation needs, rather than focusing only on correctness. The paper is both a system description and an evaluation of multiple interventions developed over years of iterative design.

The intervention combines several components: adaptive problem selection based on an effort-based tutoring algorithm, multimedia hints and worked examples, math fact retrieval training for basic fluency, open student models and progress pages for self-monitoring, affective learning companions, and teacher-facing reports. These features aim to keep students in an appropriate challenge range, provide scaffolds during problem solving, encourage reflection and goal setting, and support motivation when students show signs of boredom, disengagement, or low effort. The system is designed around standardized-test-style mathematics problems drawn from MCAS, SAT, and teacher-generated items.

The empirical studies reported involved middle- and high-school students in Massachusetts, including a 2012 study with 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students and earlier classroom deployments since 2004. Some studies used randomized or controlled comparisons, and the paper reports improved short-term learning, better longer-term standardized test performance, and gains in math fluency, especially when math fact retrieval training was combined with tutoring. The authors conclude that a single intelligent tutor can meaningfully support mathematics learning when it integrates cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and teacher-facing supports, but the effectiveness depends on how adaptivity, scaffolding, and motivational feedback are implemented.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper with multiple classroom studies, including a controlled study, but it is not a single clean RCT with fully reported design details across all outcomes in the excerpt. Evidence is reasonably strong for an applied ITS, though some outcome reporting is mixed and not all analyses include complete effect-size information.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest-to-medium positive impacts on priority middle-school math populations, including standardized test gains and improved algebra-pattern learning (e.g., d=0.38 and d=0.77). The broader engagement/metacognitive benefits are meaningful but less precisely quantified, so the overall impact is best characterized as green rather than blue.

interventions.use_case: multimedia adaptive mathematics tutoring for middle and high school students using personalized problem selection, step-by-step hints, worked examples, affective learning companions, and teacher dashboards

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports repeated positive effects of the Wayang Outpost/MathSpring ITS on math achievement. In a 2012 controlled study with 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students, 7th graders using Wayang had a near-significant MCAS score advantage over controls (Mean Wayang=244.82 vs. Mean Control=239.50; F(1,93)=2.2, p=0.14), and the combined 7th/8th grade MAP patterns and algebra gains were significantly higher for the Wayang group (p<0.01, Cohen’s d=0.38). For 8th graders alone, gains in MAP-Algebra/Patterns were larger (d=0.77), especially when teachers tailored the system toward algebra content.
finding.measure: MCAS standardized test scores; Measures of Academic Progress (MAP) patterns and algebra subtest gains
finding.study_size: n=198 (2012 controlled study); additional aggregated comparisons across earlier cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and evaluated to improve engagement, affect, and motivation through affective companions, progress reports, and effort-based tutoring. The paper reports that these mechanisms increased supportive behaviors and reduced disengagement, with evidence from student gaming-of-the-system records, self-reports, and affect detectors; however, specific standardized effect sizes for engagement/affect are not consistently reported in the excerpted results.
finding.measure: student gaming-of-the-system records; affect detector outputs; student self-reports of emotion/engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies metacognitive support, especially self-regulation via open student models, progress pages, and help-seeking scaffolds. It argues that these interventions encourage reflection, goal setting, monitoring, and informed choice, and presents evidence that higher student progress-page use is associated with better self-regulatory behaviors, though the excerpt does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: student progress page usage; self-regulation behaviors; help-seeking and monitoring measures

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing reports provided immediate, fine-grained information on student mastery, engagement, affect, and problem-level difficulty, enabling teachers to identify struggling students and challenging skills in real time. The paper presents this as a practical benefit for classroom management and instruction, but does not report a formal effect size for teacher workload or time savings.
finding.measure: teacher dashboard/report use; real-time progress monitoring and class analytics

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding and dialogic teaching in mathematics education: introduction and review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces and reviews a special issue on scaffolding and dialogic teaching in mathematics education. The authors ask how scaffolding has been conceptualized, how it has been extended from one-to-one tutoring to classroom, peer, and technology-mediated contexts, and how dialogic teaching can deepen or refine the scaffolding idea. Rather than reporting a single intervention, the article synthesizes conceptual and empirical work to clarify what counts as scaffolding, what its defining characteristics are, and how it relates to dialogue and participation in mathematics learning.

The review covers recent mathematics-education scaffolding studies published between 2010 and 2015, plus papers in the special issue, along with a brief survey of dialogic teaching literature. The population context is broad: elementary through high school students, low-attaining and low-SES learners, future teachers, and even parents in some cited studies. Settings include classrooms, small-group work, one-to-one tutoring, and computer-supported environments, with mathematics topics ranging from arithmetic and graphs to geometry, modelling, probability, statistics, and algebra.

The main conclusion is that scaffolding is most usefully understood as contingent, responsive, and intended support that gradually transfers responsibility to learners, but that it should not be reduced to simple input or any generic support. The authors argue that scaffolding becomes more powerful when enriched by dialogic teaching, because dialogue highlights responsiveness, shared meaning-making, and the possibility of open-ended inquiry and creativity. They also caution that research should clearly separate the scaffolding intervention from its learning effects and pay greater attention to long-term, layered, distributed, and cumulative implementation processes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed survey/review paper, not an empirical intervention study. It synthesizes prior scaffolding and dialogic teaching literature in mathematics education using a clear search-and-screen approach, but it does not itself estimate causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has scholarly impact as a conceptual and review article, especially for framing scaffolding and dialogic teaching in mathematics education. However, it reports no direct intervention effect sizes or learner outcome impacts from this paper itself.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions of ChatGPT as a tool for teaching and learning mathematics, with a focus on whether the system can support mathematical instruction and where it falls short. The authors ask how students, educators, and other stakeholders view ChatGPT after its launch, and whether it can be used safely and effectively in mathematics education.

The study uses a qualitative case study approach with two stages: content analysis of interview data and user-experience testing. In the interview phase, 30 people with experience discussing or using ChatGPT in mathematics were selected from public blogs and interviews; in the user-experience phase, three educators used ChatGPT for one week across a set of mathematics scenarios. The tasks included solving linear and cubic equations, evaluating limits and derivatives, and explaining geometry, especially Pythagoras’ theorem.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is promising for mathematics education because it can generate fast explanations, examples, and step-by-step solutions, especially for basic or introductory material. However, it also produces mathematical errors, misinterprets geometry, and cannot reliably detect or correct misconceptions. The authors argue that ChatGPT should be treated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human teachers, and that safe, responsible use in mathematics education requires caution, guidelines, and further research.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study with interview content analysis and small-scale user testing, not an experimental or causal design. It provides useful early evidence about ChatGPT’s strengths and weaknesses in math education, but it does not estimate achievement effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct achievement effect size on middle school mathematics outcomes. Its findings indicate mixed and context-dependent usefulness, with some correct explanations but also substantial errors, so the net educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a math-supporting conversational tutor and explanatory assistant for middle school–level mathematics topics, including algebraic equations, limits/derivatives, and geometry explanations.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study did not measure student achievement directly; instead, it tested ChatGPT on several math tasks and solicited stakeholder perceptions. ChatGPT produced correct explanatory text for some geometry prompts (e.g., Pythagoras’ theorem) but also made multiple computation and reasoning errors on algebra, limits, derivatives, and geometry (e.g., incorrect solutions to 3x+4(1-5x)=-9 and x^3+1=0; incorrect evaluation of limits/derivatives and triangle geometry).
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT responses to math prompts; user experience observations; stakeholder interview content analysis
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user testing

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived ChatGPT as helpful for providing instant feedback, step-by-step explanations, and support for problem solving, which could support metacognitive and self-directed learning. However, the study also emphasized that ChatGPT can reinforce misconceptions, fail to correct errors, and encourage overreliance rather than deeper reasoning.
finding.measure: Interview themes on perceived learning support and limitations; qualitative user experience judgments
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can produce explanations and examples quickly, sometimes faster than manual drafting, and may help educators generate instructional content and responses within seconds. No quantitative productivity metric was reported, but the study repeatedly frames ChatGPT as a time-saving tool for explaining mathematics and generating instructional text.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of speed and convenience in generating instructional responses
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators in user testing

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes and, if so, under what conditions. It addresses three outcome domains: learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking. The motivation is that prior studies on ChatGPT in education have reported mixed results, ranging from positive effects to null or negative findings, and the field lacked a consolidated quantitative estimate.

The authors conducted a PRISMA-guided meta-analysis of 51 experimental or quasi-experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025, extracting 72 independent effect sizes. Included studies compared an experimental group using ChatGPT with a control group not using ChatGPT, and the control condition was limited to standard instructional approaches or conventional tools. The sample spans primary, secondary, and college settings, but most included studies were at the college level; the subject areas included STEM, language/academic writing, and skills/competencies development.

Overall, the meta-analysis found that ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance and moderate positive effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking. Moderator analyses suggested that effects on learning performance were strongest in skills/competencies courses, problem-based learning, and 4–8 week interventions. For learning perception, longer interventions showed stronger effects. For higher-order thinking, the strongest effects appeared in STEM-related courses and when ChatGPT functioned as an intelligent tutor. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support student learning, but its impact depends on how it is integrated into instruction and for how long it is used.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 51 experimental/quasi-experimental studies, which is the strongest design tier in the provided framework. The authors also report heterogeneity, publication-bias checks, and sensitivity analyses, supporting methodological credibility despite substantial between-study variation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled learning-performance effect is large (g=0.867), exceeding the threshold for medium/large impact. Even the secondary outcomes are positive and nontrivial, so the overall evidence suggests meaningful educational impact, though this paper is not specific to middle school mathematics.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT used as a generative AI learning support tool in experimental and quasi-experimental education studies, including tutoring, intelligent partnering, assessment feedback, and personalized recommendation across subjects such as STEM, language/writing, and skills development.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent effects (51 studies total), ChatGPT significantly improved learning performance with a large pooled effect, g=0.867 (95% CI 0.683 to 1.052, p<0.001). The meta-analysis included post-test and pre-post data from experimental/quasi-experimental comparisons against non-ChatGPT instruction; the included paper’s primary learning-performance outcome was broad academic achievement rather than a single K-12 subject measure.
finding.measure: Learning performance / achievement tests and exam scores
finding.study_size: n=5051 studies; 44 independent effects for learning performance

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT also improved learning perception with a moderate pooled effect, g=0.456 (95% CI 0.287 to 0.625, p<0.001) across 19 independent effects. The paper operationalized this construct with scale/questionnaire-based outcomes such as motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, and related perceptions of learning experience.
finding.measure: Learning perception scales/questionnaires (e.g., motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, attitudes toward learning)

finding.finding_summary: For higher-order thinking, the pooled effect was positive and moderate, g=0.457 (95% CI 0.255 to 0.650, p<0.001) across 9 independent effects. This outcome was measured with questionnaire/scales targeting higher-order thinking, critical thinking, and related reasoning outcomes, indicating a beneficial but more modest effect than learning performance.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking / critical thinking scales and questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students perceived and trusted ChatGPT when it was used as a virtual tutor in a physics class. The authors were interested in three questions: how accurate ChatGPT was at answering physics problems, whether students’ trust depended on answer accuracy, and how trust shaped perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use. The study is framed around growing interest in generative AI in education and concern that students may over-trust AI outputs despite errors.

The intervention was a ChatGPT-supported make-up exam assignment in an introductory college physics course at a public university in the southern United States. Forty students completed an exam on light and radioactivity, then had up to a week and a half to interact with ChatGPT to work through incorrect answers and regain lost credit. After the assignment, students completed a survey and submitted drawings representing their perceptions of ChatGPT. The study also analyzed the accuracy of ChatGPT responses across 362 questions and compared trust groups using statistical analyses.

Results showed that ChatGPT answered 85% of physics questions correctly, but many students still trusted its answers uncritically, including incorrect ones. Higher trust was associated with more favorable perceptions of ChatGPT, especially ease of use and future intention to use. The drawing analysis suggested that students often anthropomorphized ChatGPT or viewed it as a robot, machine, or “super-intelligent” system. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be error-prone and that AI literacy, critical evaluation skills, and careful design of educational GenAI tools are needed to reduce misconceptions and blind trust.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study, but it is a descriptive, single-class observational study focused on perceptions and answer accuracy rather than a controlled comparison of learning outcomes. It provides useful qualitative and correlational evidence, but not the kind of causal evidence needed for strong claims about achievement effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate middle school mathematics achievement or compare ChatGPT with standard instruction or no-AI support. Its main findings concern trust, perceptions, and response accuracy in college physics, so there is no direct achievement impact relevant to the retrieval topic.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual tutor/assistant to answer students' physics exam questions in an introductory college physics class, including follow-up questioning and explanation-seeking during make-up exam work.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 85% of the 362 physics questions correctly (307/362), but accuracy varied by item and sometimes changed after follow-up prompts. This paper did not test learning gains versus standard instruction; instead, it shows that students' responses to ChatGPT were often uncritical even when the model was wrong, with the trust group agreeing with ChatGPT 100% of the time despite only 82% answer accuracy in that group.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics questions; student agreement/trust in ChatGPT answers

finding.finding_summary: Trust in ChatGPT was associated with students' perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use, and students displayed misconceptions requiring critical evaluation of AI outputs. The study suggests a need for AI literacy and critical thinking, but it does not measure middle school mathematics achievement or direct skill gains.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, intention to use, trust clustering, and qualitative drawing-based conceptions of AI
finding.effect_size: η2=0.257 (ANOVA on accuracy across trust groups); η2=0.175 (MANOVA on perceptions)

finding.finding_summary: Students largely trusted ChatGPT despite documented inaccuracy, with 19 students in the Trust group agreeing with the model 100% of the time. Perceptions differed by trust level, and higher trust was associated with higher perceived ease of use and somewhat higher intention to use ChatGPT again, but the study is descriptive rather than an achievement experiment.
finding.measure: Trust/agreement with ChatGPT, perceived ease of use, intention to use

paper_profiles.title: Acceptance of artificial intelligence among pre-service teachers: a multigroup analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what drives pre-service teachers’ acceptance of AI-based educational applications and whether those drivers differ by gender. The study is framed around the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3) and asks which factors predict behavioral intention to use AI in education, with particular attention to AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, job relevance, and subjective norm.

The study did not evaluate a specific AI product or instructional intervention. Instead, it used a survey of 452 pre-service teachers enrolled at one German university in teacher education programs, collecting self-reported perceptions of AI use in education. Analyses included confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, measurement invariance testing, latent mean comparisons, and multigroup analysis by gender.

Results showed that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were the strongest predictors of intention to use AI, with AI self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment also contributing indirectly through perceived ease of use. AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use in the overall model, although gender moderated some relationships: female pre-service teachers showed higher AI anxiety, and the path from AI anxiety to perceived ease of use differed by gender. The authors conclude that AI acceptance in teacher education depends mainly on perceived usefulness and ease of use, and that training programs should address gender-specific concerns and provide better preparation for AI-supported teaching.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical correlational study using survey data, SEM, and multigroup invariance analysis, but it does not evaluate an instructional intervention or learning outcomes. It is useful for understanding acceptance determinants, yet it provides only indirect evidence for educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct evidence of achievement or other student outcome effects; it measures intentions, perceptions, and gender differences in AI acceptance among pre-service teachers. Any impact on K-12 learning is speculative and indirect.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based acceptance of AI-based educational applications among pre-service teachers, including general AI tools and references to AI-powered educational products such as chatbots, learning analytics, recommendations, diagnostics, and adaptive learning applications; no specific classroom intervention was implemented.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: The ChatGPT Effect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and related generative AI tools in education, with a specific focus on higher education rather than on a single empirical intervention study. It aims to explain what generative AI is, why it matters, and how educators and institutions can respond through AI literacy, curriculum design, assessment redesign, policy development, and technical understanding of the technology.

The volume is written primarily for educators, students, policymakers, and institutional leaders in higher education. It synthesizes literature, examples, practical scenarios, and author perspective to propose ways generative AI can be integrated responsibly into teaching and learning. The book also presents conceptual frameworks such as an AI literacy model, an AI assessment integration framework, and guidance for institutional AI policy.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT/GenAI should be embraced as a partner in education rather than a replacement for human teaching, with strong emphasis on ethics, assessment integrity, AI literacy, and policy readiness. It does not report direct empirical evidence on middle school mathematics achievement or comparison against standard instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive, conceptual trade book/chapter on generative AI in higher education, not an empirical study. It does not present a research design, sample, or causal evidence on middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct evidence is reported on ChatGPT or related generative AI tools for middle school mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or no AI support. The paper offers general discussion, examples, and policy/practice guidance only.

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Machine Learning in School: A Systematic Mapping of the State of the Art
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what instructional units exist for teaching machine learning (ML) concepts in elementary through high school, and what their characteristics are. The authors conduct a systematic mapping study of ML education resources and publications from 2009–2019 to identify and synthesize available instructional units (IUs), the ML concepts they cover, how they are taught, and how they are developed and evaluated.

The study does not test a single intervention; instead, it maps 30 ML instructional units found across articles and online materials. These units include workshops, courses, challenges, tutorials, summer programs, and extracurricular activities, often using block-based programming environments, Python, unplugged activities, or web-based tools. The population spans K-12 learners, with many units aimed at high school and some at elementary/middle school, often beginners with no prior ML experience. The context is mainly school or school-adjacent learning settings, sometimes family-oriented or community-oriented, and many units focus on practical applications such as image classification, robotics, and game-based projects.

The authors conclude that ML education is already appearing in K-12, mostly in recent years, but the field is still immature. Most units emphasize supervised learning, neural networks, and hands-on application, while few address assessment rigorously or provide detailed development/evaluation methods. The paper argues for more systematic instructional design, clearer assessment practices, and better balance between abstracted and explicit ML processes to support meaningful student learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic mapping study, but it does not evaluate a ChatGPT-like tool or any direct middle-school mathematics achievement intervention. Its evidence is descriptive and qualitative, summarizing existing K-12 ML instructional units rather than testing learning outcomes against standard instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct empirical impact on middle school mathematics achievement or generative AI use. It provides background mapping of ML education interventions in K-12, but no evidence of effect relative to standard instruction or no AI support.

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second-language writing, with a particular focus on students from refugee and migrant backgrounds. The authors frame the study around the broader question of how AI language models may support language learning, especially for socially vulnerable learners who face additional barriers in acquiring a second language.

The intervention was a simple before-and-after writing activity. Eight 15-year-old junior high school students in Greece first wrote a personal email in German to a friend. The researchers then used ChatGPT to revise the texts for vocabulary and grammar, showed the improved versions to students, and asked them to write a second, related email on a similar topic.
