Outcomes were derived from text characteristics such as total words, unique words, and average words per sentence, compared before and after the ChatGPT-assisted feedback.

The study reports increases in the measured writing features after the ChatGPT-supported revision phase, suggesting that the tool may help students generate longer and more varied German texts. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise as a supportive language-learning tool in multilingual classrooms, but they also emphasize that further research is needed in other contexts and with larger samples before stronger claims can be made.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot classroom study with an uncontrolled pre-post design and no randomization or comparison group. It provides direct empirical evidence, but methodological rigor and generalizability are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed changes were positive but based on a very small sample and descriptive outcomes rather than standardized achievement measures. The impact on generalizable educational achievement is therefore modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a feedback and revision tool to improve German as a foreign language writing by enhancing vocabulary and grammar for junior high school students with migrant/refugee backgrounds.

finding.finding_summary: In this 8-student pilot study, ChatGPT-assisted revision was associated with improved foreign-language writing output. Across students, the revised texts showed increases in total words (2% to 62%, mean increase 38%), unique words (mean increase 19.1 per student), and average words per sentence (mean increase about 42%).
finding.measure: Foreign-language writing quality/quantity indicators: total words, unique words, average words per sentence in pre- vs post-intervention German emails

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of large language models (LLMs), motivated by the rapid rise of ChatGPT and related models. It does not investigate an educational intervention or student outcomes; instead, it synthesizes recent advances in LLM architectures, training methods, alignment techniques, datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and applications. The survey covers major LLM families such as GPT, LLaMA, and PaLM, and also discusses other representative models and emerging capabilities like in-context learning, instruction following, reasoning, and tool use.

The paper focuses on the technical development of LLMs, including pre-training, fine-tuning, RLHF, decoding strategies, data cleaning, tokenization, and augmentation with external knowledge or tools. It uses examples from general-purpose AI systems such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, and other LLMs, but these are discussed as model examples rather than as interventions studied in schools or classrooms.

Because this is a review article, it does not report a participant population, setting, experimental comparison, or outcome measures relevant to middle school mathematics achievement. Its main conclusion is that LLMs are rapidly advancing and have strong potential across many tasks, while still facing challenges related to efficiency, safety, multimodality, and responsible deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey of large language models, not an empirical study of ChatGPT or any educational intervention. It does not report a study design, sample, comparison group, or outcome data relevant to middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 mathematics achievement or any student outcome. It is background/review literature only, so no effect size or intervention impact can be inferred.

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German school-level content. The authors argue that many existing multimodal benchmarks are either English-only, multiple-choice heavy, or too decontextualized, and therefore do not adequately measure real visual reasoning combined with subject knowledge. Their dataset consists of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions drawn from German school textbooks and related sources across nine domains, including mathematics, history, biology, geography, physics, music, religion, arts, and sports.

The benchmark is designed around middle school-level knowledge, specifically grades 8–10 in the German school system, and includes questions requiring direct visual interpretation, background knowledge, calculation, and in some cases adversarial reasoning about information not present in the image. The authors evaluate 13 open-weight VLMs using multiple LLM judges for scoring. They find that the benchmark is challenging: the best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in music and mathematics, and very low accuracy on adversarial questions.

The paper concludes that middle school curricula provide a useful stress test for current VLMs, particularly in German and in open-ended settings. It also shows that strong performance on public benchmarks such as MMMU does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic benchmark. The work is primarily a benchmark paper rather than an intervention study, and it highlights the need for better visual reasoning, stronger language robustness, and improved ability for models to say when they do not know an answer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a study of an educational intervention with learners. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically systematic, but it does not meet criteria for causal evidence on student outcomes relative to instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured student achievement impact from ChatGPT or any generative AI tutoring tool. The paper reports model benchmark accuracy only, so educational impact on middle school mathematics achievement is not demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Benchmark evaluation of vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions, including open-ended visual reasoning and adversarial unanswerable questions; not an instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This is not an instructional study, but a benchmark paper. For the math subset, the best model achieved only 34.09% accuracy (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with other models ranging down to 9.09% on the math questions. The paper reports that models were better at calculating than counting, but there is no comparison to standard instruction or no-AI instruction, so no educational achievement effect can be inferred.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle school math benchmark questions requiring image-based reasoning and basic calculations

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates model performance across several non-math school subjects, but it does not test student learning or compare against instruction. In the overall benchmark, the best model reached 43.26% accuracy and the weakest 23.53%, with subject-specific highs such as 54.36% in history and 52.92% in religion, indicating challenging multimodal understanding rather than educational impact.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended benchmark questions across arts, biology, geography, history, music, physics, religion, and sports

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how generative AI can support personalized middle school mathematics tasks when teachers remain actively involved in the creation process. The central question is not whether ChatGPT can generate math problems, but how teachers use it to adapt existing curriculum problems to students’ interests, and what tradeoffs arise in terms of efficiency, task quality, and student response.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers worked with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum for students’ popular culture interests. Teachers first received training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then used ChatGPT in recorded sessions to modify problems from Unit 4 and later Unit 6. The personalized assignments were delivered through ASSISTments to 521 middle school students, who provided closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback about interest and closeness to their own interests.

The study found that teachers used ChatGPT in diverse ways, including broad topical personalization, inserting specific references, checking realism, adjusting numerical quantities, and revising readability. Students tended to prefer more specific, fine-grained references, but they often focused on surface-level interest rather than the realism of the problems. Teachers needed about 4 minutes per problem on average, and there was little evidence that the process became time-efficient with practice; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit while also producing problems students rated more positively. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can improve instructional relevance and offer professional learning benefits, but it remains time-intensive and may not easily achieve the fine-grained personalization students want.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory observational study with qualitative coding and mixed-effects regression, but it has no control group for achievement and is not randomized. The evidence is useful for understanding implementation and student reactions, but it does not directly test learning gains against standard instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of middle school mathematics achievement effects from ChatGPT or generative AI versus standard instruction. Its findings are mainly about student interest and teacher efficiency, so any instructional impact on achievement remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize middle school mathematics word problems by rewriting existing IM curriculum tasks around students' interests, popular culture references, age group, location, and realism.

finding.finding_summary: The paper did not measure achievement; it measured students' interest and perceived closeness of personalized math problems. On 5-point ratings (subsample of 52 problems), personalization was rated low overall (mean interest 2.46, mean closeness 2.53), and students preferred more specific popular-culture references rather than broad topics.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for using 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts on student ratings

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing personalization with ChatGPT was not time-efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 personalized problems, averaging 3.2 prompts and 246 seconds (about 4 minutes) per problem; time increased rather than decreased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 by 70.4 seconds per problem, and prompts increased by 1.26 per problem.
finding.measure: Teacher time per problem and number of prompts used to personalize problems
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=1.26 additional prompts

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT and GPT-4 by benchmarking them on a newly created set of natural-language mathematics datasets, GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS. The authors ask what kinds of mathematical tasks large language models can handle, where they fail, and whether newer versions improve over earlier ones. The evaluation focuses on advanced mathematical reasoning rather than educational intervention or student learning outcomes.

The study tests two ChatGPT versions (9-Jan-2023 and 30-Jan-2023) and GPT-4 on prompts spanning graduate-textbook exercises, proof completion, olympiad-style problems, symbolic integration, MATH problems, and mathematical search/retrieval tasks. The benchmark is manually annotated using detailed rating and error codes, with human experts judging model outputs. The paper is not about classroom use or a student population; rather, it evaluates models as tools for mathematical reasoning, including use cases relevant to professional mathematicians and upper undergraduate/graduate-level mathematics.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT performs inconsistently and is generally below graduate-student level on advanced mathematics, though it can be useful for factual lookup and some easier tasks. GPT-4 performs better than ChatGPT, especially on undergraduate-level material, but still fails on graduate-level difficulty and many proof-based or complex reasoning tasks. The authors conclude that these models can function as assistants or search interfaces for knowledgeable users, but are not reliable substitutes for rigorous mathematical problem solving.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical benchmark study with a clear methodology, but it is not an education study and does not evaluate learner outcomes or a K-12 intervention. Evidence is observational/benchmark-based rather than an RCT or QED in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not show impact on middle school mathematics achievement or student learning relative to standard instruction. It evaluates model capability on advanced math benchmarks, so there is no demonstrated educational impact for the target population.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT (two January 2023 versions) and GPT-4 on natural-language mathematics prompts, including proof completion, theorem stating, symbolic integration, and search-engine-like math fact retrieval; evaluates their use as math assistants rather than as a student-facing tutor.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports benchmark performance of ChatGPT and GPT-4 on advanced mathematics tasks rather than student learning outcomes. ChatGPT averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) on GHOSTS for 9-Jan-2023 and 3.29/5 (SD=1.28) for 30-Jan-2023, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15/5 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS; performance was strong on fact retrieval but weak on proofs, olympiad problems, and graduate-level exercises. On symbolic integration, ChatGPT averaged 2.51/5 (SD=0.87) and GPT-4 3.50/5 (SD=1.43), both below specialized models and below the implied passing threshold in many cases.
finding.measure: Human-rated correctness/quality scores (1-5) on mathematics prompts across GHOSTS/miniGHOSTS subdatasets; average rating, standard deviation, and distribution of perfect scores
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts total; GPT-4 evaluated on n=170 miniGHOSTS prompts
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT 9-Jan SD=1.23; ChatGPT 30-Jan SD=1.28; GPT-4 SD=1.12 overall, and 1.43 on symbolic integration subset

finding.finding_summary: The authors find ChatGPT can be useful as a mathematical search engine or knowledge-base interface for professional mathematicians, especially for querying facts and retrieving definitions or theorem outlines. This is framed as workflow assistance that can speed up lookup tasks, although no direct productivity effect size or user-study evidence is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of utility for search-engine-like mathematical lookup tasks and assistant use cases

paper_profiles.title: Search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos with the ATLAS experiment at the LHC
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a particle physics search for long-lived massive particles produced in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, specifically coloured supersymmetric sparticles that may hadronize into stable R-hadrons. The central question is whether ATLAS can observe slow-moving, charged or intermittently neutral particles through detector signatures such as ionisation energy loss in the pixel detector and time-of-flight in the tile calorimeter.

The study uses 34 pb−1 of ATLAS data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. Candidate events are selected with missing transverse energy triggers and tracks consistent with a heavy, slowly moving particle; background is estimated with a data-driven approach. The analysis considers several interaction models for R-hadrons in matter and evaluates stop, sbottom, and gluino hypotheses.

No significant excess over Standard Model expectations is found. The paper sets 95% confidence-level lower mass limits of 294 GeV for sbottoms, 309 GeV for stops, and 562–586 GeV for gluinos depending on the interaction model, concluding that these are the most stringent limits available at the time.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a high-energy physics search from the ATLAS experiment, not an education study. It contains no intervention, learner, or instructional methodology relevant to ChatGPT, generative AI, or middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational outcome or instructional impact reported. The paper provides no evidence about student achievement, technology-supported learning, or school practice.

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) is sufficient to address market concentration and gatekeeping risks in generative AI. The authors argue that the DMA, which was designed for established digital platform services, does not adequately cover standalone generative AI systems even though these systems may become important gateways for downstream AI-based services.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any participant population. Instead, it analyzes generative AI markets and platforms, using examples such as OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta to show how computing power, early mover advantages, data resources, and integrated systems can create entrenched positions. The discussion focuses on how generative AI might function as a core platform service and how DMA obligations could apply to AI providers.

The main conclusion is normative and policy-oriented: generative AI should be explicitly incorporated into the DMA’s framework to preserve contestability, diversity, and fairness in AI markets. The paper proposes that certain AI developers could be treated as gatekeepers and that selected DMA obligations would help prevent anti-competitive practices and data leverage in generative AI ecosystems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/policy paper about the EU Digital Markets Act and generative AI market structure, not an empirical study of ChatGPT or any educational intervention. It contains no original study design, sample, or outcome data relevant to K-12 mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact, and nothing in the paper evaluates middle school mathematics achievement or instructional effectiveness. The paper is outside the requested evidence domain and provides no direct impact estimate.

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that general-purpose generative AI models may produce medical product recommendations that go beyond approved labeling, creating potential public-health and regulatory harms. The author argues that because these models are trained on broad internet-scale data with limited oversight, they can learn and reproduce off-label product-indication associations that are not FDA-approved.

The paper proposes a post-hoc detection approach for identifying potentially harmful off-label promotion in generative AI outputs. The method standardizes user queries, applies biomedical named entity recognition to extract products and diseases, matches them against FDA labeling resources, and then uses a zero-shot classifier to determine whether an identified product-indication pairing constitutes a recommendation. The approach is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style medical question-answering setup where the model is provided with product-label images and user queries.

For evaluation, the author generated 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with known off-label uses. The system identified off-label indications in 15.4% of model responses, and human annotation on a sample of 2,000 responses yielded reasonable detection performance. The conclusion is that generative AI models can surface unvetted medical uses and that guardrails are needed to ensure outputs adhere to approved product labels. This is a proof-of-concept safety paper, not an educational intervention study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style technical/preprint paper, but it is not an educational impact study and does not evaluate learner outcomes. The methodology is a synthetic red-teaming/guardrail demonstration in a medical product setting, not a rigorous causal design for education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report direct educational impact or student achievement effects. Its findings concern model safety and regulatory risk in medical product recommendations, so there is no measurable positive educational impact in the requested sense.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating Claude 3 Sonnet as a multimodal generative AI system answering user questions about medical product labels in a shopping context, including whether it produces harmful off-label recommendations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on regulatory and safety implications of generative AI rather than learner outcomes. In a synthetic red-teaming evaluation of 14,300 queries across 35 pharmaceuticals, 15.4% of model responses were judged to contain off-label indications, indicating a substantial safety and governance concern for deployment.
finding.measure: Rate of off-label medical product recommendations in Claude 3 Sonnet responses; precision/recall/F1 of the detection method
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; 35 products; 2000 human-annotated sample for validation

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how mixing different instruction-tuning datasets affects the behavior of large language models (LLMs). The authors focus on three instruction types: NLP downstream tasks, coding, and general chat, and ask how these mixtures influence performance across task-specific benchmarks and alignment-related chat skills.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention but a machine learning fine-tuning procedure. The authors fine-tune LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models on combinations of Alpaca (general instructions), CodeAlpaca (coding), and P3 (NLP task instructions). They compare eight dataset combinations and evaluate the resulting models on NLP benchmarks, HumanEval code generation, and FLASK-based alignment skill assessments.

The paper reports that specialized instruction data tends to help in its own domain, but mixing all instruction types does not uniformly improve all outcomes. General instructions improve alignment and NLP performance; coding instructions improve coding and can also help chat quality; and P3-style NLP task instructions can harm alignment/chat abilities when combined with other data. Larger models appear better able to benefit from diverse instruction mixtures. Because the paper is a model-training study rather than a study of learners or classrooms, it does not provide evidence about student learning or mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a model-training and benchmark paper about instruction mixing in LLMs, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate classroom instruction, student learning, or K-12 mathematics outcomes, so it does not meet credibility criteria for the retrieved education topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on middle school mathematics achievement is reported. The paper only reports benchmark changes in NLP, code generation, and alignment skills for fine-tuned LLMs, with no student-level educational outcome evidence.

interventions.use_case: Fine-tuning LLaMA-2 chat-style large language models with general instruction data (Alpaca), code instructions (CodeAlpaca), and NLP task instructions (P3) to study how instruction mixing affects downstream chat/alignment capabilities.

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper is a conceptual overview of generative information retrieval (GenIR) and, more broadly, how modern generative AI models reshape information access systems. It contrasts traditional AI-based information retrieval with generative AI systems, arguing that large language models and other generative models create new opportunities through two main paradigms: information generation and information synthesis.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any human participant population. Instead, it surveys model architectures, scaling laws, training stages, prompt optimization, multimodal applications, retrieval-augmented generation, generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling. It uses examples such as ChatGPT, Bing, and Midjourney to illustrate how generative models can directly produce responses or synthesize grounded outputs from external sources.

Its main conclusion is that generative AI can improve information access by either generating tailored content or synthesizing external knowledge more reliably than unconstrained generation. At the same time, the paper emphasizes persistent challenges, especially hallucination, inference cost, controllability, and the difficulty of integrating retrieval with generation. The paper is a theoretical and survey-style chapter rather than an empirical study, and it does not provide evidence about student learning, mathematics achievement, or school-based implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual chapter on generative AI and information retrieval, not an empirical study of ChatGPT or any education intervention. It reports no original methods, sample, or outcome analysis relevant to middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct evidence on educational impact, and nothing in the paper evaluates middle school mathematics learning or comparison against standard instruction/no AI support.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Computer Science Education: Accelerating Python Learning with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether integrating ChatGPT into introductory Python instruction can accelerate programming skill acquisition in a professional training context. The authors focus on a practical instructional problem: many learners, especially those without prior programming experience, struggle with syntax, debugging, and abstract programming concepts, which can slow progress in computer science education. The study asks whether generative AI can provide immediate, personalized support that helps learners reach basic Python proficiency more quickly.

The intervention was a self-paced, asynchronous Python module embedded within a 16-week university-affiliated professional course on applied generative AI. Participants used OpenAI’s ChatGPT to generate code, interpret code behavior, and debug errors during Weeks 3–4 of the course. The paper reports on 86 adult learners with varied programming backgrounds, grouped into prior Python experience, other programming experience, and no programming experience. Outcomes were measured through 30 assessments across the course, including code-based tasks and quizzes, and analyzed using mixed-design ANOVA and follow-up tests.

Results showed that learners without prior programming experience initially performed worse than those with programming backgrounds, but these gaps diminished after the Python module. By the end of the module, group differences were no longer statistically significant on most assessments, suggesting that the AI-supported instruction helped close early skill gaps. Qualitative mentor feedback also indicated that learners used ChatGPT as just-in-time support for troubleshooting and understanding code. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support accelerated foundational programming learning, while also noting the need for careful scaffolding so learners do not over-rely on AI-generated help.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-design observational study with within-subject and between-group comparisons, but it is not randomized and lacks a no-AI control group. Evidence is useful but limited by confounding from prior programming experience and by the study’s professional-training context.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gains are modest-to-moderate during the instructional window (η²=.06–.17) and suggest meaningful help for novices in a priority upskilling population. However, the evidence is for adult programming, not K-12 mathematics, so the transferable impact for the retrieval topic is limited.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-supported self-paced Python instruction where learners used the model to generate code, interpret code functionality, and debug syntax/logic errors in an asynchronous programming module.

finding.finding_summary: This study found that ChatGPT-supported Python instruction improved programming proficiency in an adult learner cohort (n=86). Early group differences favoring learners with prior programming experience were no longer statistically significant after the Python module, suggesting that the intervention helped novices catch up; the paper reports small-to-moderate improvement effects during instruction (η²=.06–.17) and smaller group-difference effects later (η²<.05).
finding.measure: Timed code-based Python assessments and code evaluation quizzes across 30 assessments, including conditional statements, loops, functions, fundamentals, and control flow
finding.effect_size: η²=.06–.17 during instruction; η²<.05 for later group differences

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appears to have supported metacognitive and troubleshooting skills, as learners used ChatGPT for just-in-time help to understand code and resolve errors independently. The authors and mentors describe improved comfort with Python and stronger self-directed problem solving, though this is based on qualitative observations rather than a separate measured scale.
finding.measure: Mentor observations and qualitative feedback about independent troubleshooting, code understanding, and comfort with Python

paper_profiles.title: Conversational AI: The Science Behind the Alexa Prize
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the Alexa Prize, a university competition created by Amazon to advance conversational AI. The paper’s main question is not about educational effectiveness, but about how to build, deploy, and evaluate open-domain social conversational agents at scale using live user interactions. It outlines the technical and organizational infrastructure provided to participating university teams, including shared data, cloud resources, feedback systems, monitoring, and evaluation metrics.

The intervention studied is the Alexa Prize competition itself: 15 university-built socialbots were made available to millions of Alexa users through the "Alexa, let’s chat" experience. Users conversed freely with the bots, rated conversations, and provided feedback that teams used to iteratively improve their systems. The paper describes the system architecture, customer experience design, conversational ASR, NLU, dialogue management, response generation, ranking, topic tracking, offensive speech filtering, and evaluation methods developed during the competition.

The context was a large-scale, real-world deployment in the United States with Amazon Alexa users and university research teams. The paper reports that user engagement was high, ratings improved over the competition, and top teams benefited from strong NLU, dialogue management, and conversational user experience components. It concludes that large-scale live interaction data and iterative feedback can accelerate progress in conversational AI, but it does not address schooling or mathematics learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed proceedings paper describing a technology competition and system engineering advances, not a controlled empirical study of an educational intervention. It provides observational performance data and correlational analyses, but no rigorous causal design relevant to the requested educational outcome.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact on middle school mathematics achievement and does not evaluate ChatGPT or any comparable generative AI tutor in a school setting. Its findings concern conversational AI engagement and system quality, so educational impact for the target question is absent.

interventions.use_case: Large-scale conversational AI/socialbot platform (Alexa Prize) used to support open-domain chatbots evaluated with live user interactions, ratings, and feedback; includes ASR, NLU, dialog management, and response generation infrastructure rather than tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports high and improving user engagement with conversational agents, indicating positive social/engagement outcomes for users of the Alexa Prize system. Across the competition, customers spent over 40,000 hours in conversation, and finalist ratings improved by 24.6% from 2.77 to 3.45 over the competition period; conversation duration also increased to a median of 1:53 and 90th percentile of 8:08 for finalists.
finding.measure: User ratings of conversations; conversation duration; number of dialog turns; engagement ratings
finding.effect_size: 24.6% rating increase; 14.0% median duration increase; 56.8% 90th percentile duration increase

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines the promise and challenges of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, it synthesises emerging work on large language models, diffusion models, and related GenAI systems to argue that these tools may transform learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. The authors also emphasise the risks of hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, inequity, and the possibility that AI assistance could create an illusion of learning without genuine skill development.

The paper discusses GenAI in educational contexts such as AI tutors (for example, ChatGPT- or GPT-4-based systems like Khanmigo), AI-generated learning materials, automated feedback on student work, and adaptive assessment systems. The discussion is framed around human-centred theories of learning, including constructivism, inquiry-based learning, and the zone of proximal development, and it repeatedly calls for rigorous empirical studies to test GenAI’s effects across learning settings.

The article does not focus on a specific age group, school level, or country, and it does not present direct evidence on middle school mathematics achievement versus standard instruction. Its main conclusion is that GenAI has substantial potential in education, but responsible adoption requires AI literacy, stakeholder involvement, ethical safeguards, and stronger methodological rigour before educational benefits can be assumed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed perspective article, not an empirical study, and it does not present original data or a formal evaluation design. It synthesizes and interprets prior literature on generative AI in education, so there is no direct evidence to grade under an experimental or observational evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper makes broad conceptual claims about GenAI’s potential and challenges, but it does not report measured impacts on middle school mathematics achievement or any other outcome. There is therefore no direct demonstrated effect to classify as educational impact for the retrieval question.

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broader question of how artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in research involving teachers, with particular attention to the promises and challenges of AI in teaching practice. The authors systematically reviewed empirical studies published over the last 20 years that involved in-service or pre-service teachers and AI-based systems or machine learning methods. Their goal was to synthesize what kinds of data were collected from teachers, what roles teachers played in AI research, what benefits AI offered, what challenges appeared, and which AI methods were most common.

The review is not a study of a single intervention or trial, but rather a synthesis of 44 empirical studies identified from Web of Science. Across these studies, teachers were often sources of data for training AI systems, for grading/assessment validation, or for providing background information about students and teaching contexts. Most of the reviewed work involved machine learning approaches such as artificial neural networks and decision trees, and the applications centered on planning, classroom monitoring, immediate feedback, and automated assessment.

The paper concludes that AI can support teachers in planning, implementation, and assessment, especially by reducing workload and enabling timely feedback and intervention. However, the reviewed literature also shows important limitations, including limited reliability, limited technical capacity, and weak transferability across contexts. The authors argue that teacher involvement in AI design is still limited and that future work should use richer multimodal data and involve teachers more deeply in development and decision-making.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not itself an empirical intervention study and does not provide causal evidence for ChatGPT or generative AI on middle school mathematics achievement. Its methodology is qualitative/synthesis-based, so it offers only indirect contextual evidence for AI use in education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate any intervention effect on student mathematics outcomes, nor does it report effect sizes relevant to the retrieval topic. It mainly summarizes teacher-facing AI applications and challenges across heterogeneous studies, with no direct evidence on ChatGPT or comparable generative AI for middle school math achievement.

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of Parental Involvement, Parental Support and Family Education on Pupil Achievements and Adjustment: A Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report reviews English-language research on how parental involvement, parental support, and family education relate to pupil achievement and adjustment. Rather than testing a new instructional intervention, it synthesizes evidence on both spontaneous parental involvement (for example, home-based parenting, discussions, and support for learning) and attempts to increase involvement through interventions such as parent training, home-school link initiatives, and family/community education programs.

The paper draws on studies across the UK, the United States, Spain, and other contexts, with evidence spanning preschool, primary, and secondary-aged learners. Much of the review focuses on large cohort and longitudinal datasets, such as the UK National Child Development Study and the US National Educational Longitudinal Study, to examine associations between family background, parental involvement, and student outcomes in reading, mathematics, adjustment, aspirations, and persistence in education. It also reviews intervention evaluations intended to raise parental involvement.

The central conclusion is that at-home parenting and home learning support have a strong positive association with achievement and adjustment, often more strongly than school-based forms of parental involvement. The influence of parental involvement is partly indirect, working through children’s self-concept, aspirations, and learning-related attitudes. However, the review also concludes that evaluations of interventions designed to increase parental involvement are generally too weak methodologically to establish their impact on achievement with confidence, even though such initiatives are widespread and often well received.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative literature review summarizing correlational and cohort studies rather than direct intervention research. The evidence discussed includes some technically strong observational studies, but the paper itself does not present a controlled evaluation of an AI or ChatGPT-based intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct empirical evidence here on ChatGPT, generative AI, or middle school mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or no AI support. Because the retrieved paper is unrelated to the target intervention and outcome, its impact for the requested research question is effectively none.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a literature review of parental involvement and family education, not a study of ChatGPT or any generative AI tool. It synthesizes evidence that at-home parental support is positively associated with pupil achievement, while many school-based involvement interventions have weak or inconsistent evidence; however, it reports no direct empirical results for middle school mathematics or any AI-supported instruction.
finding.measure: N/A for this review; synthesized across studies using standardized tests, reading and mathematics scores, and adjustment scales

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that parental involvement, especially at-home good parenting and home learning environments, is associated with better child adjustment, self-concept, and reduced anti-social or worried/upset behavior. These findings are based on multiple observational studies and cohort analyses, not on AI intervention experiments; no effect sizes are reported in the text provided.
finding.measure: Psychological/personal adjustment scales; British Social Adjustment Guide; behavior and self-concept measures

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset and evaluation protocol for testing vision-language models on German middle school knowledge. The authors ask whether current AI systems can answer open-ended, subject-specific questions that require both visual interpretation and background knowledge, rather than relying on text-only cues or multiple-choice guessing.

The dataset was built from German school textbooks for grades 8–10 and related educational materials. It includes 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine domains: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. The benchmark also includes adversarial questions that are intentionally misleading or unanswerable from the image alone. No students or teachers were participants; the study evaluates open-weight VLMs such as InternVL3, Ovis2, Qwen2.5 VL, Gemma 3, Llama 4 Scout, and Mistral 3.1 small.

Results show that the benchmark is challenging and selective: the best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with much lower performance on adversarial items. The authors conclude that middle school-level multimodal questions in German remain difficult for current VLMs and that public benchmark performance does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic educational setting. They argue that carefully constructed, native-language, open-ended benchmarks are useful for stress-testing AI systems and exposing weaknesses in visual reasoning, domain knowledge, and refusal behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a study of an educational intervention or a student outcome study. It provides no causal evidence on learning effects, no comparison to standard instruction, and no experimental design with learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on student achievement; the paper only reports model accuracy on benchmark questions. As such, it does not demonstrate educational benefit or harm for middle school mathematics instruction.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking and evaluating vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions requiring visual understanding plus subject knowledge; not an instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an instructional intervention on student math achievement; instead it evaluates VLM performance on middle school math benchmark questions. The strongest model reached only 34.09% accuracy on math questions (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with the best overall model achieving 43.26% accuracy across all domains, indicating limited capability on these math items rather than an educational gain relative to instruction.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended middle school math benchmark questions requiring visual interpretation and simple calculations

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the didactic challenges posed by generative AI in school mathematics, especially the risk that students can bypass interpretation, decision-making, and validation by relying on AI-generated solutions. The author asks how mathematics teaching can preserve students’ mathematical activity and epistemic control in so-called post-AI contexts, where generative AI tools are broadly available.

To address this issue, the study analyzes a classroom experience in secondary education in which open mathematical tasks were implemented as a response to the presence of generative AI. The intervention was organized through a didactic regulation device called COMPAS, which structures task work into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, producing and exploring results, analysis and validation, and socialization/synthesis. The classroom experience was observed through student written work, classroom interaction records, and teacher-researcher observations.

The paper argues that open tasks, when explicitly regulated, can prevent premature closure of mathematical activity and keep students engaged in modeling, justification, and validation. The findings suggest that generative AI can be integrated as a subordinate support tool rather than a substitute for student reasoning, and that students retain epistemic control when task design requires them to make and defend mathematical decisions. The study concludes that task design and didactic regulation are central to preserving the formative value of school mathematics in post-AI settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive classroom study with no experimental comparison or quantitative effect estimation. It provides direct empirical classroom evidence, but the design limits causal inference and generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports promising classroom-level effects on mathematical agency and validation practices, but without quantitative achievement data or a comparison condition. Impact is therefore suggestive and modest/unclear rather than demonstrated at scale.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative secondary classroom study reports that open mathematical tasks, regulated through the COMPAS device, helped students maintain epistemic control and engage in interpretation, modeling, and validation even when generative AI was available. No achievement test scores or effect sizes are reported; the evidence is based on classroom observations, student written work, and teacher-researcher notes rather than a comparison against standard instruction.
finding.measure: Students' mathematical work, written productions, classroom interactions, and observed modeling/validation practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that students' mathematical agency, decision-making, and critical validation practices were strengthened by task design and explicit didactic regulation. The study argues that students retained responsibility for assumptions, model construction, and checking plausibility, but it does not report quantitative effect sizes or achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Observed agency, argumentation, and validation behaviors during task resolution

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that the COMPAS regulation structure organized the classroom use of generative AI and prevented premature task closure, making the resolution process more purposeful. However, it does not report workload, time-on-task, or efficiency metrics, so the evidence is descriptive rather than measured.
finding.measure: Classroom task-process organization and teacher-mediated regulation of AI use

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer in collaborative mathematics problem solving, and what behaviors, features, and controls they want from such a system. The motivation is that while generative AI tools are increasingly used for tutoring and feedback, far less is known about AI designed as a peer collaborator inside small-group mathematics work.

To study this, the authors ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students in the United States. Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks and then interacted with two LLM-based AI peers in a technology-probe web application built on GPT-4o. They experienced both individual and small-group AI-supported problem solving, then co-designed their ideal AI peer through posters, example dialogues, reflections, interviews, and a preference survey. The study also collected GEQ and NASA-TLX ratings after the human-only and AI-supported sessions.

The main conclusion is that students prefer an AI peer that scaffolds rather than solves: it should offer hints, checks, and concept refreshers, speak only when appropriate, and remain under student control. Students wanted the AI to feel peer-like and competent, but not domineering or overly “teachery,” and they strongly preferred a friendly expert tone, clear responsiveness, and emotional attunement. The paper argues that AI peer design for middle-school mathematics should emphasize co-agency, adjustable help, and collaboration norms rather than tutor-like authority.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative/participatory design study with some paired survey comparisons, but it is not an efficacy trial and does not directly measure achievement outcomes. It provides useful evidence about student experience and design requirements, but credibility for causal claims is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large effects on perceived workload and coordination, but these are process outcomes rather than learning achievement, and the study does not test whether the AI peer improves math performance. Its practical impact is promising for design, but its evidence for educational impact is indirect.

interventions.use_case: A sandboxed GPT-4o-based AI peer system for middle-school collaborative mathematical problem solving, where two generative AI agents (Alice and Bob) participate as text-based student collaborators, provide hints, checks, explanations, and dialogue during CPS tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not measure math achievement test scores; instead, it examined how middle school students experienced GenAI peers during mathematics CPS tasks. The paper reports that the AI peer condition could reduce temporal demand and support procedural progress, but it also introduced higher physical workload and lower perceived task coordination, suggesting mixed effects on the mathematical problem-solving process rather than direct achievement gains (n=22 paired survey comparisons for GEQ/NASA-TLX).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX workload ratings; GEQ group coordination/cohesion ratings during mathematics collaborative problem solving
finding.effect_size: Temporal demand d=1.15; physical demand d=1.14; ATGS d=0.94; GIT d=0.81
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs 4.13; physical demand SD=4.65 vs 2.41; ATGS SD=1.81 vs 2.05; GIT SD=1.58 vs 1.52

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower social attraction to the group when working with AI peers than in human-only CPS, and qualitative data showed frustration when AI peers repeated themselves, ignored students, or failed to provide emotional attunement. The paper argues that lack of affective responsiveness led students to feel less supported and sometimes self-blame during difficult problem solving (n=22 for GEQ; n=18 interviews).
finding.measure: GEQ Attractions to Group-Social (ATGS); interview/reflection themes about frustration, trust, and emotional support

finding.finding_summary: The AI peers improved perceived efficiency but reduced perceived collaboration quality, with students emphasizing that they wanted co-agency, shared reasoning, and negotiated methods rather than the AI doing the work for them. Quantitatively, task coordination was lower in the AI condition (GIT d=0.81), and qualitatively students criticized rigid, teacher-like behavior and non-responsive turns as undermining collaborative problem solving.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task (GIT); qualitative analysis of collaborative problem solving discourse and design preferences
finding.study_size: n=22 for survey comparisons; n=18 interviews

finding.finding_summary: Compared with human-only CPS, the AI peer condition significantly reduced perceived temporal demand, indicating that students felt the work moved faster and less time pressure was required. This came with a large effect size on NASA-TLX temporal demand (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002; d=1.15; n=22 paired comparisons).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand rating

finding.finding_summary: Although the AI peers reduced perceived time pressure, they increased physical demand because students had to manage typing, navigation, and reading text-based outputs while solving math problems. The physical-demand difference was large (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014; d=1.14; n=22 paired comparisons), showing an operational cost of the interface.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX physical demand rating

paper_profiles.title: Analysis of the User Perception of Chatbots in Education Using A Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines user perceptions and acceptance of chatbots in education, with explicit discussion of LLM-based tools such as ChatGPT and Google Bard. The central question is not whether chatbots improve academic achievement, but which human and technology-readiness factors shape students' willingness to use them and how those perceptions relate to decision-making.

The study uses a survey-based design grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technology Readiness Index (TRI), plus additional constructs for interaction/engagement, accuracy/responsiveness, transparency/ethics, intention to use, and perception of decision-making. Data were collected via Qualtrics from undergraduate and graduate students between April and July 2023; 142 complete responses were analyzed. Most respondents reported using ChatGPT or related AI tools, but the paper did not test a classroom intervention or compare learning outcomes against standard instruction.

Results from PLS-SEM suggest that optimism and innovativeness positively predict perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while discomfort and insecurity generally reduce acceptance. Perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness both increase intention to use, and interaction/engagement and accuracy/responsiveness also positively predict intention to use. Transparency and ethics negatively predict intention to use. The paper concludes that these factors shape willingness to adopt educational chatbots and that intention to use mediates their relationship with decision-making perception, but it does not provide direct empirical evidence about middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational survey using PLS-SEM, not an experimental study. It provides indirect evidence about acceptance and perceptions of ChatGPT-like tools, but it does not test learning outcomes or causal effects on mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not measure academic achievement or instructional impact, and it is not specific to middle school mathematics. Its findings concern user perceptions and intention to use, so direct educational impact is absent.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based evaluation of students' perceptions and intention to use ChatGPT and closely related educational chatbots/interactive AI (e.g., Google Bard, Jasper, Notion AI) in educational contexts, focusing on acceptance, responsiveness, transparency, and decision-making rather than tutoring performance.

finding.finding_summary: This survey/PLS-SEM study with n=142 analyzed students' perceptions of chatbots rather than achievement. Optimism and innovativeness positively predicted perceived ease of use and usefulness (e.g., OP→PU path=0.462, t=14.363; OP→PEOU path=0.398, t=5.947), while discomfort and insecurity negatively affected ease of use and insecurity negatively affected usefulness. Intention to use was positively associated with perceived decision-making (IOE→PDM path=0.458, t=5.295), but transparency and ethics negatively influenced intention to use (TE→IOE path=-0.128, t=2.468).
finding.measure: Technology acceptance / readiness survey constructs; intention to use; perceived decision-making; interaction/engagement perceptions

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Words: Infusing Conversational Agents with Human-like Typing Behaviors
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conversational User Interfaces 2024 (CUI ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adding human-like typing behaviors to a ChatGPT-based conversational agent changes how users perceive the agent’s naturalness, human-likeness, competence, friendliness, and trustworthiness. The authors note that ChatGPT responds quickly and fluently, which can make it feel less like a human interlocutor. They therefore explore whether visualized hesitation and self-editing behaviors during typing could make the system seem more natural and engaging.

The intervention is a design framework and prototype platform that uses the OpenAI API / GPT-3.5 to generate content, then presents it with three typing styles: a baseline agent, an agent with hesitation delays, and an agent with both hesitation and self-editing (deletions, insertions, and modifications). The study is a within-subject pilot user experiment in which participants chatted casually with each of the three agents about everyday topics such as hobbies, then completed questionnaires and open-ended feedback.

The sample consisted of 11 adult participants aged 18–34 recruited online via snowball sampling; they interacted with the agents on PC or mobile in an online setting. Results suggested that hesitation alone was not beneficial, but the combination of hesitation and self-editing was generally preferred and perceived as more natural, human-like, competent, and friendly, though differences were not statistically significant. Qualitative feedback also showed that typing behavior influenced perceptions, but content quality and contextual coherence from the underlying model strongly shaped user judgments as well.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pilot user study with a within-subject design, but it is small (n=11 analyzed), exploratory, and focused on subjective perceptions rather than robust causal inference. The paper itself reports that observed differences were not statistically significant, so the evidence is suggestive rather than strong.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest positive effects on perceived naturalness and engagement for a modified ChatGPT interface, but the effects are small, non-significant, and not about learning outcomes. It has unclear direct educational impact, especially for middle school mathematics achievement.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT/GPT-3.5 used as the core conversational agent in a user study, with the output presentation manipulated to simulate human-like typing behaviors such as hesitation and self-editing.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject pilot with n=11 participants (33 agent-level observations), the red agent (hesitation + self-editing) was preferred over the baseline and hesitation-only agents for perceived naturalness, human-likeness, competence, and friendliness, but these differences were not statistically significant. By contrast, the hesitation-only agent was rated lowest on naturalness (M=2.272, SD=1.272) and human-likeness (M=1.727, SD=1.103), while the baseline was fastest on response time (M=4.550, SD=0.688).
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of naturalness, human-likeness, competence, friendliness, satisfaction, response time; user preference and interaction duration
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported for several ratings; e.g., response time SD=0.688 (blue), 1.401 (red), 1.036 (green)

finding.finding_summary: User engagement differed across agent types: participants interacted longest with the red agent (M=238.73 s, SD=224.22) and entered more words and sentences, while the green agent elicited the least engagement (word entries M=49.10, SD=27.95; sentence entries M=7.0, SD=4.03; duration M=161.60 s, SD=102.31). The relationship between agent and user word counts was positively correlated overall (linear model Y=0.67X+6.81, R2=0.79), suggesting conversational behavior influenced participation, but this was an exploratory descriptive finding rather than a causal effect estimate.
finding.measure: Interaction duration, user word count, user sentence count, agent-user word count correlation
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported for duration and entries; e.g., red duration SD=224.22, green duration SD=102.31

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how generative AI can support teacher-led personalization of middle school mathematics tasks. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves test scores directly, but how teachers use it to modify existing curriculum problems, how much effort that requires, and how students react to the resulting personalized problems. The authors frame the work around context personalization and the tension between teacher-in-the-loop and teacher-out-of-the-loop approaches to GenAI in education.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools collaborated with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize 143 mathematics problems from an Illustrative Mathematics curriculum. Teachers used the system to adapt problems around broad or specific popular-culture interests, while the researchers logged prompts, recorded teacher sessions, and collected student survey feedback. In total, 521 students received the personalized assignments in ASSISTments. Students also provided closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, and some provided open-ended feedback.

The study found that teachers frequently used ChatGPT to adjust both the topic and realism of problems, but most personalization remained at a relatively broad grain size because doing finer-grained personalization for individual students was time-consuming. Teachers typically needed several prompts per item, and the process did not become clearly more efficient over time. Student feedback suggested that learners preferred more specific, small-grain personalization, but also that many students cared more about whether the references matched their own interests than about deeper realism issues. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop GenAI personalization has promise for professional learning and monitoring quality, but is difficult to scale efficiently and may not align well with students’ desire for highly individualized content.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with systematic qualitative coding and regression analyses, but it is not an experimental comparison of achievement outcomes. Credibility is limited for the user's question because there is no control group and no direct learning/achievement measure.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of middle school mathematics achievement gains from ChatGPT or related generative AI compared with standard instruction or no AI support. The reported effects concern student interest and teacher efficiency, not achievement, so impact on the target outcome is unproven.

interventions.use_case: Teachers used ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize middle school mathematics word problems by rewriting Illustrative Mathematics tasks around students' popular culture interests, age group, geography, names, and contextual realism.

finding.finding_summary: The paper did not measure student achievement or test scores; it focused on how personalized math tasks were created and how students rated them. Student feedback suggested the AI-personalized tasks were more appealing when they matched specific interests, but the study provides no direct evidence of improved mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or no AI support (n=521 students; 143 problems).
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students' responses indicated mostly low-to-moderate interest ratings (M=2.46) and moderate closeness ratings (M=2.53) on 5-point scales, with preference for specific popular-culture references rather than broad themes. The direction is mixed because some students liked the personalization, but many did not, and the paper reports no direct behavioral or learning gains.
finding.measure: 1-5 student ratings of interestingness and closeness; open-ended interest feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 53 problems
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 (for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts on ratings)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers needed substantial effort to personalize problems with ChatGPT: 558 prompts for 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts and about 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7). Efficiency did not clearly improve over time; in fact, Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 (B=70.4 seconds, p=0.0189) and required more prompts (B=1.26, p=0.0025), though 3-5 prompts per problem was associated with better student ratings.
finding.measure: Prompt counts per problem; time spent creating each problem; regression models of prompts/time
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 prompts; B=70.4 seconds; B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other counts

paper_profiles.title: “EHLO WORLD” - Checking If Your Conversational AI Knows Right from Wrong
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate and validate ethical claims made about conversational AI systems. The authors ask whether ethical behavior in chatbots and similar agents should be governed primarily through top-down regulation, bottom-up technical processes, or a hybrid of the two. The discussion is motivated by concerns about privacy, manipulation, bias, and the social impact of conversational agents in real-world deployments.

Rather than studying an educational intervention or a generative AI tool in a learning setting, the paper is a conceptual framework paper. It uses customer service chatbots as the main example to illustrate how ethical standards might be specified and checked. The paper argues that top-down regulation can define what systems should not do, while bottom-up processes such as bias-checking checklists, certified components, repeatable builds, and automated tests can verify what systems do in practice.

The context is broad commercial conversational AI rather than a specific user population, school level, or country. The main conclusion is that neither regulation nor technical certification alone is sufficient; instead, an interdependent hybrid approach is needed to create small, verifiable claims about chatbot behavior and to better protect users from harmful or manipulative AI outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/position paper about ethics and governance of conversational AI, not an empirical study of educational outcomes. It does not present a research design, sample, or measured effects relevant to middle school mathematics achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on student achievement outcomes and does not evaluate ChatGPT or any generative AI tool in a middle school mathematics context. Its relevance is only indirect, through general discussion of conversational AI ethics and regulation.

paper_profiles.title: Effect of Static vs. Conversational AI-Generated Messages on Colorectal Cancer Screening Intent: a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) generated communication can more effectively increase intentions to undergo colorectal cancer (CRC) screening than standard educational material or no message at all. It directly compares a concise static AI-generated message with a more interactive AI chatbot conversation designed around motivational interviewing principles.

In a preregistered four-arm randomized controlled trial, 915 U.S. adults aged 45–75 who had never completed CRC screening were recruited online. Participants were assigned to one of four conditions: no-message control, a JAMA patient-page educational handout, a single GPT-4.1-generated personalized message, or a GPT-4.1 chatbot conversation personalized with demographic information and prompted to use motivational interviewing techniques. Everyone had to spend at least three minutes with their assigned material.

The primary outcomes were post-intervention self-reported 12-month intentions to complete colonoscopy and stool testing. Both AI conditions increased screening intentions relative to no message, but they did not outperform expert-written materials for colonoscopy intent. For stool-test intent, both AI conditions performed better than the expert materials, with the single-message AI and chatbot showing similar effects. The main conclusion is that brief, demographically tailored AI messages may be as persuasive as more complex chatbot conversations, and that AI may be especially useful for promoting less familiar, lower-burden screening options such as stool testing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with a clear comparison arm structure, large sample size, and robust statistical analysis. It directly tests causal effects of LLM-generated interventions versus standard materials and no-message control, with credible implementation and reported effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects are modest-to-medium on intentions, with the strongest effects on stool-test intent (d≈0.60-0.64) but not on colonoscopy intent relative to expert materials. The study is in a general adult population, not the target K-12 middle-school mathematics population, so practical educational relevance for the retrieval topic is very low despite the methodologically strong evidence.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4.1-generated persuasive messaging and a multi-turn motivational-interviewing chatbot used to encourage colorectal cancer screening intentions; both AI arms were personalized with participant demographics and compared against expert-written materials and no-message control.

finding.finding_summary: Both AI interventions increased self-reported comfort discussing colorectal cancer screening with a provider relative to no-message control and expert-written materials. The paper reports that participants found both AI conditions more empathetic than expert materials, but it does not provide a numeric effect size for this secondary outcome.
finding.measure: Self-reported comfort discussing CRC screening with a provider; perceived empathy of message/interaction

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the single AI message may be more scalable than the longer chatbot because it achieved similar intent gains with less participant time. Participants spent on average 180 seconds more with the chatbot than with the single AI message, yet the two AI formats did not differ in screening-intent effects.
finding.measure: Surplus time spent engaging with intervention
finding.std_deviation: Chatbot surplus time SD=260.46 sec; single AI message SD=69.61 sec; expert material SD=78.46 sec

paper_profiles.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Conversational AI
paper_profiles.venue: ICTIR’ 17 Workshop on Search-Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI’ 2017)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews deep reinforcement learning (DRL) as an approach for conversational AI. It explains basic reinforcement learning concepts, contrasts reinforcement learning with supervised learning, and discusses why DRL is promising for dialogue systems and intelligent assistants. The paper does not investigate a specific educational intervention or measure learner outcomes; instead, it synthesizes conceptual issues and prior work in conversational AI.

A major focus is the set of challenges involved in applying DRL to conversational agents, especially reward design, trade-offs among multiple goals, coherent dialogue generation, and evaluation of agents. The paper argues that conversational AI requires balancing performance, informativeness, personalization, and user experience, which makes reward functions difficult to design and optimize.

The paper also surveys example conversational models based on DRL and deep learning, including dialogue systems and related neural approaches. It briefly mentions educational uses such as AutoTutor as an example of conversational AI in education, but it does not present an empirical study of middle school mathematics, ChatGPT, or any comparable generative AI tool. The conclusion is that DRL has substantial potential for conversational AI, but important methodological challenges remain, especially around reward formulation and evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review-style paper with no direct empirical study, no comparison group, and no student outcome data. It is peer-reviewed workshop proceedings, but it does not meet criteria for an evaluative impact study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact on student learning or middle school mathematics achievement is measured. The paper is informative about conversational AI methods but provides no direct evidence of instructional effect.

interventions.use_case: The paper reviews deep reinforcement learning and neural conversational models as the basis for conversational AI systems, including dialogue generation, strategic dialogue management, and chatbot-style assistants. It discusses potential educational use in conversational tutoring systems such as AutoTutor, but does not test a live classroom tutoring intervention.

paper_profiles.title: AI Conversational Tutors in Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings 14th Panhellenic Conference iCT in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines AI conversational tutors for foreign language learning, focusing on how well current state-of-the-art systems support conversational practice, feedback, and learner experience. The author frames the work as an empirical mixed-methods evaluation and asks three questions: what design patterns are common in AI language tutors, how their interaction experience compares with general-purpose AI models, and how such tools can be systematically evaluated for quality.

The study first assesses four specialized language-learning applications (Talkio, TalkPal, Univerbal, and Langua) through simulated use by the researcher acting as a Spanish learner at B1/B2 level. The tools are examined in free chat and other conversational modes, with attention to turn-taking, correction, feedback, breakdown repair, transcript availability, and privacy handling. The paper then compares these specialized tutors with ChatGPT and Gemini in voice mode using a Spanish role-play prompt, and finally applies a 10-dimensional transcript-based evaluation framework to six tutors total using five LLM-based evaluators.

The main conclusion is that AI conversational tutors can provide supportive, natural-feeling language practice, but they vary substantially in interaction quality, feedback quality, and handling of conversational breakdowns. The author finds that some specialized tools offer stronger language-specific correction and annotated feedback, while ChatGPT can produce high-quality conversational feedback even as a general-purpose tool. The paper also highlights design concerns such as missing transcript segments, limited transparency about voice-data storage, and the need for better contextual error correction and privacy safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference paper with a clear mixed-methods design, but it is primarily qualitative/descriptive and relies on a single evaluator for the user-experience phase plus transcript-based ratings by artificial experts. It does not include a controlled learning-outcome comparison or randomized design.
