Across the 20 interviewees, themes indicated that AI models functioned as 'patient tutors,' 'mentors,' and 'math buddies' that made mathematics feel less intimidating; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of interview reports of math anxiety, confidence, and coping

finding.finding_summary: The paper also suggests a positive effect on independent learning and persistence: students said AI use encouraged them to practice more, rely less on others, and engage in self-guided learning. This was based on interview themes rather than a measured skill outcome, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Interview themes related to independence, persistence, and self-guided learning

paper_profiles.title: An explanatory study of factors influencing engagement in AI education at the K-12 Level: an extension of the classic TAM model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what factors shape K-12 students’ acceptance and engagement with artificial intelligence education when generative AI tools are used in instruction. The authors argue that existing technology acceptance models do not fully capture the cognitive and human–computer interaction factors that matter for students learning AI with tools such as ChatGPT and Midjourney, so they extend TAM with additional constructs related to AI motivation, readiness, confidence, anxiety, interface design, content, and interactivity.

The study was conducted with 210 Chinese students in grades 7–9 who took part in a one-month AI course centered on creating AI-related visual narratives and picture books. During the course, students used GenAI tools including ChatGPT, Midjourney, and translation software. After the course, 197 valid survey responses were analyzed using structural equation modeling. The outcome measures were students’ perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and attitudes toward AI learning, all assessed through self-report questionnaires.

Results showed that AI intrinsic motivation, AI readiness, AI confidence, user interface, content quality, and learner-interface interactivity positively predicted perceived usefulness and ease of use, while AI anxiety had negative effects. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, in turn, positively predicted attitudes toward AI learning. The paper concludes that both cognitive and interface-related factors are important for designing AI4K12 instruction and that GenAI-based AI courses can support student engagement when the learning experience is well designed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational SEM study with post-course survey data, not an experiment or RCT. It provides useful evidence on acceptance and engagement constructs, but it does not estimate causal learning effects or achievement outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects are modest to moderate on attitudinal and acceptance variables, not academic achievement, and the study focuses on one Chinese K-9 sample. Because it is about engagement/acceptance rather than direct learning gains, the practical impact on the requested topic is unclear for math achievement.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-supported K-12 AI course activities using ChatGPT for idea generation, narrative continuity, and question answering while students create AI-themed picture books; Midjourney is also used as a generative image tool within the same instructional workflow.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not measure achievement; it examined K-12 students' acceptance of AI courses using GenAI tools (n=197 valid responses after exclusions from 210 initial participants). Cognitive factors AIIM, AIRD, and AICF were positively associated with perceived usefulness and ease of use (e.g., AIIM→PU β=0.211), while AIAX was negatively associated (AIAX→PEOU β=-0.162).
finding.measure: Survey-based technology acceptance constructs: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and attitudes toward learning AI through GenAI
finding.effect_size: β values reported; AIIM→PU=0.211, AIRD→PU=0.152, AICF→PU=0.158, AIAX→PEOU=-0.162

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that GenAI course design features were positively related to students' attitudes toward learning AI, with HCI factors such as content and learner-interface interactivity showing meaningful associations with perceived usefulness and ease of use (e.g., LINT→PEOU β=0.203, C→PEOU β=0.184). Overall, the model suggests GenAI can support students' engagement, perceived usability, and willingness to learn in AI4K12 settings.
finding.measure: Attitudes toward AI learning, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use
finding.effect_size: β values reported; UI→PEOU=0.173, C→PU=0.168, C→PEOU=0.184, LINT→PEOU=0.203, PU→ATT=0.208, PEOU→ATT=0.228

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of two versions of ChatGPT (released 9 January 2023 and 30 January 2023) and GPT-4. The authors ask whether these models can solve or assist with a wide range of mathematical tasks, and whether they are useful as tools for professional mathematicians. To do so, they introduce two natural-language mathematics benchmarks, GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS, designed to cover advanced mathematical reasoning and multiple dimensions of task difficulty.

The benchmark includes prompts drawn from graduate- and undergraduate-level textbooks, proofs with missing steps, olympiad-style problems, symbolic integration tasks, and search-engine-style queries about definitions and named theorems. The study uses manually labeled ratings, error codes, and warning codes to score model outputs on correctness, logic, and failure modes. Although the paper is not an education study in the classroom sense, it does include educationally relevant mathematical levels such as undergraduate and graduate mathematics.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is useful mainly as a lookup or factual assistant, while GPT-4 performs better and can handle some undergraduate-level mathematics, but still fails on graduate-level tasks and many proof-based or complex problems. The authors conclude that despite public enthusiasm, these models are not reliable for consistently producing high-quality mathematical proofs or calculations, though they may be integrated into expert workflows as supportive tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmark study with manual human ratings and a clearly described methodology, but it is not a K-12 study, not an RCT/QED in educational settings, and uses custom evaluation rather than learner outcomes. It provides useful evidence about model capability, but only limited direct relevance to classroom education.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear performance differences in mathematical task-solving, including GPT-4’s moderate-to-large gains over earlier ChatGPT versions, but these are not measured in student learning outcomes. Its practical impact for education is indirect and mainly concerns potential productivity gains for expert users rather than demonstrated learner achievement.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating ChatGPT and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for advanced math tasks, including fact retrieval, proof completion, symbolic integration, and solving undergraduate-to-graduate level problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper benchmarks ChatGPT (9-Jan and 30-Jan versions) and GPT-4 on 709 math prompts (1636 human ratings). ChatGPT averaged 3.20 (SD=1.23) and 3.29 (SD=1.28), below a passing threshold of 3.5 for most subdatasets; GPT-4 improved to 4.15 (SD=1.12) on the 170-prompt miniGHOSTS subset, with particularly strong results on undergraduate-level items but continued failure on graduate-level difficulty and Olympiad-style problems.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical problem-solving performance (1-5 rating scale) across proof, computation, fact-retrieval, integration, and problem-solving tasks
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts total; GPT-4 on n=170 miniGHOSTS prompts

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that ChatGPT is most useful as a mathematical search engine / knowledge-base interface for query answering and lookup tasks, especially for professional mathematicians who can verify outputs. This is a workflow-efficiency benefit rather than a direct learning gain, and the paper describes it qualitatively rather than with an experimental effect size.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of utility for fact querying, theorem/definition retrieval, and proof-outline lookup

paper_profiles.title: On the Robustness of ChatGPT in Teaching Korean Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how well ChatGPT performs on Korean mathematics problems and whether it can also rate and categorize mathematics questions in ways that align with human judgment and educational theory. The authors frame the work as addressing two questions: the accuracy of ChatGPT on multilingual math problem solving, and its usefulness for evaluating question characteristics such as difficulty, cognitive demand, clarity, and engagement.

The approach uses a validated dataset of 586 Korean mathematics questions from the South Korean CSAT (College Scholastic Ability Test). ChatGPT is evaluated in a zero-shot setting on answer correctness, and then asked to rate each question on eleven criteria using Likert-style scales. The paper also includes correlation analysis, chi-squared significance testing, topic analysis, and some prompt-engineering follow-up experiments (including translation to English and use of GPT-4o / o1-preview on subsets of incorrect items).

The study context is high-stakes university-admissions mathematics in South Korea, which is multilingual from the model’s perspective because the questions are in Korean and include both textual and diagram-based items. The main findings are that ChatGPT answers about 66.72% of the questions correctly, performs better on lower-marked and non-diagram questions, and struggles with sequential reasoning, visual information, and low-resource-language handling. At the same time, its ratings of difficulty and other question attributes are broadly consistent with human annotations and educational theory, suggesting possible utility for assessment analysis and adaptive learning support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-paper observational evaluation of ChatGPT on a fixed exam dataset, with descriptive accuracy analysis and correlational/statistical associations, not an experimental study. The methodology is clear and systematic, but it does not meet RCT or strong QED standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a moderate accuracy level (66.72%) on a specialized Korean mathematics dataset, but it also highlights substantial limitations on harder, sequential, and diagram-based items. The practical impact is promising yet mixed and not clearly generalizable to middle school mathematics achievement.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating ChatGPT as a multilingual mathematics-solving and question-rating assistant for Korean CSAT math items, including zero-shot answering and rubric-based categorization of exam questions.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 391 of 586 Korean CSAT mathematics questions correctly, for an overall accuracy of 66.72% (n=586; n=391 correct). Performance was higher on lower-marked questions and dropped to about 50% on 4-point questions, with notable weaknesses on sequential and diagram-based items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on CSAT mathematics questions; correctness by item type/mark value and diagram presence

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s rubric-based ratings of difficulty, cognitive demand, time requirement, clarity, and other item-quality criteria were reported as substantially good and broadly consistent with educational theory and human perspectives, but the paper also notes weaknesses on sequential reasoning and complex multi-step problems. No formal effect size was reported, but correlations were described as positive between predicted cognitive demand/difficulty and question marks.
finding.measure: Rubric-based ratings/categorization of mathematics questions; correlations with item marks and human annotations

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests ChatGPT can support assessment design and item analysis by rating/categorizing questions across eleven criteria and by identifying topic distributions, potentially reducing manual analysis effort. This is a descriptive utility finding rather than a direct workload experiment, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Ability to rate, categorize, and analyze exam items across 11 criteria

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT A Good Translator? Yes With GPT-4 As The Engine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can function as a machine translation system and how its performance compares with commercial translation products. The authors focus on three questions: how to prompt ChatGPT for translation, how it performs across language pairs with different resource levels and language families, and how robust it is on domain-specific or noisy text.

The approach is an empirical benchmark evaluation rather than an educational intervention. The study tests several translation prompts on ChatGPT, compares ChatGPT against Google Translate, DeepL, and Tencent TranSmart, and evaluates translation quality using BLEU, ChrF++, and TER. It examines multiple language directions involving German, English, Romanian, and Chinese, plus robustness sets from biomedical abstracts, Reddit comments, and speech-like data. The authors also test a pivot prompting strategy and later re-evaluate performance with GPT-4 as the engine.

The paper finds that ChatGPT with GPT-3.5 performs reasonably well on high-resource European language pairs but lags on low-resource and distant language pairs, and it is less robust than commercial systems on biomedical and noisy text. Pivot prompting improves performance for distant languages, and GPT-4 substantially improves translation quality to near-commercial levels. The authors conclude that ChatGPT becomes a strong translator with GPT-4, though the work is limited by small samples and early-access constraints.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed technical report on machine translation, not an education study, and it does not evaluate any K-12 learning intervention or student outcome. It provides benchmark-based comparisons of translation systems rather than empirical evidence about educational achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct impact on middle school mathematics achievement or any education outcome. The paper's findings concern translation quality for GPT-3.5/GPT-4 versus commercial MT systems, which is outside the retrieved research topic.

paper_profiles.title: Utilizing ChatGPT to Enhance Clinical Trial Enrollment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving clinical trial enrollment by automating the initial step of identifying eligible trials from patient information in electronic health records. The authors focus on the challenge that clinical notes are unstructured, lengthy, and difficult to search effectively with standard retrieval methods.

The proposed approach uses ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) as an intermediate component in a retrieval pipeline. Given a clinical note, ChatGPT is prompted to extract patient-related information, disambiguate entities, handle negation in combination with a transformer-based model, and generate search queries for retrieving potentially eligible clinical trials. The study compares multiple prompt designs, including zero-shot prompts with different system roles and task instructions, and evaluates query effectiveness on two benchmark clinical trial retrieval collections.

The paper is not an education study; it does not involve students, teachers, or classroom implementation. The main findings are that ChatGPT-generated queries can improve retrieval performance over existing approaches under several prompting strategies, and in some cases even outperform human-generated queries. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has potential to support clinical trial enrollment by reducing human effort, while noting that its role is limited to structured information extraction and query formulation rather than direct decision-making.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative retrieval study, but it is not an educational study and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design relevant to K-12 evidence standards. The paper reports benchmark evaluations rather than a rigorously controlled impact study on learners or schools.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests operational gains in a medical retrieval workflow, but it does not report educational impact or effect sizes that map to K-12 outcomes. Any impact is indirect and specific to clinical trial enrollment, so it is not evidence of educational impact.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT is used as an intermediate NLP tool to extract patient-related information from unstructured clinical notes and generate search queries for identifying eligible clinical trials.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT-generated search queries improve retrieval performance for clinical trial enrollment compared with existing approaches, and in some settings outperform human-generated queries. No student learning outcomes are studied; the practical contribution is reduced human effort in the trial-matching workflow and faster query formulation. Sample sizes and effect sizes are not reported in the abstracted text.
finding.measure: Retrieval performance for clinical trial search (e.g., ranking effectiveness on two benchmark retrieval collections)

paper_profiles.title: Points of convergence - music meets mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: More UK Success Stories in Industrial Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter discusses a piece of pure mathematics on phase-locking in the Arnold family of circle maps and uses it as a case study for how frontier research can influence creative collaboration. The central mathematical question is whether hyperbolic parameters are dense in the Arnold family, meaning that stable behavior can be found arbitrarily close to chaotic behavior. The paper explains the result that hyperbolic maps are dense and outlines the key ideas behind the proof, including complex extension, rigidity, and perturbation arguments.

The second half describes a collaboration between the author and composer Emily Howard during her 2015 artist-in-residence appointment in Liverpool’s mathematics department. The collaboration turned research ideas into numerical datasets that inspired musical works such as Orbits, Torus, sphere, and Antisphere. The paper presents this as an example of research-led creative exchange rather than an educational intervention.

The paper’s main conclusion is that mathematically rich, conceptually accessible research can support productive interdisciplinary collaboration when there is a shared language and a carefully chosen topic. It argues that the success of the collaboration came from Howard’s mathematical background and the suitability of the hyperbolicity result for creative interpretation, including its themes of stability near chaos and the role of hidden structure in the proof.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/mathematical research chapter describing dynamical systems results and a music collaboration, not an empirical study of an educational or AI intervention. There is no student sample, no comparison condition, and no outcome measurement relevant to K-12 learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct educational or AI intervention effects and provides no evidence of impact on learners or schools. Its relevance to the retrieval topic is only indirect through a non-educational collaboration narrative.

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT in the generative AI era. It addresses the rapid rise of ChatGPT after its release in late 2022 and argues that a comprehensive review is needed because many early articles were already appearing across technical and application domains. The paper aims to synthesize what ChatGPT is, how it works, what it can do, and what limitations and risks it poses.

The survey reviews the underlying technology behind ChatGPT, including the Transformer backbone, autoregressive generation, and the GPT model family from GPT-1 through GPT-4. It then organizes applications into scientific writing, education, medical uses, software development, management, and miscellaneous domains. In education, the paper discusses ChatGPT’s use for teaching and learning support, assessment, and subject-specific tasks such as physics, mathematics, economics, and law, but these are presented as examples from other studies rather than a single empirical study conducted by the authors.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is highly capable for text generation, tutoring-like support, brainstorming, and assistance across many fields, while also emphasizing major limitations such as incorrectness, illogical outputs, inconsistency, lack of consciousness, plagiarism risks, overreliance, misuse, and misinformation. Because it is a survey rather than an intervention study, it does not report participant populations, implementation details, or outcome effects for a specific educational experiment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It does not report a study design, comparison group, or original outcome data for educational achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of impact on student outcomes such as middle school mathematics achievement. It is descriptive and theoretical rather than outcome-based.

interventions.use_case: Survey of ChatGPT as a general-purpose conversational AI, including its use in education as an AI assistant for tutoring, answering questions, generating explanations, and supporting teaching/learning tasks.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as a Learning Assistant in Distance Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how Large Language Models, particularly ChatGPT, can be used in higher education to support active learning and student engagement. The first article in the excerpt presents ChatGPT as a role-playing simulation tool for a master's-level course, where students practice negotiation and decision-making in an applied cloud computing context. The goal is to show how conversational AI can be programmed with prompts to simulate realistic interaction scenarios that students can practice asynchronously.

The implementation described is a case study in the master's programme "Cloud Computing Engineering" at the University of Applied Sciences Burgenland in Austria. Students took on a role-playing task in which they negotiated for approval of a cloud migration project budget using ChatGPT as the interlocutor. The paper also includes a second, related article about a ChatGPT-based Learning Assistant in distance learning programmes at the same institution, where ChatGPT is integrated into the LMS to answer student questions based on course content, with teacher review of responses within 24 hours.

Across both examples, the paper is primarily exploratory and conceptual rather than a controlled evaluation of learning outcomes. The authors argue that ChatGPT can broaden the range of educational uses beyond text generation, enabling interactive simulations and always-available support. They conclude that these uses are promising for higher education, while noting that the work is an initial exploration and that more extensive future case studies are needed to assess broader applicability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a brief practice-oriented article describing a case study and future plans, not a rigorous empirical evaluation. No controlled design, quantitative outcome data, or analytic methodology is reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measurable evidence of impact on learning outcomes or other outcomes. The paper offers an illustrative use case only, so impact cannot be estimated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational role-playing partner in a simulation game, where students practice negotiation and real-life scenario dialogue asynchronously.
Role-playing simulation game for active learning in which students negotiate a cloud migration project and interact with ChatGPT as the simulated interlocutor.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT-enabled role-play can support durable skills such as negotiation, decision-making, analytical thinking, and problem solving. However, it reports only a conceptual case study/pilot use in a master's course and provides no quantitative pre/post outcome data, effect sizes, or inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Not empirically quantified; course assignment reflections and described skill targets

finding.finding_summary: The article claims the simulation increased student interest and motivation by making learning more engaging and interactive. This is presented as a rationale and preliminary classroom observation rather than measured evidence, so no effect size or sample-based estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement/motivation implied through classroom participation and reflection

paper_profiles.title: Development of a test in German language to assess middle school students’ physics proficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of readily accessible German-language, subject-specific achievement tests for middle-school physics. The authors aim to develop a test that can be used in educational research to assess students’ physics proficiency in a test-economic, objective manner, replacing ad hoc pencil-and-paper measures assembled from published TIMSS items.

The intervention/approach is not a teaching intervention, but a test-development process. The authors selected 40 physics-related TIMSS items, translated English items into German, and converted some open-ended items into multiple-choice single-select format. They then administered the resulting item pool to 177 eighth-grade students in Hamburg, Germany and used Rasch modeling to evaluate item fit, differential item functioning, reliability, and correlational validity with science interest, science self-concept, physics grades, and cultural/economic capital.

The final instrument retained 20 items spanning content areas typical of middle-school physics, especially mechanics and optics. The results suggested adequate model fit, sufficient person-separation reliability, excellent item-separation reliability, and expected correlations with external variables, leading the authors to conclude that the test provides a valid measure of middle-school students’ physics proficiency in German. They also note that the test is limited by its Hamburg-only sample and weaker coverage of electrics and the extreme ends of ability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/test-development study using Rasch analysis, not an RCT or quasi-experiment. It provides useful psychometric evidence, but the design does not support causal claims about an educational intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct instructional effect on achievement; its contribution is a validated assessment instrument. Any practical impact is indirect and modest, mainly improving measurement efficiency and research capability rather than student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports development and psychometric validation of a German-language middle-school physics proficiency test based on adapted TIMSS items, not an intervention effect. In a sample of n=177 eighth-grade students, the resulting 20-item test showed acceptable Rasch model fit (Andersen LR=11.82, df=19, p=0.89), person-separation reliability of 0.78, and item-separation reliability of 0.97, supporting valid measurement of physics proficiency.
finding.measure: Physics proficiency test scores / Rasch person parameters; item fit and reliability indices

finding.finding_summary: The test was explicitly designed to be highly test-economic and objective, using 20 multiple-choice single-select items with an estimated completion time of 20 minutes. This is a measurement-development finding rather than a student-outcome effect, but it indicates improved efficiency for assessing middle-school physics proficiency compared with longer open-ended formats.
finding.measure: Test length / estimated administration time / objective scoring properties

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT Assess Human Personalities? A General Evaluation Framework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models, especially ChatGPT, can be used to assess human personalities rather than only model their own personalities or biases. The authors frame this as a general evaluation problem and propose a framework for querying LLMs with MBTI-style personality items in a way that elicits clearer, less self-referential answers.

Their approach has three main components: unbiased prompts that randomize response-option order and average across repeated testings, subject-replaced queries that swap "you" for a target group such as men, women, or professions, and correctness-evaluated instructions that ask the model to judge whether statements are correct rather than whether it personally agrees. They then define three metrics for consistency, robustness to prompt-order perturbations, and fairness across genders.

The experiments evaluate InstructGPT, ChatGPT, and GPT-4 on general population groups and representative professions using the MBTI questionnaire. The results suggest that ChatGPT and GPT-4 can produce stable personality-type assignments for groups of people, often with higher consistency and fairness than InstructGPT, though they are still sensitive to prompt bias. The paper is exploratory and methodological rather than educational, and it concludes with cautions about misuse, bias, and the limited scientific validity of MBTI as a personality measure.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study with a clearly described evaluation framework and repeated prompting experiments, but it is not a K-12 intervention study and does not use a randomized or educational design. The evidence is indirect for education and focuses on model behavior rather than learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational achievement effects, no middle school mathematics outcomes, and no intervention impact on students. Its findings are about LLM assessment behavior, consistency, robustness, and fairness in personality evaluation, so educational impact is absent for the requested topic.

interventions.use_case: Evaluates ChatGPT, GPT-4, and InstructGPT as general-purpose language models used to assess human personalities via rewritten MBTI questionnaire prompts, including subject-replaced queries and correctness-evaluated instructions.

paper_profiles.title: Identification of Books That are Suitable for Middle School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of selecting books that are suitable for middle school students, motivated by concerns that books with inappropriate content can negatively affect children’s development. Rather than studying reader responses or reviews, the authors propose analyzing the books themselves using natural language processing and sentiment analysis.

The intervention/approach is a custom algorithm built in Python that preprocesses book text, applies VADER sentiment analysis at the word and sentence level, adds a manually created bad-words list, and computes 14 textual and semantic features. These features are then used to train an artificial neural network (ANN) to classify books as suitable or unsuitable for middle school students. The dataset is original and contains 416 books drawn from Turkish Ministry of National Education-approved books, Oxford/Cambridge sources, school libraries, Gutenberg Project books, and books with R ratings or age ratings indicating inappropriate content.

The context is middle-school reading materials in Turkey and English-language books from international sources. The paper frames the tool as potentially useful for the Ministry of National Education, schools, teachers, parents, and students to screen books for curriculum or reading-list use. The authors report that the trained ANN achieved 90.06% consistency on a sample of 83 test books and conclude that the method can help expedite book selection, though it needs a larger dataset and better handling of academic jargon.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical machine-learning classification study, but it is not a causal educational intervention study and does not use a randomized or strong quasi-experimental design. The evidence is mainly a model-development evaluation on a small custom dataset with limited external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported accuracy is reasonably high for the classification task, but the paper does not measure student learning outcomes and therefore has unclear educational impact. Any benefit is indirect, via book screening efficiency and institutional decision support.

interventions.use_case: NLP-based book suitability classification for middle school texts using VADER sentiment analysis, custom bad-words filtering, and an artificial neural network to screen books for age-appropriateness.

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to speed up and standardize the book-selection process for middle school curricula and as a screening tool for Ministry of Education, schools, teachers, parents, and students. The paper reports 90.06% consistency on a test set of 83 books and 91.2% accuracy for appropriate books and 80.7% accuracy for inappropriate books, suggesting improved efficiency in identifying age-suitable texts.
finding.measure: Book suitability classification accuracy / consistency rate; correct classification of suitable and unsuitable books

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues the model could support institutional book-selection decisions for curricula and age-group screening, reducing subjective bias in evaluations by producing numerical suitability scores. Reported performance included 90.06% overall consistency, with proposed use by the Ministry of National Education and schools as a preliminary reference system.
finding.measure: Institutional screening utility and classification consistency

paper_profiles.title: Examining pre-service mathematics teachers' purposes of using ChatGPT in lesson plan development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines why pre-service middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT while developing lesson plans. The study asks how the tool supported lesson content creation and how it helped participants deepen their own knowledge and address deficiencies during planning.

The intervention/approach was not a classroom teaching intervention but a structured use of ChatGPT during lesson-plan preparation. Participants were asked to choose one or more mathematics curriculum outcomes, prepare a lesson plan using ChatGPT, and then respond to an open-ended questionnaire. The qualitative analysis focused on the purposes for which ChatGPT was used, including generating activities, problems, examples, evaluation tools, course flow, creative ideas, conceptual explanations, and revisions.

The sample included 56 third-year pre-service middle school mathematics teachers at a state university in Turkey. The study was conducted in the spring semester of the 2023–2024 academic year. Findings showed that ChatGPT was used mainly to create lesson content, especially learning activities, problems/examples, assessment tools, and course flow, and secondarily to deepen pedagogical and conceptual knowledge. The author concludes that ChatGPT can be a useful support tool in teacher education for lesson planning, but it should complement, not replace, teachers' expertise, and its outputs should be checked carefully for accuracy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative phenomenological study using convenience sampling and open-ended questionnaire data with content analysis. It provides useful descriptive evidence, but it does not estimate causal impact and has limited generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical usefulness of ChatGPT for teacher lesson planning, but it does not measure student learning gains or quantify impact. The evidence indicates potential benefits for planning efficiency and teacher cognition, but the impact on educational outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Pre-service middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT to support lesson plan development, including generating activities, problems, examples, assessment tools, course flow, creative ideas, concept explanations, and revisions.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative phenomenological study (n=56 pre-service middle school mathematics teachers) found that ChatGPT was widely used to speed and structure lesson-plan development. Participants reported using it to generate course flow, activities, problems, assessments, and revisions, suggesting improved planning efficiency, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported uses/purposes of ChatGPT in lesson plan development from open-ended questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT supported durable skills such as creativity, idea generation, and pedagogical problem-solving during lesson planning. Pre-service teachers reported that it helped them think of novel activities, connect concepts, and deepen their own pedagogical and conceptual understanding; however, the evidence is qualitative and descriptive with no effect size reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported pedagogical idea generation, conceptual understanding, and lesson-plan revision purposes

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions and practical issues surrounding the use of ChatGPT in mathematics education shortly after the tool’s release. The authors ask how different stakeholders view ChatGPT’s usefulness, accuracy, and risks for teaching and learning mathematics, and whether it can support mathematical problem solving and geometry instruction.

The study uses a qualitative instrumental case study design with two components: content analysis of interviews and a user-experience investigation. Interview data were collected from 30 people drawn from public blogs and discussions about ChatGPT use in mathematics, including students and math educators. In addition, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for one week across several teaching scenarios, including solving equations, evaluating limits, and teaching geometry. The paper focuses on ChatGPT as an AI chatbot rather than a formal instructional intervention in a classroom setting.

The findings suggest that participants viewed ChatGPT as promising for improving access to explanations, instant feedback, and basic mathematical support, especially for geometry. However, the authors also found clear weaknesses: ChatGPT produced incorrect algebra and calculus answers in some cases, misunderstood geometric concepts, and lacked the deeper understanding needed to diagnose misconceptions. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be a useful supplementary tool in mathematics education, but its use should be cautious, ethically guided, and supported by human review.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study using interviews, social media/content analysis, and user-experience testing, but it does not employ a controlled experimental design or quantitative causal inference. The evidence is useful for descriptive understanding of early ChatGPT use in mathematics, yet it has substantial methodological limitations and a small sample.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful instructional usefulness, but the direct evidence on mathematics performance is mixed and largely qualitative rather than showing measurable achievement gains. Any impact on middle school mathematics achievement is therefore unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI tutor for middle-school and general mathematics support, including solving equations, limits, derivatives, and explaining geometry concepts such as Pythagoras' theorem.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative case study does not report a quantitative achievement effect, but it presents direct task-based evidence that ChatGPT can solve some basic algebra/geometry prompts while making several important errors on equations, limits, derivatives, and geometric reasoning. In user scenarios, ChatGPT answered some geometry explanation prompts well, yet it produced incorrect results for a linear equation (correct answer 13/17 vs ChatGPT's 13/20), a cubic equation, a limit problem, and a derivative evaluation, indicating inconsistent mathematical performance rather than reliable achievement gains.
finding.measure: Task-based correctness on math problem-solving prompts and qualitative assessment of geometry explanations
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators for user experience scenarios

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can provide rapid, step-by-step explanations and generate responses within seconds, suggesting potential productivity gains for teachers and learners. However, this is a qualitative assessment only and is tempered by concerns about reliability and the need for human verification.
finding.measure: Perceived speed/efficiency of response generation and instructional support

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves student learning and under what conditions its effects are strongest. It addresses three outcomes: learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking, responding to mixed findings in the prior literature about whether ChatGPT helps, has no effect, or may even hinder learning.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis of 51 quasi-experimental and experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025, extracting 72 independent effect sizes. The included studies covered primary, secondary, and college learners, though the quantitative moderator analyses were mainly driven by secondary and college samples. The contexts included STEM and related courses, language learning and academic writing, and skills/competencies development; learning models included personalized learning, problem-based learning, project-based learning, contextual learning, reflective learning, and mixed designs. ChatGPT was used in roles such as intelligent tutor, intelligent partner, intelligent learning tool, and mixed roles, and in applications such as assessment/evaluation, tutoring, and personalized recommendation.

The meta-analysis found a large positive effect of ChatGPT on learning performance, and moderate positive effects on learning perception and higher-order thinking. For learning performance, effects were stronger in skills/competencies courses, problem-based learning, and 4–8 week interventions. For learning perception, duration was the only significant moderator, with longer interventions producing larger effects. For higher-order thinking, effects varied by course type and were strongest when ChatGPT functioned as an intelligent tutor. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can support learning outcomes, but its effectiveness depends on instructional design, duration, and how it is integrated into teaching and learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 51 experimental/quasi-experimental studies with standardized effect sizes, heterogeneity tests, publication-bias checks, and sensitivity analyses. The design is strong for causal synthesis, though there is substantial heterogeneity across included studies.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effects are medium-to-large and positive for the main outcomes, especially learning performance (g=0.867) and moderate effects for learning perception and higher-order thinking (g≈0.46). This indicates meaningful impact on general student learning outcomes, although the evidence spans mixed contexts rather than middle school mathematics specifically.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT used as an intelligent tutor, learning partner, or educational tool in experimental and quasi-experimental learning interventions across K-12 and college settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent studies, ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance (Hedges's g=0.867, 95% CI 0.683 to 1.052). Outcomes were measured with post-test scores, exams, and comparable achievement assessments in experimental and quasi-experimental studies (total studies in the overall meta-analysis: 51; performance subset k=44).
finding.measure: Learning performance tests/exams/post-test achievement scores

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception across 19 independent studies (g=0.456, 95% CI 0.287 to 0.625). The paper reports this construct as learner perceptions measured primarily through scales and questionnaires, indicating improved attitudes/experience with ChatGPT-supported learning.
finding.measure: Learning perception scales/questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on higher-order thinking across 9 independent studies (g=0.457, 95% CI 0.255 to 0.650). The included studies measured higher-order thinking with scales/questionnaires, capturing outcomes such as critical thinking and related cognitive processes.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking scales/questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: The ChatGPT Effect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and other generative AI tools and asks how they should be understood, governed, and used in higher education. Rather than testing a single classroom intervention, it synthesizes concepts, practical examples, policy issues, and technical background to help educators and institutions respond to GenAI’s impact on teaching, learning, assessment, and administration.

The approach is a broad conceptual and practice-oriented treatment of GenAI in higher education. It discusses AI literacy, the strengths and weaknesses of ChatGPT in curriculum design, redesigning assessment for the AI era, and developing institutional AI policies. The book also includes illustrative scenarios, prompts, and a framework for assessment integration, alongside a qualitative study of perceptions of GenAI policy in Hong Kong and a technical overview of how GenAI works.

The intended users are primarily higher-education educators, students, and administrators/policymakers, with examples centered on post-secondary contexts. The book’s main conclusion is that GenAI should be embraced thoughtfully as a partner to human teaching and assessment, supported by AI literacy, ethical policy, and redesigned pedagogy rather than used as a replacement for human judgment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a book introduction/preview and review-style text about generative AI in higher education, not an empirical study. It contains no direct methodology, no sample, and no evaluated intervention or measured educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct empirical evidence of impact on middle school mathematics achievement or any other student outcome. The text is conceptual and policy-oriented rather than outcome-evaluative.

paper_profiles.title: Acceptance of artificial intelligence among pre-service teachers: a multigroup analysis
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what factors shape pre-service teachers’ acceptance and intended use of AI-based educational applications, and whether these relationships differ by gender. The authors frame the problem as an important but under-studied issue in teacher education, especially as AI tools such as ChatGPT and related educational applications become more visible in schooling. They argue that understanding acceptance among future teachers is important because their attitudes may influence how AI is adopted in classrooms later on.

The study used a questionnaire grounded in Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM3), measuring AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, subjective norm, job relevance, and behavioral intention. Data were collected online from 452 pre-service teachers at one German university enrolled in teacher education programs. The analysis used structural equation modeling, measurement invariance testing, latent mean comparisons, and multigroup analysis to examine both overall relationships and gender differences.

Results showed that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were the strongest predictors of intention to use AI, with perceived usefulness having the larger effect. AI self-efficacy and perceived enjoyment predicted perceived ease of use, while subjective norm and job relevance predicted perceived usefulness. AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use in the full sample, but gender moderated some paths: female participants reported higher AI anxiety and the anxiety-to-ease-of-use path differed by gender, as did the ease-of-use-to-usefulness path. The authors conclude that teacher education should address AI-related anxiety, especially among female pre-service teachers, and should emphasize the practical usefulness and usability of AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with structural equation modeling and multigroup invariance testing, but it is correlational and does not evaluate an intervention or causal effect. The evidence is methodologically solid for acceptance modeling, yet it lacks experimental manipulation or direct outcome measurement in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has unclear direct impact on K-12 learning outcomes because it measures pre-service teacher acceptance rather than student achievement or implementation effects. Its main contribution is institutional and preparatory, informing future adoption of AI in education rather than demonstrating measurable educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based acceptance of AI-based educational applications among pre-service teachers, using TAM3 constructs (AI self-efficacy, perceived enjoyment, AI anxiety, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, job relevance, subjective norm, behavioral intention); no specific AI tool was deployed.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that pre-service teachers’ AI acceptance was shaped by affective and self-belief factors, but anxiety was not a direct predictor of behavioral intention. AI self-efficacy positively predicted perceived ease of use (β=0.359, p<0.001; n=452), while perceived enjoyment also positively predicted perceived ease of use (β=0.518, p<0.001). AI anxiety did not significantly predict perceived ease of use (β=-0.037, p>0.05), and gender differences showed higher AI anxiety among female pre-service teachers (z=-3.217, p<0.01).
finding.measure: TAM3 survey constructs: AI anxiety, perceived enjoyment, AI self-efficacy, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention

finding.finding_summary: The paper found strong positive associations between perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and intention to use AI-based educational applications. Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention (β=0.501, p<0.001), followed by perceived ease of use (β=0.297, p<0.001); together, SN, PE, and PEOU explained 65% of the variance in behavioral intention (R²=0.65).
finding.measure: Behavioral intention to use AI-based educational applications; TAM3 structural equation modeling

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence relevant to teacher education institutions by showing that AI acceptance among pre-service teachers is measurable and gender-invariant at the configural, metric, and scalar levels, with only partial strict invariance requiring one freed item. Gender significantly moderated two paths in the model: AI anxiety to perceived ease of use (female β=-0.119 vs male β=0.254; Δχ²=5.638, p=0.018) and perceived ease of use to perceived usefulness (female β=0.530 vs male β=0.283; Δχ²=9.987, p=0.002).
finding.measure: Measurement invariance and multigroup SEM by gender
finding.effect_size: ΔCFI=0.011 for strict invariance rejection; Δχ²=5.638 and 9.987 for moderated paths

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in-the-loop” when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The authors focus on a central tension in AI-supported personalization: teacher involvement may improve relevance, realism, and instructional quality, but it may also reduce efficiency and limit the fine-grained personalization that students may want.

The study involved seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers who used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so they better matched students’ interests, especially popular culture interests. Teachers participated in training, then worked through two curriculum units (Unit 4 and Unit 6) while their ChatGPT prompts, time spent, and spoken interactions were recorded. The personalized problems were delivered to 521 middle school students through ASSISTments, and students provided both closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback about how interesting the problems were and how closely they matched their interests.

The authors found that teachers used ChatGPT in varied ways, including broad prompts for general interest areas and more specific prompts to insert or refine particular cultural references, improve realism, and adjust readability or mathematical clarity. Students tended to prefer more specific, small-grain personalization, but teachers often operated at broader grain sizes because of time and feasibility constraints. On average, personalizing one problem took about four minutes, and the process did not become clearly more time-efficient over time. Teachers did improve the quality of their work across the second unit, and student ratings were higher in Unit 6 than in Unit 4, but the study concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization is expensive in time and still struggles to match the fine-grained personalization students want.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory mixed-methods study with teacher/student observations and regression analyses, but it is not a controlled efficacy trial and does not measure learning outcomes directly. The evidence is useful but mainly qualitative/correlational for the key achievement question.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows modest positive effects on student interest/relevance ratings and highlights substantial teacher workload, but it does not demonstrate direct math achievement gains. For the retrieved topic on ChatGPT and middle school mathematics achievement, the impact is therefore unclear rather than strong.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to rewrite existing middle school mathematics problems into personalized tasks aligned with students' interests, with iterative prompting to improve realism, readability, and cultural relevance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates math task personalization, not direct achievement. It reports that students rated problems created with 3-5 prompts more favorably on interestingness and closeness to interests, and that Unit 6 personalized problems received higher ratings than Unit 4 (interestingness: 2.56 vs 2.27; closeness: 2.66 vs 2.28). However, the study did not measure test scores or learning gains, so no direct achievement effect on middle school mathematics can be inferred.
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to students' interests; no direct math achievement measure reported
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs Unit 4 on ratings
finding.std_deviation: interestingness SD=1.24; closeness SD=1.28; prompts per problem SD=2.6

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-created personalization with ChatGPT was time-intensive. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6) and 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), with no evidence that time decreased as teachers gained experience; in fact, time increased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 by about 70 seconds per problem (B=70.4, p=0.0189). The paper concludes that this workflow did not become particularly time efficient, despite some gains in task quality and student ratings.
finding.measure: Time to create each personalized problem; number of prompts per problem
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=1.26 more prompts per problem from Unit 4 to Unit 6

finding.finding_summary: The personalized problems elicited moderate but generally low student interest and perceived relevance (mean interestingness=2.46/5; mean closeness=2.53/5). Students tended to prefer narrower, more specific pop-culture references, but disliked them when the reference did not match their own interests, indicating a mixed engagement response rather than uniformly positive affect.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback on why problems were interesting/uninteresting
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454-449 open-ended responses depending on item
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for optimal 3-5 prompt zone; unit-level rating increase B=0.33

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students perceive and want AI to behave when it is framed as a peer in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS), rather than as a tutor. The authors note that while generative AI has been widely explored for one-to-one tutoring, much less is known about AI as a collaborator inside small-group classroom work. Their research questions ask how students perceive AI peer support during mathematics CPS and what features, behaviors, and controls they want from such a peer.

To study this, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising Grades 6–8 students in the United States. The camp combined human-only CPS tasks, interactions with two AI peers through a web-based technology probe, reflections on AI dialogue, and participatory design activities in which students co-designed their ideal AI peer. The AI peers were built as a sandboxed prototype using GPT-4o, with conversation-stage control and individualized peer schemas intended to simulate middle-school mathematical reasoning and peer-like dialogue. Data included questionnaires, workload and group-climate surveys, interviews, reflections, and student artifacts.

The main conclusion is that students wanted an AI peer that supports collaboration without taking over: they preferred hints, checks, and concept refreshers before direct answers; explicit control over when the AI speaks and how much it says; and a friendly, peer-like tone with genuine expertise. Students reacted negatively when the AI felt too directive, repetitive, emotionally flat, or insufficiently responsive to their ideas. Overall, the study argues that effective AI peers for middle-school mathematics should be scaffold-first, socially attuned, and designed around student agency and classroom norms of collaborative problem solving.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative participatory design study with a small sample and a limited within-cohort comparison, not a controlled efficacy trial. It provides useful formative evidence, but the methodology primarily supports perception and design insights rather than causal claims about learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful but mixed effects on collaboration experience and workload, with medium-to-large effect sizes on some process measures. However, it does not provide direct evidence of improved mathematics achievement, so the overall impact on learning outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI peers for middle school mathematics collaborative problem solving, implemented with GPT-4o in a web-based chat probe that provided step-by-step discussion, hints, error detection, conceptual refreshers, and peer-like dialogue during group math tasks.

finding.finding_summary: This participatory design study did not measure math achievement directly, but it did evaluate mathematics problem-solving support in a CPS setting with n=22 paired comparisons on workload/climate measures. Students reported that AI peers could reduce temporal demand during math problem solving (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs M=9.62, SD=4.13; d=1.15), but they also described the AI as sometimes giving answers too quickly or failing to support the intended reasoning process.
finding.measure: Mathematics collaborative problem-solving experience; NASA-TLX temporal demand during math tasks; qualitative reflections on math reasoning support
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 for temporal demand; other math-achievement effects not reported
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 (AI-peer temporal demand), SD=4.13 (human-only temporal demand)

finding.finding_summary: Students expected AI peers to support collaboration, co-agency, and negotiation rather than simply provide procedures, and many found the AI’s rigid or repetitive dialogue disruptive to collaborative reasoning. The study reports significantly lower perceived task coordination with AI peers on GEQ Group Integration-Task (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs M=5.54, SD=1.52; d=0.81), but also rich qualitative preference for scaffolds that prompted explanation, turn-taking, and shared problem solving.
finding.measure: Group integration/task coordination, collaboration quality, co-agency, peer interaction norms
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey analyses; n=24 overall

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower social cohesion and less positive group affect when working with AI peers. GEQ Attractions to Group-Social was significantly lower in the AI-peer condition (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in pure human CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05), d=0.94, and students frequently described the AI as rude, not listening, or emotionally unresponsive.
finding.measure: GEQ social cohesion/attraction to group, qualitative affective responses
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey analyses; n=18 interviews plus 5 whole-class reflection sessions

finding.finding_summary: The AI peers reduced perceived time pressure during collaborative math work, indicating improved procedural efficiency. However, this came with significantly higher physical demand from typing and interface navigation (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41; d=1.14), so the overall efficiency impact was trade-off driven rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand during math CPS
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 vs 4.13 (temporal demand); SD=4.65 vs 2.41 (physical demand)

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive the roles, benefits, and challenges of using a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) in mathematics learning. Rather than testing achievement effects, the study asks what students think the TA should do, what opportunities it creates for learning, and what barriers arise when the system is used in a real classroom.

The intervention was a GenAI-powered TA built with GPT-4-Turbo and additional design features such as personalized topic/difficulty selection, gamification, contrasting cases, and retrieval-augmented generation from a large math Q&A corpus. Students interacted with the agent through text-based problem-solving activities in a 6th-grade rate-and-ratio unit. The study drew on classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 108 sixth-grade students in a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States.

Findings suggest that students viewed the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They reported that it supported a student-centered climate, autonomy, cognitive/social/emotional growth, deeper subject-matter understanding, and more positive attitudes toward math and AI. At the same time, students identified barriers related to the TA’s question quality, difficulty adapting to learning styles, technical issues, interface design, and the need for teacher facilitation. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can meaningfully extend teachable-agent design, but effective classroom use still depends on better pedagogical design, multimodal interaction, and human teacher support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative classroom study using observations, focus groups, and open-ended surveys. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically systematic for exploratory insight, but it does not provide causal identification or quantitative outcome estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for middle school math learning and motivation, but the evidence is self-reported and qualitative rather than measured achievement impact. There are no effect sizes, so the magnitude of impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: A generative AI-powered teachable agent for middle school math, using GPT-4-Turbo to simulate a less-knowledgeable peer that converses with students, asks elaboration questions, and supports learning-by-teaching in rate-and-ratio problems.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent helped them better understand middle school rate-and-ratio content. They described clearer grasp of core concepts and formulas, and said teaching the agent helped them recognize and correct misconceptions, but the evidence is qualitative rather than a measured achievement gain (n=108 students; 14 interviewed).
finding.measure: Students’ qualitative reports about math understanding and application of knowledge in rate-and-ratio tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the GenAI-powered TA as increasing enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and positive attitudes toward AI. The study is based on observation, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 108 sixth graders, so the finding reflects perceived affective benefits rather than a quantified causal effect.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of joy of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and attitudes toward AI

finding.finding_summary: Students said the tool fostered cognitive, social, and emotional capacities, including elaboration, perspective-taking, communication, and resilience. They described being pushed to explain reasoning, communicate more clearly, and persist after errors, but no standardized durable-skills measure was administered.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of reasoning, communication, perspective-taking, and resilience

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students saw opportunities for interdisciplinary learning, especially connecting computer science and mathematics through AI use. This was captured through students’ open-ended responses and interviews, not through a formal content assessment.
finding.measure: Students’ qualitative perceptions of interdisciplinary learning (computer science + math)

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to assess specific tutoring behaviors in authentic tutoring dialogues at scale. The authors focus on two tutor moves linked to effective instruction: delivering process-focused praise and responding appropriately to student math errors. Their central question is whether LLMs can reliably detect when these situations occur in transcripts and whether they can judge the quality of the tutor’s response in a way that matches human raters.

The study analyzes 50 randomly selected audio transcripts from remote math tutoring sessions in which college-student tutors worked with middle school students. The transcripts came from real tutoring interactions delivered via video conferencing and then transcribed; the work uses lightly processed text only, without video, screenshots, or chat logs. The authors compare several models, including GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM, using prompt-engineering strategies such as few-shot prompting, rationale forcing, chain-of-thought, prompt chaining, and self-consistency.

Results show that the models were highly accurate at identifying tutor praise and student math errors, and they also aligned fairly well with human judgments when evaluating whether tutor responses were pedagogically appropriate. Performance was consistently above chance across models, with no single model clearly outperforming the others. The authors conclude that LLMs can provide a scalable and cost-effective method for assessing tutor moves in real-world educational dialogues, while also noting that more work is needed to handle missing multimodal context and improve speaker identification in transcripts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed feasibility/benchmarking study with clear methods, but it is not an RCT or impact evaluation of student learning. The evidence is primarily qualitative/technical performance testing of LLM classification on a small sample of transcripts.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper demonstrates useful but indirect impact: it improves the scalability of assessing tutoring interactions, not student achievement itself. Reported performance is strong, but there is no direct evidence of learning gains or measurable educational impact on students.

interventions.use_case: Feasibility study using GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM to assess tutor moves in real-life middle school mathematics tutoring transcripts, including praise quality and responses to student math errors.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that LLMs can scale assessment of tutoring dialogue with high accuracy, suggesting a practical efficiency gain for research and quality assurance. Across 50 transcript cases, models achieved 94-98% accuracy for detecting praise and 82-88% for detecting student math errors, with 83-89% accuracy for praise-quality evaluation and 73-77% for error-response evaluation; no model significantly outperformed the others.
finding.measure: Accuracy of LLM classification of tutor-move filter and evaluation prompts on transcript coding
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported as ranges in table (e.g., GPT-4 praise filter 94-100; error filter 74-94; praise eval 82-95; error eval 65-86)

paper_profiles.title: LLM-Driven Rubric-Based Assessment of Algebraic Competence in Multi-Stage Block Coding Tasks with Design and Field Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of assessing middle school students’ mathematical achievement in multi-step algebra tasks more holistically than answer-only scoring allows. The authors argue that in algebra, and especially in multi-stage problem solving, evaluation should capture not just correctness but also reasoning quality, procedural fluency, and attitudes toward using computational tools.

To address this, the study proposes an LLM-driven rubric-based assessment framework for online mathematics tasks that combine quadratic-equation reasoning with block coding. Domain experts designed a rubric with three main domains—Knowledge and Understanding, Procedural Skills, and Values and Attitudes—and mapped problem segments to rubric subcategories so that evidence could be accumulated across stages. The platform automatically graded objective responses, logged intermediate attempts, and used few-shot prompting with an LLM to judge open-ended explanations and synthesize rubric-aligned achievement levels.

The field evaluation involved 42 middle school students from two schools in South Korea during a guided classroom implementation. Students worked through a six-stage sequence centered on finding consecutive natural numbers via quadratic equations and block coding, with teachers introducing the platform and a teaching assistant providing technical support. The study also incorporated learner self-assessments and expert ratings to benchmark the system’s outputs. The results showed that the LLM-based rubric scores aligned strongly with expert judgments and that the framework could provide process-oriented feedback and scalable assessment for online mathematics education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a field study with descriptive and correlational validation analyses, not a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study. It provides useful empirical evidence on assessment validity and feasibility, but does not isolate causal effects on student achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear feasibility and strong agreement between LLM scoring and expert ratings, but it does not demonstrate measurable learning gains from the intervention. The observed correlations and group differences are meaningful for assessment practice, yet the educational impact on student outcomes remains indirect and modest.

interventions.use_case: LLM-driven rubric-based assessment and process-oriented feedback for middle school algebra tasks embedded in block coding, with rubric-aligned scoring of student work and iterative formative feedback on intermediate submissions

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to assess middle school students' algebraic competence in multi-stage quadratic equation tasks using block coding, but it did not test learning gains from the intervention. Instead, it reported students' achievement distributions on rubric-based scores (overall mean = 69.81, SD = 17.03; n=42) and showed differentiated rubric performance, with higher scores on conceptual and structured tasks and lower scores on computational/proactive-use rubrics.
finding.measure: Rubric-based academic achievement scores across five rubrics; overall performance score; rubric-wise scores on quadratic equation and block-coding tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that LLM-based rubric scoring closely matched expert judgments, indicating potential for reducing manual grading burden while maintaining validity. Agreement with experts was strong (r=0.79, ρ=0.76, both p<0.001), with modest error (MAE=12.4, RMSE=15.8) and only a small upward bias (M=5.1 points) across n=42 students.
finding.measure: Agreement between LLM-generated rubric scores and expert ratings; MAE, RMSE, Pearson/Spearman correlations, bias

finding.finding_summary: The framework explicitly evaluated process-oriented problem solving, explanation, and self-assessment/metacognitive reflection in addition to correctness. Students' self-check surveys and one-sentence reflections were incorporated as auxiliary evidence, and higher rubric performance was associated with successful completion of keystone block-coding tasks (e.g., Rubric 3: M=78.8 vs 52.5, t=4.28, p<0.001 for path-completed vs incomplete groups).
finding.measure: Self-check Likert survey, reflection item, and rubric scores for procedural reasoning/block coding

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of providing scalable, individualized grading and formative feedback for open-ended mathematics tasks, especially constructive geometry tasks that require multi-step reasoning and digital geometric construction. The authors argue that traditional answer-based grading is insufficient for capturing student reasoning in these settings and that teachers need support when students submit diverse, partially correct, or open-ended responses.

To address this, the paper presents a personalized auto-grading and feedback system built with large language models, including GPT-4, and deployed on the Algeomath online geometry platform. The system uses rule-based grading for closed-ended and geometry-construction items, and few-shot LLM prompting for open-ended explanations. It also generates attempt-aware feedback using teacher-authored exemplars, with different feedback styles across retries so that hints become progressively more explicit as attempts run out.

The system was piloted in four middle-school classes in South Korea with 79 students. The study evaluated grading agreement with teacher judgments, feedback quality rated by a mathematics education expert, and student response changes across attempts. Results showed strong agreement with teachers for rule-based items and substantial agreement for LLM-graded explanations, while feedback often helped students correct errors on later attempts. However, some feedback leaked answers, used imprecise terminology, or became too directive, and longer-term transfer effects were not clearly demonstrated.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site field study with 79 students and no randomized control group, so it provides direct empirical evidence but limited causal identification. The paper combines quantitative agreement/learning analyses with qualitative feedback evaluation, supporting a solid descriptive design rather than a high-credibility experimental one.
