paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The system shows modest, mixed instructional impact: 36.7% immediate correction after feedback and improved within-item performance, but no statistically significant transfer effects on later questions. The observed benefits are promising for a priority middle-school population, yet the absence of strong causal evidence and transfer limits the overall impact rating.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted auto-grading and personalized formative feedback for middle-school constructive geometry tasks on an online math platform
GPT-4-based generation of context-sensitive hints and explanatory feedback for student math responses across multiple attempts

finding.finding_summary: In a field study with 79 middle-school students across 18 geometry items, the system showed strong grading performance and some evidence of learning support, but academic gains were uneven. Post-feedback conversion from incorrect to correct occurred on 36.7% of 708 feedback-supported incorrect attempts, and learning curves rose from about 0.60 correct on attempt 1 to about 0.80 by attempt 4; however, longer-term transfer to later target questions was not statistically significant (all p > 0.05).
finding.measure: Item correctness across geometry tasks; post-feedback conversion rate; cumulative learning curves by attempt

finding.finding_summary: The system achieved perfect agreement (100%) with teacher judgments on the rule-based closed-ended and CGT items, and substantial agreement on open-ended explanations (overall agreement 0.866, Cohen's κ=0.737 across 878 explanatory responses). This indicates the LLM/rule hybrid can scale teacher-aligned grading and feedback in middle-school geometry with reduced human workload, though some items showed lower agreement (e.g., Q15 κ=0.434).
finding.measure: Agreement rate with teacher grading; Cohen’s κ for open-ended scoring; qualitative feedback rubric scores

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS’23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of large-language-model responses for middle-school math question answering, and how prompt design affects the trade-off between groundedness in source materials and human preference. The authors focus on conceptual math QA rather than procedural problem solving, motivated by the risk that unconstrained LLMs may hallucinate or give answers that are not aligned with a school’s curriculum.

The intervention is a RAG-based chatbot pipeline that retrieves relevant content from the OpenStax Prealgebra textbook and uses GPT-3.5-turbo to generate responses. The authors test three prompt-guidance conditions: no guidance, low guidance, and high guidance, plus an information-retrieval baseline. They evaluate the system on 51 real student questions from the Math Nation discussion board and collect human judgments from 9 educators and education-technology designers who rank response quality and judge groundedness. They also annotate retrieval relevance to understand when grounding improves.

The main findings are that retrieval-augmented responses are generally preferred over non-RAG responses, but only when the prompt is not overly constrained by the textbook. High-guidance responses are perceived as more grounded, but low-guidance responses are most preferred overall, suggesting a trade-off between strict textual grounding and conversational usefulness. The paper concludes that math QA systems should balance faithfulness to source materials with pedagogical usefulness, and it highlights the need for future work that connects response preference to actual student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear comparative human-evaluation design, but it is not an experiment on student learning outcomes. The evidence is qualitative/correlational with a very small evaluator sample (n=9) and no direct achievement measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest promise for improving the quality of middle-school math chatbot responses, but it does not demonstrate learning gains or behavior change. Impact on educational outcomes remains unclear because the study evaluates preferences and groundedness rather than student achievement.

interventions.use_case: Retrieval-augmented generation for middle-school math question answering in a chatbot tutor, using GPT-3.5 with prompt guidance to answer algebra and geometry questions grounded in an OpenStax prealgebra textbook.
The LLM/RAG system is developed in the context of an existing WhatsApp-based math tutor (Rori) that uses an ITS-style mastery-based tutoring approach and is being extended to support conceptual QA.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure student learning gains; instead, it evaluates middle-school math QA responses on human preference and groundedness. In a survey of 9 educators/designers rating responses to 51 student questions, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, suggesting improved response quality, but the paper reports no direct achievement outcome for students.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings of generated responses; groundedness judgments against textbook document
finding.study_size: n=9 annotators; 51 student queries; 153-? response judgments reported for groundedness analyses

finding.finding_summary: For the tutorial interaction itself, respondents preferred RAG-assisted answers that better balanced being helpful and grounded, indicating potentially better instructional communication. However, the paper explicitly treats this as a proxy for conversation quality and not as evidence of improved student learning, persistence, or metacognition.
finding.measure: Survey-based response preference and groundedness ratings

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting differentiated instruction in heterogeneous mathematics classrooms. The authors argue that existing AI personalization tools are often performance-focused, student-facing, and insufficiently attentive to motivational and pedagogical factors that teachers must manage when creating instructional materials for diverse learners.

To address this problem, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-centered, large language model-based multi-agent framework for generating individualized worksheets. FACET uses three specialized agents: learner agents that simulate student profiles, a teacher agent that creates didactically structured worksheets aligned with Bloom’s taxonomy, and an evaluator agent that provides quality feedback. The system is built to personalize tasks using both cognitive factors such as mathematical proficiency and motivational factors such as intrinsic motivation.

The framework is tested with authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education. Evaluation combines automated agent-based scoring across multiple worksheet iterations and exploratory feedback from five K-12 in-service teachers. The results suggest that the system produces stable, high-quality, and learner-aligned worksheets, with especially strong ratings for task suitability and clarity. Teacher feedback was broadly positive and emphasized the usefulness of adjustable difficulty, scaffolding, and motivational tailoring.

The authors conclude that multi-agent LLM architectures can feasibly support scalable teacher-facing personalization in mathematics education, but they also note that the current study is preliminary. They call for richer learner profiles, stronger curricular integration, and future in-classroom validation with real learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed feasibility and qualitative evaluation, not an experimental study of learning outcomes. It uses internal agent-based ratings and exploratory teacher feedback, so it provides some empirical evidence but with limited causal credibility and external validity.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect benefits, mainly on worksheet quality and perceived suitability rather than student achievement. Because there is no measured effect on learning gains and no effect size, the practical impact on K-12 outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: teacher-facing LLM-based multi-agent system that simulates learner profiles and generates personalized mathematics worksheets with scaffolding, hints, motivational comments, and didactical sequencing for grade 8 classrooms

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that FACET generated personalized grade 8 mathematics worksheets aligned to learner profiles, with high evaluator ratings for suitability and clarity. Across 10 internal evaluations per worksheet, suitability was very high (M=4.78, SD=0.06) and clarity was also high (M=4.76, SD=0.12) on a 1–6 inverted scale, suggesting the system can produce math tasks matched to cognitive level and motivation. However, this is a feasibility/quality study rather than a direct achievement test, so no learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Automated evaluator ratings and teacher ratings of worksheet quality/suitability for grade 8 mathematics tasks
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles x 10 internal evaluations; n=5 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The system explicitly models intrinsic motivation alongside mathematical proficiency, and teacher feedback indicated that motivational tailoring was valuable, especially for low-motivation learners. Teachers suggested that narrative framing and everyday-life relevance could further improve engagement, implying the generated worksheets already supported motivation to some extent. No direct student motivation outcome was experimentally measured; evidence is based on expert judgments of motivational fit.
finding.measure: Teacher expert ratings and qualitative think-aloud feedback on motivational suitability

finding.finding_summary: The framework is presented as a teacher-facing tool intended to reduce prompting overhead and support scalable differentiation, and teachers described it as useful for adjusting tasks without moving students to other topics. While the paper does not quantify workload reduction, the qualitative feedback indicates potential efficiency gains in preparing differentiated worksheets for heterogeneous classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback on usability and preparation burden reduction

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based lessons for training novice human tutors who teach middle school mathematics online. The focus is on lesson creation rather than student learning outcomes: the authors investigate how different levels of prompt decomposition affect the quality of generated lessons, and how LLM-generated lessons compare with human-crafted lessons.

The intervention/approach combines retrieval-augmented generation with GPT-4o. The authors used retrieved research articles on tutoring practices to prompt the model to generate structured lessons in English, each following a five-part format: title page, scenario 1, instruction, scenario 2, and conclusion. They tested one-, two-, three-, four-, and five-segment prompting strategies, where later segments were conditioned on earlier generated content.

The setting is online tutor professional development for novice tutors in middle school mathematics, with lesson quality evaluated by two experienced human coders and compared against lessons written by two human instructional designers. The paper finds that the three-segment strategy produced the best overall lesson ratings, outperforming single-step generation and slightly outperforming more highly decomposed approaches. Human reviewers saw clear benefits in time savings, diverse scenario generation, and generally appropriate content, but also noted weaknesses such as generic feedback, unclear writing in some sections, and unreliable references. The authors conclude that LLMs can support lesson drafting in a human-AI workflow, but human review remains necessary for quality, clarity, and citation accuracy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical qualitative/benchmarking study of generated lesson quality, but it does not test learning outcomes and relies on human ratings and expert reflections rather than a controlled causal design. The evidence is informative for content generation quality, but it meets only limited credibility criteria for efficacy claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear promise for reducing authoring time and improving scalable lesson production, but it does not demonstrate measurable effects on student learning. Reported impacts are practical and workflow-oriented rather than direct educational gains.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4o with retrieval-augmented generation and prompt decomposition to automatically generate interactive, scenario-based tutor training lessons for novice tutors teaching middle school mathematics online

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that LLM-generated lessons substantially reduced lesson-drafting burden, especially for scenario sections and multiple-choice question creation. Two human lesson designers judged the system as time-saving and useful for creating reusable lesson drafts; however, no quantitative productivity effect size was reported (n=2 evaluators).
finding.measure: Human designer questionnaire / qualitative review of authoring workload and time-saving potential

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that hybrid human-AI workflows could help scale tutor-training content production, potentially expanding access to lesson development for middle school math tutoring programs. This is based on qualitative judgments from two designers and human ratings of generated lessons; no learner outcome data or institutional effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Expert judgments about scalability, reusability, and collaboration potential

paper_profiles.title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can accurately interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work. The authors frame the problem as a practical educational challenge: teachers spend substantial time grading handwritten work, but that work contains valuable evidence of student thinking that is difficult to assess at scale. The study asks whether MLLMs can separate visual recognition from mathematical grading, and whether they can handle both routine arithmetic and more complex mathematical illustrations.

The paper reports two experiments. Experiment A uses 288 scanned handwritten responses from Ghanaian middle school students solving arithmetic, fractions, percentages, and basic algebra problems with objective answers. Four MLLMs (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4.1) were prompted to extract student answers and judge correctness. Experiment B uses 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations from the DrawEDU dataset, involving number lines, geometry, coordinate planes, and other visual representations. In this second experiment, models were tested first on images alone and then with human-written descriptions of the images to isolate visual interpretation from grading ability.

Results show that MLLMs can perform very well on routine handwritten arithmetic, with Gemini 2.5 Pro reaching 95% grading accuracy and near-human agreement. However, performance drops substantially on mathematical illustrations, and even with human descriptions supplied, model agreement only rises to moderate levels around kappa 0.47, similar to initial human inter-rater agreement but still below what would be needed for autonomous deployment. The authors conclude that current MLLMs are promising for routine arithmetic grading but remain limited for richer pedagogical interpretation of student mathematical thinking, especially where tacit educator knowledge and contextual judgment are required.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmarking study with two small evaluation datasets and clear quantitative methods, but it is not an RCT or causal intervention study. It primarily measures model performance on task benchmarks rather than student learning outcomes or classroom implementation effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance is strong for routine arithmetic grading (95% accuracy, LWK = 0.90), suggesting meaningful potential impact on assessment efficiency. However, the practical impact is constrained by poor performance on complex illustrations and the lack of evidence on real-world deployment or student learning gains.

interventions.use_case: evaluating multimodal LLMs for automated grading and interpretation of handwritten middle-school mathematics work, including arithmetic worksheets and student-drawn mathematical illustrations

finding.finding_summary: On routine handwritten arithmetic with objective answers, the best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) reached near-human grading performance: 95% accuracy and linear weighted kappa (LWK) = 0.90 on n=288 middle-school responses. On harder mathematical illustrations, performance dropped substantially: direct image-only grading reached only 61-64% accuracy with kappa as low as 0.15-0.38 on n=150, improving to 72-75% accuracy and kappa 0.43-0.47 when provided human descriptions, still below deployment-ready levels.
finding.measure: Accuracy, F1, precision/recall, linear weighted kappa on handwritten arithmetic grading and mathematical illustration judgment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues these models could reduce teacher workload by automating routine grading of handwritten arithmetic, where Gemini 2.5 Pro achieved 95% accuracy and LWK = 0.90 on n=288 responses. For more ambiguous illustrations, however, the models were not accurate enough for autonomous use, suggesting only limited efficiency gains via human-in-the-loop screening and pre-sorting rather than full automation.
finding.measure: Grading accuracy and agreement as a proxy for feasibility of automating assessment workflows

paper_profiles.title: Improving Multimodal LLM’s Ability in Geometry Problem Solving, Reasoning, and Multistep Scoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving multimodal large language models (LVLMs) on geometry problem solving, especially for secondary-school mathematics. The authors argue that existing geometry datasets are too small, too narrow, and often limited to multiple-choice or objective items, which makes them insufficient for evaluating and training models on numerical-answer and theorem-based geometry reasoning.

To address this gap, the paper introduces GPSM4K, a multimodal geometry dataset built from grades 7-12 mathematics textbooks and Indian board exam materials. The dataset includes image-question-answer pairs, augmented questions, and step-by-step solutions generated and reconstructed with Gemini Pro Vision and Gemini Pro. The work also explores related methods such as image captioning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to support inference in LVLMs, and evaluates several models including LLaVA, G-LLaVA, Gemini Pro, and GPT-4 on geometry tasks.

The paper reports that finetuning on GPSM4K improves model performance compared with finetuning on prior datasets such as PGPS9K and GeoQA++. It also finds that higher-quality captions and multimodal RAG can further improve results. The authors conclude that dataset design, caption quality, and retrieval support matter for geometry reasoning, while also noting that theorem-based reasoning remains a challenge and that the dataset is still relatively small.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference-style empirical benchmark paper with clear experimental procedures and comparative evaluations, but it is not a randomized study of learners and does not directly evaluate educational outcomes in classrooms. The evidence is therefore useful but primarily correlational/benchmark-based rather than high-credibility causal evidence for instruction.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows moderate gains in model accuracy for geometry problem solving, but the effects are on AI system performance rather than student learning, and no classroom or learner impact is measured. The practical educational impact is therefore indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: Multimodal large language models (e.g., LLaVA, G-LLaVA, Gemini Pro, GPT-4) are evaluated on geometry problem solving, reasoning, caption-assisted inference, and retrieval-augmented generation for textbook-style grade 7-12 math problems.

LLM-assisted final-answer checking and step-by-step chain-of-thought scoring, using Gemini Pro to compare predicted versus ground-truth solutions and label intermediate reasoning steps as correct/incorrect.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved geometry problem-solving performance after finetuning and multimodal augmentation, with accuracy on the GPSM4K test set rising from 7.33%-8.66% for LLaVA 1.6 models trained on PGPS9K to 22.66%-24.66% when trained on GPSM4K. In zero-shot inference, stronger proprietary models also performed better (Gemini Pro 44% on GPSM4K; GPT-4 60%), and 1-shot multimodal RAG further improved Gemini from 35.33% to 38% and LLaMa 3 8B from 22.6% to 26%.
finding.measure: Top-1 accuracy on geometry problem-solving test sets (GPSM4K, PGPS9K, Geometry3K)
finding.study_size: n=150 test problems for main evaluation; GPSM4K test set also described as 200 inference samples in dataset statistics

finding.finding_summary: Adding image captions to geometry prompts improved performance for finetuned GLLaVA models. With Gemini-generated captions, GLLaVA 7B reached 21.33% accuracy and GLLaVA 13B reached 22.66%, while human captions improved them further to 24.66% and 26.66%, respectively, on the GPSM4K test set. The authors also report that a text-only LLaMa3 8B setup achieved 28.66% in their caption-based comparison discussion, suggesting captions can materially support geometry reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GPSM4K test set after adding image captions to inference prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM-based automation for geometry dataset construction and evaluation, including Gemini Vision Pro for diagram caption generation, Gemini Pro for question/solution regeneration, and Gemini Pro for answer extraction and step-by-step scoring. These methods are presented as reducing manual effort in building multimodal geometry resources and in grading model outputs, but no formal time-savings or workload effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Automation of caption generation, question regeneration, final-answer extraction, and chain-of-thought evaluation workflows

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight: A Multi-Agent Adversarial Framework for Reliable AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
The paper addresses a reliability problem in AI tutoring systems built on large language models: these systems can validate incorrect student reasoning, give overly direct answers, or otherwise fail to provide pedagogically appropriate guidance. The authors frame this as a need for more reliable automated pedagogical oversight, especially for middle-school mathematics dialogues where student misconceptions must be detected and classified accurately.

To address this, the paper proposes Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight (HPO), a multi-agent adversarial framework that separates context distillation, structured debate, and final synthesis. The system uses specialist agents to summarize the dialogue, then pits permissive and strict pedagogical critics against each other in a five-act adversarial debate moderated by a Devil’s Advocate, and finally uses a judge/stress-analyst/lead-evaluator pipeline to produce labels for mistake identification and guidance quality. The implementation uses AutoGen with a Llama-3-8B-Instruct backbone and QLoRA fine-tuning of the final evaluator.

The evaluation is conducted on MRBench, a dataset of 1,214 middle-school mathematics dialogues, with GPT-4o and several agentic baselines as comparators. The reported results show that the full HPO system achieves higher Macro F1 than GPT-4o while using far fewer parameters, and ablations suggest that the adversarial structure—especially the Devil’s Advocate and the contextual distillation phase—drives much of the gain. The authors conclude that structured adversarial interaction can be more important than raw model scale for reliable AI tutoring, though they note that cross-domain validation and deployment studies are still needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed/accepted conference-style paper with a clear experimental benchmark and ablation study, but it is not a randomized educational trial and evaluates model classification performance rather than direct student learning. The evidence is therefore methodologically informative but limited for causal claims about educational outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance gain on MRBench is modest but meaningful for the benchmark task (Macro F1 +0.033 vs GPT-4o), yet it concerns automated evaluation reliability rather than direct student achievement. Impact on real K-12 learning is therefore indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: A multi-agent LLM tutoring/oversight framework for evaluating middle-school mathematics tutor responses, including mistake identification and guidance-quality classification using debate, synthesis, and fine-tuning.

finding.finding_summary: On the MRBench middle-school mathematics dialogue benchmark (n=1,214), the proposed HPO-FT system achieved Macro F1=0.845, outperforming GPT-4o at 0.812 by 0.033. The paper reports statistically significant gains for the guidance-quality task and overall benchmark performance, indicating better detection/classification of math tutoring errors and scaffolding quality.
finding.measure: MRBench classification performance on mistake identification and guidance quality; Macro F1, accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The framework is positioned as a lower-compute alternative to larger models: an 8B-parameter system outperformed GPT-4o by 3.3% Macro F1 while using 20× fewer parameters. However, inference latency was 4.2s versus 0.4s for a single Llama-3-8B call, so the operational benefit is mainly in compute/parameter efficiency rather than raw speed.
finding.measure: Parameter count, inference latency, and benchmark performance

paper_profiles.title: Can MLLMs Read Students’ Minds? Unpacking Multimodal Error Analysis in Handwritten Math
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can diagnose the causes of students’ mistakes from handwritten mathematics scratchwork, rather than simply produce correct answers. The authors argue that existing educational NLP and MLLM benchmarks focus too much on textual responses, structured inputs, or answer generation, and do not adequately capture the visual and reasoning complexity of authentic handwritten work.

To study this, they introduce ScratchMath, a benchmark for two tasks: Error Cause Explanation (ECE), where a model explains why a student made a mistake, and Error Cause Classification (ECC), where it assigns the error to one of seven categories. The dataset contains 1,720 Chinese math samples from primary and middle school students, collected from an online K-12 education platform and annotated through a human-machine workflow with five professional teachers. The benchmark covers five math topic areas and includes handwritten scratchwork images, reference answers, student answers, and expert-labeled error causes.

The paper evaluates 16 MLLMs on the benchmark and finds large gaps between current models and human experts. Proprietary and larger reasoning-oriented models perform best, especially on the explanation task, but all models struggle with visual recognition, logical inference, and precise error classification. The authors conclude that diagnosing student reasoning from handwritten work remains a difficult problem for current MLLMs and that more robust visual understanding, better reasoning alignment, and educationally grounded evaluation are needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical benchmark study with a clearly described dataset construction and evaluation protocol, but it is not an intervention study and does not estimate causal effects on learners. Its evidence is primarily observational/benchmarking rather than experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear potential relevance for educational AI tools that diagnose math errors, but it reports no student outcome gains and no effect sizes on achievement or efficiency. Its impact is therefore indirect and currently unclear for K-12 practice.

interventions.use_case: benchmarking multimodal large language models for error diagnosis in authentic handwritten middle and primary school mathematics scratchwork

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test a student-facing intervention on math achievement; it benchmarks 16 MLLMs on error cause explanation (ECE) and error cause classification (ECC) for handwritten math scratchwork. The reported results are model-performance scores on diagnostic tasks, not changes in student math learning or achievement (n=1,720 samples).
finding.measure: ECE judge score / semantic alignment for error explanations; ECC classification accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is intended to support automated diagnosis and personalized feedback by identifying student error causes from handwritten work, which could reduce teacher workload in reviewing scratchwork. However, the paper does not directly measure workload reduction; it only evaluates model performance on error diagnosis tasks over n=1,720 samples.
finding.measure: Model performance on error diagnosis tasks as a proxy for automated grading/feedback utility

paper_profiles.title: LEGO-PROVER: NEURAL THEOREM PROVING WITH GROWING LIBRARIES
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of neural theorem proving, specifically the difficulty large language models (LLMs) face when trying to prove formal mathematical theorems, including some at the middle-school level. The authors argue that existing approaches are limited by using a fixed theorem library during proving, which prevents reuse of useful lemmas across problems and makes long-chain proofs especially difficult.

To address this, they introduce LEGO-Prover, a system that uses ChatGPT as the LLM and combines a prover with an evolver around a growing skill library. The prover decomposes a theorem into subgoals, retrieves relevant verified lemmas from the library, and constructs proofs in a modular block-by-block fashion. The evolver then generalizes or solves newly proposed requests to create additional reusable skills, which are verified in Isabelle and added back to the library. The evaluation is conducted on the miniF2F benchmark, which consists of high-school mathematics competition problems formalized in Isabelle; the system is not an educational intervention with human learners.

The paper reports that LEGO-Prover improves pass rates on miniF2F compared with prior methods, reaching 57.0% on validation and 50.0% on test. The authors conclude that a growing library of verified lemmas can substantially improve theorem-proving performance and help bridge the gap between informal and formal mathematical reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is about neural theorem proving for formal mathematics, not an educational intervention study. It reports benchmark performance on miniF2F and ablations of an AI proof system, but there is no K-12 or student learning evaluation and no study design relevant to education evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational impact on learners or schools. The reported gains are on theorem-proving pass rates in a formal mathematics benchmark (e.g., 57.0% vs 48.0%), which does not map to middle school mathematics achievement or classroom outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence is reshaping education and argues that effective use of AI in academic work and classrooms depends on three core capabilities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than testing an intervention with measured outcomes, the article makes a conceptual and practice-oriented argument about how institutions should respond to tools such as ChatGPT and related large language models.

The paper combines a case study from Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, with a narrative literature review. The case study describes how the institution developed internal AI guidelines for students, including transparency requirements for documenting which AI tools were used, why they were used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. It also discusses practical classroom uses such as AI experiments, AI-generated case studies, curriculum support, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The paper’s main conclusion is that banning AI outright or allowing it without restrictions are both inadequate. Instead, universities should foster a broader “culture of AI” through workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, written guidance, and staff roles focused on AI. The author argues that AI literacy courses and prompt-engineering instruction can help students and educators use AI responsibly, while critical thinking remains essential to avoid overreliance, hallucinations, and ethical misuse.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual discussion with a case study and narrative literature review, not an empirical evaluation with a rigorous comparison design. It does not report primary quantitative outcomes or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear practical relevance for AI governance and classroom practice, but it provides no measured effect sizes or demonstrated student outcome gains. Its influence is therefore best characterized as conceptually useful but empirically unverified.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT and related large language models as classroom supports, including using them as an 'informed conversational partner' or sparring partner for brainstorming, case-study generation, and guided student use with transparency requirements.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that responsible AI use may strengthen critical thinking and metacognition if students critically evaluate outputs rather than copy them, but it may also weaken independent cognitive work if students over-rely on the model. No quantitative effect size is reported because this is a conceptual and narrative review paper, not an outcomes study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflective evaluation of AI outputs, and student self-reported/observed responsible use

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI tools can improve efficiency in tasks such as creating curricula, generating case studies, and supporting academic writing workflows, while noting that prompt quality can be time-consuming and sometimes offset gains. No quantitative effect size is reported; the evidence is anecdotal and practice-oriented.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, curriculum design efficiency, and writing support productivity

finding.finding_summary: The article proposes institutional AI guidelines, transparency requirements, workshops, budgets, and dedicated staffing as mechanisms to improve responsible AI adoption across the university. These are presented as recommendations rather than measured effects, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy, governance, and implementation practices

paper_profiles.title: LLM-based collaborative programming: impact on students’ computational thinking and self-efﬁcacy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs), including GPT-4, can improve middle school students’ outcomes in collaborative programming compared with conventional collaborative programming without AI support. The main questions are whether LLM-supported collaboration improves computational thinking, self-efficacy, and cognitive load.

The intervention was an LLM-based collaborative programming framework that embedded GPT-4 as a scaffold during problem analysis, code development, debugging, and monitoring/evaluation. Students could interact with an adapted SpeechGPT platform and an online code assessment platform, while the teacher also provided instruction on using LLMs responsibly for programming support. The control group received standard collaborative programming instruction. The study used a randomized controlled trial with 82 sixth- and seventh-grade students in China over five weeks, with 12 programming sessions in C++.

Results showed that the LLM-supported group performed significantly better on computational thinking than the control group and reported lower cognitive load. Self-efficacy did not differ significantly between groups, although both groups declined from pretest to posttest, with a smaller decline in the LLM group. Interview data suggested that students found LLM support helpful for interest, ease of learning, and problem solving, but also noted drawbacks such as misunderstanding prompts and network issues. Overall, the study concludes that LLMs can be effective scaffolds in middle school programming education, especially for reducing cognitive load and supporting computational thinking.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with random assignment to conditions, pre/post measures, and inferential analyses, but it is not a full RCT and relies on a single short intervention in one school context. Some methodological concerns remain, including limited duration, small sample size, and incomplete reporting of some statistics.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a modest-to-medium impact on a priority population (middle school students), with a small effect on computational thinking (η2=0.04) and medium effects on cognitive load (d around 0.52-0.59). However, the lack of a self-efficacy improvement and the short intervention period keep the overall impact modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-0314 used as a learning partner/scaffold in middle school collaborative programming, providing hints, code debugging support, problem analysis prompts, and feedback without giving full solutions.

finding.finding_summary: LLM-supported collaborative programming significantly improved students' computational thinking compared with conventional collaborative programming in a quasi-experiment with n=82 sixth- and seventh-grade students. The adjusted post-test means were 81.35 vs 73.08, with ANCOVA showing F=4.39, p<0.05 and a small effect size η2=0.04; interviews also suggested better problem-solving and collaboration.
finding.measure: Computational thinking post-test (Bebras-based items) with ANCOVA-adjusted comparison

finding.finding_summary: Self-efficacy did not differ significantly between groups after the intervention. In the post-test, the experimental group mean was 3.41 (SD=0.83) and the control group mean was 3.26 (SD=0.92), with Mann–Whitney U=756, p=0.43; both groups showed some decline from pre-test levels.
finding.measure: Programming self-efficacy post-test questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: LLM-supported collaborative programming reduced students' cognitive load relative to conventional collaborative programming. Total cognitive load was lower in the experimental group (M=3.96, SD=0.765) than the control group (M=4.39, SD=0.887), t=-2.20, p<0.05, d=-0.518; mental load was also lower (M=3.91 vs 4.38), t=-2.51, p<0.05, d=-0.592, while mental effort was not significantly different.
finding.measure: Cognitive load questionnaire; subscales mental load and mental effort
finding.std_deviation: Total load SDs: 0.765 vs 0.887; Mental load SDs: 0.713 vs 0.844; Mental effort SDs: 0.927 vs 1.037

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT for medical education: the technical perspective
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a ChatGPT-based chatbot can improve bedside history-taking education and facilitate international collaboration in medical training. The authors build on an earlier Dialogflow-based chatbot, Bennie and the Chats, which had limited flexibility, weak handling of unexpected questions, and high maintenance requirements. They ask whether a generative AI chatbot can provide a more natural, scalable, and adaptable simulated patient interaction for students.

The intervention is an improved version of the chatbot implemented with ChatGPT-3.5 Turbo through Azure OpenAI. Students act as physicians and converse with virtual patients whose cases are stored as de-identified JSON records and converted into prompts. The system also includes configurable patient personalities, multilingual interaction, profanity filtering, and an administrator interface for adding, editing, and deleting cases. The study was conducted as a cross-territory virtual bedside teaching activity co-hosted by the University of Hong Kong and the National University of Singapore.

A total of 70 undergraduate medical students and 13 patients participated, and 45 students completed an 11-point Likert questionnaire. Quantitative findings showed generally positive ratings for learning efficacy, learning experience, and the value of cross-university exposure, with strong positive correlations between usability-related ratings and overall learning outcomes. The qualitative comparison found that the ChatGPT version was simpler to maintain, better at handling irrelevant or multi-intent questions, and able to support multilingual, personality-based, and education-level variation. The paper concludes that ChatGPT-enabled virtual bedside teaching is a feasible supplementary tool for clinical history-taking education and could support broader international case sharing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-method study using survey data and qualitative comparison, but it is not an RCT and lacks an objective achievement outcome or controlled causal design. The main evidence is self-reported perception and descriptive statistics, so only correlational/qualitative credibility is present.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceptions and feasibility for a medical education chatbot, but it does not provide a measured learning gain effect size or strong causal evidence. Impact appears promising yet modest/unclear in terms of demonstrated educational achievement.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-powered virtual patient chatbot for bedside history-taking practice in medical education, using role-play prompts, patient personas, and multilingual conversation support.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports generally positive learning outcomes from a ChatGPT-based virtual bedside teaching system. Among 45 student survey respondents, the median rating for learning efficacy was 7/10 and 75.6% rated efficacy at 7 or above; the median for learning experience was 8/10 and 73.3% rated experience at 7 or above. This is a self-reported perception measure rather than an objective achievement test, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student Likert ratings of learning efficacy and overall learning experience in virtual bedside/history-taking teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the chatbot supports clinical reasoning, communication, and history-taking practice through realistic patient dialogue, handling irrelevant and complex questions, and role-play with different personalities. Students rated interaction-related aspects positively (median 7/10; mean 6.64/10), but the evidence is based on perceptions and correlations rather than direct skill tests.
finding.measure: Student ratings of user-friendliness, keyword/input identification, interaction, and perceived learning effectiveness/experience

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable learning experience and engagement with the chatbot, and 73.3% rated the overall experience at 7 or above. The system design features such as different patient personalities and flexible multilingual interaction are presented as enhancing engagement, though the study does not directly measure motivation or persistence with validated instruments.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction/experience ratings and feedback on chatbot interaction

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that cross-territory virtual bedside teaching between HKU and NUS was feasible and perceived positively for international teaching collaboration. Among respondents, 82.2% agreed that exchanging patient cases helped them gain experience with diseases less prevalent in their own locality, suggesting institutional value for broader case sharing and collaboration.
finding.measure: Student agreement that international peer collaboration and case exchange improved learning outcomes/insights

finding.finding_summary: The technical comparison with the prior Dialogflow-based version indicates the ChatGPT system is simpler to develop and maintain, with lower maintenance cost and easier data updates by non-technical administrators. This is a qualitative assessment rather than a productivity experiment, so no numerical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of system design complexity, maintenance burden, and administrator usability

paper_profiles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly growing but still fragmented literature on generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in K-12 education. The author’s aim is to map how AI and GAI—especially ChatGPT and related tools—have been used in teaching and learning, what opportunities and challenges they present, what teachers need in order to integrate them effectively, and where the main gaps remain in the literature.

The study is a systematic review conducted using PRISMA. It searched multiple databases and journals for work published between 2016 and 2024, ultimately identifying 197 relevant studies, with additional papers gathered through backward snowballing. The review includes research on GAI-supported teaching, AI literacy, teacher professional development, adaptive learning, assessment, and broader AI-in-education frameworks. The population of interest is K-12 students and the educators who teach them, with the context explicitly limited to primary and secondary school settings, including classroom, hybrid, and distance learning possibilities.

The review concludes that AI and GAI can support personalized learning, feedback, assessment, engagement, and teacher workload reduction, but that effective use depends heavily on teacher training, pedagogical framing, and clear guidelines. It also identifies major gaps: a shortage of concrete experiments in K-12 settings, limited evidence outside STEM, and insufficient practical models for everyday classroom use. The paper emphasizes that future research should focus on age-appropriate design, ethical and privacy issues, and teacher preparation for responsible integration of GAI in schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review with a stated PRISMA method and transparent search/exclusion process, but it is still a qualitative evidence synthesis rather than a meta-analysis or causal study. The paper aggregates heterogeneous studies and does not provide pooled effect estimates for achievement outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad positive potential for K-12 uses of GAI, but the paper itself reports no direct quantitative impact on student achievement or other outcomes. Because findings are narrative and not effect-size-based, the overall demonstrated impact remains modest and unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT and closely related generative AI tools used in K-12 teaching and learning, including conversational support for personalized learning, adaptive materials, and teacher assistance.
Review includes GAI-enabled adaptive learning use cases where systems tailor content, pacing, or feedback to students' needs in K-12 settings.
Review covers GAI-supported assessment and automated feedback applications for student work and learning tasks in K-12 education.
Review includes broader AI/GAI-supported instructional software and digitally mediated teaching workflows used to enhance classroom instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic review of 197 K-12 studies on generative AI and related AI tools, and it reports that the literature broadly supports improved teaching and learning processes rather than a single quantified achievement effect. Across the reviewed studies, GAI was repeatedly linked to personalized learning, improved assessment, and more innovative instructional practices, but the review does not report a pooled effect size or a single achievement metric.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported educational uses and outcomes across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that GAI can increase motivation, engagement, and interest in learning, especially through more interactive and personalized experiences. However, these conclusions are qualitative and drawn from heterogeneous studies; no pooled effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of engagement/motivation findings in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly identifies benefits for collaboration, creativity, critical reflection, and inclusive learning, framing these as major opportunities of GAI in K-12. These claims are based on a descriptive synthesis of the literature rather than direct experimental estimates, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, and inclusion outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A major theme in the review is that GAI can improve teacher productivity through support for assessment, lesson adaptation, and the automation of repetitive tasks. The paper emphasizes reduced workload and more efficient educational processes, but it does not provide quantitative estimates such as d or g.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of teacher workload, assessment efficiency, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The review finds strong potential for GAI to transform K-12 systems, but it also stresses major implementation barriers including ethics, privacy, teacher training, and lack of policy guidance. The overall pattern is mixed: promising institutional benefits alongside significant governance and readiness concerns, with no quantitative effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of policy, ethics, teacher training, and institutional implementation themes

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The authors ask how teachers prompt ChatGPT, how much time and effort is required, and how students respond to the resulting personalized problems. The study is framed around issues of depth, grain size, and ownership in personalization, with a particular focus on context personalization using students’ popular culture interests.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to adapt 143 Illustrative Mathematics problems across two units: proportional relationships/percentages and expressions/equations/inequalities. Teachers received a 2-hour training session, then participated in recorded Zoom sessions where they iteratively prompted ChatGPT to generate personalized versions of problems. The personalized assignments were delivered through ASSISTments to 521 students, who provided closed-ended ratings and some open-ended feedback about interestingness, closeness to their interests, and realism.

The study found that teachers commonly used prompts to add specific or broad popular-culture references, but they also spent substantial effort correcting realism, numerical plausibility, readability, and age appropriateness. Students generally preferred more fine-grained, specific references, but often cared less about deeper realism unless something was obviously wrong. Teachers needed about 4 minutes per problem on average, and efficiency did not clearly improve over time; in fact, the second round of personalization took more prompts and more time, though student ratings were higher in Unit 6. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and quality control, but it is not especially time efficient and may not match students’ desire for finer-grained personalization.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/observational classroom study with mixed-effects analyses, not a randomized trial. It provides useful process evidence about prompting, student reactions, and teacher time, but lacks a control group and causal identification.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest improvements in student interest/closeness ratings, but these are subjective engagement outcomes rather than achievement gains. Teacher workload was substantial, and the paper reports no direct learning or test-score impact, so overall impact on achievement is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize middle school mathematics word problems from Illustrative Mathematics to students' interests, including iterative prompting to adjust context, realism, readability, and numerical plausibility.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers took an average of 246 seconds per personalized problem (SD=165.7; 143 problems total), which suggests substantial time cost for creating GenAI-personalized math tasks. Efficiency did not improve over time; teachers spent significantly more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (286 vs. 204 seconds per problem; B=70.4, SE=29.6, p=0.0189) and used more prompts (4.6 vs. 3.2; B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025).
finding.measure: Teacher time per problem; number of prompts per problem; regression comparison of Unit 4 vs Unit 6
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds (time increase Unit 6 vs Unit 4); B=1.26 prompts (prompt increase Unit 6 vs Unit 4)
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds per problem; SD=2.6 prompts per problem

finding.finding_summary: Student reactions to the personalized problems were generally favorable when the context aligned with their interests, especially for more specific popular-culture references. Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests improved from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (interestingness: 2.27 to 2.56; closeness: 2.28 to 2.66), with a significant combined increase of about 0.33 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student 1-5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback
finding.effect_size: B=0.33 points on 5-point scale; also B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts
finding.std_deviation: Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German, middle school–level subject knowledge. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice based, and not sufficiently reflective of real-world reasoning needs. To address this, they construct a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, including mathematics, history, biology, physics, arts, music, religion, geography, and sports.

The benchmark is built from German school textbooks for grades 8–10 and supplemented with some non-school educational material and internet images. Questions are designed to require both visual understanding and subject-specific background knowledge, and some items are adversarial, meaning they cannot be answered from the image and are intended to test whether models can correctly abstain. The paper evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs using LLM-as-a-judge with a panel of models for scoring.

Results show that the benchmark is difficult: the best model achieves under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in music and mathematics and very low accuracy on adversarial questions. The authors conclude that middle school tasks are a useful stress test for VLMs, particularly in German, and that current models often fail when they must integrate visual interpretation with domain knowledge or recognize unanswerable questions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear dataset and systematic model comparison, but it is not a causal or experimental K-12 learning intervention study. It provides useful empirical evidence about model capability, yet the educational relevance is indirect and there is no human learner outcome or controlled instructional design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test an intervention on students, so there is no direct educational effect size to attribute to learning impact. Its contribution is primarily diagnostic for AI capability and benchmark design, with only indirect implications for classroom use and therefore unclear learner impact.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that math performance was the weakest among the benchmarked school subjects, with the best model reaching only about 34.09% accuracy on math questions and some models much lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors note that models struggled especially with counting, geometric reasoning, identifying formulas from diagrams, and reading coordinate values, indicating substantial limitations in multimodal math understanding rather than simple calculation alone.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on middle school math questions drawn from textbook images
finding.study_size: n=308 questions (math subset of 486 images total)

finding.finding_summary: This benchmark study evaluates multimodal understanding across multiple middle-school subjects and reports overall accuracies below 45% for all tested models, with subject-specific weaknesses in history, arts, music, religion, biology, geography, and sports. For example, the strongest model reached 54.36% in history and 52.92% in religion, but many domains remained substantially below ceiling, showing that current open-weight VLMs do not reliably handle curriculum-grounded school tasks in German.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy across 9 curriculum domains; domain-level accuracies and adversarial-question accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s adversarial question design directly probes whether models can reject misleading prompts and say they do not know when the answer is not in the image. Performance was very low overall: the best models reached only about 31.32% and 32.83% on adversarial questions, while many models were below 15%, suggesting poor reliability for contextual reasoning and resistance to hallucination.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring refusal/non-answer recognition

finding.finding_summary: Physics and biology items required diagram interpretation plus domain knowledge, and the models often failed on explanatory reasoning even when they could identify the diagram type. The best physics scores were around 47.65% and the paper notes failures on cause-effect explanations such as why stars become red giants or why adding a resistor changes bulb brightness, indicating weak scientific reasoning from multimodal input.
finding.measure: Open-ended accuracy on physics and biology reasoning questions involving diagrams and explanations
finding.study_size: n=234 physics questions; n=169 biology questions

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT in the AIGC era, aiming to synthesize the model’s underlying technology, capabilities, applications, challenges, and future directions toward AGI. Rather than testing a specific educational intervention, it reviews prior work on ChatGPT and related large language models, including their architecture, training methods, and the transition from GPT-1 through GPT-4.

The paper discusses applications across several domains, with a substantial section on education. In education, it summarizes reported uses of ChatGPT for teaching and learning support, assessment, language translation, concept explanation, and subject-specific tasks, including mathematics, physics, engineering, economics, and law. The paper cites studies showing that ChatGPT can perform at or above average on some academic tasks and standardized exams, while also noting important weaknesses such as inaccuracies, logical inconsistency, and sensitivity to prompts.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT is a powerful and versatile generative AI tool with promising educational applications, but it should be used as an assistant rather than a replacement for human judgment or learning. It emphasizes technical, ethical, and misuse-related challenges, especially hallucinations, plagiarism, overreliance, and misinformation, and argues that further development and careful governance are needed before such systems can reliably support broader educational and societal use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey/review paper, not an empirical study with a clear experimental or quasi-experimental design. It does not provide original participant-level data or causal identification of achievement impacts.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to ChatGPT in education, but it reports no direct intervention impact on middle school mathematics achievement. Its influence is therefore conceptual and indirect rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.

interventions.use_case: Broad survey of ChatGPT as a generative AI chatbot for education, including personalized tutoring, interactive dialogue, assessment support, and student assistance across subjects.

finding.finding_summary: This is a broad survey paper, not an empirical study, so it does not report a new causal effect on achievement outcomes. It synthesizes prior reports that ChatGPT can perform at around average-to-above-average levels on some educational tasks (e.g., physics essays scored 71±2% vs module average 71±5%, economics questions correct on 63.3% of microeconomics and 86.7% of macroeconomics items), while also noting weaknesses in advanced mathematics and other tasks.
finding.measure: Reported performance on educational tasks and exams summarized from prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The survey summarizes prior work indicating that ChatGPT can assist with some mathematical retrieval/search tasks, but also explicitly states that it performs poorly in advanced mathematics and arithmetic. No original middle-school math achievement study is reported, and no effect sizes are provided.
finding.measure: Mathematical task performance in cited studies

finding.finding_summary: Across education examples, the paper reports that ChatGPT can support course material generation, tutoring, and some subject-specific exam performance, including passing or near-passing levels on certain non-math assessments. However, these are literature summaries rather than direct evaluations in this paper, and the evidence is uneven across domains.
finding.measure: Summarized performance on subject exams and educational tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that ChatGPT may aid brainstorming, explanation, and problem-solving, but it also warns that overreliance could weaken independent and critical thinking. No quantitative causal evidence is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Summarized claims about brainstorming, problem-solving, and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior reports that ChatGPT can reduce time and labor in writing, literature review, data analysis, proofreading, and course material preparation. These are qualitative efficiency claims rather than a single measured intervention effect, and no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Task efficiency / productivity in writing, review, analysis, and grading support

finding.finding_summary: The survey highlights institutional benefits such as automated assessment support and course design, but also major concerns including plagiarism, misuse, misinformation, and policy/regulatory challenges. Because it is a narrative review, it provides no direct outcome estimate or effect size.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, and institutional concerns around educational use of ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive and want AI to function as a peer collaborator in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS), rather than as a tutor or teacher-like assistant. The authors argue that while generative AI has been explored heavily for one-on-one tutoring, much less is known about how AI should behave inside small-group mathematics work where students are expected to co-construct solutions.

To investigate this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students in the United States. Students first experienced human-only CPS and then CPS with two AI peers using a technology probe built around GPT-4o. The camp combined surveys, interviews, whole-class reflections, and design artifacts such as posters and example dialogues. Students also completed comparative measures after human-only versus AI-assisted sessions, including NASA-TLX and the Group Environment Questionnaire.

Findings show that students preferred an AI peer that gives progressive scaffolds such as hints, checks, and concept refreshers before direct answers, and one that remains under clear student control over when it speaks and how much it says. They strongly favored a peer-like but competent and friendly tone, and rejected exaggerated personas or rigid, teacher-like behavior. The study concludes that effective AI peers for middle school mathematics should support co-agency, social attunement, and emotional scaffolding, not just correctness or efficiency.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative participatory design study with some within-subject survey comparisons, not a controlled efficacy trial. It provides useful user-centered evidence, but the main contribution is design requirements rather than causal impact on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report direct achievement gains; its strongest effects are on perceived workload and collaboration experience. Implications for learning impact are important but indirect and therefore unclear for achievement.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT/GPT-4o-based AI peer technology probe for middle school collaborative mathematics problem solving, using two conversational AI peers (Alice and Bob) to provide hints, checks, explanations, and peer-like dialogue during group work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studied middle school students’ mathematics collaborative problem solving with and without AI peers, but it did not report achievement test gains. In the AI-peer condition (n=22 paired comparisons for survey measures), students perceived lower temporal demand during math work (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. 9.62, SD=4.13; d=1.15, p=0.002) but also higher physical demand and lower task coordination/social cohesion, suggesting that the AI altered how students experienced math problem solving rather than clearly improving achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Math CPS task experience and perceived workload/coordination during middle-school mathematics problem solving (NASA-TLX, GEQ); no direct math achievement test reported
finding.study_size: n=24 (qualitative/PD sample); n=22 paired survey comparisons
finding.effect_size: d=1.15 for temporal demand; d=1.14 for physical demand; d=0.94 for ATGS; d=0.81 for GIT
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SDs: 4.38 (AI) vs 4.13 (human); physical demand SDs: 4.65 (AI) vs 2.41 (human); ATGS SDs: 1.81 vs 2.05; GIT SDs: 1.58 vs 1.52

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI peers reduced time pressure but also made collaboration feel colder and more frustrating, indicating mixed social-emotional effects. Qualitatively, students wanted encouragement, emotional attunement, and a partner that would not trigger self-blame; quantitatively, the AI condition lowered group social attraction (ATGS: M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. 6.50, SD=2.05; d=0.94, p=0.029).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal/physical demand, GEQ social attraction, and interview/reﬂection themes about frustration, encouragement, and trust
finding.study_size: n=24; n=22 paired survey comparisons; interviews n=18
finding.effect_size: d=0.94 for ATGS; d=1.15 for temporal demand (beneficial but not social-emotional); d=1.14 for physical demand
finding.std_deviation: ATGS SDs: 1.81 (AI) vs 2.05 (human); NASA-TLX relevant SDs reported above

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on collaboration, co-agency, turn-taking, and coordination in middle school mathematics CPS, showing that students valued AI peers that supported shared problem solving rather than taking over. Quantitatively, perceived group integration-task was lower with AI peers (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. 5.54, SD=1.52; d=0.81, p=0.047), indicating weaker coordination even though the AI reduced temporal demand.
finding.measure: Group cohesion and coordination in collaborative problem solving (GEQ Group Integration-Task and related reflections/interviews)
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey comparisons; qualitative sample n=18 interviews plus whole-class reflections

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT and GPT-4 rather than studying a classroom intervention. The authors ask how well these language models handle different kinds of mathematical tasks, with particular attention to advanced mathematics, proof completion, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search-like retrieval of mathematical facts and definitions. To do this, they introduce two new natural-language benchmark datasets, GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS, designed to probe multiple dimensions of mathematical reasoning in a fine-grained way.

The benchmark includes both hand-crafted prompts and prompts drawn from existing sources such as graduate-level textbooks, Math StackExchange, the MATH dataset, and a symbolic integration dataset. The tasks span undergraduate and graduate-level material, with emphasis on problems that are unlikely to have been memorized from training data. The paper uses manual expert ratings and error codes to characterize model behavior and compares two ChatGPT versions from January 2023 with GPT-4.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is useful mainly as a mathematical lookup aid: it performs best when querying facts or acting like a search engine/knowledge base interface. GPT-4 performs better overall and can sometimes handle undergraduate-level mathematics, but still falls short on graduate-level tasks and proof-heavy problems. The authors conclude that neither model is reliable enough for consistently solving advanced mathematics problems, though GPT-4 shows clear improvement over earlier ChatGPT versions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style benchmark study with a clear, manual evaluation methodology, but it is not an education trial and does not test student learning outcomes. The evidence is primarily descriptive/qualitative with human ratings, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows potentially useful support for mathematics lookup and assistant tasks, but it does not demonstrate learner impact in educational settings. Any impact is therefore modest and indirect, with no measured student achievement gains.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT (9-Jan-2023 and 30-Jan-2023 versions) and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for university-level and graduate-level problem solving, proof completion, definition retrieval, and fact lookup in natural-language mathematics prompts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates mathematical performance across 709 prompts (GPT-4 on a 170-prompt miniGHOSTS subset) and finds highly uneven results. ChatGPT averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) on the 9-Jan version and 3.29/5 (SD=1.28) on 30-Jan, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15/5 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS; GPT-4 passed all subdatasets except graduate-level functional analysis and olympiad problem solving. The authors conclude ChatGPT is useful mainly for fact lookup/search-like tasks, but is not reliable for proofs or complex calculations.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical solution quality on GHOSTS/miniGHOSTS prompts (1-5 rubric; subdataset averages; correctness on proof, computation, fact-retrieval, and integration tasks)
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts total; 1636 human ratings; GPT-4 on n=170 prompts

finding.finding_summary: Although not tested as a classroom intervention, the paper reports that ChatGPT can speed up certain lookup tasks for mathematically proficient users, functioning as a search engine or knowledge-base interface. This benefit is qualitative rather than experimentally quantified, and is strongest for querying facts and recalling definitions/theorems rather than solving hard problems.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of usefulness as a mathematical assistant for search/lookup tasks

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concentration of power in generative AI from an antitrust law perspective. Rather than studying educational use or learner outcomes, it analyzes how major technology companies control key layers of the generative AI stack, including data, talent, infrastructure, funding, and model development. The authors argue that these structural advantages create barriers to entry and may entrench incumbent firms' dominance.

The paper discusses the role of vertically integrated technology companies such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Apple in shaping the generative AI market. It reviews how access to data, proprietary infrastructure, large-scale funding, human feedback labor, and influence over academic research contribute to competitive advantage. The analysis is framed through existing antitrust doctrine in the US and EU, with attention to the difficulty of defining relevant markets and proving abuse of dominance in digital technologies.

The main conclusion is that current generative AI markets may be reinforcing existing concentrations of platform power. The authors suggest that new entrants are disadvantaged by historical dominance in adjacent markets and by the capital-intensive nature of large-scale model development. They conclude that future regulation, including the EU AI Act, may either mitigate or worsen these inequities, and they call for more substantial quantitative analysis of market definition, access conditions, and dominance in generative AI systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a legal/technology policy analysis paper about antitrust and platform power in generative AI, not an empirical study of educational intervention or student outcomes. It contains no research design, sample, or measured effects relevant to K-12 learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational outcomes or intervention effects, so there is no demonstrated impact on student learning or school practice for the retrieved topic.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring large language model (LLM)-based applications across their full lifecycle. The authors argue that current workflows for LLM applications are often manual, slow, and reliant on trial-and-error prompt engineering, which makes it difficult to ensure quality, robustness, and scalability.

To address this, the paper introduces the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework intended to automate DevOps-style workflows for LLM-based applications and agents. The toolkit supports agent bootstrapping, user-defined evaluation metrics, repeatable test cases, model/prompt permutation testing, CI/CD integration, deployment via infrastructure-as-code, and logging/monitoring with traces. The paper demonstrates the toolkit on several representative use cases, including a text-to-SQL agent, a RAG-based restaurant menu agent, an in-vehicle assistant, and model comparison experiments.

The paper does not study students, teachers, or schools. Its context is software engineering and industrial generative AI application development at BMW Group and Amazon Web Services.
