The main conclusion is that the toolkit can reduce manual effort, shorten release cycles, and improve the quality and observability of LLM-based systems, though the authors note that generic quantitative claims about benefit are difficult to make.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint framework/tool paper, not an empirical study with a controlled design. It provides illustrative use cases and descriptive claims, but no rigorous outcome evaluation suitable for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable educational effect size or student outcome is reported, and the paper is not about K-12 learning intervention impact. Its contribution is tooling for LLM application development, so educational impact is absent or unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM application lifecycle tooling for configuring, testing, monitoring, and optimizing generative AI agents via DevOps/LLMOps workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the Generative AI Toolkit significantly reduces cycle time and manual work in developing and operating LLM-based applications. However, no quantitative effect size, sample size, or CI is reported; the evidence is presented descriptively across representative use cases rather than as a controlled evaluation.
finding.measure: Development cycle time, manual work, automated testing/monitoring workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is positioned as an end-to-end framework that standardizes testing, deployment, and monitoring practices for LLM-based applications, with the aim of improving quality and release processes across teams. The paper claims improved quality and audit-proof logging, but does not provide quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Quality assurance workflow standardization, auditability, CI/CD integration, monitoring coverage

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that general-purpose generative AI models may recommend medical products for off-label uses that are not approved by regulators and may therefore be unsafe or illegal to promote. The authors frame this as a public-health and regulatory problem, arguing that large multimodal models can learn unvetted product-indication associations from broad internet-scale training data.

To address the problem, the paper proposes a post-hoc detection approach for identifying potentially harmful off-label promotion in generative AI outputs. The method standardizes user queries, performs named entity recognition for drugs and diseases, matches entities against FDA labeling data, and then checks whether the model response contains a non-approved product-indication association that is phrased as a recommendation. The paper demonstrates the approach using Anthropic’s Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style scenario where a user submits an image of a product label and asks questions about it.

The experimental setup is synthetic rather than human-subject based: the authors generated 14,300 queries across 35 pharmaceuticals with known off-label uses and evaluated model responses against FDA-approved labeling. They report that 15.4% of responses contained off-label indications, and that their detector achieved good precision and recall on a human-annotated sample. The main conclusion is that generalist MLLMs can surface off-label medical recommendations, and that guardrails are needed to filter or block such outputs before they reach users.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical/technical paper with a clear methodology, but it is not an educational impact study and does not use a randomized or causal design. The evidence is best characterized as descriptive and diagnostic rather than high-credibility outcome evaluation for learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not measure educational achievement or learner outcomes, and its findings are about model safety/regulatory risk in medical product recommendations. There is no demonstrated positive educational impact, and the directly measured impact is negative in a non-education domain.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating a multimodal generative AI chatbot (Claude 3 Sonnet) used in a medical product question-answering setting, where users ask questions about product labels and the model generates textual recommendations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a multimodal GenAI system can generate potentially harmful off-label medical product recommendations, highlighting a regulatory and safety failure mode rather than a student-learning outcome. In 14,300 synthetic queries across 35 pharmaceuticals, 15.4% of responses were identified as containing off-label indications; the authors also report a detection method with precision 85.75%, recall 80.47%, and F1 83.02% on a 2,000-sample human-annotated evaluation.
finding.measure: Rate of off-label indications in model responses; precision/recall/F1 of off-label detection method
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 human-annotated sample

paper_profiles.title: Developers and Generative AI: A Study of Self-Admitted Usage in Open Source Projects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how developers self-admit the use of generative AI tools in open-source software development, focusing on ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot. The central question is what software-related tasks developers document as being supported by these LLM-based assistants, and whether the tools were perceived as useful in those contexts. The motivation is to better understand real-world usage patterns, provenance, and traceability of AI-assisted software artifacts.

The study mined GitHub commits, issues, and pull requests containing references to ChatGPT or Copilot, then manually inspected a stratified sample of 1,161 candidate instances. After filtering false positives, the authors analyzed 343 ChatGPT cases and 281 Copilot cases and performed qualitative coding to derive taxonomies of usage tasks. The analysis covered open-source projects hosted on GitHub and included both automatically classifiable Copilot template cases and manually coded instances. No educational intervention, student sample, or achievement outcome is involved.

The paper concludes that developers use generative AI across a broad range of software engineering activities, including feature implementation, process automation, learning, data generation/manipulation, development environment support, software quality, and documentation. ChatGPT was used for a wider and more diverse set of tasks, while Copilot was more concentrated in IDE-integrated workflows such as commit/message generation and development-environment support. The authors argue that these self-admitted traces provide a biased but useful view into LLM adoption in practice, and that future research should better capture AI involvement and evaluate its effects on productivity, code ownership, and quality.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative mining study with manual coding and taxonomy construction, but it is not an experimental or causal design. The evidence is useful for mapping real-world usage patterns, yet it has clear observational bias and no randomized comparison.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s impact is mainly descriptive and methodological rather than demonstrably outcome-changing. It shows broad adoption of LLMs in development workflows, but reports no measured educational effect sizes or direct impact on student achievement.

interventions.use_case: Self-admitted use of ChatGPT to support software-development tasks in open-source projects, including code generation, debugging, refactoring, documentation drafting, brainstorming, and CI/CD assistance.
Self-admitted use of GitHub Copilot for IDE-integrated assistance on development tasks such as commit/PR description generation, code completion, and workflow/script generation.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative mining study does not estimate a causal effect, but it shows that developers frequently used ChatGPT and Copilot to automate or speed up work such as feature implementation, bug fixing, documentation, and CI/CD scripting. The paper identified 624 valid instances (343 ChatGPT, 281 Copilot) and reports that many task categories were judged useful, especially process automation (21/21 successful for ChatGPT) and several feature- and quality-related tasks.
finding.measure: Self-admitted usage instances and developer-reported usefulness across GitHub commits, issues, and pull requests
finding.study_size: n=624 valid instances (ChatGPT n=343; Copilot n=281)

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents LLM use for brainstorming, program comprehension, and design decisions, suggesting support for problem solving and metacognitive work rather than direct instruction. At the same time, it highlights limitations such as hallucinations and ownership concerns, so the net effect on deeper understanding is mixed and not quantified.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of learning/brainstorming/comprehension usage in developer artifacts
finding.study_size: n=624 valid instances overall; learning-related instances are a subset (e.g., ChatGPT learning n=64 in the taxonomy)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that widespread self-admitted AI use raises provenance, code ownership, trust, licensing, and review-process concerns for open-source projects. It reports no quantitative institutional effect, but provides evidence that projects may need new contribution and review guidelines for AI-generated code and that mining studies must adapt to harder-to-detect AI involvement.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of governance/provenance implications discussed in developer artifacts and author interpretation

paper_profiles.title: Experimenting with Generative AI: Does ChatGPT Really Increase Everyone’s Productivity?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT improves performance on tasks where the model may be less strong than in English writing or Python/SQL coding. The authors focus on two task domains: writing analysis tasks in Thai and math/data analysis tasks in Stata. They ask whether generative AI can increase productivity in these less-common language and programming settings, and whether the benefits differ across students with different academic and digital-skill backgrounds.

The study is an experiment with 121 economics students from Chulalongkorn University and Thammasat University in Thailand. Participants completed two rounds of writing analysis tasks and two rounds of math/data analysis tasks, doing each task set once without ChatGPT and once with ChatGPT. The design used random assignment to task order and task set, and performance was measured with expert-rated scores and completion time. Students also reported academic indicators such as GPAX, econometrics grades, and self-assessed skills.

The results show that, on average, students scored higher and finished faster when using ChatGPT in both task domains. However, the gains were uneven: about one-third of participants did not improve in writing tasks and about two-fifths did not improve in math/data tasks. Higher-ability students, proxied by econometrics grades, tended to do worse with ChatGPT on writing tasks, while students with stronger digital skills performed better with ChatGPT, especially on math/data tasks. The paper concludes that generative AI can boost productivity on average, but benefits depend on user skills and task type.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized within-subject experiment with 121 college students and repeated measures, which supports internal validity. However, it is not a K-12 study, is not peer reviewed in the provided text, and the focus is on productivity/achievement in economics students rather than a fully validated education intervention trial.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The estimated gains are modest to moderate in task performance, but the population is college economics students and the outcomes are short-horizon task scores rather than durable learning gains. The evidence suggests positive productivity effects, yet general educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a generative AI support tool while economics students completed Thai writing analysis tasks and Stata-based math/data analysis tasks, to compare performance with vs. without LLM assistance.

finding.finding_summary: In Thai writing analysis tasks, students scored higher with ChatGPT than without it by 0.43 points on a 10-point scale (n=121). The paper also reports faster completion times with ChatGPT by 1.73 minutes, and the improvement was not universal: 34% of participants saw no score gain.
finding.measure: Expert-rated writing analysis score out of 10; task completion time in minutes

finding.finding_summary: In math & data analysis tasks using Stata, students scored higher with ChatGPT by 1.65 points on a 10-point scale (n=121). They also finished faster by 0.99 minutes on average, though 42% did not improve, indicating heterogeneous benefits rather than uniform gains.
finding.measure: Expert-rated math/data analysis score out of 10; task completion time in minutes

finding.finding_summary: Across both task types, ChatGPT reduced completion time relative to no ChatGPT, indicating improved task efficiency. The reported average time gains were 1.73 minutes for writing tasks and 0.99 minutes for math/data tasks, both measured within 20-minute timed sessions.
finding.measure: Task completion time in minutes
finding.std_deviation: 3.43 (writing time diff SD); 2.90 (math/data time diff SD)

paper_profiles.title: On the Robustness of ChatGPT in Teaching Korean Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT can solve and evaluate Korean mathematics questions, addressing a broader concern about whether large language models are reliable in multilingual educational settings. The authors frame the work as a test of ChatGPT’s robustness in non-English math problem solving and its ability to rate math questions using pedagogical criteria. Two research questions guide the study: the accuracy of ChatGPT on Korean CSAT mathematics items and the effectiveness of ChatGPT in rating and categorizing those items at the university-entrance level.

The intervention or approach is a zero-shot evaluation of ChatGPT on a validated dataset of 586 Korean mathematics questions from the South Korean CSAT. The model is asked both to answer the questions and to rate them on eleven dimensions such as difficulty, cognitive demand, clarity, time requirement, scoring fairness, originality, discrimination power, error-proneness, and analytical depth. The paper also performs topic analysis and compares performance across questions with and without diagrams, as well as across prompt/model variants including GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, translation into English, and limited tests with o1-preview.

The study population is not human participants but high-school-level standardized test items drawn from South Korea’s college admissions context. The setting is an assessment-analysis workflow using official exam PDFs processed into machine-readable formats, with model outputs compared against answer keys and human annotations where available. The authors conclude that ChatGPT achieves moderate accuracy overall (66.72%) and performs better on simpler, lower-marked questions than on more complex, sequential, or diagram-based items. They also find that ChatGPT’s ratings are broadly consistent with educational theory and human perceptions, suggesting usefulness for assessment design and personalized education, while emphasizing the need for better multilingual support, stronger reasoning, and improved diagram comprehension.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational, non-randomized evaluation of a single LLM on a fixed test set, with correlation and descriptive analyses rather than causal inference. It is methodologically clear and data-based, but it does not meet RCT/QED standards for stronger evidence tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports a moderate direct performance level (66.72% accuracy) but on a benchmark/test-set task rather than a demonstrated classroom intervention with measured learning gains. The practical implications are promising, yet the evidence for actual educational impact remains indirect.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating ChatGPT as a multilingual mathematics-solving and question-rating assistant for Korean CSAT math items, including zero-shot problem solving and automated rating/categorization of question difficulty, cognitive demand, clarity, and topic coverage.

finding.finding_summary: Across 586 Korean CSAT mathematics questions, ChatGPT answered 391 correctly for an overall accuracy of 66.72%. Performance was much higher on easier/lower-marked items (near 100% on 2-point questions) and dropped to about 50% on 4-point questions, with especially poor performance on sequential and diagram-based problems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Korean mathematics questions; correct response rate by item point value and format (diagram vs non-diagram)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s ratings of Korean CSAT math items were reported as substantially consistent with educational theory and with human test-taker/educator perspectives. The model also aligned on higher-order features such as cognitive demand, difficulty, and analytical depth, suggesting utility for classification and assessment design rather than direct student achievement gains.
finding.measure: Correlation/consistency of AI-generated ratings with human annotations and educational theory across 11 question criteria

finding.finding_summary: The study shows ChatGPT can automate rating and categorization of mathematics questions using 11 criteria, including difficulty, cognitive demand, time requirement, and originality/engagement. Although no formal workload metric was reported, the model’s strong agreement with human-style judgments suggests practical value for assessment design and content analysis efficiency.
finding.measure: Automated question rating/categorization quality and agreement with theory/human perspectives

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Computer Science Education: Accelerating Python Learning with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether integrating ChatGPT into introductory Python instruction can help adult learners rapidly acquire foundational programming skills. The central problem is the difficulty many novice programmers face with syntax, debugging, abstraction, and timely feedback, especially in compressed online training formats. The authors frame generative AI as a possible way to provide immediate, personalized support that reduces barriers to learning programming.

The intervention was a self-paced, asynchronous Python module embedded in a sixteen-week professional training course on applied generative AI. Learners were instructed to use ChatGPT to generate code, interpret code behavior, and debug errors while completing coding assignments and assessments. The module was delivered online to 86 adult learners with mixed prior programming backgrounds, including people with Python experience, experience in other languages only, and no prior programming experience.

Using repeated assessments across the course and a mixed-design ANOVA, the study found that learners without prior programming experience initially scored lower than peers, but these gaps largely disappeared after the Python module. The authors conclude that ChatGPT-supported instruction can accelerate foundational programming learning, close initial skill gaps, and help adult learners reach proficiency quickly. They also caution that AI assistance should be balanced with opportunities for independent problem-solving, and note that human mentorship and instructional scaffolding remain important.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear repeated-measures quantitative design, but it is not randomized and lacks a comparison group independent of prior experience. The evidence is therefore suggestive rather than high-credibility causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gains appear practically meaningful for a priority population of adult reskilling learners, with early performance gaps closing and post-intervention group differences becoming negligible (η²<.05). The overall impact is modest-to-moderate and concentrated in foundational programming proficiency rather than broad academic outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-supported self-paced introductory Python learning, where learners used the chatbot to generate code snippets, interpret code, and debug syntax/logic errors during a compressed programming module

finding.finding_summary: The study found that learners improved in foundational Python programming proficiency after the ChatGPT-supported instructional module. Early in the course, novices without prior programming experience scored lower than peers (e.g., group effects on conditional statements F(2,114)=4.05, p=.020; looping F(2,105)=4.90, p=.009), but these gaps were no longer statistically significant after the module, with later group effects generally small (η² < .05).
finding.measure: Timed code-based assessments and multiple-choice programming quizzes across 30 course assessments, including conditional statements, loops, functions, and Python fundamentals

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT helped learners develop metacognitive and problem-solving skills such as troubleshooting, solution synthesis, and adaptive debugging. This conclusion is supported qualitatively by mentor observations that learners increasingly used ChatGPT for just-in-time support and independent error resolution, though no direct standardized durable-skills measure was reported.
finding.measure: Instructor/mentor qualitative observations of learner troubleshooting and code interpretation behaviors

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how 3D generative AI can be connected to physical fabrication, arguing that improving text-to-3D generation alone is not enough to realize practical physical making. The authors identify a mismatch between fast digital generation and the constraints of real-world fabrication, and they propose that fabrication methods should be evaluated in terms of whether they can accommodate generative AI outputs.

As a case study, the paper presents a system that combines 3D generative AI with discrete robotic assembly. The system takes a user prompt, generates a 3D model using Meshy.AI, discretizes the geometry into modular components, and uses a UR10 robotic arm to assemble the object from prefabricated parts. The paper emphasizes five design considerations: fabrication constraints, time, sustainability, functionality, and accessibility.

The paper does not study an educational population; it is an HCI / fabrication workshop paper from researchers at MIT. The authors report that discrete robotic assembly can better support variable AI-generated designs, produce large objects quickly, and enable reuse of components for more sustainable fabrication. However, they also find limits in ensuring functionality and note that accessibility is still constrained by the cost and equipment requirements of robotic fabrication.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a workshop case study/framework paper with no experimental comparison, no controlled design, and no inferential statistics. It is peer-reviewed workshop literature, but the evidence is largely demonstrative and conceptual rather than rigorous empirical evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical benefits for prompt-to-production fabrication, especially faster assembly and component reuse, but provides no measured educational or population-level impact. Effects are qualitative and application-specific, so the broader impact is unclear and modest.

interventions.use_case: text-to-3D generative AI combined with discrete robotic assembly to create physical objects from speech prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the prompt-to-physical workflow can produce large objects quickly, with nearly all assembled objects completed in under five minutes. The authors emphasize this as a promising faster iterative design loop between humans and AI, but no controlled comparison or formal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: fabrication/assembly time from user prompt to completed physical object

finding.finding_summary: The system is presented as a more sustainable and accessible approach to physical making: 40 modular components were reused to assemble seven distinct objects, and the authors argue that lower-cost robotic alternatives could broaden access. However, accessibility remains limited by the high cost of the UR10 arm used in the study ($40,000-$50,000), so the impact is promising but constrained.
finding.measure: component reuse across objects; cost/accessibility analysis of fabrication hardware

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Efficacy of a Professional Development Program in Formative Classroom Assessment in Middle School English Language Arts and Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a professional development program in formative classroom assessment improved middle school teachers’ assessment knowledge and their students’ achievement. The study was motivated by the claim that better classroom assessment practices should help teachers identify student learning needs and adjust instruction, but prior studies had produced mixed findings.

The intervention was a year-long professional development course developed by the South Carolina Department of Education. Teachers learned to align assessments to standards, write multiple-choice and performance items, build rubrics and checklists, interpret standardized tests, and use assessment results formatively and summatively. In Year 1, treatment schools received the program through trained assessment coaches while control schools received no professional development. In Years 2 and 3, the study compared the same professional development delivered by trained coaches versus relatively untrained facilitators, with matched comparison schools serving as controls.

The participants were sixth-, seventh-, and eighth-grade English language arts and mathematics teachers and their students in state-identified low-performing middle schools in South Carolina. Teacher knowledge was measured with pre/post assessment tests, and student achievement was measured using state PACT scores analyzed with multilevel models. The findings showed that the professional development improved teachers’ assessment knowledge in all years, regardless of whether it was delivered by a coach or facilitator. However, student achievement did not improve; in fact, treatment students often scored lower than comparison students, including significant negative effects in English language arts across all three years and in mathematics in Year 3. The authors conclude that improving teachers’ assessment skill alone may not be enough to raise achievement and that formative assessment must be linked to effective instructional action.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed multi-year study with a randomized cluster trial in Year 1 and quasi-experimental matched comparisons in Years 2-3, using multilevel modeling and standardized outcomes. However, only one year is fully randomized and later years rely on matched controls, so the design has some credibility concerns relative to a pure RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The key student achievement effects are negative or null, with effect sizes mostly small and the largest magnitude around d=-0.33 in mathematics. Although teacher knowledge improved meaningfully, the paper reports no positive student achievement impact and in some cases a detrimental effect, which places overall impact in the red tier.

finding.finding_summary: This three-year study of middle school English language arts and mathematics teachers found that a formative assessment professional development program increased teacher assessment skill, but student achievement declined relative to matched controls. In English language arts, adjusted PACT scores were lower in the treatment schools by 2.39 points in Year 1 (d≈-0.16), 1.15 points in Year 2 (d≈-0.08), and 3.46 points in Year 3 (d≈-0.26); all three differences were statistically significant.
finding.measure: State standardized PACT English language arts scale scores

finding.finding_summary: In mathematics, there were no significant treatment effects in Years 1 and 2, but Year 3 showed significantly lower adjusted PACT scores for professional-development schools. The Year 3 adjusted difference was -3.76 points, with a standardized effect size of d≈-0.33; Years 1 and 2 were near zero (d≈0.03 and -0.01).
finding.measure: State standardized PACT mathematics scale scores

finding.finding_summary: The professional development produced clear gains in teachers’ assessment knowledge and related measurement skills, including aligning items to standards and identifying cognitive levels. On the teacher posttest, the treatment group improved by 8.51 points in Year 1 versus 1.85 points for controls, and both treatment conditions improved substantially in Years 2 and 3 (e.g., 10.99-11.77 points in Year 2; 8.00-8.23 points in Year 3), with significant pre-post effects (e.g., ω²=0.60 and 0.56).
finding.measure: Teacher assessment knowledge test / assessment skill pretest-posttest scores
finding.study_size: Year 1 n=151; Year 2 n=146; Year 3 n=71

paper_profiles.title: A Meta-Analysis of ChatGPT’s Influence on Learning Achievement
paper_profiles.venue: International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves learning achievement and whether its effects differ by learner level, learning domain, instructional approach, and research method. The authors conducted a meta-analysis of empirical studies published from November 2022 to December 2024, synthesizing 22 publications and 86 independent effect sizes using a random-effects model.

The intervention studied was the use of ChatGPT as a generative AI support tool across educational settings and subjects. The coded studies included elementary, middle/high school, undergraduate, and adult/clinical-teacher participants, with most evidence coming from higher education and from studies using quasi-experimental or experimental designs. Instructional approaches ranged from lecture and problem-based learning to self-regulated learning, game-based learning, flipped learning, and case-based learning.

The main finding is that ChatGPT has a moderate positive overall effect on learning achievement (g = 0.573). Effects were larger for middle and high school learners than for undergraduates, though the subgroup difference was not statistically significant. Effects did not significantly differ across cognitive, affective, and metacognitive outcomes, but they did vary by instructional approach, with self-regulated learning showing the largest gains and game-based learning the smallest. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support achievement across contexts, especially when used in learner-centered designs, but more research is needed in K–12 settings and across diverse learning domains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 86 independent studies across 22 publications and uses random-effects models with heterogeneity, subgroup analyses, and publication-bias checks. That makes it high on methodological credibility for evidence grading, though the included primary studies vary in design and quality.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled overall effect is moderate (g = 0.573), which exceeds the threshold for meaningful impact. Effects are also positive for priority K–12/secondary populations, with middle and high school students showing a comparatively large subgroup effect (g = 0.928).

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT use as a conversational AI tutor/support tool across learning settings, including lecture, self-regulated learning, case-based, problem-based, project-based, flipped, and game-based instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across 86 independent studies from 22 publications, ChatGPT showed a moderate positive effect on learning achievement overall (g = 0.573, 95% CI [0.451, 0.696]). The meta-analysis used a random-effects model and found substantial heterogeneity (Q = 511.1, I2 = 83.37), but the pooled result remained statistically significant (p < .001).
finding.measure: Learning achievement / learning outcomes across cognitive, affective, and metacognitive domains

finding.finding_summary: For affective outcomes, ChatGPT had a positive pooled effect (g = 0.481, 95% CI [0.262, 0.700]; k = 27, n = 1,808). Outcomes included motivation, emotional engagement, flow, attitudes, satisfaction, frustration, and anxiety; the subgroup effect was statistically significant (p < .001).
finding.measure: Affective learning outcomes (motivation, engagement, satisfaction, anxiety, attitudes, flow)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT also improved cognitive and metacognitive outcomes, with pooled effects of g = 0.612 (95% CI [0.446, 0.779]; k = 46, n = 3,757) for cognitive outcomes and g = 0.619 (95% CI [0.319, 0.919]; k = 13, n = 1,427) for metacognitive outcomes. The paper interprets this as support for problem solving, knowledge construction, higher-order thinking, critical thinking, planning, monitoring, and self-regulated learning.
finding.measure: Cognitive and metacognitive learning outcomes (problem solving, higher-order thinking, critical thinking, self-regulation)

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Activities on Academic Achievement, Critical Thinking and Innovation Skills in Social Studies Classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether artificial intelligence-supported activities improve middle school students’ academic achievement, critical thinking disposition, and innovation skills in social studies. The author frames the work around the growing use of AI and large language models in education and the need for empirical evidence on their effects, especially on higher-order thinking outcomes that may be helped or hindered by AI use.

The study used an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Quantitatively, it employed a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design; qualitatively, it used a case study approach. The intervention was built with Microsoft Copilot and implemented over six weeks in the 7th-grade “Global Connections” unit. The experimental group consisted of 25 students who used AI-supported activities in a public middle school, while the control group of 24 students followed textbook-based instruction. Data came from an academic achievement test, a critical thinking disposition scale, an innovation skills scale, and semi-structured interviews with eight students from the experimental group.

Results showed that the AI-supported activities significantly improved academic achievement and innovation skills compared with the textbook condition. However, they did not significantly improve critical thinking disposition; in fact, the control group outperformed the experimental group on the posttest critical thinking measure. Interview data suggested that students saw AI as helpful for learning, research, motivation, and creativity, but also noted risks such as misdirection, overreliance, and potential harm to critical thinking. The paper concludes that AI can support learning and innovation in social studies, but its classroom use should be carefully designed and supported by appropriate infrastructure and reliable educational fine-tuning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with pretest-posttest control group design, but it is not randomized and has a small sample (n=49). The qualitative component and non-equivalent groups reduce internal validity relative to blue-tier evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large positive effects on academic achievement (d=.77, η2=.305) and innovation skills (r=.49 between groups; r=.83 within-group change), which meet the threshold for meaningful impact. However, the effect on critical thinking was null/negative, so the overall intervention impact is mixed but still substantial for the positive outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Microsoft Copilot used to support lesson planning and generate six weeks of AI-supported social studies activities for the 7th-grade 'Global Connections' unit, with students also using the AI tool during class activities for research and learning support.

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported activities significantly improved 7th-grade social studies academic achievement in the experimental group. The experimental group's AAT scores increased from 12.96 to 17.00 over 6 weeks (n=25), and the adjusted posttest mean was significantly higher than the control group (16.97 vs 13.50), with a large ANCOVA effect (F(1,46)=20.22, p<.05, η2=.305).
finding.measure: Academic Achievement Test (AAT) for the 'Global Connections' unit
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pre SD=5.18, post SD=5.27; control pre SD=3.72, post SD=3.93

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported activities did not improve critical thinking disposition relative to either pretest levels or textbook-based instruction. The experimental group showed no significant pre-post change on the CTDS (Z=-1.14, p>.05), and the posttest comparison favored the control group with a large difference (U=83.50, Z=-4.33, p<.05, r=.62).
finding.measure: Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS)

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported activities substantially improved innovation skills in the experimental group. The total ISS score increased significantly from pretest to posttest, and the posttest comparison showed the experimental group outperforming the control group (U=127.00, Z=-3.46, p<.05, r=.49), with moderate effects across all subscales.
finding.measure: Innovation Skills Scale (ISS), including creativity, leadership, energy, self-efficacy, and risk-taking tendency
finding.effect_size: r=.83 pre-post within experimental group; r=.49 between-group posttest

paper_profiles.title: Measuring the impact of ChatGPT in enhancing number sense acquisition: A mixed-method study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether integrating ChatGPT into mathematics instruction improves junior high school students’ understanding of number concepts, and how students perceive the tool’s usefulness. The authors note debate over whether generative AI can meaningfully improve achievement in mathematics, especially for foundational number sense skills.

The intervention was a quasi-experimental classroom study combined with qualitative analysis. One 7th-grade class at Junior High School State 10 Manado used ChatGPT during seven 90-minute mathematics sessions, while a control class received conventional teaching. In the experimental condition, ChatGPT was used for explanations, question-answering, problem solving in pairs, and independent exercises. Quantitative data came from pre-test and post-test math scores, including both LOTS and HOTS items; qualitative data came from student essays about their experiences with ChatGPT.

The quantitative results showed significant pre-post gains within both the ChatGPT and control groups, but no significant difference between the two groups’ post-test performance. The effect sizes were small, indicating that ChatGPT did not directly improve measured mathematics achievement in number concepts. Qualitatively, however, students reported that ChatGPT increased efficiency, improved understanding, provided generally accurate help, and supported them when they were stuck. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is better viewed as a supplementary tool that may support learning processes and higher-order problem solving, rather than as a replacement for traditional instruction or a guaranteed driver of achievement gains.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental mixed-method study with a control group and pretest-posttest design, which provides moderate causal evidence but not full RCT rigor. Credibility is limited by the small sample, single school setting, and the reliance on qualitative perceptions for some claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The main academic outcome showed no significant benefit of ChatGPT on mathematics achievement (p=0.913), so overall impact is unclear to modest at best. There was a small within-group gain in the experimental class (d=0.265) and positive perceptions about efficiency, but not enough for a stronger impact rating.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-supported mathematics learning for 7th-grade students, used by the teacher for additional explanations, by students for question-answering, problem solving, and independent अभ्यास on number concepts

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental mixed-method study with 7th-grade students (experimental n=39; control n=37), ChatGPT integration did not significantly improve number sense / number-concept achievement compared with conventional instruction. Post-test scores were not significantly different between groups (p=0.913), and the reported pretest-posttest effect within the experimental group was small (d=0.265).
finding.measure: Mathematics test scores on 20 multiple-choice items covering number concepts, including LOTS and HOTS questions; pretest and posttest; independent and paired t-tests

finding.finding_summary: Although the quantitative achievement results were null, the qualitative findings suggested ChatGPT supported higher-order thinking and problem solving, especially on HOTS items where scores increased from 12.820 to 18.590 in the experimental class. Students also reported improved understanding and easier handling of difficult problems, but these were perception-based findings rather than a direct standardized measure of critical thinking.
finding.measure: Descriptive performance on HOTS versus LOTS math items; student essays on perceived understanding/problem-solving support
finding.study_size: n=39 qualitative; n=39 experimental for HOTS/LOTS descriptives

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported that ChatGPT improved efficiency and speed in studying, helping them find answers quickly and complete exercises faster. This was a qualitative finding from 39 student essays, not a quantified productivity metric, but the direction of perceived effect was clearly positive.
finding.measure: Student perceived efficiency/speed in learning and task completion from open-ended essays

paper_profiles.title: The impact of AI-supported online classroom management (AIS-OCM) on attitudes toward english lessons, self-directed online learning, and academic achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-supported online classroom management (AIS-OCM) can improve middle school students’ attitudes toward English as a Foreign Language (EFL), their self-directed online learning skills, and their academic achievement. The authors argue that online learning often suffers from reduced interaction, weaker motivation, and limited feedback, especially in language learning contexts that require frequent communication and timely correction.

To address this problem, the study implemented AIS-OCM in a seventh-grade EFL setting using the Zoom platform and the AI-supported language learning tool Rosetta Stone. The intervention combined adaptive content, automated speech-recognition feedback, individualized practice, automated monitoring, and teacher use of AI-generated dashboards and reports. A control group received the same online instruction without AI integration. The study used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design over eight weeks with two seventh-grade classes from the same school in Turkey.

Results from mixed ANOVA showed that both groups improved over time, but the AIS-OCM group generally performed better. The strongest and most consistent benefits appeared for self-directed online learning and academic achievement, while attitude gains were positive but sometimes not significantly different in growth rate between groups. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-supported online classroom management can meaningfully enhance online EFL instruction by supporting learner autonomy, improving feedback and monitoring, and contributing to better academic outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group study with baseline comparisons, standardized instruction, and a comparison group, but it lacks random assignment and is limited to one school and small sample sizes. Internal validity is reasonably supported, though not at the level of a well-controlled RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports modest-to-moderate positive effects, with several outcomes showing partial η2 values around or above 0.06 and one achievement interaction effect at ηp2=0.062. Impacts are meaningful for a priority middle-school EFL population, but generalizability is limited by the quasi-experimental single-site design.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported EFL instruction using Rosetta Stone with speech recognition, automated pronunciation feedback, personalized language practice, and adaptive content during synchronous online classroom management
Adaptive learning pathways and personalized time-management/learning recommendations based on student performance analytics within the AIS-OCM setup
Teacher dashboards and automated monitoring reports used to track participation, progress, and learning difficulties during online English lessons

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved English-language performance in a middle-school EFL context over an 8-week quasi-experiment (n=65; 32 experimental, 33 control). Academic achievement scores rose significantly over time in both groups, with a significant group difference and Time×Group interaction for Unit 2 (F(1,63)=4.14, p=0.046, ηp2=0.062), indicating greater gains for the AI-supported group.
finding.measure: English academic achievement tests for Unit 1 (Appearance and Personality) and Unit 2 (Sports)
finding.effect_size: ηp2=0.062 (Unit 2 Time×Group); ηp2=0.941 and 0.957 for time main effects

finding.finding_summary: AIS-OCM improved students’ attitudes toward English lessons, with significant main effects of time and group for both affective and behavioral subdimensions. For example, affective attitudes showed F(1,63)=11.29, p=0.001, ηp2=0.152 and behavioral attitudes showed F(1,63)=16.41, p<0.001, ηp2=0.207, suggesting moderate improvements across the 8-week intervention (n=65).
finding.measure: Attitudes toward English Lessons Scale (ATELS), affective and behavioral subdimensions

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported condition improved self-directed online learning, especially autonomous learning. The autonomous learning subscale showed a significant Time×Group interaction (F(1,63)=4.20, p=0.045, ηp2=0.063), and both self-directed learning subdimensions favored the experimental group overall (n=65).
finding.measure: Self-Directed Online Learning Scale (SDOLS), autonomous learning and asynchronous online learning subdimensions
finding.effect_size: ηp2=0.063 (autonomous Time×Group); ηp2=0.198 (group main effect, autonomous)

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Generative AI-assisted programming on the computational thinking of high school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Generative AI-assisted programming improves high school students’ computational thinking, and whether its effects differ across sub-skills. The authors note that most prior work on ChatGPT-like support has focused on higher education, while K-12 evidence—especially on fine-grained computational thinking dimensions—is limited. They frame Generative AI as a potential scaffolding tool that can reduce syntactic burden, support debugging, and free students’ cognitive resources for higher-order problem solving.

The study was conducted with 83 tenth-grade students at one high school in western China. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods quasi-experimental design, one intact class was assigned to the Generative AI-assisted condition and another to teacher-led instruction. The intervention lasted 8 weeks and used iFlytek Spark to help students learn Python syntax, understand code, and debug programs during programming projects. Quantitative data came from pre/post computational thinking tests based on the Bebras CT Challenge, and qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 18 students.

Results showed that the Generative AI group improved significantly more than the control group on overall computational thinking, algorithmic modeling, and abstraction/decomposition, but not on pattern recognition and evaluation. Interview data suggested that students valued the AI for personalized support, immediate feedback, code explanation, and efficiency, but some worried about over-dependence and occasionally unclear answers. The authors conclude that Generative AI can be an effective scaffold for high school programming instruction, though its benefits may vary by computational thinking dimension and require careful classroom guidance to avoid dependency.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with a comparison group, pretest-posttest design, and clearly reported quantitative analyses, but it lacks random assignment at the individual level and is limited to one school. Those design constraints keep it below blue, though it is stronger than a purely qualitative or correlational study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-to-large effects on a priority population: high school students learning programming, with partial η² values of 0.120 to 0.216 for key computational thinking subskills. The impact is meaningfully positive overall, despite one null subscale result.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-assisted programming support using iFlytek Spark (ChatGPT-like conversational AI) to explain Python code, answer syntax questions, generate examples, and provide debugging help during middle/high school programming lessons.

finding.finding_summary: Generative AI-assisted programming produced significant gains in overall computational thinking for the experimental group (n=42) compared with teacher-led instruction (n=41). The repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant method-by-time interaction, F(1,81)=14.29, p<0.001, partial η²=0.150, indicating a large effect on computational thinking as measured by the Bebras CT Challenge.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge overall computational thinking score

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was especially effective for algorithmic modeling. The experimental group improved from M=17.17 to 21.38, while the control group changed from M=17.78 to 17.80; the method-by-time interaction was significant, F(1,81)=22.315, p<0.001, partial η²=0.216, a large effect. This suggests the conversational AI mainly supported structured problem solving and algorithm design.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge algorithmic modeling subscale

finding.finding_summary: For abstraction and decomposition, the experimental group improved from M=13.76 to 22.43, compared with the control group’s increase from M=13.89 to 18.13. The interaction was significant, F(1,81)=11.065, p=0.001, partial η²=0.120, indicating a medium effect favoring Generative AI-assisted learning.
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge abstraction and decomposition subscale

finding.finding_summary: Pattern recognition and evaluation did not show a statistically reliable advantage for Generative AI after Bonferroni correction. The interaction was F(1,81)=5.194, p=0.025, partial η²=0.060, but this did not meet the corrected alpha of 0.0125; the experimental group showed a slight non-significant decline (M=-0.26) while the control group improved significantly (M=1.59).
finding.measure: Bebras CT Challenge pattern recognition and evaluation subscale

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated that students perceived the AI as increasing initiative, motivation, and willingness to ask questions. Students emphasized individualized support, ease of use, and rapid responses as reasons they felt more engaged and less intimidated by programming; these are qualitative findings from 18 interviewed students rather than a separate quantified outcome.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on learning initiative, engagement, and perceived motivation

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning Integrated with Artificial Intelligence on Self-Regulated Learning Tendencies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Problem-Based Learning (PBL) integrated with artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen junior high school students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) tendencies. The authors frame the study around a gap in prior research: although PBL and AI-supported learning have each been linked to SRL, fewer studies have tested AI as an adaptive scaffolding component within PBL, especially in school settings.

The intervention was implemented as an AI-integrated PBL lesson design that supported students through problem orientation, investigation, solution development, presentation, and reflection. AI was described as providing guided support such as prompts, feedback, scaffolding, and information exploration assistance rather than being used simply as a standalone technology. The study used a one-group posttest-only quasi-experimental design, with SRL measured by a Likert-scale questionnaire covering goal setting, strategy use, self-monitoring, time and resource management, motivational control, and self-reflection.

The participants were 60 seventh-grade students from SMP Negeri 1 Telaga Biru in Indonesia, drawn purposively from two classes during the first semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. Quantitative analysis used normality testing followed by either a one-sample t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test against a reference value. The results showed SRL scores in the good-to-high range and significantly above the benchmark in both classes. The strongest areas were forethought, motivational belief, and self-reflection, while help-seeking and collaboration were comparatively weaker. The authors conclude that AI-integrated PBL can positively support SRL, but social regulation components such as peer collaboration and structured help-seeking still need to be deliberately designed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study, but it uses a one-group posttest-only design with no comparison group or pretest, which limits internal validity and causal inference. The paper also reports no effect sizes for the main outcomes, further reducing evidentiary strength.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests a positive effect on SRL tendencies, but the practical magnitude is unclear because effect sizes are not reported and the design is criterion-referenced rather than comparative. The findings are promising for a priority population (junior high students) but remain modest and uncertain in generalizability.

interventions.use_case: problem-based learning integrated with AI-based pedagogical scaffolding, including prompts, guided information exploration, rapid feedback, and reflection support for grade 7 junior high students

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental one-group posttest-only study of 60 grade 7 students (n=30 in VII-1; n=30 in VII-3), AI-integrated PBL was associated with good-to-high self-regulated learning tendencies. SRL scores were significantly above the reference value of 75 in both classes: VII-1 showed a one-sample t-test result of t=15.777, p<.001, mean difference=11.56, 95% CI [10.06, 13.06], while VII-3 showed a Wilcoxon signed-rank result of Z=4.792, p<.001.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning questionnaire/survey covering goal setting, strategy use, self-monitoring, time/resource management, motivational control, and self-reflection

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a strong post-intervention SRL profile, especially in forethought, performance/control, and self-reflection, which are durable-skill components of metacognition and self-management. However, help-seeking and collaboration were comparatively lower, suggesting the intervention strengthened individual regulation more than social regulation.
finding.measure: SRL indicator scores by dimension (forethought, performance/implementation & control, motivational belief, self-control & persistence, help-seeking & collaboration, self-reflection/evaluation)

paper_profiles.title: Fostering students’ creative thinking through inquiry-design-based STEM water purification project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding an explicit engineering design cycle to inquiry-based STEM learning improves secondary students’ creative thinking. The authors focus on a sustainability problem—designing a low-cost water purification system—and ask whether an Inquiry-Design-Based Learning integrated STEM model (IDBL-STEM) produces stronger gains than traditional inquiry-based learning (IBL) alone across four creativity dimensions: fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration.

The study was conducted with 10th-grade students in a public senior high school in Padang, West Sumatra, Indonesia. Two intact classes participated in a non-equivalent pretest-posttest control group design: one class received the IDBL-STEM intervention and the other received conventional inquiry instruction. The intervention lasted five sessions over three weeks and included problem exploration, investigation, prototype development, testing, and reflection. Students designed and built water purifier prototypes using recycled and locally available materials, and they also used AI-assisted image generation tools such as Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, or Google Gemini to visualize design ideas.

Results from ANCOVA showed that the IDBL-STEM group improved significantly more than the control group in fluency, flexibility, and originality, but not in elaboration. The authors conclude that iterative design embedded within inquiry is a strong mechanism for fostering divergent creative thinking in STEM classrooms, especially when learning is grounded in authentic environmental problems. They also note that elaboration may require more time and scaffolding, and they position the approach as relevant for sustainability education and the SDGs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental non-equivalent pretest-posttest control group study with ANCOVA and baseline equivalence checks, which supports moderate credibility. It is not randomized, so selection bias remains a concern, but the design and reporting are substantially stronger than purely descriptive work.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports large effects for fluency and flexibility and a medium-to-large effect for originality (partial η²=.140-.262), indicating meaningful impact. However, the outcome is creativity rather than direct mathematics achievement, so the impact is strong on the measured construct but only indirectly relevant to the retrieval topic.

interventions.use_case: Inquiry-Design-Based Learning integrated with a STEM water purification project, where students iteratively designed, prototyped, tested, and refined low-cost water filters using recycled/local materials; AI image generation tools (e.g., Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) were used only as a support for visualizing designs, not as the main intervention.

AI-assisted image generation/visualization support for student design sketches during the water purifier project, including use of tools named ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, or Google Gemini to digitally visualize prototype concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The IDBL-STEM group showed significantly greater gains than the traditional IBL group in three creative-thinking dimensions: fluency, flexibility, and originality, but not elaboration. For fluency, the ANCOVA group effect was significant (F=25.17, p<.001, partial η²=.262) with n=72; for flexibility, F=22.84, p<.001, partial η²=.248; and for originality, F=11.23, p=.001, partial η²=.140. These outcomes were measured with a 10-item creative thinking scale using pretest-posttest scores, indicating stronger divergent thinking under the iterative design condition.
finding.measure: Creative thinking test scores and observational evidence for fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was delivered in a science/biology context around environmental change and water purification, and students used scientific investigation, testing, and redesign to build and evaluate filtration prototypes. The paper reports that the IDBL-STEM condition improved students’ ability to connect scientific concepts with evidence-based testing and iterative refinement, although the primary measured outcome remained creative thinking rather than a direct science achievement test.
finding.measure: Prototype testing, data analysis during filtration trials, and science-based design performance documented through classroom observation

paper_profiles.title: Impact of AI-assisted microlearning on student engagement in an online environment in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-assisted microlearning can improve student engagement in an online higher-education course. The authors focus on the problem that traditional online microlearning is often static and non-adaptive, while generative AI may enable personalized, bite-sized learning experiences that better sustain attention, participation, and motivation.

The intervention was implemented in a multimedia course in the Technology Education department at Palestine Technical University–Kadoorie. The experimental condition used AI-assisted microlearning modules supported by tools such as ChatGPT for generating quizzes and feedback, Canva AI for producing short instructional videos and visual materials, and adaptive learning elements such as quizzes, chatbots, and leaderboards. The comparison group received traditional online learning materials without AI personalization. The study used a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with pre- and post-engagement measures plus forum comments and semi-structured interviews.

Participants were 50 pre-service teachers at the third- and fourth-year undergraduate level in Palestine. Quantitative results showed significant gains in overall engagement and in cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement for the AI-assisted group. Qualitative findings suggested that AI-assisted microlearning increased attention, reduced frustration, supported task completion, encouraged sharing and peer interaction, and made learning feel more personalized. The authors conclude that generative AI combined with microlearning can enhance engagement in online higher education, especially by strengthening cognitive engagement through adaptive and personalized content delivery.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with pre/post comparison and an ANCOVA, but it is not a true randomized controlled trial and uses a small single-site sample. The evidence is strengthened by qualitative triangulation, yet overall credibility is limited by design and generalizability concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on engagement are large in magnitude, especially for cognitive engagement, but the study population is narrow and the outcome is engagement rather than achievement. Given the size of the observed effects but limited external validity, the impact is modest-to-strong for the studied context rather than broadly generalizable.

interventions.use_case: AI-assisted microlearning for an online multimedia course, delivering bite-sized videos, infographics, quizzes, forums, and adaptive content personalized to learner performance and preferences
ChatGPT used to generate personalized quizzes and provide instant feedback and question-answer support within the microlearning workflow
Adaptive personalization of microlearning content, adjusting difficulty and recommending resources based on quiz results and interaction patterns
Gamified microlearning elements including leaderboards, badges, and point-based competition to increase participation and task completion

finding.finding_summary: AI-assisted microlearning significantly improved overall student engagement in a quasi-experimental study of n=50 college students (experimental n=25, control n=25). ANCOVA controlling for pre-test scores found a significant group effect on total engagement, F(1,47)=23.882, p<.001, with partial eta squared reported as 0.825 for total engagement; the authors interpreted this as a large impact. The intervention was also associated with reduced frustration, higher motivation, and greater comfort with learning activities.
finding.measure: Student engagement scale and qualitative interview/forum themes related to engagement, frustration, motivation, and attention

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved multiple engagement-related durable skill dimensions, including cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement. Reported ANCOVA effects were significant for cognitive engagement, F(1,47)=47.171, partial eta squared=0.849; behavioral engagement, F(1,47)=12.215, partial eta squared=0.413; emotional engagement, F(1,47)=7.113, partial eta squared=0.634; and social engagement, F(1,47)=10.018, partial eta squared=0.327, all p<.001. Qualitative themes indicated gains in attention, personalized learning, task completion, sharing, and peer interaction.
finding.measure: Cognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement subscales plus forum/interview coding

finding.finding_summary: The paper was situated in a multimedia course and reported that AI-assisted microlearning helped students understand course concepts, apply multimedia tools, and complete course tasks more effectively. However, the primary measured outcomes were engagement-related rather than direct achievement test scores, so any academic achievement inference is indirect and not tied to a standardized learning outcome.
finding.measure: Qualitative course-related understanding and task completion; no direct achievement test reported

paper_profiles.title: LLAMA LIMA: A Living Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Generative AI on Learning Mathematics (Version 2, 03/26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly evolving evidence base on whether generative AI can improve mathematics learning, and under what conditions such effects occur. The authors argue that conventional meta-analyses become outdated quickly in this area, so they propose a living meta-analysis (LLAMA LIMA) that can be updated regularly as new studies appear.

The intervention under study is not a single educational program but the collection of experimental and quasi-experimental interventions that use generative AI in mathematics education. The authors synthesize studies involving tools such as ChatGPT and closely related generative AI systems used as mathematics experts, tutors/feedback providers, instructors, collaborative-learning facilitators, or teacher-support tools. The meta-analysis includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, and preprints that were undergoing peer review.

The evidence base spans learners from primary school through university and adults, with many studies situated in lower secondary, upper secondary, and bachelor-level settings. Across 21 studies and 38 effect sizes, the pooled effect was positive but modest (g = 0.42), with substantial heterogeneity across studies. The authors conclude that generative AI may support mathematics learning, but effects depend strongly on context, design, and implementation, and the current evidence is still too limited for strong generalizations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a living meta-analysis synthesizing experimental and quasi-experimental studies with a Bayesian multilevel model, which is strong evidence by the requested framework. It is not a single RCT, but the methodology is rigorous and transparent, with PRISMA-LSR reporting and sensitivity analyses.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on mathematics learning is g=0.42, which exceeds the 0.20 threshold for medium/large impact. Although heterogeneity is substantial and the evidence base is still limited, the average effect suggests meaningful potential impact on mathematics achievement.

interventions.use_case: Living meta-analysis of generative AI interventions in mathematics education, including ChatGPT-like systems used for adaptive assessment/tutoring, instructor-style explanations, and problem-solving support in school mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Across 21 studies and 38 effect sizes (n=4,071), the Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis found a positive pooled effect of generative AI interventions on mathematics learning outcomes, g=0.42 with a wide 95% credible interval [0.13, 0.72]. This suggests a small-to-moderate average benefit, though substantial heterogeneity (study-level SD=0.28; within-study SD=0.71) indicates effects vary widely by context and implementation.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning/performance outcomes across included intervention studies

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a didactic problem raised by the widespread availability of generative AI in school mathematics: many traditional tasks can now be solved automatically, reducing students’ engagement in interpretation, decision-making, and mathematical validation. The author asks how mathematics teaching can preserve students’ meaningful mathematical activity in so-called post-AI contexts.

To respond to this issue, the paper studies a classroom experience in which open mathematical tasks are used alongside a didactic regulation device called COMPAS. COMPAS organizes the resolution process into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, generating and exploring results, validating, and socializing/synthesizing. The design intentionally avoids closed prompts and explicit numerical data so that students cannot simply delegate the work to AI and instead must formulate assumptions and make mathematical decisions.

The study was conducted in secondary education in Peru and uses a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach. Data came from student written work, classroom interaction records, and teacher-researcher observations. The findings suggest that when AI use is explicitly regulated and tasks are designed to require interpretation and validation, students retain epistemic control of the mathematical activity. The paper concludes that open task design and didactic regulation can preserve the formative value of mathematics learning even when generative AI is readily available.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative descriptive-interpretive classroom study, not a controlled trial or correlational design. It provides useful practice-based evidence, but causal claims and generalizability are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially meaningful way to preserve mathematical activity in post-AI classrooms, but it reports no quantitative achievement effect sizes. The observed impact is descriptive and unclear in magnitude beyond the single classroom experience.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative secondary-school classroom study, open mathematical tasks regulated through COMPAS were associated with students maintaining epistemic control over mathematical activity even when generative AI was available. The paper does not report effect sizes, but it provides descriptive evidence that students still engaged in interpretation, model construction, and validation rather than delegating the task to AI.
finding.measure: Observed mathematical activity, student written work, classroom interactions, and validation/modeling practices

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the task design fostered mathematical agency, justification, and critical validation of AI-generated or AI-assisted answers. Students were described as retaining control over assumptions, model selection, and plausibility checking, indicating support for higher-order reasoning and metacognitive regulation rather than direct achievement gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative indicators of agency, argumentation, and validation in classroom discourse and student productions

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students perceive and want generative AI to function as a peer collaborator during collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors argue that most prior GenAI in education has focused on tutor-like, one-to-one support, leaving open the question of how AI might work as a teammate in small-group math activity.

To study this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students in the United States. Students experienced grade-aligned math CPS both without AI and with a text-based AI peer technology probe built on GPT-4o. They interacted with two AI peers that differed in proficiency and style, then reflected on the experience through group discussions, interviews, surveys, and design activities where they sketched, revised, and presented their ideal AI peers.

The study found that students wanted AI peers to be mathematically competent but deferential, providing scaffolds such as hints, checks, concept refreshers, and examples rather than full answers. They strongly preferred explicit student control over when the AI speaks and what kind of help it gives. Students also wanted the AI to sound friendly and expert without exaggerated persona effects. Across the study, students judged AI not only by correctness, but by whether it supported co-agency, respected social norms, and offered emotional attunement during struggle.

The paper concludes with design recommendations for future AI peers in middle-school mathematics CPS, emphasizing scaffold-first support, configurable participation control, and peer-like social tone. It also presents the participatory design process itself as a reusable approach for eliciting youth-grounded requirements for classroom AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative participatory design study with some paired survey comparisons, not a controlled efficacy trial. It provides useful evidence about student preferences and interactional effects, but credibility for achievement impact is limited because no direct learning outcome was tested.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report direct achievement gains, only mixed effects on workload and collaboration perceptions. The observed impacts are meaningful for design, but learning impact on mathematics achievement is unclear.

interventions.use_case: A sandboxed GPT-4o-based AI peer used in middle school collaborative mathematics problem solving, where two conversational agents (Alice and Bob) supported student groups with hints, checks, dialogue acts, and peer-like problem solving rather than direct tutoring.

A technology-probe prototype for simulating AI peers in collaborative mathematical problem solving, including a conversation-level CPS stage monitor and individual-level peer-schema simulation to study desired AI peer behaviors and controls.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure achievement gains directly; instead it examined how middle school students experienced AI peers during grade-aligned mathematics problem solving. Students reported that AI peers could reduce temporal demand during CPS (NASA-TLX temporal demand M=5.67, SD=4.38 with AI vs M=9.62, SD=4.13 human-only; p=0.002, d=1.15), but they also found the AI’s help sometimes distracting or overly procedural rather than mathematically productive.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand during math CPS; qualitative perceptions of mathematical help and problem-solving support
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: Students valued encouragement, listening, and emotional attunement from AI peers, but reported that correctness-focused responses often felt cold or frustrating and could increase self-blame. The AI condition was associated with lower group social attraction (GEQ ATGS M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs M=6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94), indicating weaker affective engagement even when the system supported task flow.
finding.measure: GEQ social cohesion / attraction to group-social; qualitative accounts of frustration, encouragement, and trust
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviewees

finding.finding_summary: The AI peer changed how students experienced collaboration: it lowered perceived task coordination in the GEQ (Group Integration-Task M=4.76, SD=1.58 with AI vs M=5.54, SD=1.52 human-only; p=0.047, d=0.81) even while prompting students to articulate preferences for co-agency, turn-taking, and negotiation. Qualitatively, students wanted the AI to support collaboration as a peer rather than control the solution path, highlighting collaboration and metacognitive coordination as central outcomes.
finding.measure: GEQ task coordination; qualitative judgments about co-agency, collaboration, turn-taking, and method negotiation
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; n=18 interviewees

finding.finding_summary: The AI peer reduced perceived time pressure during problem solving, suggesting procedural support improved efficiency (NASA-TLX temporal demand M=5.67, SD=4.38 with AI vs M=9.62, SD=4.13 human-only; p=0.002, d=1.15).
