However, this came with substantially higher physical/interactional workload because students had to manage a text-based interface and interpret AI outputs (physical demand M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand during mathematics CPS

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how teachers should remain involved when generative AI is used to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The central question is whether a "teacher-in-the-loop" approach can produce personalized problems that are both educationally meaningful and efficient to create, especially compared with the promise of student-facing AI personalization that can target finer-grained interests.

In the study, seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers worked with ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify problems from the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum so they better matched their students’ popular-culture interests. Teachers participated in training on personalization, then used ChatGPT during recorded Zoom sessions to generate personalized versions of problems from Unit 4 and later Unit 6 of the curriculum. Their interactions with ChatGPT were logged and coded, and 521 middle school students completed the personalized assignments through ASSISTments. Students also provided closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, plus open-ended feedback on what they liked or wanted changed.

The study finds that teachers used ChatGPT in ways that reflected tradeoffs among grain size, depth, and ownership of personalization. Teachers often asked for broad topical personalization or specific references (brands, celebrities, games, etc.), while also spending substantial effort fixing realism, quantities, readability, and age-appropriateness. Students generally preferred more specific popular-culture references, but they also cared less about whether problems were deeply realistic than teachers did. Personalizing a problem took about four minutes on average, and there was no clear evidence that this became faster over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit. However, problems created with an intermediate number of prompts (about 3-5) received the most favorable student ratings. Overall, the authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports teacher learning and quality control, but it is time-consuming and may not achieve the fine-grained personalization students prefer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/observational study with mixed-methods coding and regression analyses, not an RCT or meta-analysis. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it lacks a control group and does not measure achievement outcomes directly.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear but modest evidence about student preferences and teacher workflow, not direct learning gains. Its practical impact is informative for design and implementation, but the absence of achievement effects and the relatively small, context-specific sample limit claims of broader impact.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students' interests, including rewriting Illustrative Mathematics tasks with popular culture references and checking realism/readability.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not measure math achievement directly, but it did examine how the personalized math tasks were rated on closeness to students' interests and interestingness, which the authors treat as proximal indicators relevant to mathematics learning contexts. Student ratings were higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts to generate a problem (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), and Unit 6 tasks were rated more favorably than Unit 4 tasks (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012), but no test scores or learning gains were reported.
finding.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests for personalized mathematics problems
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 143 problems; ratings available for 52-53 problems depending on measure
finding.effect_size: B=0.240 for 3-5 prompts vs other prompt counts; B=0.33 for Unit 6 vs Unit 4

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded positively to personalized tasks when the content matched their preferred popular culture interests, but many also disliked tasks when the reference did not align with their own interests. In the open-ended feedback, 163 responses implied the problem was interesting versus 243 implying it was not, and students most often requested narrower, more specific references rather than broad topic changes.
finding.measure: Student open-ended interest feedback and 1-5 interestingness/closeness ratings
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454, 449, and 446 open-ended responses across the three survey items

finding.finding_summary: Teacher use of ChatGPT was time-consuming rather than time-saving. On average, personalizing a single problem took 246 seconds (about 4 minutes; SD=165.7) and required 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), with no evidence that efficiency improved over time; in fact, Unit 6 required more prompts and more time than Unit 4 (B=1.26 additional prompts, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; B=70.4 additional seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher time per personalized problem and number of prompts used in ChatGPT
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 prompts; B=70.4 seconds; B=0.240 for optimal 3-5 prompt zone on student ratings

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT and GPT-4 by benchmarking them on a newly created set of natural-language mathematics prompts called GHOSTS, plus a smaller subset called miniGHOSTS. The authors ask what kinds of mathematical tasks these models can handle, where they fail, and whether they can function as useful assistants in mathematical work. The evaluation is not about teaching or learning in classrooms; it is a model-capability study focused on advanced mathematical reasoning.

The intervention/approach is the use of ChatGPT and GPT-4 as mathematical problem-solvers and assistants on tasks spanning graduate-textbook exercises, proof completion, olympiad-style problems, symbolic integration, MATH dataset items, and search-engine-like factual retrieval tasks. The paper introduces a fine-grained manual rating scheme with error codes and warning codes, and it compares different model versions over time. It also uses hand-crafted prompts designed to test specific reasoning behaviors, including filling gaps in proofs and retrieving definitions or theorem names.

The paper’s context is advanced mathematics rather than school instruction. The datasets draw from university-level and graduate-level textbooks, math.stackexchange, symbolic mathematics benchmarks, and olympiad resources. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is only intermittently useful, performing best as a fact/query retrieval aid, while GPT-4 improves performance and can sometimes handle undergraduate-level material. However, both models fall well short of reliable graduate-level mathematical performance, and GPT-4 still makes substantial mistakes.

Overall, the paper argues that ChatGPT can assist knowledgeable users as a search engine or knowledge-base interface for mathematics, but it is not yet dependable for consistently solving proofs or advanced calculations. The work is primarily a benchmark and model analysis paper rather than a study of educational outcomes in schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic benchmark study with human expert ratings, but it is not an experimental study in a K-12 educational setting and does not test learner outcomes. The methodology is clear and careful, yet it is fundamentally an evaluation/benchmark paper rather than causal evidence of instructional impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no direct educational impact on students; it measures model performance on mathematics tasks. Any relevance to education is indirect, so there is no demonstrated effect size on learner achievement to classify as positive impact.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarks ChatGPT and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for solving, completing, and retrieving information for advanced mathematics prompts, including proof completion, definition retrieval, and symbolic integration.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates ChatGPT (9-Jan-2023 and 30-Jan-2023) and GPT-4 on 709 mathematical prompts (miniGHOSTS subset for GPT-4, n=170). Performance varies strongly by task: ChatGPT averaged 3.20 (SD=1.23) and 3.29 (SD=1.28) across versions, while GPT-4 averaged 4.15 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS. The models did best on factual retrieval and some undergraduate-level tasks, but performed poorly on graduate-level proofs, olympiad problems, and more complex symbolic calculations; e.g., ChatGPT scored 2.51 (SD=0.87) on the symbolic-integration subset and only 29% perfect scores on MATH samples, while GPT-4 reached 70% perfect scores on corresponding miniGHOSTS MATH questions.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical solution quality on curated math prompts (1-5 rating scale), including proof completion, theorem/fact retrieval, symbolic integration, olympiad problem solving, and MATH accuracy

paper_profiles.title: A mathematical model for the bullying dynamics in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of bullying dynamics in schools and asks under what conditions bullying can persist or be controlled. Rather than analyzing a classroom intervention or educational technology, it develops a mathematical compartmental model to represent how bullying-related states evolve over time within a school population. The model divides individuals into four groups: susceptible, bullies, exposed victims, and violent individuals.

The proposed approach combines analytical ordinary differential equations with numerical simulations on two-dimensional grids. Transitions between states are driven by interaction-based contagion-like processes and spontaneous changes, with parameters intended to represent social pressure, exposure to bullying, student aggression, parental intervention, and anti-bullying school programs. The paper examines both a homogeneous mixing setting and a spatially localized agent-based grid simulation.

The population context is school-aged students in schools, with parents, teachers, and administrators discussed as relevant actors in bullying prevention and intervention. The main conclusion is that bullying-free and endemic equilibria can both arise, with the outcome depending mainly on the balance between bullying recruitment and control/recovery processes. In particular, stronger anti-bullying school programs and other interventions that increase the rate at which bullying stops can reduce or eliminate bullying, while higher contagion can sustain bullying and associated violent behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/mathematical modeling paper, not an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention or AI system. It contains no randomized design, observational dataset, or measured student achievement outcomes relevant to the retrieved topic.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on middle school mathematics achievement or ChatGPT/GenAI support. Its findings concern bullying dynamics and institutional control in a stylized model, with no evidence of educational performance effects.

finding.finding_summary: This paper models bullying dynamics and anti-bullying control mechanisms rather than testing an educational technology intervention. The main empirical-like result is theoretical: bullying-free equilibrium is locally stable when α<γ (equivalently R0<1), while endemic bullying persists when α>γ; no student-level achievement outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Theoretical equilibrium stability and simulated compartment densities (s, b, e, v) in an ordinary differential equation model and lattice simulations

finding.finding_summary: The model suggests that stronger anti-bullying school programs and parental interventions reduce the equilibrium bullying density and can eradicate bullying when the contagion parameter α is below the control parameter γ. This is supported by analytical fixed-point and stability analysis plus agent-based simulations on a 60x60 lattice, but the study does not report behavioral effect sizes from real schools.
finding.measure: Analytical threshold condition (α vs γ), equilibrium densities, and numerical simulation outcomes under varying α

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how to broaden access to AI education by embedding a foundational AI problem-solving concept, Breadth-First Search (BFS), into ordinary middle school science instruction. The authors ask whether middle school students can learn BFS meaningfully through an integrated curriculum and whether teachers view the curriculum as a good fit for classroom science instruction. The work is motivated by the broader problem that many AI learning opportunities are stand-alone experiences and may not reach most students.

The intervention was a seven-day module, co-designed with a classroom teacher, that combined simulation-based activities in an interactive Snap!-based environment called i-SAIL with unplugged tracing and science-context activities. Students first learned BFS using map-based pathfinding and then applied it to contact tracing and virus transmission scenarios in a rural middle school health science unit. The implementation occurred in six classrooms across grades 6 to 8 in one U.S. public middle school, with data drawn from pre/post knowledge assessments, a paper-based BFS worksheet, student artifacts, and a teacher interview.

Findings showed significant gains on the BFS assessment from pre to post, and most students could correctly identify the shortest path on the unplugged worksheet, though many struggled to document the procedure fully and accurately. Teacher interview feedback suggested the module fit well within the science curriculum and helped students understand both the AI ideas and the science content. The teacher also noted opportunities for improvement, including simpler language, more explicit vocabulary support, and additional teacher-facing scaffolds. Overall, the study concludes that AI problem-solving can be taught productively in middle school subject-area instruction when the curriculum is interactive, well scaffolded, and locally co-designed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom-based implementation study with pre/post assessment, student artifacts, and a teacher interview, but it is not a randomized or controlled design. Evidence is useful and directly relevant, but credibility is limited by the single-group, small-sample, mostly qualitative/quasi-experimental methodology.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pre/post gain on BFS understanding was moderate (dz=0.453), which exceeds the 0.20 threshold for blue on the effect-size rule, but the study is small and context-specific. Given the rural middle-school setting and strong curriculum fit, the impact is promising for a priority population, though broader generalization remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Interactive BFS learning simulation in I-SAIL/Snap! where middle school students trace breadth-first search on map-based graphs, use frontier/visited lists, and apply the algorithm to shortest-path and contact-tracing scenarios.

Unplugged paper-based BFS tracing and science-integrated contact-network activities (including a Glo Germ virus-spread simulation) used to reinforce algorithmic reasoning within middle school science instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Students showed improved understanding of BFS and AI problem-solving after the curriculum. On the matched pre/post assessment, scores increased from M=0.683 (SD=0.219) to M=0.790 (SD=0.232) for n=41, with statistically significant gains in a paired t-test, t(40)=2.90, p=.006, and Wilcoxon signed-rank test, W=87, p=.008; effect size was moderate (Cohen’s dz=0.453).
finding.measure: Matched pre/post BFS knowledge assessment (5-item multiple-choice score proportion correct)

finding.finding_summary: On the post-activity worksheet, most students (64.5%) were able to correctly identify the shortest path using BFS, indicating practical application of the procedure after instruction. However, many written traces were incomplete, especially in documenting intermediate expansions and exploration order, suggesting partial rather than fully procedural mastery.
finding.measure: Paper-based BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and completeness

finding.finding_summary: Teacher interview feedback indicated that students were engaged productively with the module and that movement-based, interactive tasks helped students retain and recall the material. The teacher described the curriculum as fitting well within the science unit and noted that students 'started to really understand' on days with more active participation.
finding.measure: Semi-structured teacher interview on engagement, recall, and classroom fit

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Pretesting with Conversational AI on Retention of Needed Information
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether pretesting before using conversational AI can improve learning and retention, extending prior work on “thinking before googling” to ChatGPT. The authors investigate whether asking learners to attempt a problem from memory before consulting ChatGPT leads to better later recall than giving immediate access to the AI.

The intervention was a pretest condition versus a no-pretest condition. In the pretest group, participants first attempted to solve a complex problem before receiving ChatGPT assistance; in the control group, participants accessed ChatGPT immediately. The task involved chi-square analysis in a cybersecurity scenario, and the learning materials were embedded in a statistics course context.

Participants were 61 undergraduate information sciences students at a large public research university in Pennsylvania, United States, after exclusions from an initial sample of 73. The study found no difference between groups on the earlier recall test, but the pretest group performed significantly better on the final transfer test. The authors conclude that pretesting can improve retention and application of complex statistical concepts even when learners use conversational AI as the information source.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized true experimental study with a clear comparison condition and posttest/transfer outcome, which supports causal inference. Confidence is tempered by the small sample, single course context, and an unusually large reported effect size that may warrant caution about robustness and generalizability.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect on the final transfer test is very large (d=8.59), exceeding the threshold for a large impact. The intervention appears to substantially improve learning outcomes in this sample when pretesting is combined with ChatGPT use.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational AI information source during a problem-solving task in intermediate statistics, providing step-by-step help for two-way chi-square analysis after or without an initial pretesting attempt.

finding.finding_summary: Students who completed a pretest before using ChatGPT scored significantly higher on the delayed transfer/final test than students who accessed ChatGPT immediately. Final test performance was M=91.85 (SD=9.52) for the pretest group versus M=78.59 (SD=7.62) for the no-pretest group, t(58)=-5.974, p<.001, Cohen’s d=8.59 (as reported).
finding.measure: 11-item multiple-choice transfer/final test on two-way chi-square analysis and concept application

finding.finding_summary: The study indicates that pretesting before ChatGPT use improved retention and transfer of learned statistical concepts, suggesting stronger learning-related metacognitive engagement and problem-solving persistence. However, the recall test for prior one-way chi-square knowledge showed no group difference, t(58)=0.584, p=.562, with similar means (M=71.03 vs M=72.90), so the measured benefit emerged primarily on later application rather than baseline recall.
finding.measure: Delayed recall test and final transfer test
finding.effect_size: final test d=8.59; recall test not_reported
finding.std_deviation: recall SDs=13.72 and 11.01; final SDs=9.52 and 7.62

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations. The authors focus on a practical concern in educational use of large language models: students may accept fluent but wrong AI outputs without sufficient verification.

The study tested a short educational text explaining ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations, risks, and appropriate use, compared with a control text that only introduced ChatGPT more generally. High school seniors in Estonia were randomly assigned to intervention or control conditions, then solved eight math reasoning puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were intentionally incorrect. The task was designed to measure both over-reliance on wrong advice and under-reliance on correct advice, along with response times and self-reported perceptions of AI literacy.

Results showed widespread over-reliance overall: students adopted incorrect ChatGPT recommendations in about half of the cases. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance, although it did increase self-reported knowledge about ChatGPT’s working mechanism and usage, and it unexpectedly increased under-reliance, meaning participants were more likely to ignore correct recommendations. The authors conclude that short AI literacy texts may be insufficient to counter over-reliance on LLM outputs and that improving AI literacy alone may not be enough to change reliance behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized experiment with a clear intervention and outcome measures, but the sample is very small (n=36) and the study relies on self-report plus a bespoke task, limiting generalizability and precision. It is best characterized as a small experimental study with some methodological concerns rather than a fully robust RCT.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention showed no beneficial effect on reducing over-reliance and instead significantly increased under-reliance, with one moderate effect (d=0.78) in the undesired direction. Overall impact is unclear to negative for the target population.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT to support high school students as a conversational problem-solving aid for math puzzles, with students deciding whether to adopt ChatGPT’s recommendations.
A short AI literacy educational text about ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations/risks, prompt writing, and tips for wise use, used as an intervention to reduce over-reliance on ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment with 36 12th-grade students (n=19 intervention, n=17 control), the short AI literacy text did not significantly reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations on math puzzles: over-reliance was 48.68% vs 55.88%, Welch’s t(28.78)=-0.73, p=.236, d=-0.25. However, it significantly increased under-reliance on correct recommendations: 36.84% vs 19.12%, t(34)=2.35, p=.025, d=0.78, suggesting a shift toward excessive skepticism rather than calibrated reliance.
finding.measure: Over-reliance and under-reliance rates while solving eight math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations; initial decision time as a related behavioral measure
finding.std_deviation: Over-reliance SD=24.26 (intervention) and 33.69 (control); under-reliance SD=24.11 (intervention) and 20.78 (control)

finding.finding_summary: The study also found that longer deliberation was associated with less over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT advice (Spearman rs=-0.41, p=.013) and more under-reliance on correct advice (rs=0.35, p=.038). This indicates that slower, more analytical decision-making reduced blind acceptance of erroneous AI output but also increased the chance of ignoring correct AI suggestions.
finding.measure: Initial decision time for puzzles with incorrect recommendations and correct recommendations, correlated with reliance behavior

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a policy and competition-law question rather than an educational intervention: whether generative AI systems should be covered by the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA). The authors argue that the current DMA framework, which targets established platform services and gatekeepers, does not adequately address the emerging market power of generative AI providers.

The paper examines generative AI as a potential platform service, using OpenAI and similar systems as examples of how foundation models can be monetized through public-facing tools and APIs. It analyzes why major generative AI developers may become gatekeepers due to computing power requirements, early-mover advantages, data resources, network effects, and integrated service ecosystems.

Rather than studying participants or an instructional context, the paper develops a legal and regulatory framework for amending the DMA. Its main conclusion is that generative AI services should be explicitly integrated into the DMA’s core platform services list, and that some developers may already meet the criteria for gatekeeper designation. The paper argues that this would help preserve contestability, fairness, diversity, and innovation in the generative AI market.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/policy paper about the EU Digital Markets Act and generative AI market structure, not an empirical education study. It contains no experimental, quasi-experimental, or observational methodology evaluating learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measured educational intervention effects or student outcomes, so there is no evidence of impact on learning, engagement, or efficiency in the retrieved topic area.

paper_profiles.title: The mathematics in middle-aged Arab caliphate and it application to contemporary teaching in high schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys major mathematical contributions of scholars from the medieval Arab caliphate and argues that this historical material can be used to stimulate students’ interest and mutual respect in contemporary mathematics teaching. Rather than evaluating a new instructional technology or intervention, the article presents historical and mathematical exposition centered on the development of algebra, number theory, trigonometry, and related topics in Islamic civilization.

The paper discusses a series of classical mathematical puzzles and then summarizes the work of figures such as al-Khwarizmi, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Haytham, al-Karaji, Ibn Tahir al-Baghdadi, Omar Khayyam, al-Samawal, al-Tusi, and al-Qalasadi. These contributions are framed as content that can be incorporated into high school mathematics lessons, especially to enrich algebra and mathematical history teaching.

The context is contemporary high school mathematics education, but the paper does not report an empirical classroom study, participant sample, or measured achievement outcomes. Its main conclusion is that Arabic and Islamic mathematical heritage is rich and pedagogically useful as cultural and historical material for secondary mathematics instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a historical review/opinion-style article rather than an empirical study. It reports no research design, no participant sample, and no measured outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no evidence of measurable educational impact and no intervention effects. Its contribution is descriptive and curricular, not evaluative.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate any instructional technology, AI system, or student learning intervention. It is a historical/expository article describing Arab mathematicians and suggesting that some problems and historical content could be used in high school teaching. No achievement data, sample, control group, or effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: On the Robustness of ChatGPT in Teaching Korean Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT can solve and evaluate Korean mathematics questions, with a focus on understanding the model’s robustness in a multilingual educational setting. The authors frame the work as addressing a key limitation of current large language models: strong performance in English but weaker performance in non-English mathematical contexts. They ask two questions: how accurately ChatGPT solves Korean math problems, and how effectively it can rate and categorize those questions.

The study uses a validated set of 586 Korean mathematics questions drawn from the South Korean CSAT, a high-stakes college admissions exam. ChatGPT is used in a zero-shot setting to answer the questions and to rate them on eleven criteria such as difficulty, cognitive demand, clarity, fairness, and analytical depth. The paper also conducts topic analysis and additional prompt-engineering experiments, including translation to English and use of GPT-4o and o1-preview for some incorrect items.

Results show that ChatGPT solved 66.72% of the questions correctly, with better performance on simpler, lower-marked items and worse performance on sequential and diagram-based problems. At the same time, the model’s ratings were broadly consistent with human and educational-theory expectations, suggesting it can be useful for assessment analysis and personalized learning support. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise in multilingual mathematics education, but improvements are needed for low-resource languages, multi-step reasoning, and visual/diagram interpretation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational/benchmarking study of a single AI model on a fixed exam dataset, with no randomized comparison to instructional alternatives. It is methodologically useful but does not meet stronger causal-evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are mainly descriptive and context-specific, with no demonstrated classroom-level achievement effect. The model shows promise for multilingual math support and assessment analysis, but the evidence of educational impact remains indirect and modest.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT to solve Korean CSAT mathematics questions and to rate/categorize mathematics items on eleven assessment criteria, including difficulty, cognitive demand, clarity, and analytical depth.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 391 of 586 Korean mathematics questions correctly, for an overall accuracy of 66.72% in zero-shot evaluation. Performance was much stronger on lower-mark questions (near 100% accuracy on 2-point items) and dropped to about 50% on the most complex 4-point items, with notably poorer results on sequential and diagram-based questions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on CSAT mathematics questions; correctness by point value; performance on diagram vs non-diagram items

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s item-rating outputs were reported as substantially consistent with educational theory and test-taker perspectives, suggesting utility for higher-order judgment tasks rather than direct instruction alone. The model’s predicted difficulty, cognitive demand, and analytical depth aligned with question marks and with the notion that harder questions require more advanced reasoning and longer solution time.
finding.measure: Correlation/consistency of predicted difficulty, cognitive demand, time requirement, originality/engagement, and analytical depth with question marks and human/educational expectations

finding.finding_summary: The paper found ChatGPT could classify and rate CSAT mathematics questions across eleven criteria and perform topic analysis, indicating potential to support assessment design and content analysis workflows. The authors further showed that prompt translation and GPT-4o improved correction of previously wrong answers, increasing accuracy from 66.72% to 75.09% in the best reported scenario for incorrect items, which suggests efficiency gains for multilingual problem-solving workflows.
finding.measure: Accuracy on incorrect-question repair scenarios; rating and categorization performance; topic analysis utility
finding.study_size: n=586 questions; n=195 initially incorrect items

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in education. The authors ask what kinds of data are collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI-based research, what benefits AI offers teachers, what challenges teachers face, and which AI methods are used in studies involving teachers. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes 44 journal articles published in the Web of Science over the previous 20 years.

The review shows that teachers are involved in AI studies mainly through self-reports, grades, observations, video, interviews, and other data sources used to train or evaluate AI systems. Teachers often serve as models for AI training, provide data about their professional development, help define assessment criteria, and validate automated scoring systems. The most common benefits identified are support for planning, implementation, and assessment, such as identifying student needs, enabling timely monitoring and feedback, and assisting with automated scoring and evaluation.

The paper concludes that AI can reduce teacher workload and support instructional decision-making, but current systems still face important limitations, including limited reliability, restricted technical capacity, weak adaptability across contexts, and insufficient infrastructure or teacher expertise. The authors also note that pre-service teachers are underrepresented, multimodal data are rarely used, and teachers are only minimally involved in the design of AI systems. They argue that future AI-for-education research should involve teachers more deeply and expand beyond narrow data types and prediction tasks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it does not present a new causal evaluation of an intervention. The paper synthesizes qualitative/coding results from 44 empirical studies, so it provides descriptive evidence rather than direct experimental evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests broad implications for teacher use of AI in planning, implementation, and assessment, but it reports no single pooled effect size or directly tested outcome impact. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and field-mapping rather than measurable K-12 impact.

paper_profiles.title: An explanatory study of factors influencing engagement in AI education at the K-12 Level: an extension of the classic TAM model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what factors influence K-12 students’ engagement and attitudes toward AI education when learning with generative AI tools. The authors extend the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) by adding four cognitive factors—AI intrinsic motivation, AI readiness, AI confidence, and AI anxiety—and three human-computer interaction factors—user interface, content, and learner-interface interactivity—to explain perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and attitudes toward AI learning.

The study was conducted with 210 Chinese students in grades 7 to 9 who completed a one-month AI course. The course centered on creating AI-themed picture books and included use of ChatGPT, Midjourney, and AI translation tools. Students completed post-course questionnaires, and the authors analyzed the data using structural equation modeling. After screening, 197 valid responses were used in the final analysis.

Results showed that intrinsic motivation, readiness, confidence, interface quality, content quality, and learner-interface interactivity all positively predicted perceived usefulness and/or perceived ease of use, while AI anxiety had negative effects on both. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, in turn, positively predicted attitudes toward learning AI. The paper concludes that both cognitive and interface-related factors matter for K-12 AI course acceptance and suggests that AI4K12 curriculum design should account for these dimensions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational SEM study with a clear survey-based methodology, but it is not an experimental or causal design. Credibility is limited for subgroup effects or learning gains because outcomes are attitudes and acceptance perceptions rather than academic achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports modest positive path coefficients for acceptance and attitude constructs, but these are not direct achievement effects. The impacts are meaningful for engagement and adoption of GenAI in K-12, yet they are indirect and based on self-report rather than performance gains.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-supported K-12 AI course activities using ChatGPT for generating narrative text, discussing AI concepts, and supporting students' creation of AI-themed picture books; Midjourney is also used as a generative AI companion for image creation in the same course.

finding.finding_summary: This correlational SEM study (valid n=197) found that students' AI intrinsic motivation, readiness, confidence, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use were positively associated with attitudes toward learning AI through GenAI, while AI anxiety was negatively associated. Reported path coefficients included AIIM→PU β=0.211, AIRD→PU β=0.152, AICF→PU β=0.158, AIAX→PU β=-0.130, and AIAX→PEOU β=-0.162; PU→ATT β=0.208 and PEOU→ATT β=0.228.
finding.measure: Survey-based TAM constructs: attitudes toward AI learning, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, intrinsic motivation, readiness, confidence, and anxiety
finding.effect_size: β=0.211 to -0.162 across paths; PU→ATT β=0.208; PEOU→ATT β=0.228

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes engagement, learner-interface interactivity, and attitude formation as key outcomes of using GenAI in K-12 AI education. Students rated the course and GenAI-supported learning positively, and the model showed that perceived usefulness and ease of use significantly predicted attitudes toward the AI course (PU→ATT β=0.208; PEOU→ATT β=0.228) in the valid sample of n=197.
finding.measure: Attitudes toward AI course learning; perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as proximal engagement-related outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic research. A multi-group analysis of students’ awareness and perceptions using gender and programme type
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether university students’ awareness of artificial intelligence (AI), their perceptions of AI, and their actual use of AI tools in academic research are related, and whether these relationships differ by gender and programme type. The authors frame the work as addressing a gap in the literature, since prior studies have focused more on AI for instruction and classroom use than on students’ use of AI for research activities such as literature review, summarisation, paraphrasing, plagiarism checking, and data analysis.

The study surveyed 5,554 students from six universities in Nigeria, including undergraduate, master’s, and doctoral-level students. It measured awareness, perception, and utilisation of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, Turnitin, Elicit, Consensus, Mendeley, and others. Using exploratory factor analysis, t-tests, structural equation modelling, mediation analysis, and multi-group analysis, the authors tested whether awareness predicted perception and utilisation, whether perception mediated the awareness–utilisation link, and whether these paths differed for male versus female students and undergraduate versus postgraduate students.

The main findings were that students reported high awareness, positive perceptions, and high utilisation of AI tools in research. Awareness positively predicted perception, and both awareness and perception predicted utilisation; perception partially mediated the awareness–utilisation relationship. Subgroup analysis showed notable gender and programme differences: males were generally more aware and more positive in perception, while females reported higher utilisation; postgraduate students were consistently higher than undergraduates on awareness and utilisation. The authors conclude that AI is already widely present in students’ research practices and that curriculum and support strategies should account for differences by gender and academic level when integrating AI into higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional correlational survey with SEM and multi-group analysis, but it is not an intervention study and has no causal design. It provides useful subgroup evidence, but causal credibility is limited and the measures are self-reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports high self-reported use of AI tools and statistically significant subgroup differences, but the practical effect sizes are mostly not reported and the outcome is descriptive rather than demonstrated learning impact. This suggests unclear-to-modest impact on general higher-education research behavior rather than strong educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based assessment of university students' awareness, perceptions, and self-reported utilisation of AI tools for academic research, including tools such as ChatGPT, SciSpace, Elicit, Consensus, Grammarly, QuillBot, Turnitin, and Mendeley.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported a high level of utilisation of AI tools for academic research (M=20.932, SD=5.67, t(5419)=303.776, p<.001). The paper treats this as evidence that AI tools are widely used to support research tasks such as literature review, paraphrasing, editing, plagiarism checking, and report writing.
finding.measure: Self-reported utilisation of AI tools for academic research

paper_profiles.title: A cross-sectional look at teacher reactions, worries, and professional development needs related to generative AI in an urban school district
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers in a large urban school district responded to the rapid emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The study asks whether teacher attitudes toward AI chatbots vary by grade level taught, subject area, and years of teaching experience, and it also investigates the concerns, benefits, and professional development needs teachers associate with AI use in schools.

The researchers used a mixed-methods design based on a districtwide survey of certificated educators in one large U.S. urban district. The sample included 1,454 completed responses after cleaning. Teachers answered close-ended questions about AI chatbot allowability for several academic tasks (idea generation, editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation), plus open-ended questions about perceived benefits, concerns, and professional learning needs. The study also used logistic regression for quantitative associations and thematic coding for qualitative responses.

Results showed that willingness to allow AI chatbot use decreased as grade level increased, with elementary teachers generally more permissive than middle and high school teachers. More experienced teachers, especially in elementary and high school settings, were generally more restrictive than less experienced teachers. Teachers also distinguished between risks and benefits for themselves versus students: plagiarism and overreliance were seen as especially serious risks for students, while misinformation and insufficient AI knowledge were more salient for teachers. Professional development needs differed by grade level, with elementary and middle school teachers wanting basic AI literacy and high school teachers emphasizing guidance on student use and detecting AI-generated work. Overall, the paper argues for grade-specific and role-specific professional development and policy support for AI integration in K-12 education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed cross-sectional mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, logistic regression, and chi-square analyses, but it is not experimental and cannot support causal claims. The evidence is useful for understanding teacher attitudes and subgroup differences, but it is correlational and based on a single district.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s findings have clear policy and professional-development relevance, but the outcomes are perceptions and intended allowability rather than student achievement or behavior change. The practical impact is important but indirect and of unclear magnitude for learners.

interventions.use_case: Teachers’ perceptions, allowability judgments, concerns, and professional development needs related to generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT for student and teacher academic tasks (idea generation, paper editing, full-paper writing, concept explanation, and code generation).

finding.finding_summary: This cross-sectional survey of 1,454 teachers found substantial grade-level differences in attitudes toward generative AI adoption and in professional development needs. Teachers in higher grade levels were less willing to allow AI chatbot use, with marginal effects showing decreases in allowability probability of 0.121 for idea generation, 0.117 for paper editing, 0.135 for full-paper writing, 0.125 for concept explanation, and 0.150 for code generation across grade levels. Elementary and middle school teachers prioritized basic AI literacy, while high school teachers more often wanted guidance on managing student AI use and detecting AI-generated work.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses on allowability of AI chatbot uses, reported concerns/benefits, and professional development needs; logistic regression and chi-square tests

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that generative AI chatbots could improve their own work efficiency, especially for lesson planning and information retrieval. In the coded open-ended responses, 21.41% identified preparing lesson plans or materials as a benefit for teachers, and 13.62% identified increased efficiency; 9.13% mentioned information search support. By contrast, only 4.19% believed chatbots would increase students’ efficiency, suggesting the main perceived productivity gains were for educators rather than learners.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses coded for perceived benefits of AI chatbots

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ comments emphasized both potential support for learning and concerns about students’ overreliance, plagiarism, and reduced independent thinking. Overreliance was the most frequently named concern for students (29.52%), and plagiarism/misuse was cited by 26.35% of teachers for student use; this indicates strong perceived risk to critical thinking and authentic writing development. At the same time, some teachers saw AI as useful for idea generation and concept explanation, suggesting a mixed perceived effect on durable skills rather than a simple positive or negative impact.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses coded for concerns and benefits, especially overreliance, plagiarism, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined teacher allowability of AI use for writing-related tasks. Teachers were least willing to allow AI to edit or complete a paper, and allowability declined with grade level; more experienced elementary teachers were also substantially less likely to allow idea generation, paper editing, and full-paper writing (e.g., dy/dx = -0.489, -0.502, and -0.587 respectively, all p<0.001, n=113-115). These results indicate strong resistance to generative AI for student writing support, especially in higher grades and among more experienced teachers.
finding.measure: Logistic regression on teacher allowability judgments for idea generation, paper editing/completion, and full-paper writing
finding.effect_size: dy/dx reported as negative marginal effects; exact standardized effect not reported
finding.confidence_interval: [0.025, 0.975] reported for marginal effects in tables; exact CI values vary by item

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Impact of ChatGPT on Mathematics Performance: The Influential Role of Student Interest
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT use is associated with mathematics performance and whether student interest in mathematics changes that relationship. The authors frame the study around a concern in mathematics education: students often struggle with abstract concepts and procedural problem solving, while AI tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being used as study supports. The paper asks not only whether ChatGPT relates to achievement, but also whether interest in mathematics serves as a moderator of that relationship.

The study used a quantitative survey design with structured questionnaires administered to 250 mathematics education students at Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (AAMUSTED) in Kumasi, Ghana. Participants included undergraduate Bachelor of Science students and postgraduate students pursuing MPhil and PhD degrees. The data were analyzed with SPSS and AMOS using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling with path analysis. Measures captured self-reported ChatGPT use, mathematics interest, and mathematics performance.

Results showed that ChatGPT use was positively associated with mathematics interest, but its direct association with mathematics performance was negative and statistically significant. Mathematics interest was positively associated with performance, and the interaction term between ChatGPT use and mathematics interest was also positive and significant, indicating moderation. The authors conclude that ChatGPT should be used cautiously in mathematics education and should complement, not replace, conventional learning. They argue that students’ interest in mathematics can help offset the negative direct association observed between ChatGPT use and performance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quantitative correlational/path analysis study using questionnaires and SEM, not an experimental or randomized design. It provides reported coefficients and model fit, but the evidence is observational and vulnerable to self-report bias and confounding.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a large negative direct association between ChatGPT use and mathematics performance, alongside a positive moderation by interest, but these are correlational path estimates rather than causal effects. Overall impact is unclear for K-12 because the sample is university mathematics education students, not middle school learners.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT as an AI chatbot for mathematics learning, problem solving, and explanation of complex math concepts among university mathematics education students.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of n=250 mathematics education students, ChatGPT usage had a direct negative association with mathematics performance (standardized estimate β=-0.757, p<.01), while the ChatGPT × mathematics interest interaction was positive and significant (β=0.206, p<.01). The paper also reports a positive direct association between mathematics interest and performance (β=0.442, p<.01), suggesting that interest buffers the negative performance link from ChatGPT use.
finding.measure: Mathematics performance scale in a questionnaire; path analysis in SEM
finding.effect_size: β=-0.757 for ChatGPT→performance; β=0.206 for interaction; β=0.442 for interest→performance

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT usage was positively associated with students’ interest in mathematics in the same sample of n=250 (β=0.839, p<.01). Interest in mathematics also positively predicted mathematics performance (β=0.442, p<.01), and the authors interpret ChatGPT as increasing motivation/interest rather than directly improving achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics interest scale in a questionnaire
finding.effect_size: β=0.839 for ChatGPT→interest; β=0.442 for interest→performance

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive Insights from Emotional Intelligence: A Systematic Review of EI Models in Educational Achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how emotional intelligence (EI) relates to educational achievement and whether different EI models—especially Trait EI, Ability EI, and Mixed EI—are associated with students’ performance, engagement, motivation, and classroom behavior. The authors frame EI as an increasingly important construct in education because emotions, regulation, and social functioning may shape learning outcomes alongside cognitive ability.

The study is a systematic review of 64 peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 2023, following PRISMA guidelines and assessed with AMSTAR-2. The included evidence spans randomized controlled trials, longitudinal studies, reviews, and meta-analyses, and covers both students and teachers across educational contexts. The review synthesizes findings on interventions and correlational evidence rather than testing a single intervention directly.

Across the literature, the authors conclude that all three EI models are positively related to academic success, but in different ways. Trait EI is emphasized as influencing motivation, engagement, resilience, stress management, and teacher-student relationships through self-perceptions and personality-related competencies. Ability EI is highlighted as more directly tied to cognitive processes such as attention, memory, problem-solving, and emotional regulation, which can support grades and test performance. Mixed EI is presented as the most comprehensive approach because it combines self-perceived and actual emotional skills. The review argues that embedding EI-oriented curricula and interventions in schools may improve academic outcomes and the learning environment, though the paper also notes that effects vary by model, age, and educational context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review using PRISMA methods and includes a large set of peer-reviewed studies, including RCTs, longitudinal studies, and meta-analyses. The paper also reports quality appraisal using AMSTAR-2, which strengthens methodological transparency, though the review itself is not a new primary experiment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad positive relationships between EI and academic/social-emotional outcomes, but it does not report a single pooled intervention effect for the review itself. The impact is therefore promising but somewhat unclear for direct educational practice, especially for the requested middle school mathematics/ChatGPT topic.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a systematic review of 64 studies on emotional intelligence (EI) and academic achievement, not an intervention study. Across the reviewed literature, both Ability EI and Trait EI are reported as positively associated with academic success, with the strongest evidence coming from studies linking EI to grades, achievement, and related performance outcomes. No pooled effect size was reported for the review as a whole, but the paper summarizes consistent positive relations across studies.
finding.measure: Academic achievement, school grades, standardized test performance, and related educational outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review places substantial emphasis on EI-related social-emotional outcomes, including engagement, motivation, stress management, behavioral adjustment, and resilience. It reports that Trait EI and Ability EI are associated with better engagement and motivation, and that achievement emotions show meaningful relations with performance, including a meta-analytic correlation of ρ=.27 for enjoyment of learning and academic performance, and negative correlations for anger (ρ=-.35) and boredom (ρ=-.25).
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, stress management, burnout, resilience, and achievement emotions
finding.study_size: n=64 studies reviewed; specific cited meta-analytic samples vary

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that EI supports durable skills such as problem-solving, self-regulation, and metacognitive functioning, which in turn contribute to academic success. This is presented as a synthesis of the included literature rather than a single causal estimate; one cited meta-analysis on executive functions reports a moderate relation with academic performance (r=.365), with working memory showing r=.370.
finding.measure: Executive functions, self-regulation, cognition, problem-solving, and metacognitive-related competencies
finding.study_size: n=64 studies reviewed; cited meta-analysis n=7,947 children

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an activity-based teaching method improves secondary school students’ mathematics achievement compared with the traditional lecture method. The motivation is the persistent poor performance of Nigerian secondary students in mathematics and the need for more effective instructional approaches.

The intervention studied is an activity-based method of teaching mathematics, contrasted with lecture-based instruction. The study used a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with intact classes and analyzed the results using ANCOVA to control for pretest scores. The content focus was Senior Secondary II mathematics topics, specifically circle geometry and construction.

The participants were 96 Senior Secondary II students from two government-owned schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. Students were split into an experimental group taught with activity-based methods and a control group taught with lecture methods. Results showed significantly higher posttest achievement for the activity-based group, with the authors concluding that activity-based teaching can improve mathematics learning and should be adopted more widely in secondary schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with intact classes and ANCOVA, but it is not randomized at the individual level and has limited sample size from two schools. It provides suggestive causal evidence, but credibility is below a strong RCT standard.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect on mathematics achievement is substantial for the study context (η²=0.261, well above a modest threshold). The intervention targets a priority population of secondary school students in a low-performing mathematics context, supporting a green impact rating.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study of SSS 2 students in Nigeria (n=96; 48 activity-based, 48 lecture), students taught with the activity-based method achieved significantly higher posttest mathematics scores than those taught with lecture after controlling for pretest scores. The paper reports ANCOVA results of F(1,93)=114.461, p<0.001, with partial eta squared η²=0.261 for teaching method; pretest also explained substantial variance (η²=0.552).
finding.measure: 20-item Essay Mathematics Test (MT) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest scores
finding.std_deviation: Experimental posttest SD=8.84; Control posttest SD=6.22

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German-language tasks grounded in middle school curricula. The main problem addressed is that existing multimodal benchmarks are largely English-language, often multiple-choice, and may not reflect real-world visual reasoning with subject-specific background knowledge. The authors argue that such benchmarks can overestimate practical understanding and do not adequately test open-ended reasoning in non-English contexts.

The paper’s approach is to assemble a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine school subjects, including mathematics, history, geography, biology, arts, music, physics, religion, and sports. The questions were collected from German school textbooks for grades 8–10 and supplemented with author-created items; some images also contain the question text or require adversarial handling of unanswerable questions. The study evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs, using LLM-as-a-judge methods for scoring free-text answers.

The benchmark targets middle school-level content in Germany, specifically grades eight to ten, and includes tasks that require combining visual interpretation with background knowledge. The results show that even strong VLMs struggle substantially, with best overall accuracy below 45% and especially weak performance in math, music, and adversarial questions. The authors conclude that middle school tasks are a meaningful and underused stress test for multimodal AI, and that German-language, open-ended benchmarks reveal weaknesses that are not obvious from standard leaderboard scores.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear methodology and a substantial test set, but it is not an intervention study and does not use randomized or quasi-experimental designs in educational settings. It provides correlational-style performance evidence about model capabilities rather than causal evidence of student learning impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows that current VLMs achieve only moderate accuracy on middle-school-level German tasks, but it does not evaluate educational outcomes for students or teachers. Its practical impact is mainly diagnostic for AI system capability, with unclear direct impact on K-12 learning.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking and evaluating vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions with open-ended answers, including image-grounded reasoning and adversarial unanswerable questions.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students. The authors focus on a central question in AI-assisted instruction: whether teacher-mediated personalization can balance instructional quality, realism, and student interest, and whether it is efficient enough to be practical in real classrooms.

In the study, seven middle school mathematics teachers used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to adapt existing Illustrative Mathematics problems to students’ interests, especially popular culture topics. Teachers worked on problems from two 7th-grade units, participated in training on personalization and bias/readability/cultural relevance, and then created personalized versions that were assigned through ASSISTments to 521 seventh-grade students across six U.S. schools. The study analyzed teacher prompts and interaction logs, video-recorded sessions, student survey ratings, and open-ended student feedback.

The findings show that teachers most often used ChatGPT to introduce broad or specific popular-culture references, but they also spent substantial effort correcting realism, numbers, readability, and age-appropriateness. Students tended to prefer more specific, fine-grained references and often judged problems mainly by whether the reference matched their personal interests. Personalizing one problem took about four minutes on average, and there was no clear evidence that the process became faster over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit, although student ratings also improved. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and quality control, but it is time-consuming and may be too coarse-grained to satisfy many students’ preferences.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods observational study with teacher and student data, not a randomized or quasi-experimental evaluation of learning outcomes. It is well described and uses mixed-effects models, but credibility is limited by lack of a control group and the absence of direct achievement measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest and mixed effects on student interest perceptions and clear costs in teacher time, but no direct evidence of academic learning gains. Overall impact appears unclear and limited to process outcomes rather than strong student achievement effects.

interventions.use_case: Teachers used ChatGPT/GPT-4o as a co-authoring tool to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students' interests, iteratively prompting the model to rewrite or adapt Illustrative Mathematics tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper did not measure student achievement directly, but it did examine whether the personalized math tasks were perceived as more interesting and closer to students' interests. Student ratings were modest overall; tasks created with 3-5 prompts were associated with higher ratings by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), suggesting a small positive effect on the quality of math task personalization rather than on math learning itself.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher-created personalized mathematics problems

finding.finding_summary: Students generally gave low-to-moderate interest and closeness ratings for the personalized problems (mean interestingness=2.46/5, mean closeness=2.53/5), and many open-ended responses said the problems were not especially interesting. However, students were more positive when the problems matched their specific popular-culture preferences, and Unit 6 problems were rated higher than Unit 4 (interestingness: 2.27 to 2.56; closeness: 2.28 to 2.66; B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: 1-5 student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454/449/446 open-ended responses across questions

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was time-intensive. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds or roughly 4 minutes (SD=165.7) to create; the authors conclude this did not become notably more time-efficient with practice and that Unit 6 actually took longer than Unit 4 (286 vs. 204 seconds; B=70.4, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher prompt counts and time spent creating personalized problems

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT (two January 2023 versions) and GPT-4 using a newly created benchmark of natural-language mathematics problems called GHOSTS, plus a smaller miniGHOSTS subset for GPT-4. The authors focus on whether large language models can handle different kinds of mathematical reasoning, including factual recall, filling in gaps in proofs, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search-engine-like retrieval of definitions and theorem statements.

The study does not involve classroom instruction or an educational intervention; instead, it is a benchmark/evaluation paper using hand-crafted and sourced prompts from graduate-level textbooks, math.stackexchange, the MATH dataset, symbolic mathematics datasets, and olympiad materials. The relevant population is therefore the mathematical knowledge domain represented by undergraduate and graduate-level exercises rather than human learners in a school setting.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is most useful as a mathematical assistant for factual lookup and search-like tasks, while GPT-4 improves on ChatGPT and can sometimes handle undergraduate-level tasks, but still falls short on graduate-level mathematics and complex proofs. The authors conclude that, despite public hype, these models are not yet reliable for advanced mathematics, although they may be helpful as workflow aids for mathematically proficient users who can verify the output.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic benchmark study with human annotation and clear evaluation methodology, but it is not an intervention study in K-12 education and does not use an experimental or quasi-experimental design with learners. It provides descriptive performance evidence rather than causal evidence of educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear capability differences in mathematical problem solving and assistant usefulness, but it does not measure student learning gains or educational outcomes directly. Its likely impact is on model evaluation and downstream tutoring use, not demonstrated population-level educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT (two 2023 versions) and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for querying facts, filling gaps in proofs, solving undergraduate/graduate math problems, symbolic integration, and theorem/definition retrieval.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT and GPT-4 have uneven mathematical performance across task types. On GHOSTS, the 9-Jan-2023 ChatGPT version averaged rating 3.20 (SD=1.23) and the 30-Jan-2023 version averaged 3.29 (SD=1.28), while GPT-4 averaged 4.15 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS; GPT-4 still failed on graduate-level and olympiad-style tasks. For symbolic integration, ChatGPT averaged 2.51 (SD=0.87) on a random sample, and GPT-4 reached 3.50 (SD=1.43), indicating better but still limited mathematical competence overall.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical solution quality across task sets (rating 1-5) on GHOSTS/miniGHOSTS; also exact-answer success on subsets such as MATH and symbolic integration
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts (1636 human ratings); GPT-4 evaluated on n=170 prompts

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter/paper discusses the foundational role of generative AI models in information access (IA) systems. It argues that modern generative models, especially large language models (LLMs), create new opportunities for IA through two broad paradigms: information generation and information synthesis. Information generation refers to directly producing tailored outputs from user instructions, while information synthesis refers to integrating external sources to produce grounded responses and reduce hallucinations.

The paper is a conceptual survey and framework paper rather than an empirical study. It reviews model architectures such as Transformers, scaling laws, training stages including pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF, prompt optimization, and multimodal applications. It also surveys retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), modular RAG, and related approaches for using LLMs to combine retrieval with generation.

The paper further discusses generative retrieval and domain-specific modeling as ways of using generative AI to model corpora and answer information needs directly. Its main conclusion is that generative AI can substantially enhance information access, but important challenges remain, including hallucination, efficiency, controllability, and the difficulty of effectively integrating external knowledge with large models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/chapter-style review of generative AI foundations and information access, not an empirical study with a measured educational intervention. It provides no study design, sample, or outcome evaluation relevant to K-12 evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any educational outcomes, effect sizes, or student-level impacts. Its relevance to middle school mathematics or subgroup effects is only indirect through broad discussion of LLMs like ChatGPT.

interventions.use_case: Uses ChatGPT and related large language models as examples of generative AI systems that can directly answer user questions and support information access, including chatbot-style query answering and retrieval-augmented generation.

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, are changing software development work practices and team collaboration. The authors focus on questions such as what GenAI is used for, how people interact with it, and what effects it has on productivity, learning, and teamwork. The study is framed as an exploratory investigation because GenAI in this context was described as a new and under-studied phenomenon.

The intervention/approach studied is the use of GenAI systems in everyday software development tasks, including getting unstuck on problems, learning new topics, creating virtual environments, copywriting, generating boilerplate code, and working with existing code such as refactoring, debugging, and writing tests. The paper reports on semi-structured interviews with 13 professionals working in software-related roles, including developers, data scientists, managers, designers, and technical leaders, drawn from companies that had introduced GenAI into their product development processes.

The main conclusions are that GenAI often increases individual efficiency, lowers the barrier to asking for help, and supports faster learning and more enjoyable work. At the same time, the authors argue that frequent reliance on GenAI may reduce peer-to-peer communication and weaken the team learning loop, potentially harming collaboration and knowledge sharing in agile teams. They also note important challenges such as privacy concerns, lack of tool integration, outdated training data, and the need for careful prompt engineering to get useful output.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory multi-case interview study with 13 participants, which provides useful descriptive evidence but not causal identification. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful workflow and collaboration changes, but all evidence is self-reported and qualitative with no quantified effect sizes. Its impact is therefore plausible but unclear in magnitude, especially for education-related outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT as a conversational assistant for software development tasks, including rubber-duck debugging, code explanation, boilerplate generation, learning new topics, and prompt-engineered roleplay for coding and review support.

finding.finding_summary: Interviewees consistently reported that ChatGPT/GenAI reduced time spent on repetitive and manual tasks, improved speed of getting unstuck, and shortened writing or coding workflows. No numeric effect size was reported; the evidence is qualitative from n=13 participants across developer, manager, designer, and data science roles.
finding.measure: Interview-reported productivity, time savings, and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI supported learning, problem solving, and prompting as a form of metacognitive support, but also reduced human-to-human collaboration and pair programming in some cases. Participants described faster learning and better thought structuring, alongside concerns about weaker knowledge sharing in teams.
finding.measure: Interview themes on learning, debugging, collaboration, and knowledge sharing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction when GenAI removed tedious work and made interactions feel more natural and less socially taxing than asking colleagues. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes; findings are based on n=13 interviews.
finding.measure: Interview-reported motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that GenAI may reshape team structures and knowledge-sharing norms, potentially disrupting agile learning loops while also enabling new practices such as pair prompt engineering. Evidence is qualitative and exploratory, with no effect size reported; conclusions are drawn from n=13 interviews.
finding.measure: Interview themes on teamwork, knowledge sharing, and agile team dynamics

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools are being used in YouTube content creation, with a focus on understanding specific use cases across the video production workflow. The authors note that although tools like ChatGPT, MidJourney, and related systems are increasingly popular among creators, there was limited understanding of how these tools are actually applied throughout planning, production, editing, and uploading.

To address this, the study analyzed 274 YouTube how-to videos showing the use of GenAI in content creation.
