The researchers used thematic analysis to code 2,829 video clips and developed a conceptual framework of GenAI use cases across four phases: planning, production, editing, and uploading. The dataset was collected from YouTube videos posted between September 2023 and February 2024, filtered to English videos with captions and durations in a specified range, and then manually screened for relevance to GenAI-based video creation.

The findings show that creators use GenAI for tasks such as identifying video topics, generating scripts, refining prompts, creating images, avatars, voiceovers, and music, as well as editing tasks like lip-syncing, restyling, increasing resolution, clipping long videos, and translating speech. In the uploading phase, GenAI is used to generate subtitles and titles. The paper concludes that GenAI is already deeply embedded in creator workflows and argues for future tool designs that better support prompting, multimodal content creation, accessibility, and transparency around AI-generated media.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of YouTube how-to videos, not an experiment or causal evaluation. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically systematic, but it primarily documents use patterns rather than testing outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful productivity support for content creators, but it does not estimate effect sizes on learner or creator outcomes. Its impact is therefore indirect and observational, with unclear magnitude for educational settings.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools are used to segment transcripts, refine prompts, generate video scripts, suggest topics, titles, and subtitles, and support YouTube content-creation workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generative AI is widely used to streamline YouTube video production workflows across planning, production, editing, and uploading. In the 274-video sample, creators used GenAI for scripting (n=85), image/video generation (n=167), voiceover creation (n=93), and automatic subtitle generation (n=28), indicating substantial workflow support rather than a measured causal effect on performance.
finding.measure: Qualitative content analysis of GenAI use cases in YouTube how-to videos; frequency counts of observed use cases

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications Over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring large language model (LLM)-based applications, which the authors argue is still largely manual, slow, and dependent on trial-and-error workflows. The paper proposes the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework intended to automate DevOps-style processes across the full life cycle of LLM applications, from project bootstrapping and prompt/model experimentation to CI/CD integration and post-deployment monitoring.

The intervention is not an educational tool or student-facing chatbot; it is a software engineering toolkit for developers. It provides templates for creating agents, support for custom metrics, repeatable evaluation cases, parameter permutation across prompts and models, automated testing, deployment via infrastructure-as-code, and logging/monitoring through traces and dashboards. The paper illustrates these capabilities through several representative use cases: a text-to-SQL agent, a restaurant menu RAG agent, an in-car voice assistant, and model-comparison experiments on the assistant use case.

The population and context are adult developers working on LLM-based applications in industry settings, specifically at BMW Group and Amazon Web Services. The use cases are technical software examples rather than a study of learners, teachers, or classrooms, and no education-related participants are reported. The main conclusion is that the toolkit can improve quality assurance, reduce manual work, shorten cycle times, and make it easier to test and monitor LLM applications at scale, although the authors note that quantitative benefits are hard to generalize from the showcased examples.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preprint framework paper with illustrative use cases and no controlled educational study, randomized design, or quantitative comparison against a baseline. It provides implementation details and qualitative claims, but not empirical evidence meeting K-12 study standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate educational outcomes or student learning effects, and it is not an intervention study in schooling. Any impact is indirect and operational, focused on software development workflows rather than learner outcomes.

interventions.use_case: framework for developing, testing, deploying, and monitoring LLM-based applications and agents with user-defined metrics and CI/CD automation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the Generative AI Toolkit reduces manual work and shortens release cycles for LLM-based applications by automating development, testing, deployment, and monitoring workflows. However, the authors do not provide a controlled evaluation with numerical effect sizes; benefits are described qualitatively across representative use cases (e.g., text-to-SQL, RAG menu agent, in-car assistant).
finding.measure: development cycle time, manual work, and automation coverage in LLM application life cycle

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is presented as an open-source framework intended to improve the quality and operationalization of LLM systems at scale, including CI/CD integration, logging, monitoring, and audit-friendly evaluation. The evidence is descriptive rather than inferential, so no formal impact estimate is reported.
finding.measure: framework capability and lifecycle support for large-scale LLM operations

paper_profiles.title: Comparison of Methods That Combine Multiple Randomized Trials to Estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: A Preprint
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects when data are available from multiple randomized controlled trials. The authors note that single trials are often underpowered to detect treatment effect heterogeneity and may not generalize well, so they compare methods for combining multiple RCTs to estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) more flexibly than traditional meta-analysis.

The paper evaluates several single-study machine learning approaches—S-learner, X-learner, and causal forest—and then extends them to multi-trial settings through complete pooling, pooling with trial indicators, ensemble methods, IPD meta-analysis, and no-pooling approaches. These methods are assessed through extensive simulations under varying levels of cross-trial heterogeneity, nonlinear treatment effect structure, unequal trial sizes, covariate shift, and larger numbers of trials. The study also includes an applied example using four randomized trials of depression medications (duloxetine vs vortioxetine) in adults with major depressive disorder.

The main conclusion is that methods allowing trial-level heterogeneity generally outperform complete pooling when treatment effects differ across studies. In particular, pooling with trial indicators and ensemble forests performed consistently well, especially when combined with causal forests as the base learner. The causal forest was the most robust single-study method overall, while parametric approaches such as lasso-based ensembles and mixed-effects meta-analysis worked best only when their functional-form assumptions matched the true data-generating process. In the real depression dataset, methods broadly agreed on an overall positive treatment effect and suggested limited heterogeneity, with age emerging as a possible moderator.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methods preprint on combining randomized trials to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects, not an education intervention study. It contains no empirical evaluation of a K-12 educational technology or learning outcome, so it does not fit the evidence tiers for intervention effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact results; its contribution is methodological and applied to depression trials, not schooling or AI-in-education outcomes. Therefore there is no measurable impact on the requested education-relevant population or outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines antitrust and platform power in the generative AI ecosystem. Rather than studying an educational intervention or learner outcomes, it asks how market dominance is structured across the generative AI technology stack and whether current legal frameworks are adequate to address concentration of power among major technology firms.

The authors analyze the inputs and dependencies that shape success in generative AI, including access to large-scale data, top engineering talent, substantial capital, proprietary infrastructure, and the ability to fund and influence research. They discuss examples such as OpenAI/Microsoft, Google, Amazon, GitHub Copilot, and BloombergGPT to illustrate how incumbent firms may leverage existing advantages across adjacent markets.

The paper’s main conclusion is that generative AI is currently highly concentrated and vertically integrated, making it difficult for new entrants to compete. The authors argue that antitrust law and emerging AI regulation may unintentionally reinforce existing market power rather than reduce it, and they call for more substantial quantitative analysis of relevant AI markets in future work. The paper is a legal/technical position piece with no empirical study of participants or educational settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/legal analysis of antitrust and platform power in generative AI, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate a learning intervention, report a study design, or present student outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or learner outcome is assessed, so there is no measurable K-12 impact to assign.

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve middle school students’ math learning, particularly for students from low-income backgrounds and for lower-performing subgroups. The authors are motivated by persistent access and engagement gaps in mathematics tutoring, and they ask whether combining adaptive math software with human tutoring can increase students’ learning opportunities and whether effects differ by baseline ability.

The intervention is a hybrid tutoring approach in which students work with AI-based math software while human tutors provide motivational, relational, and content support. Across three quasi-experimental studies, the model was implemented during the school day in three urban U.S. middle schools using different software platforms: IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia. Two sites used a round-robin tutoring structure without a dashboard, while the third piloted a tutor-facing dashboard intended to guide support. The sites included largely low-income student populations, including a Pennsylvania middle school, a large California middle school, and a small Pennsylvania charter school serving Black male students.

The findings indicate that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased engagement and intermediate learning outcomes such as time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, lesson completion, and workspace progress. The strongest pattern was that lower-pretest or below-grade-level students benefited more than higher-performing students. The authors conclude that hybrid tutoring can improve learning opportunities at relatively low marginal cost, and that dashboard-guided support and more targeted tutor allocation may further increase equity and effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental, multi-site field study with mixed-effects models and interrupted time series analyses, but it lacks random assignment and has site-specific implementation differences. The design provides reasonably strong causal evidence, though internal validity concerns keep it below blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest-to-meaningful positive effects on key engagement and progress measures in a priority population of low-income middle school students, including a statistically significant tutoring effect and evidence of stronger benefits for lower-pretest students. The reported effects are promising but are mostly intermediate outcomes rather than external achievement test gains, so overall impact is best classified as green.

interventions.use_case: hybrid human-AI tutoring in middle school math, where students work in software such as IXL, i-Ready, or MATHia while remote human tutors provide motivational, relationship-building, and occasional content support; in one site tutors were guided by a live dashboard

finding.finding_summary: This three-study quasi-experimental investigation found that hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software alone. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then tutoring increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; the mixed-effects model showed a positive tutoring effect on time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006) over n=125 students, with similar positive effects for questions answered and skills proficient. In Site 2, tutoring increased lessons passed per week (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], p<0.001; n=385), and in Site 3 students completed 0.36 more MATHia workspaces per hour after tutor-to-student ratios improved from 1:8 to 1:4 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=.03; n=75).
finding.measure: Math software usage and progress: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed per week, and MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved engagement with learning software, a proximate social-emotional/behavioral outcome emphasized throughout the paper. Across sites, students spent more time on task during hybrid tutoring than with software alone (e.g., Site 2 increased from 24 to 33 minutes per week), suggesting greater persistence and participation. The authors interpret these gains as especially strong for lower-pretest students, who appear to respond more to tutor support and relationship-building.
finding.measure: Time on task / minutes spent using math software; participation and engagement indicators
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 on time spent; observed increase from 24 to 33 minutes/week
finding.confidence_interval: [0.057, 0.347] for tutoring effect on time spent; other site-level intervals reported in text

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the hybrid model can improve tutoring efficiency and scalability by allowing one tutor to serve more students and by using dashboard guidance to allocate attention. The discussion emphasizes a lower marginal cost of about $700 per student annually, substantially below traditional high-dosage tutoring costs of $3,500-$4,300, while still producing positive engagement and progress outcomes.
finding.measure: Marginal cost per student; tutor-to-student ratio; time per tutor session

paper_profiles.title: Robust Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects in Randomized Trials Leveraging External Data
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in randomized trials when the trial sample is too small to reliably detect subgroup differences. The specific focus is on conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which are used to understand how treatment effects vary across covariates and support personalized or subgroup-specific decision-making. The authors argue that trial-only estimators often have high variance and limited power for detecting heterogeneity, motivating the use of external data from other trials or observational studies.

The paper proposes the QR-learner, a model-agnostic method that uses external data to improve the first-stage estimation of nuisance functions while preserving robustness to mismatch between the external and trial populations. It also introduces a combined learner that stacks the QR-learner with a trial-only doubly robust learner, aiming to achieve performance at least as good as either method alone. The methods are evaluated in simulations and in a case study using the Tennessee STAR project, where rural and urban schools form two populations and transportability is intentionally violated by omitting school location from the covariates.

Across simulations and the STAR application, the proposed approaches generally improve CATE estimation accuracy and, in some settings, increase statistical power to detect treatment effect heterogeneity. The main conclusion is that external data can be leveraged safely and effectively for subgroup effect estimation in randomized trials, even when the external data are imperfectly aligned with the trial population. The combined learner is particularly attractive because it retains robustness while often matching or improving on the best component learner.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methods paper with simulation studies and a real-world case study, not a peer-reviewed education intervention trial. It does not evaluate a classroom or student-facing AI intervention in the K-12 sense, so it does not meet evidence criteria for educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially important downstream implications for how heterogeneous effects are estimated in education research, but it reports methodological gains rather than direct student outcome effects. Any practical impact on education is indirect and currently unclear.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a methodological/statistical learning contribution rather than an educational intervention study. It proposes the QR-learner and a combined learner for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects, showing improved CATE prediction mean squared error and greater power to detect treatment effect heterogeneity in simulations and in the STAR case study. Reported results include RMSE improvements such as 0.23 vs 0.28 for the DR-learner in one aligned external-data scenario (n1=250) and higher interaction-test power by about 10-20 percentage points in the simulation study, but these are methodological performance metrics rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: CATE prediction RMSE; statistical power to detect interaction effects; model-selection risk

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that augmenting randomized trials with external data can improve the detection of treatment effect heterogeneity and the precision of subgroup estimation, which has implications for trial design and personalized decision-making. In simulations, the proposed method maintained nominal type I error and increased power by roughly 10-20 percentage points for detecting effect modification, while the STAR case study showed lower held-out RMSE than trial-only baselines in smaller-sample settings.
finding.measure: Type I error; power for interaction tests; held-out RMSE in STAR case study

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how tutoring systems in education have evolved and what benefits, limitations, and ethical concerns accompany their use. The authors review the literature on intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), robot tutoring systems (RTS), and multimodal/hybrid tutoring systems, with particular attention to artificial intelligence methods, system behavior, engagement features, affordances, and responsible AI considerations.

The approach is a systematic literature review following PRISMA. The paper synthesizes 86 representative studies drawn from 1972 to 2024, spanning early computer-assisted instruction through contemporary systems using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, large language models, and social robots. The reviewed systems cover computer-based, robot-based, and multimodal tutoring environments rather than a single intervention, and the paper does not report a single participant sample for this review itself.

The review concludes that ITS generally provide stronger cognitive adaptability and scalability, while RTS are better at social and emotional engagement through verbal, gestural, and physical interaction. Multimodal systems combine strengths of both but introduce greater complexity and ethical concerns. The paper highlights persistent issues around privacy, fairness, transparency, scalability, and limited cognitive adaptability in robot-based systems, and argues that future tutoring technologies should better integrate cognitive personalization with social engagement while strengthening responsible AI safeguards.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review with PRISMA procedures and latent class analysis, but it is not a primary causal study and does not itself report experimental effects. Evidence quality is therefore observational/synthetic rather than RCT-level.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful benefits for engagement and learning in tutoring systems, but it provides no pooled effect sizes or direct impact estimates from a single intervention study. Its conclusions are broad and largely qualitative, so impact is plausible but unclear from this paper alone.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of classical and modern intelligent tutoring systems, including Bayesian Knowledge Tracing- and LLM-enabled adaptive tutoring for individualized instruction, with a specific example of middle school mathematics tutoring.

Review of generative-AI and LLM-enabled tutoring systems that provide conversational feedback, adaptive explanations, and chat-based tutoring (e.g., ChatGPT-like tutor models and LLM-as-tutor chatbots).
Systematic review of robot tutoring systems used as embodied tutors or peer tutors, including social-robot tutoring with verbal feedback, gestures, and multimodal interaction.
Historical review of early computer-assisted instruction systems as predecessors to modern tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that tutoring systems, especially AI-driven ITS, have improved learning outcomes in mathematics and other core subjects, and specifically cites an ITS for middle school mathematics as evidence of adaptive learning support. However, this paper is a systematic review and does not report a pooled effect size or primary-study estimate for math outcomes.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes / academic performance in tutoring-system studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, robot-based and multimodal tutoring systems are described as improving engagement, motivation, and social-emotional engagement through verbal encouragement, gestures, and human-like interaction. The review synthesizes these as recurring positive outcomes, but does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and social-emotional engagement outcomes reported in prior studies

finding.finding_summary: LLM-based and conversational tutoring systems are described as increasing interactivity and engagement through real-time, personalized dialogue and feedback. The review emphasizes improved responsiveness and learner engagement, but does not report a quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement and interaction quality in LLM-based tutoring studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial ethical, privacy, scalability, and equity concerns across tutoring systems, especially for AI-driven and robot-based approaches, while also noting proposed mitigation strategies such as encryption, audits, access controls, and governance oversight. Because the paper is a synthesis rather than an intervention trial, it provides no effect size or institutional outcome estimate.
finding.measure: Ethical risk, privacy, governance, scalability, and responsible AI considerations

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can accurately evaluate human tutors’ responses when middle school students make math errors during tutoring. The motivating problem is that expert human evaluation of these tutoring moves is time-consuming, especially for nuanced skills such as responding indirectly and supportively to student mistakes. The authors focus on a specific tutoring skill taught in a scenario-based lesson, "Reacting to Errors," which trains tutors to respond in ways that are process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and mathematically accurate.

The approach compares GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 on 50 real-life tutoring dialogues, after first using GPT-4 to generate synthetic dialogues for human rater calibration. The real tutoring corpus involved online tutoring of middle school students in 6th–8th grade from two schools, with tutors who were college students at a university in Pennsylvania. Tutors interacted remotely via Pencil, and human annotators scored each dialogue on five criteria and whether the student had made an error.

The main conclusion is that both LLMs can assess several tutor-response criteria reasonably well, especially immediate and accurate feedback, but both struggle to reliably detect when the student actually made an error. GPT-4 performs slightly better than GPT-3.5-Turbo overall, yet the improvement may not justify the much higher cost for scalable use. The authors suggest that prompt refinement, larger datasets, and future analyses of learning transfer could improve this approach, but caution that LLMs alone are not yet sufficient for fully evaluating and guiding tutors in this setting.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, descriptive evaluation study using 50 tutoring dialogues rather than a controlled experiment. It is peer-reviewed workshop work, but the evidence is mainly methodological/benchmarking and does not establish causal effects on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest practical value for scaling tutor evaluation, but it does not demonstrate direct student learning gains. Its impact is therefore unclear to modest, centered on operational efficiency rather than educational effect sizes.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 to assess middle school math tutoring dialogues, specifically scoring whether tutors responded effectively to student math errors in a Reacting to Errors scenario-based lesson context.

finding.finding_summary: This paper shows that LLMs can be used to automate assessment of tutor performance in real tutoring dialogues, reducing the need for time-consuming human evaluation. In 50 real-life tutoring dialogues, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 performed fairly well on most criteria, with GPT-4 generally slightly better, suggesting practical utility for scalable tutor feedback workflows.
finding.measure: Accuracy/F1 for scoring tutor response criteria against human graders; ability to identify whether a student made an error

paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that many current AI tutoring systems, especially in mathematics, are too reactive: they tend to provide direct answers rather than supporting deep understanding, structured practice, and individualized learning. The authors ask how AI tutoring can move beyond simple response generation toward guided, tool-assisted, and personalized learning experiences.

To address this, the paper proposes a multi-agent AI tutoring platform built around large language models, Socratic tutoring, dual-memory personalization, GraphRAG-based textbook retrieval, and DAG-based course planning. The system is designed to support adaptive feedback, targeted practice generation, exam revision planning, and retrieval-grounded explanations, with the Tutor Agent orchestrating specialized components such as memory, retrieval, task creation, and course planning.

The paper is primarily a system/design contribution rather than a student intervention study. It evaluates prompting and model choices using the MathDial benchmark, showing that a tutor prompt emphasizing Socratic questioning and scaffolding performs better than a base prompt on success and telling metrics, and that o3-mini(high) performs well on math problem-solving tasks. The authors conclude that the architecture is promising for personalized STEM learning, but they explicitly note that real student evaluation is still needed before claims about learning effectiveness can be made.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a system description and benchmark-validation paper without a real-student evaluation, randomization, or causal design. The authors explicitly note the lack of empirical learning-environment validation, so it does not meet strong evidence criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising benchmark improvements in guided tutoring behavior and math task accuracy, but these are component-level results rather than learner outcomes. Because no student learning gains are measured, the real-world impact remains unclear despite the potentially useful system design.

interventions.use_case: multi-agent GPT-4o-based math tutoring with Socratic questioning, adaptive feedback, textbook-grounded retrieval, and personalized exercise/course generation
AI tutoring platform designed as an intelligent tutoring environment with adaptive support, student modeling, and guided learning workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a pedagogically informed Tutor Prompt improved guided tutoring behavior in simulated MathDial dialogues, with higher Success@K and lower Telling@K than a Base Prompt. This indicates better support for self-explanation, metacognitive engagement, and independent problem solving, although the paper does not provide numeric effect sizes for these benchmark outcomes.
finding.measure: MathDial benchmark dialogue metrics: Success@K and Telling@K

finding.finding_summary: On the MathDial problem set, the system evaluated several LLMs with SymPy access for mathematical problem-solving accuracy. o3-mini(high) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved the highest accuracy at 90.00%, followed by Gemini 2.0 Flash at 88.67%, while GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were lower at 78.67% and 77.33%, respectively.
finding.measure: Problem-solving accuracy on MathDial math problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that the platform automates personalized exercise generation and structured course planning, reducing the need for manual authoring of practice items and learning paths. However, this is a system-design claim supported by benchmarked component performance rather than a direct teacher-workload study, and no quantitative workload reduction effect is reported.
finding.measure: Automated exercise generation and course-planning capability; component benchmark performance

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve middle school mathematics learning, especially for students from low-income backgrounds, and whether the benefits differ by prior achievement. The authors frame the problem as a persistent equity and access challenge: tutoring is effective but expensive and difficult to scale, while AI-based math software alone may not sufficiently engage students who need the most support.

To address this, the study evaluates a hybrid model in which students use adaptive math software while human tutors provide motivational, relational, and content support. The system is implemented in three separate urban U.S. middle school settings using different platforms: IXL, i-Ready, and Carnegie Learning’s MATHia. Across the sites, the tutoring format varied from round-robin human support to a dashboard-guided model, allowing comparison of software-only conditions versus software plus teacher support versus software plus teacher and tutor support. The sample includes 125 students in Pennsylvania, 385 students in California, and 75 students in a Pennsylvania charter school, with students largely from low-income backgrounds and with site-specific racial/ethnic compositions.

The authors report that hybrid human-AI tutoring generally increased engagement and learning-process indicators such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, and lesson completion. They also find evidence of subgroup effects: lower-pretest or below-grade-level students benefited more than higher-pretest students, while the presence of a math teacher during software use tended to benefit higher-pretest students more. The paper concludes that hybrid tutoring is promising for improving middle school math learning at relatively low cost, and that dashboard-guided systems and better allocation of tutor attention may further strengthen equity and effectiveness.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed three-study quasi-experimental investigation with repeated measures and mixed-effects models, but it lacks random assignment and includes site-specific implementation differences and small samples at some sites. The design is stronger than simple correlational work, but not RCT-level evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed effects on math engagement and lesson progression are practically meaningful and directly relevant to a priority middle school population from low-income backgrounds. Several reported effects are at or above a medium magnitude in the learning-process domain, particularly the increases in time on task and workspaces completed per hour.

interventions.use_case: hybrid human-AI tutoring in middle school math using adaptive practice software (IXL, i-Ready, MATHia) paired with remote human tutor support and, in one site, a live tutor dashboard

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental middle school sites, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software only. In Site 1 (n=125), mixed-effects models found tutoring increased time spent practicing (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and improved skills proficient, with stronger benefits for lower pretest students (pretest:Tutoring β=-0.212, 95% CI [-0.325, -0.096]). In Site 2 (n=385), tutoring increased weekly minutes on task from 24 to 33 and increased lessons passed, especially for below-grade-level students (lesson_grade:during_treatment β=-0.05261, p=0.000217). In Site 3 (n=75), moving from 1:8 to 1:4 tutor:student ratio increased MATHia workspaces completed per hour by 0.36 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: IXL time spent, questions answered, skills proficient; i-Ready time on task and lessons passed; MATHia workspaces completed per hour
finding.study_size: n=585 total across three sites (Site 1 n=125, Site 2 n=385, Site 3 n=75)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports consistent gains in engagement and participation, which it treats as a core mechanism linking tutoring to learning. In Site 1, tutoring significantly increased time spent on software, and in Site 2 weekly time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes during treatment, suggesting higher engagement with the math platform. The authors interpret these changes as increased learning opportunities and improved participation, especially for lower-performing students.
finding.measure: time spent on task, engagement/participation with math software
finding.study_size: n=585 total across three sites (Site 1 n=125, Site 2 n=385, Site 3 n=75)
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 for time spent; 24 to 33 minutes/week

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the hybrid model can increase the efficiency of tutoring delivery by enabling more student progress with a lower tutor:student ratio and using dashboard-guided support. In Site 3, reducing the tutor:student ratio from about 1:8 to 1:4 increased progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]), indicating better throughput when tutors had more availability. The authors also frame the model as scalable and lower-cost than exclusive human tutoring, with estimated marginal costs around $700 per student annually.
finding.measure: workspaces completed per hour; tutor:student ratio; estimated marginal cost per student
finding.study_size: n=75 for Site 3; cost estimate across three sites

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark designed to evaluate vision-language models on German-language, middle school-level knowledge tasks. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-centric, overreliant on multiple-choice formats, and sometimes too artificial or text-solvable to test genuine visual reasoning. To address this, they construct a dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, with many tasks requiring the model to combine image interpretation with subject-specific background knowledge. The benchmark also includes adversarial questions that are intentionally unanswerable from the image alone, to test whether models can resist guessing and appropriately express uncertainty.

The study evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs, including InternVL3, Ovis2, Qwen2.5 VL, Gemma 3, Llama 4 Scout, and Mistral Small 3.1. Models were run on the benchmark using automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring with a panel of three judges. The context is German middle school curricula for grades 8–10, with tasks drawn from textbooks and related educational materials in arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. The paper focuses on model behavior rather than human learners, so no student intervention or classroom implementation is studied.

Results show that the benchmark is difficult for current VLMs: the best overall accuracy is under 45%, with particularly weak performance in math, music, and adversarial settings. The authors find that model rankings on this benchmark do not perfectly align with public benchmark performance such as MMMU, and that larger model size does not always yield large gains beyond the medium-scale range. They conclude that middle school-level German tasks provide a useful stress test for VLMs, especially in non-English contexts, and that current models still struggle with precise visual reasoning, domain-specific knowledge, and recognizing when a question cannot be answered from the image.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear methodology, but it is not an intervention study and does not use randomized assignment or causal identification. It provides descriptive comparative evidence about model performance, so credibility is moderate but not experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for educational AI benchmarking and model selection, but it does not test a learner-facing intervention or show student outcome gains. Its impact is mainly indirect and methodological rather than demonstrably instructional.

interventions.use_case: Benchmark evaluation of vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions that require visual understanding, subject knowledge, and open-ended answering across math, science, history, arts, religion, music, geography, and sports.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows poor performance on middle school math questions that required interpreting figures and doing basic calculations. The best model reached only about 34% accuracy on math, and the paper reports that models were better at calculating than counting but still frequently failed when visual parsing errors led to wrong geometry answers.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended middle school mathematics questions
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; math subset n=308

finding.finding_summary: In physics and biology, models struggled to combine image interpretation with explanatory reasoning and domain knowledge. The paper reports that even strong models had difficulty explaining phenomena such as stellar evolution and circuit behavior, and biology items showed variable success when identifying labeled parts of diagrams.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology visual-reasoning questions
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; biology n=169, physics n=234

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math subjects, the benchmark found generally modest performance on German middle school knowledge questions, with best overall accuracy below 45% and domain peaks around 54% in history/religion. This indicates substantial difficulty with real-world subject knowledge in arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports when visual and textual cues had to be integrated.
finding.measure: Accuracy across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports questions
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; arts n=286, geography n=251, history n=264, music n=166, religion n=206, sports n=154

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests current VLMs have weak contextual reasoning and poor ability to recognize when a question is unanswerable. Performance on adversarial items was much lower than on the full set, with the best overall adversarial accuracy only 32.83% and several model families near or below 10-15%, showing limited robustness to misleading prompts.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring rejection of unanswerable or misleading queries
finding.study_size: n=2038 questions total; adversarial subset size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive and want AI to behave when it is framed as a peer collaborator in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS), rather than as a traditional tutor. The central question is how to design an AI peer that can participate in group mathematics work in ways that support co-agency, productive struggle, and student control.

The authors conducted a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students in the United States. Students completed human-only mathematics CPS tasks and then interacted with two AI peers through a web-based technology probe built around GPT-4o, before co-designing their own ideal AI peer behaviors, personas, and controls. The camp also included surveys, reflections, interviews, and artifact analysis, including group environment and workload measures comparing human-only versus AI-involved CPS sessions.

Findings show that students preferred an AI peer that gives hints, checks work, and provides concept refreshers before revealing answers, with explicit student control over when and how the AI speaks. Students wanted the AI to sound friendly and expert, but not overly performative, and to acknowledge social and emotional aspects of collaboration rather than just optimizing for correctness. Overall, the study argues that effective AI peers for middle school mathematics should support collaborative reasoning, emotional attunement, and user control, while avoiding overly didactic or dominant behavior.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative and mixed-methods participatory design study with a small sample and no randomized causal test of learning effects. It provides careful within-subject comparisons and credible measures of user experience, but the evidence is primarily exploratory rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows large effects on perceived workload and collaboration experience, but it does not demonstrate academic achievement gains. Its main contribution is design insight for middle-school AI peers, with indirect and still-uncertain impact on learning outcomes.

interventions.use_case: A sandboxed GPT-4o-based AI peer technology probe used in middle-school collaborative mathematics problem solving, where two conversational AI peers (Alice and Bob) interact with students using text chat, step-by-step discussion, hints, checks, and procedurally staged collaboration behaviors.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure learning gains directly, but it does evaluate how students experienced AI-mediated mathematics collaboration on grade-aligned tasks. Students reported that the AI peers helped keep problem solving moving and provided useful hints/explanations, but they also found some AI behaviors distracting or overly directive, indicating mixed implications for mathematical problem solving support.
finding.measure: Observed and self-reported experience during collaborative middle-school mathematics problem solving; qualitative reflections on task help and problem-solving process

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower social cohesion and affective engagement when working with AI peers than in human-only groups. On GEQ, Attractions to Group-Social was lower with AI peers (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than human-only collaboration (M=6.50, SD=2.05), d=0.94, and qualitative data showed students wanted more encouragement, empathy, and emotional attunement from the AI.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (ATGS), interview/reflection reports on frustration, trust, encouragement, and emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined collaboration-related outcomes and found that AI peers changed how students coordinated group work. Group Integration-Task was lower with AI peers than with human-only CPS (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs M=5.54, SD=1.52; d=0.81), while students qualitatively valued co-agency, turn-taking, and negotiation rather than didactic control.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (GIT), qualitative reflections and participatory design artifacts about collaboration, co-agency, and turn-taking
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced perceived time pressure during collaborative math work: NASA-TLX temporal demand was lower with AI peers than with human-only CPS (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15). However, this gain was offset by higher physical demand from typing and interface navigation (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14), so overall efficiency effects were mixed even though task flow improved.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand subscales

paper_profiles.title: Ensembling Large Language Models to Characterize Affective Dynamics in Student–AI Tutor Dialogues
paper_profiles.venue: 2025 13th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction Workshops and Demos (ACIIW)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students’ affective states unfold during interactions with an AI tutor, and whether large language models can be used to characterize those emotions at scale. The authors focus on the gap between prior evaluations of AI tutoring systems, which typically emphasize test scores or cognitive proxies, and the emotional experience of learners, which may shape persistence, engagement, and learning progress.

To study this, they analyze two semesters of chat logs from PyTutor, a GPT-4o–based Socratic tutor that gives hints and metacognitive prompts rather than full solutions. The dataset includes 16,986 conversational turns from 261 undergraduates enrolled in introductory Python or computing courses at MIT, Georgia State University, and Quinsigamond Community College in the United States. Instead of human coding, the paper uses three frontier LLMs (Gemini, GPT-4o mini, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to produce turn-level affect labels and valence/arousal/learning-helpfulness ratings, then fuses these outputs through an ensemble procedure.

The main findings are that student turns are generally mildly positive in valence, moderately aroused, and rated above neutral on learning helpfulness, but that confusion and curiosity are frequent and frustration still appears in a meaningful minority of turns. Temporal analysis suggests emotional states are short-lived, positive states persist longer than neutral or negative ones, negative affect often resolves quickly, and neutral states often act as a tipping point toward positive affect. The authors conclude that affect-aware scaffolding may be important for AI tutors, but they also caution that ensemble-derived labels are proxies rather than ground truth and should not be used for high-stakes decisions without human review.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference workshop paper using a clear observational/secondary-analysis methodology, but it is not an experiment and does not include human-annotated gold validation of the affect labels. Credibility is limited to descriptive and correlational evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no learning-gain effect size or causal impact on achievement; its contribution is primarily descriptive, characterizing emotional dynamics in LLM tutoring. The practical implications are plausible but the measured impact on learners is indirect and unclear.

interventions.use_case: PyTutor, a GPT-4o-based Socratic AI tutor used for on-demand hints, metacognitive questioning, and stepwise code debugging support in introductory Python/computing courses.

LLM ensemble used for automatic affect sensing in tutor–student dialogues, with Gemini, GPT-4o mini, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet producing turn-level valence, arousal, learning-helpfulness, and emotion labels.

finding.finding_summary: Across 16,986 student turns from 261 undergraduates, ensemble-fused affect ratings were mildly positive overall (median valence=5/9, arousal=5–6/9, learning-helpfulness=6/9), but negative and epistemic emotions remained common. Neutral turns often served as a pivot toward positive states, while frustration and confusion still appeared frequently enough to disrupt progress.
finding.measure: Turn-level affect annotations: valence, arousal, learning-helpfulness, and discrete emotion labels; Markov transition analysis of valence states

finding.finding_summary: The paper characterizes affect dynamics relevant to metacognition and self-regulation rather than measuring test performance. Confusion was frequent (22.15% of turns), curiosity was also common (15.83%), and negative affect often resolved quickly, suggesting the tutor context supported iterative problem solving but still required emotional regulation scaffolds.
finding.measure: Discrete emotion frequencies and valence transition dynamics during tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: A Causal Framework for Estimating Heterogeneous Effects of On-Demand Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of estimating causal effects for on-demand tutoring sessions embedded in adaptive learning systems. The authors argue that standard evaluations are confounded because students request help when they are already struggling, making naive comparisons between tutored and untutored attempts misleading. To solve this, they propose a causal inference framework that combines analytic sample construction, Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) to estimate latent student knowledge, and causal forests with doubly robust estimation to estimate both average and session-level heterogeneous tutoring effects.

The study is applied to more than 5,000 middle-school mathematics tutoring sessions from the Eedi adaptive learning platform. In Eedi, students worked on mathematics problems and could initiate brief synchronous text-chat sessions with human tutors. The sample came from a larger school-level randomized trial in which 12 schools and 2,585 students had access to the platform over two academic years, but the paper’s own analysis is observational at the tutoring-session level. Tutors were experienced teachers trained to support students through Socratic, problem-focused chat.

The authors find that requesting tutoring increases next-problem correctness by about 4 percentage points and improves accuracy on the next skill by about 3 percentage points. Effects vary substantially across sessions, ranging from strongly negative to strongly positive, and are larger for students with lower prior mastery, with slightly smaller effects for low-SES students. The paper concludes that DKT-informed causal forests can help estimate heterogeneous effects in embedded tutoring systems and could also support the evaluation and improvement of AI tutoring systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a strong observational causal-inference study with doubly robust estimation, causal forests, robustness checks, and placebo testing, but it is not a randomized evaluation of the tutoring interaction itself. The design credibly estimates heterogeneous session-level effects, yet residual confounding remains possible.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The estimated average effects are modest but meaningful for a priority population: +4.01 percentage points on immediate correctness and +2.73 percentage points on near transfer. The larger significance is methodological and operational, but the direct learning gains are in the modest-to-moderate range rather than large.

interventions.use_case: Causal evaluation framework for on-demand human tutoring embedded in an adaptive middle-school mathematics learning platform, using DKT and causal forests to estimate session-level effects and heterogeneity.
Eedi adaptive mathematics platform delivering diagnostic quizzes, hints, videos, and follow-up practice, within which on-demand tutoring was embedded.

finding.finding_summary: Across 2,585 middle-school students and 96,612 analytic problem attempts, on-demand tutoring increased immediate math correctness by 4.01 percentage points (ATE; 95% CI [2.51, 5.51]) and first-attempt accuracy on the next skill by 2.73 percentage points (95% CI [1.12, 4.35]). The paper also reports substantial session-level heterogeneity, with immediate-performance CATEs ranging from -20.25pp to +19.91pp and near-transfer CATEs ranging from -23.60pp to +47.70pp.
finding.measure: Next-problem correctness and first-attempt correctness on the subsequent skill (math problem accuracy)
finding.confidence_interval: [2.51, 5.51] for next-problem correctness; [1.12, 4.35] for near transfer

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, especially large language models such as GPT-4 and ChatGPT, can be integrated into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to make learning more personalized, adaptive, and interactive. Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, it synthesizes recent work and use cases around automated question generation, personalized feedback, and conversational tutoring dialogue. The central problem addressed is how generative AI can overcome limitations of traditional ITS that rely on static content and rule-based adaptation.

The paper discusses the kinds of capabilities generative AI adds to ITS, including generating questions tailored to learner proficiency, producing step-by-step feedback for errors, and sustaining natural-language tutoring conversations. It also highlights key implementation challenges, such as pedagogical accuracy, bias, equity, and learner engagement, and argues for hybrid systems with validation and expert oversight. Future directions include multimodal AI, affective computing, and ethical policy development.

The paper does not study a specific student population or educational setting; instead, it is a conceptual and review-style discussion aimed at the broader educational technology and ITS community. Its main conclusion is that generative AI has substantial promise for improving personalization and responsiveness in tutoring systems, but that responsible deployment requires safeguards for correctness, fairness, and sustained engagement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative conceptual report/review, not an empirical study. It does not present a defined sample, comparison group, or outcome analysis, so it provides no causal or correlational evidence under the evidence framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measured impact is reported. The paper argues for potential benefits of generative AI in tutoring systems, but it provides no effect sizes or student outcome data.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI/LLM-enhanced intelligent tutoring systems that generate personalized questions, provide real-time step-by-step feedback, and support interactive dialogue tutoring (e.g., GPT-4 in ITS).
A conceptual review of classical adaptive tutoring systems as the base architecture being augmented by generative AI for personalization and feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Estimating the Potential Impact of Combined Race and Ethnicity Reporting on Long-Term Earnings Statistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how long-term earnings differ across self-identified race and ethnicity categories when compared with country of birth and parental place of birth. The central question is not about an educational intervention, but about how changes in U.S. race/ethnicity reporting standards may affect the measurement and interpretation of statistical outcomes, especially for Hispanic and Middle Eastern/North African (MENA) groups.

The authors combine administrative place-of-birth data from the Social Security Administration with 2010 Census race and ethnicity responses and earnings records from state unemployment insurance systems. They analyze two large adult samples: foreign-born workers aged 25-55 in 2010, and U.S.-born young adults aged 25-28 with parental birthplace information from the 2000 Census. Their outcome is average real annual earnings from 2010-2015, with regression adjustments for education, age, U.S. residence duration, industry, labor-force attachment, and hours worked.

The study shows substantial heterogeneity in earnings within the same birthplace groups, especially among Mexican, Puerto Rican, Salvadoran, Cuban, Iranian, Israeli, Egyptian, and Lebanese-origin populations. The findings suggest that a single-question race/ethnicity format may obscure economically meaningful differences that are visible under the current two-question format, particularly differences associated with whether respondents identify as White, Black, Some Other Race, Hispanic alone, or MENA.

Overall, the paper concludes that the way race and ethnicity are collected can materially affect which subgroup differences remain visible in official statistics. The authors argue that birthplace information can help interpret these patterns, but some distinctions may become difficult to estimate under the new reporting format.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not an education intervention study; it is a policy/economics analysis of race/ethnicity reporting and long-term earnings using administrative and census data. There is no experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of an AI or instructional technology intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is evaluated. The paper’s findings concern measurement and classification effects in earnings statistics, not student learning, engagement, or instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Student Engagement with GenAI’s Tutoring Feedback: A Mixed Methods Study
paper_profiles.venue: Koli Calling '25 / Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Computing Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students engage with immediate AI-generated tutoring feedback in programming education. The authors focus on a gap in prior work: while many studies examine the quality of GenAI feedback, less is known about whether students actually notice, understand, and use that feedback during problem solving.

To study this, the authors built a Python learning environment in which students could request four distinct GenAI tutoring feedback components: identifying problems, providing explanations/examples, giving a next-step hint, and offering a strategic approach. The feedback was generated with GPT-4.1 and integrated into Tutor Kai. Students used the system while working on Python exercises that matched an introductory programming course. The study combined think-aloud protocols, eye-tracking, screen recordings, and questionnaire data.

The study involved 20 undergraduate students in an introductory programming course at a German university. The tasks were part of a course environment used during the summer semester, and the participants were mostly first- or second-semester students. The results show that students often understood or agreed with the feedback, but a substantial portion of their thoughts indicated they needed more information, thought the feedback was irrelevant, or judged it as not helpful. When students expressed understanding, they were more likely to improve their code; when they expressed disagreement or needed more information, they often collected another feedback component instead of acting immediately.

Overall, the paper concludes that students are active, selective consumers of GenAI tutoring feedback rather than passive recipients. The authors argue that systems should better support follow-up clarification, because students frequently evaluate feedback against their own internal understanding before deciding whether to act on it.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods study with think-aloud, eye-tracking, and screen-recording analysis rather than a causal impact evaluation. It is methodologically careful and includes inter-coder reliability, but it does not meet higher-evidence experimental standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports descriptive, process-oriented findings about how students engage with GenAI feedback rather than a measured educational impact with effect sizes. Its implications are useful for design, but the demonstrated outcome impact on learning is unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: GenAI-generated tutoring feedback for introductory Python programming tasks, delivered through four feedback components (find problems, explanations/examples, next-step hints, and strategic approach) in an online practice environment using GPT-4.1 with structured prompts and RAG-supported lecture links.

AI-generated immediate tutoring feedback on students' code submissions, with separate feedback components for error diagnosis, concept explanation, actionable next-step hints, and strategic problem-solving guidance.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students' feedback engagement reflected self-regulation, internal evaluation, and metacognitive decision-making. Students often judged whether feedback was relevant, already known, or required more detail before acting; when they expressed understanding, 76.2% of related feedback components led to code improvements, but disagreement or missing-information thoughts often led to no immediate action and seeking more feedback instead.
finding.measure: Think-aloud coded themes, feedback-selection behavior, and immediate coding actions after reading AI feedback components

finding.finding_summary: Students' engagement showed signs of help-seeking, frustration, and perceived usefulness across feedback types. Of 380 collected and read feedback components, students explicitly judged feedback as helpful 26 times and not helpful 32 times; when feedback seemed irrelevant or insufficient, they commonly collected another component rather than acting immediately.
finding.measure: Think-aloud judgments of helpfulness/not helpfulness, feedback collection rates, and no-action rates

paper_profiles.title: Training LLM-based Tutors to Improve Student Learning Outcomes in Dialogues
paper_profiles.venue: AIED 2025: The 26th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to train large language model (LLM)-based tutors so that they do more than produce pedagogically plausible dialogue: the authors want tutor utterances that actually increase the likelihood of correct student responses. The paper argues that many current AI tutors are optimized mainly to imitate good tutoring behavior, but not directly for student learning outcomes within a dialogue.

To address this, the authors propose a training pipeline that generates multiple candidate tutor utterances, scores them with two signals, and then uses those scores for preference-based optimization. One signal is a student outcome predictor (LLMKT), which estimates whether a candidate tutor turn will lead to a correct next student response. The second is a pedagogical rubric evaluated by GPT-4o, covering accuracy, progress, and guidance. These scores are combined to construct preference pairs, and a smaller open-source model (Llama 3.1 8B) is trained using distillation followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

The empirical setting is tutoring dialogues from the MathDial dataset, which contains mathematics problem-solving conversations centered on incorrect student answers. The study uses dialogue-level train/validation/test splits from MathDial and evaluates generated tutor utterances offline, not with real students. Thus the population is mathematics tutoring dialogues involving students in a math learning context, but the paper does not report an actual participant sample of middle school students; the middle-school classification comes from the topic area and math-dialogue tutoring context rather than an explicitly described human participant group.

The main conclusion is that the DPO-trained LLM tutor substantially improves predicted student correctness while maintaining high pedagogical quality, often matching or approaching GPT-4o on rubric-based evaluations. The authors also report qualitative and human evaluation evidence suggesting the model learns to pose more manageable, concrete tasks that support student progress. They conclude that the approach is promising but emphasize that real-student evaluation is still needed.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference paper with a clear experimental pipeline, but it does not test with real students and relies heavily on simulated student models and automated judgments. That makes it informative but methodologically limited for causal claims about learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports sizable improvements in predicted correctness and strong human-rated performance, but the effects are on simulated/human-judged tutor utterances rather than demonstrated student learning. Because there is no real-student outcome, the practical impact remains promising but unconfirmed.

interventions.use_case: training an open-source LLM tutor (Llama 3.1 8B) to generate math tutoring dialogue turns that maximize next-turn student correctness while preserving pedagogical quality

finding.finding_summary: The trained DPO tutor produced significantly higher predicted next-turn student correctness on MathDial math dialogues than all baselines, including GPT-4o. In the automated evaluation, DPO achieved 0.65 student-correctness prediction versus 0.49 for GPT-4o and 0.43 for the base Llama model, while human evaluation also ranked DPO best for likelihood of correct response (mean rank 1.75 vs 2.13 for GPT-4o and 2.12 for human tutors; p < 0.05).
finding.measure: LLMKT-predicted next-turn student correctness; human-annotated correctness ranking of tutor utterances
finding.study_size: n=3,101 tutor turns on the test set; human eval n=50 instances

paper_profiles.title: TutorGym: A Testbed for Evaluating AI Agents as Tutors and Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents TutorGym, a software testbed for evaluating AI agents in educational settings, especially large language models (LLMs), reinforcement learning agents, and computational models of learning. The main problem addressed is that existing LLM benchmarks usually evaluate only final answer generation, which does not capture the step-by-step, interactive behavior required for intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs). TutorGym instead embeds agents inside real tutor interfaces so they can be assessed as tutors and as simulated students.

The intervention is not a learner-facing educational treatment but a benchmarking infrastructure that connects agents to three ITS paradigms: CTAT example-tracing tutors, Apprentice Tutors, and OATutors. The system exposes tutor state to the agent and evaluates actions such as providing hints, identifying correct or incorrect steps, or demonstrating next-step solutions. It also supports training agents as simulated learners through in-context learning and compares their learning curves against human student data where available.

The paper reports an initial evaluation using several commercial LLMs, including Sonnet-3.5, Haiku-3.5, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-v2.5, across 223 tutor domains. The evaluation shows that current LLMs are weak at tutoring tasks such as grading student actions and generating stepwise demonstrations, although they can produce human-like learning curves when used as simulated learners with in-context examples. The authors conclude that TutorGym fills an important gap in AI-in-education benchmarking and may support future work on both LLM tutors and simulated learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a framework/testbed paper rather than an intervention study on student outcomes. It is peer-reviewed-style scholarly work, but it does not provide a controlled evaluation of educational effectiveness or subgroup effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s direct impact on learners is unclear because it evaluates AI agents inside tutoring systems, not student achievement. Its main contribution is methodological infrastructure for future AI-in-education research, which is useful but not itself evidence of educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking existing cognitive tutors, Apprentice Tutors, and OATutors as interactive tutoring environments for evaluating AI agents acting as tutors or simulated students

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning gains directly, but it evaluates LLMs on mathematics-tutoring tasks within 223 tutor domains. As tutors, current LLMs performed poorly: none exceeded chance at labeling incorrect actions, and next-step demonstrations were only about 52-70% accurate across models and tutor types; as simulated learners, Haiku-3.5 and GPT-4o produced learning curves qualitatively similar to human students in Apprentice Tutors.
finding.measure: Accuracy at labeling correct/incorrect student actions; accuracy of generating next-step demonstrations; first-attempt error-rate learning curves in math tutors

paper_profiles.title: An Experience Report on a Pedagogically Controlled, Curriculum-Constrained AI Tutor for SE Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how a large-language-model-based tutor can be integrated into secondary computer science / software engineering education in a way that is pedagogically controlled and constrained to curriculum content. The authors argue that generic AI chatbots are often too open-ended for educational use, so they explore an approach that preserves instructional safety, reduces hallucinations, and supports learners without replacing teachers.

The intervention is RockStartIT Tutor, an AI assistant powered by GPT-4/GPT-4o via OpenAI’s Assistant API. Rather than fine-tuning a model, the system uses a modular, tagged Markdown knowledge base and prompt engineering to keep responses grounded in approved course material, deliver hints before solutions, and maintain age-appropriate language. The tutor also uses threaded conversation memory and streaming responses to support multi-turn interaction in a web-based interface.

The evaluation involved 13 participants: 7 learners and 6 teachers/prospective teachers, all working with the tutor during a RockStartIT course on programming and computational thinking. Participants completed a TAM-based questionnaire and answered open-ended questions after a 30–45 minute use session on their own devices. Results suggested generally positive perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use, with teachers especially valuing the tutor as a complement to instruction and learners appreciating the low-pressure environment for asking questions.

The main conclusion is that a carefully constrained AI tutor can be acceptable and potentially useful in secondary-level computing education when it is tightly aligned to curriculum content and used as a support tool rather than a replacement for teachers. The study also highlights several design challenges, including onboarding, trust calibration, and the need for longer-term studies with the intended age group.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-sample mixed-methods pilot/experience report (n=13) using self-report TAM measures and qualitative feedback, not a controlled efficacy study. It provides useful descriptive evidence about acceptability and use, but limited credibility for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive acceptance and perceived support value, but it does not report learning gains or robust outcome effects. Impact is therefore unclear/modest rather than demonstrably strong.

interventions.use_case: pedagogically controlled GPT-4o chat tutor for a secondary school programming and computational thinking course, using curriculum-constrained responses, hint-first scaffolding, and threaded dialogue

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally reported that the AI tutor created a low-stakes, nonjudgmental environment that made it easier to ask questions and receive support. The study used a TAM-style questionnaire with n=13 and found strong perceived usefulness and ease of use ratings, especially on items related to clarity and comfort with interaction (e.g., PEOU1 M=4.54, PEOU2 M=4.62).
finding.measure: Technology Acceptance Model questionnaire items and open-ended feedback on usability, helpfulness, and future use

finding.finding_summary: The tutor was reported to support inquiry, reflection, and metacognitive thinking by giving hints rather than direct solutions. Qualitative comments indicated that it helped users trace reasoning errors and understand concepts, aligning with the paper’s emphasis on scaffolded problem solving and critical thinking; however, no formal learning gain effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended responses and TAM items related to usefulness for understanding tasks and learning support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived the tutor as a useful classroom support tool that could reduce cognitive load and complement instruction, with strong agreement that it could be a useful addition to teaching materials (PU8 M=4.5, SD=0.54). The study did not measure actual workload reduction, but teacher acceptance and comments suggest perceived efficiency benefits rather than demonstrated performance gains.
finding.measure: Teacher TAM items on usefulness, classroom support, and intention to use

paper_profiles.title: Unmasking the Shadows of AI: Investigating Deceptive Capabilities in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the problem of deceptive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a focus on how deception is defined, categorized, and discussed in the AI safety literature. The author argues that deceptive behavior is an inherent and evolving phenomenon in LLMs, shaped by biased training data and socio-technical dynamics, and that current debates about AI deception require clearer conceptual and governance frameworks.

Rather than studying a classroom or educational intervention, the paper is a theoretical and literature-based analysis of existing work on AI deception. It reviews four categories of deceptive behavior in LLMs: strategic deception, imitation, sycophancy, and unfaithful reasoning. The paper draws on examples involving ChatGPT, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and related systems, as well as recent AI safety and governance reports.

The context is broad AI development and policy rather than a specific population or educational setting. The paper concludes that AI deception should be treated as a serious current risk, recommends stronger regulation, context-sensitive accountability, and clearer disclosure language, and argues for interdisciplinary cooperation across philosophy, sociology, and computer science. It also suggests that digital education should include data infrastructure literacy and greater transparency around how AI generates outputs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/critical essay with literature review and policy discussion, not an empirical study. It reports no original methodology, sample, or effect estimates relevant to education or student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention impact is estimated and no student outcome is measured. The paper focuses on theoretical risks of LLM deception and governance implications rather than demonstrated effects in classrooms.

interventions.use_case: A conceptual review of ChatGPT/GPT-style large language models as conversational AI, focusing on deceptive capabilities, strategic deception, sycophancy, imitation, and unfaithful reasoning rather than tutoring per se.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM deception creates substantial governance, regulatory, and social-risk concerns, including misuse, loss of control, misinformation, and political/cultural harms.
