They compare this proposed Laplacian against standard graph-Laplacian and weighted nonlocal Laplacian approaches, examining both spectral clustering and Dirichlet-based interpolation.

The empirical illustrations are on synthetic toy datasets (2-Moons and 3-Moons) and image datasets (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST), with labels provided for only small subsets of points. The paper concludes that the proposed Laplacian improves clustering performance, particularly in low-label settings, and that the contrastive component is especially beneficial for spectral methods while the density component is helpful for constrained optimization. However, this is a graph-learning paper and does not involve educational participants, classrooms, or AI tutoring interventions.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methods paper on graph Laplacians for semi-supervised learning, not a study of an educational intervention. It does not evaluate ChatGPT, tutoring, or any K-12 learning technology, and provides no causal design or student outcome evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact evidence for middle school mathematics or any student population. Its contribution is algorithmic and theoretical within machine learning, with illustrative clustering experiments unrelated to education.

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle school subject matter. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and may not reflect real-world visual reasoning with subject-specific knowledge. To address this, they construct a dataset of over 2,000 open-ended questions tied to 486 images drawn from German school textbooks and related educational materials across nine domains, including mathematics, history, biology, physics, and others.

The benchmark is not an educational intervention but an evaluation framework for AI image understanding. Questions are designed so that models must combine visual interpretation with curricular background knowledge, and some items are deliberately adversarial or unanswerable from the image alone. The authors evaluate thirteen open-weight VLMs using a panel-of-LLMs judging setup. They report that even the strongest models achieve under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in mathematics, music, and adversarial questions. The results suggest that success on popular public benchmarks does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic German-language setting.

The study context is German grades 8-10, using school-textbook-style materials and some supplemental internet images for certain domains. The paper concludes that middle school-level multimodal questions are already difficult for current state-of-the-art VLMs, and that language, question design, and the need to integrate visual cues with background knowledge all materially affect performance. The authors propose the dataset as a testbed for future work and suggest that reasoning-style prompting or English translation may change outcomes, but these were not the focus of the reported experiments.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation paper, but it is not an educational effectiveness study and includes no student participants, assignment, or causal design. It provides model benchmarking methodology rather than evidence on an intervention's impact in classrooms.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured educational impact on learners, teachers, or institutions. The paper reports model accuracy on benchmark tasks only, with no effect size for student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking and evaluation of vision-language models on open-ended German middle school curriculum questions that require visual understanding plus subject knowledge; includes adversarial questions and some questions with text embedded in images.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test a tutoring intervention on student math learning; instead it benchmarks VLM performance on middle school math questions. Across 308 math questions, the best model reached 34.09% and the weakest 9.09%, indicating limited capability on this task rather than evidence of instructional benefit. The benchmark emphasizes counting, geometry, and simple calculations derived from images, with no student outcome measures reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended middle school math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: This is a benchmark paper rather than an educational intervention study, so there is no causal evidence of learning gains. Performance varied by subject, with best overall accuracy below 45% and domain scores around 54% in history/religion and around 31% in music, showing that current VLMs often struggle with middle school subject matter in German. No student learning outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Accuracy on subject-specific open-ended benchmark questions across arts, biology, geography, history, music, physics, religion, and sports

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different stakeholders perceive ChatGPT’s potential use in mathematics education and whether the tool can support mathematical problem solving and teaching. The central question is not a controlled comparison with another tutoring system, but rather whether ChatGPT can function as a useful educational tool and where its limitations appear, especially in mathematics.

The study uses a qualitative instrumental case study design with two parts: content analysis of interview data and a user-experience investigation. For the interview component, the authors analyzed perspectives from 30 interviewees drawn from public blogs discussing ChatGPT in mathematics. For the user-experience component, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for a week and tested several math-teaching scenarios, including algebraic equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry/Pythagorean theorem tasks. The context is mathematics teaching and learning, with some discussion framed around middle school geometry, though the sample itself is broader than middle school students alone.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is viewed positively as an accessible tool that can explain concepts, provide rapid feedback, and help with some routine mathematical tasks. However, the authors also find important weaknesses: ChatGPT can make calculation errors, misunderstand geometry, and fail to detect misconceptions or provide truly adaptive feedback. The overall conclusion is that ChatGPT has promise as a complementary educational tool, but it should be used cautiously, with human oversight and further research into safe, responsible classroom integration.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative case study with content analysis and user-experience testing, but it does not use a controlled comparison or quantitative causal design. Evidence credibility is limited by small samples and subjective interpretation, though the methodology is clearly described.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful applications of ChatGPT for math support, but it also documents notable errors and no quantified learning gains. Overall impact is unclear and modest, especially given the qualitative nature of the evidence and the lack of measured outcomes.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational mathematics tutor and problem-solving assistant for middle school algebra, limits, derivatives, and geometry explanations, including step-by-step solutions and follow-up Q&A.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents qualitative and task-based evidence that ChatGPT can explain some middle school mathematics topics well, especially basic geometry and Pythagorean theorem examples, but it also makes substantive errors on algebra, calculus, and geometry tasks. In the user-experience scenarios, ChatGPT produced incorrect results for a linear equation (13/20 vs correct 13/17), a cubic equation, a limit problem, and a derivative evaluation, while giving accurate but sometimes shallow geometry explanations.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview coding and accuracy on worked math prompts/scenarios (equations, limits, derivatives, geometry)
finding.study_size: n=33 total (30 interviewees; 3 educators in user-experience testing)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT may support mathematical problem-solving and prompt users toward step-by-step reasoning, but it also shows the model can fail to detect misconceptions or uncertainty, which limits its usefulness for deeper reasoning and metacognitive support. The evidence is qualitative rather than quantitative, based on stakeholder interviews and example prompts rather than measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of problem-solving support and error detection during math tasks
finding.study_size: n=33 total (30 interviewees; 3 educators in user-experience testing)

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently noted that ChatGPT can generate explanations and solutions quickly, making it potentially efficient for producing math help and feedback within seconds. The paper does not quantify time savings, but it repeatedly frames ChatGPT as a fast assistant for teachers and learners.
finding.measure: Perceived speed and convenience of generating math explanations/solutions
finding.study_size: n=33 total (30 interviewees; 3 educators in user-experience testing)

finding.finding_summary: The study reports generally positive enthusiasm about ChatGPT for mathematics education, but also caution and concern about overreliance, accuracy, and loss of human interaction. These findings are based on stakeholder perspectives rather than a direct measurement of motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Stakeholder perceptions of enthusiasm, caution, and reliance concerns
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees for perceptions; n=3 educators for testing

paper_profiles.title: Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This reflection paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, may affect cognitive learning processes and outcomes. Rather than reporting a new empirical intervention study, the paper critiques current research trends and argues that discussion of AI in education has often outpaced evidence, with too much emphasis on potential benefits and too little attention to instructional design, comparison conditions, and methodological rigor.

The authors develop the ISAR model, which distinguishes four types of AI effects on learning: inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition. They argue that AI can sometimes merely replace existing instructional functions, sometimes add cognitive support such as feedback and scaffolding, and sometimes transform tasks to enable deeper learning. At the same time, AI can also produce inversion effects when learners over-rely on it and engage less deeply. The paper draws on prior research on educational technologies, intelligent tutoring systems, and recent generative AI studies, but does not study a specific participant population or classroom intervention itself.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI in education should be evaluated through rigorous, evidence-based research that focuses on actual learning rather than short-term performance or satisfaction alone. The authors emphasize that AI’s educational value depends on instructional implementation, the quality of the comparison condition, and contextual factors such as students’ AI literacy and educators’ pedagogical skills. They recommend using AI to complement rather than replace human instruction and call for research that explicitly tests when AI supports learning, when it is equivalent to existing methods, and when it may be harmful.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a reflection/theoretical paper rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and proposes the ISAR framework, but does not present new primary data, an RCT, or a meta-analysis of its own.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially high conceptual impact for framing future AI-in-education research, but it does not report direct outcome effects on learners. Its empirical implications are indirect and not quantifiable from this article alone.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of ChatGPT and related generative AI as conversational tutors for learning, including Socratic multi-turn dialogue, trialogue tutoring, and AI-supported student question answering in education.

Classical and conversational ITS (e.g., AutoTutor, Socratic Playground, Ruffle & Riley) used as prior-art comparators and examples for adaptive tutoring, feedback, scaffolding, and dialogue-based learning.
AI-mediated feedback and scaffolding systems, including teacher/student dashboards, analytics-driven feedback, and AI-generated feedback on student work.
Use of ChatGPT and related generative tools to support writing, revision, and language-generation tasks in educational settings.
AI-supported problem-based, scenario-based, and game-based learning activities, including AI-generated interactive simulations for deep learning.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Solutions for Faculty and Students: A Review of Literature and Roadmap for Future Research
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of a consolidated, practice-oriented account of how generative AI (GenAI), especially ChatGPT, has been used in education. The authors argue that much of the existing literature focuses on theoretical possibilities rather than real-world applications, making it difficult for educators and policymakers to judge GenAI’s practical value, risks, and limitations.

To address this gap, the paper conducts a systematic literature review using PRISMA and thematic analysis. The review covers 44 journal articles published from 2022 to 2024 and focuses on higher education, though the examples discussed span a range of educational contexts. The paper organizes applications of GenAI into seven categories: generation of teaching materials, skill development, support for student task development, academic performance evaluation, feedback delivery, virtual assistants/chatbots, and research support. Across these cases, ChatGPT is by far the most common tool, with smaller numbers of studies using other models such as GPT-3, GPT-4, BLOOM, Codex, DALL-E, MidJourney, and LangChain.

The review concludes that GenAI has meaningful potential to support teaching, learning, assessment, feedback, administration, and research, but current tools still suffer from important limitations, especially hallucinations, inconsistent source quality, and weak performance on some open-ended or evaluative tasks. The authors emphasize that GenAI should be treated as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human judgment. They recommend more research on prompt engineering, custom education-oriented tools, ethical issues, and newer models such as GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA and thematic analysis, but it is not a primary causal evaluation and does not synthesize effects via meta-analysis. The evidence base is largely qualitative/descriptive case studies, so credibility is moderate rather than high for intervention impact estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for efficiency, tutoring, and skill development, but it reports no pooled effect sizes and repeatedly emphasizes hallucinations and accuracy limitations. Overall impact is plausible but unclear in magnitude across educational settings.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of ChatGPT and closely related generative AI models used as tutoring, conversational support, and virtual assistant tools in higher education; includes examples such as tutoring students, generating explanations, role-play dialogue, and supporting research and administrative queries.

Use of ChatGPT/GPT-3/GPT-4 and related models to generate feedback, classify student responses, and assist grading or response evaluation across open-ended answers, essays, and case-study submissions.

Use of ChatGPT to support writing, language learning, editing, translation-like tasks, grammar explanation, essay drafting, and EFL feedback, including prompting students and teachers in language-focused activities.
Use of GenAI to generate teaching materials, exercises, lesson plans, presentations, and assessment items for classroom instruction, especially in secondary and higher education.
Use of GenAI for role-play exercises, interactive gaming, and simulated case scenarios in teaching and learning activities.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports both beneficial and problematic literacy-related uses of GenAI. ChatGPT was used to support essay writing and language feedback, but the paper also highlights hallucinated references and inaccurate content, indicating that literacy support can improve drafting while introducing errors that require substantial human editing.
finding.measure: Essay writing quality, language feedback quality, and citation/reference accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The review describes ChatGPT-enabled language learning activities such as role-play, conversational practice, grammar explanation, and EFL feedback as generally supportive of language development. However, the evidence is synthesized from individual case studies rather than pooled effects, so no aggregate effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Language learning tasks, conversational practice, and EFL instructional outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a case on fourth-grade students’ open-ended mathematics responses and notes that the model performed poorly for reviewing such answers. This suggests limited reliability for math assessment and support in open-ended contexts, with no quantitative effect size reported in the review.
finding.measure: Open-ended mathematics question evaluation and response support

finding.finding_summary: GenAI was used in science and medical-education contexts to generate content, assess responses, and support topic explanation, but the review emphasizes variable accuracy. For example, it notes that only 32% of generated immunology questions were completely accurate and adequately explained in one cited study, underscoring weak reliability for scientific assessment tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy of generated science/medical questions and explanations; science learning support

finding.finding_summary: Across history, business, arts, programming, and medical education, the review finds GenAI broadly useful for supporting subject-specific learning tasks and content creation. The evidence is descriptive and case-based, showing utility in generating lessons, case scenarios, presentations, and assignment support rather than estimating a pooled academic achievement effect.
finding.measure: Subject-specific task completion, content generation, and course activities across multiple disciplines

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests GenAI can enhance student engagement and personalized learning experiences, and several included studies frame it as increasing learner participation. These claims are synthesized from qualitative and case-study evidence rather than direct standardized measures of motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Student engagement and participation in learning activities

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly identifies potential gains in critical thinking, prompting, communication, and logical reasoning, but also warns about overreliance and shallow processing. For example, one cited study noted a steep learning curve in effective ChatGPT use, while others reported improved self-perceived critical thinking; no pooled effect size is available.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, prompt engineering, communication, and logical reasoning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A major finding of the review is that GenAI can save time and reduce workload by generating teaching materials, feedback, assessments, and administrative responses. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, but it consistently frames these uses as efficiency-enhancing for faculty and staff.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction, speed of content generation, feedback turnaround, and administrative query handling

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that GenAI may reshape pedagogy, curriculum, assessment, and institutional practices, but adoption is constrained by hallucinations, ethics, and governance concerns. It emphasizes the need for training, policy, and oversight rather than reporting measurable institutional effect sizes.
finding.measure: Institutional use cases, academic integrity concerns, and recommendations for policy/pedagogical change

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions and Barriers to Adopting Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: A Survey of Educators in Fifty States
paper_profiles.venue: Reimagining Education – The Role of E-Learning, Creativity, and Technology in the Post-Pandemic Era
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines K-12 educators’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), the barriers they perceive to adopting it, and the kinds of policies, training, and infrastructure they believe are needed for classroom integration. The authors frame the study around broader questions of AI adoption in schools rather than evaluating a specific instructional tool or student outcome. The paper is positioned as especially relevant to current interest in generative AI and other classroom technologies.

The study used a nationwide survey distributed through Qualtrics to educators in all 50 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, yielding responses from 4,528 educators across PreK through grade 12. The survey asked about district AI policies, comfort with technology, prior technology training, openness to new technologies, familiarity with AI tools, perceived resource needs, and access to internet and devices. The sample included educators teaching elementary, middle school, and high school grades, working in public and private settings, and representing rural, suburban, and urban districts.

Findings indicate that most educators viewed AI positively and were open to learning and using new technologies, but they also reported gaps in district AI policies, uneven access to technology, and concerns about infrastructure, training, and awareness of free or low-training AI tools. Comfort with technology was higher among some groups than others, and access to reliable internet was notably weaker in rural districts. The authors conclude that successful AI integration in K-12 will require targeted professional development, clearer district policies, better infrastructure, and equitable resource distribution. The paper also argues that AI should be integrated through an authentic STEM model and used to support, rather than replace, teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey with descriptive statistics and no experimental manipulation or causal identification. It provides useful contextual evidence about educator perceptions, but it does not test intervention effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional implications for AI adoption, policy, and training, but it does not demonstrate measured student or teacher outcome gains. Reported findings are descriptive and therefore indicate unclear practical impact rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: Nationwide survey of K-12 educators’ perceptions, readiness, and barriers regarding AI adoption in classrooms, including generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-3/4, Bard, DALL·E-2, and scikit-learn as reported examples of use rather than an evaluated tutoring intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This survey of 4,528 educators found generally positive perceptions of AI and substantial openness to adoption, but also clear institutional barriers related to policy, infrastructure, and training. For example, 64.07% reported district AI policies, 82.53% reported policies for ethical/responsible technology use, and 75.26% said implementing AI would require substantial resources; the study is descriptive and reports percentages rather than inferential effect sizes.
finding.measure: Educator perceptions of AI, district policy presence, access to technology/training, infrastructure needs, and readiness for AI integration

finding.finding_summary: Respondents broadly viewed AI as a potential way to improve efficiency and support teaching tasks, especially through automation, personalized assistance, and reduced administrative burden. However, this was measured only as educator perceptions in a survey, not as observed workload reduction or time savings, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Educator perceptions of AI’s usefulness for administrative tasks, feedback, tutoring, and classroom support

paper_profiles.title: Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making: A Case Study on Remediating Math Mistakes
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how large language models (LLMs) and novice tutors can better remediate student math mistakes. The authors argue that a key barrier in tutoring is not only content knowledge but also the expert decision-making process behind effective remediation: identifying the student’s error, choosing an appropriate strategy, and understanding the intention behind that strategy. To study this, they develop Bridge, a cognitive-task-analysis-based framework that translates expert teachers’ latent reasoning into a structured decision-making model.

The intervention is not a classroom deployment but a modeling and benchmarking approach built from 700 real tutoring conversations collected from an existing tutoring provider. These conversations involved 1st-5th grade students in Title I schools, mostly serving low-income students of color, in a Southern U.S. school district. Four experienced math teachers helped define and validate the decision taxonomy, and they annotated the dataset with expert decisions and responses. The paper evaluates GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, and Llama-2-70B under different prompting conditions: no decision-making, expert decisions, self-generated decisions, and random decisions.

The main finding is that explicit expert-guided decision-making substantially improves LLM tutoring responses. GPT-4 responses generated with expert decisions were much more preferred, useful, and human-sounding than those generated without the decision framework, while random decisions often hurt performance. The results suggest that embedding expert thought processes into LLM tutoring can help bridge the novice-expert gap, but the paper emphasizes that this is an early framework and not yet an evaluation of student learning outcomes in real-time deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical human-evaluation study with a curated dataset and controlled comparison conditions, but it is not a student-outcome RCT or QED. Evidence is strong for model behavior and perceived response quality, but the paper does not test downstream learning impacts with students.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are meaningful for response quality and scalable tutoring workflows, but they are based on teacher judgments rather than student learning outcomes. The paper suggests practical promise, yet the impact on learners remains unmeasured.

interventions.use_case: Head-to-head evaluation of GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, and Llama-2-70B chat models as math remediation tutors for student mistakes in real tutoring conversations, with and without expert-guided decision-making (error diagnosis, strategy choice, and intention selection).
Used as a response-generation component within the Bridge framework, where expert decisions are supplied to condition LLM-generated tutoring replies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that expert-guided decision-making substantially improves LLM tutoring response quality, suggesting a more scalable way to generate higher-quality remediation than direct prompting alone. In human pairwise evaluations by teachers (40 pairs/model, 3 raters each), GPT-4 with expert decisions was 76% more preferred than GPT-4 without decisions, and overall scores improved significantly for all models under expert decision-making (p<0.05).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated pairwise comparisons of response usefulness, care, human-soundingness, and overall preference
finding.study_size: n=40 pairs per model; 3 annotators per pair; 700 tutoring conversations in the dataset

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for open-ended middle school mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned open-source LLM (GOAT, based on Mistral/Llama), a prior similarity-based method (SBERT-Canberra), and GPT-4 used in a zero-shot prompting setup. The central question is whether an LLM fine-tuned on teacher-scored student work can outperform an established non-generative benchmark for scoring, and how its feedback quality compares with GPT-4.

The study uses data from an online learning platform containing student responses to open-ended math problems, teacher-assigned scores, and teacher-written feedback. After preprocessing, the authors train and test on 50 random problems with about 5,000 total student responses, focused on middle-school math and the Illustrative Mathematics scoring rubric. GOAT and SBERT are trained or adapted on historical teacher data, while GPT-4 receives only the problem, student answer, and rubric. Quantitative scoring metrics include AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa; qualitative feedback quality is judged by two experienced teachers using criteria for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and overall preference.

Results show that GOAT outperforms SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on scoring accuracy, indicating that a fine-tuned LLM can better match teacher grading than the prior benchmark. However, GPT-4 produces feedback that teachers judge as more accurate, relevant, motivating, and preferable overall. The authors conclude that task-specific fine-tuning is promising for auto-scoring, but high-quality general-purpose LLMs remain stronger for generating feedback. They also argue that better teacher feedback data and more refined training could improve future open-source models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed comparative evaluation with a clear train/test protocol and human ratings, but it is not a randomized educational trial and lacks causal learner-outcome evidence. The study is primarily an algorithmic/qualitative benchmark rather than a rigorous classroom efficacy study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The system shows moderate promise for scoring automation and teacher assistance, especially GOAT's scoring gains over SBERT, but the work does not demonstrate direct student learning gains. Impact is therefore plausible but still unclear and limited to benchmarking and workflow support.

interventions.use_case: automated scoring and qualitative feedback generation for middle school students' open-ended mathematics responses using fine-tuned Mistral/LLM, SBERT-Canberra, and GPT-4 comparisons

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates how well three systems predict teacher scores on middle-school open-response math items. GOAT performed best on scoring accuracy (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422; n=1,000 test entries), outperforming SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, Kappa=0.266).
finding.measure: Teacher score prediction on open-ended middle school math responses; AUC, RMSE, and Cohen's kappa versus teacher-assigned scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper also assesses whether LLM-based feedback can support teacher workflow by generating usable feedback on student math responses. Human raters preferred GPT-4 most often (77.5%) over GOAT and SBERT (12% each), while GOAT outperformed SBERT on relevance and accuracy, suggesting promise for reducing teacher workload but not yet replacing human review.
finding.measure: Human evaluator ratings of feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, and model preference
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled student answers for feedback evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the extent to which secondary students are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, and Bing Copilot for school-related tasks. The authors are motivated by the rapid rise of LLMs in education, school restrictions on their use, and concerns about both cheating and inaccurate outputs. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the paper aims to document current usage patterns and student perceptions so educators and developers can better respond to students’ needs.

The study used a survey of 306 middle and high school students in the United States. Participants were recruited through a survey platform, local tutoring programs, and social media, and represented grades 6 through 12 across 43 states. The survey asked about frequency of LLM use, school subjects in which students used LLMs, perceived usefulness, policy restrictions, ethical concerns, demographic differences, and desired improvements to LLMs. Responses were primarily self-reported.

The main findings were that LLM use was widespread: about 71% of respondents had used an LLM at least once, and usage was fairly consistent across grades 7 through 12. Students reported using LLMs across multiple subjects, including math, though they were more often used for writing and language-related tasks. The authors conclude that LLMs are already deeply embedded in secondary students’ academic lives, that access and adoption may vary by socioeconomic and technological context, and that education-focused AI tools should be better adapted for student use, personalization, and equity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a cross-sectional survey study with self-reported usage and perceptions, not an experimental comparison of learning outcomes. It is peer-reviewed arXiv-style scholarly work, but the methodology is descriptive and cannot establish causal effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests widespread adoption and important equity implications, but it does not measure achievement gains or losses, so impact on learning is unclear. Its main contribution is documenting prevalence and perceived usefulness rather than demonstrating medium or large educational effects.

interventions.use_case: Survey of middle and high school students' use of ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama, and Bing Copilot for schoolwork assistance across subjects, including math, writing, history, and foreign languages; paper discusses potential AI tutoring applications rather than testing a tutoring system.

finding.finding_summary: In a survey of n=306 U.S. secondary students, 71% reported using LLMs at least once and 9% used them daily, despite generally restrictive school policies (mean strictness rating 3.48/5). The paper also finds usage gaps by context: 80.2% usage in the five most tech-advanced states versus 64.3% elsewhere, and 76.7% usage in private schools versus 71.3% in public schools, suggesting widening access inequities.
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM usage prevalence, school policy strictness ratings, and demographic comparisons across states and school types

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs for math assignments, with 28% of respondents indicating math use and 43% of LLM users finding them useful for math/STEM questions. However, the paper provides no achievement test results and notes concerns about incorrect answers and weak mathematical reasoning, so the evidence is descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Self-reported use for math and perceived usefulness for math/STEM questions

finding.finding_summary: For writing-related schoolwork, 57% of LLM users said the tools were useful for writing text. The paper is survey-based and does not report writing performance scores, but student responses suggest LLMs are viewed as helpful for producing or improving text.
finding.measure: Self-reported usefulness for writing text

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs across multiple non-math subjects, including language arts, history, and foreign languages. Responses were mixed: some said LLMs simplified complex topics, while others noted hallucinations and inaccurate factual answers, especially in history contexts.
finding.measure: Self-reported subject use and open-ended perceptions of helpfulness/accuracy

paper_profiles.title: Using Generative AI to Provide Feedback to Adult Tutors in Training and Assess Real-life Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training and evaluating adult tutors at scale, especially when human review of tutoring practice is costly and difficult. The authors argue that generative AI, particularly large language models such as GPT-4, can support tutor professional development by providing immediate feedback during training activities and by assessing tutors' real-world tutoring performance from dialogue transcripts.

The intervention described is embedded in the PLUS (Personalized Learning Squared) tutoring platform. Tutors complete online, scenario-based lessons such as Giving Effective Praise, where they answer tutoring scenarios and then receive AI-generated explanatory feedback. The paper also describes using LLMs to score real tutor-student dialogues, including identifying whether tutors praise effort versus outcomes and whether they respond appropriately to student math errors. The authors discuss prompting strategies such as prompt chaining, chain-of-thought prompting, few-shot prompting, and self-consistency to improve reliability.

The population context is adult tutors in training and in-service remote math tutors working with middle school students. The paper reports that more than 300 college students have been trained as remote math tutors serving nearly 2,500 middle school students across the United States. The setting is online, with lessons and assessments conducted through the PLUS tutoring system.

The paper concludes that generative AI shows promise as a low-cost, scalable tool for tutor feedback and performance assessment, but it should complement rather than replace human tutoring. It emphasizes practical and ethical concerns, including transparency, bias, hallucination, and the need for human-in-the-loop review. The paper is primarily a methods and use-case paper rather than a controlled evaluation of learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/practice-oriented paper with illustrative examples and references to prior conference work, not a controlled evaluation of the intervention in this paper. It is peer-reviewed and grounded in specific LLM prompting workflows, but the evidence presented here is mostly descriptive rather than causal.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential efficiency benefits for tutor training and assessment, but it does not report a measured educational outcome or effect size in this article. Impact on learners is therefore unclear and appears modest at present.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-4 and related LLMs to generate real-time explanatory feedback for adult tutors in scenario-based training lessons and to assess tutor performance from real-life tutoring transcripts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce the cost and time burden of tutor feedback and assessment compared with human evaluation. In the reported assessment use case, GPT-4 was able to evaluate 50 tutor-student dialogues with moderately high performance (F1 score reported qualitatively as moderately high), suggesting potential efficiency gains for scalable tutor coaching and monitoring.
finding.measure: Model performance on tutor dialogue assessment; workflow efficiency for feedback generation and evaluation
finding.study_size: n=50 dialogues (assessment example); program scale described as over 300 tutors and nearly 2,500 middle school students

paper_profiles.title: A scoping survey of ChatGPT in mathematics education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly emerging literature on ChatGPT in mathematics education and asks what the reported benefits and challenges are for teachers’ and students’ teaching and learning. Rather than studying a single classroom intervention, the authors conduct a scoping review of research published between November 2022 and May 2024, using Google Scholar, Web of Science, arXiv, HAL, conference proceedings, and snowball sampling to identify relevant work.

The paper focuses on ChatGPT and closely related GPT-based models as tools for mathematics education, but it also includes some studies from broader educational contexts when they are relevant to mathematics teaching and learning. The review covers a wide range of uses: mathematical problem solving, lesson planning, assessment and feedback, personalized learning, critical thinking, collaboration, and attitudes toward AI use. The literature spans primary, secondary, and tertiary contexts, with a substantial emphasis on teachers, pre-service teachers, and students in higher education, though the review also discusses K-12 and specifically middle-school-relevant mathematics topics.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as a supplementary support for mathematical explanations, planning, feedback, and personalized assistance, but its performance is inconsistent and often unreliable on more complex mathematical tasks. They highlight recurring concerns about hallucinations, inaccurate reasoning, over-reliance, and the need for human oversight. Overall, the paper argues that ChatGPT should be treated as a helpful but limited tool whose educational value depends on careful prompting, critical evaluation, and pedagogically informed use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review/editorial synthesis rather than a primary causal study. It is systematically conducted and peer-relevant, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and largely consists of early qualitative, descriptive, and small experimental studies.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful uses of ChatGPT in mathematics education, but the underlying evidence is mixed and often small-scale. Reported benefits are promising yet unclear in magnitude for general K-12 populations, so the overall impact remains modest/uncertain.

interventions.use_case: scoping review of ChatGPT use in mathematics education as a conversational AI tutor/assistant for student learning, teacher lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and collaborative support

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesized studies showing both promise and limitations for mathematics learning. ChatGPT/LLMs performed well on simple arithmetic, algebraic expressions, and some undergraduate-level tasks, but struggled with more complex problems, graduate-level difficulty, geometry misconceptions, and proof reasoning; for example, Dao and Le (2023) reported performance dropping from 82% on knowledge-level items to 10% on harder items, and Pardos and Bhandari (2024) found human-authored hints produced substantially and statistically significantly higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints across elementary and intermediate algebra.
finding.measure: Accuracy on mathematics and logic problems; exam-item performance; learning gains from hints; correctness of geometry/proof responses

finding.finding_summary: The review reported that ChatGPT could support critical thinking, reasoning, reflection, and collaboration, but also raised concerns that over-reliance might weaken these skills. Evidence included improved computational thinking and self-efficacy in a programming course (n=45; experimental group n=21), improved reflective planning and lesson-analysis skills for pre-service teachers, and better collaborative engagement in group work, alongside warnings that students may accept outputs uncritically or be less inclined to develop independent reasoning.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, programming self-efficacy, motivation, reflective planning quality, collaboration/process quality

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, ChatGPT was associated with improved motivation, engagement, and positive attitudes toward mathematics or AI-supported learning. For example, Yilmaz and Yilmaz (2023) reported significantly higher motivation in the ChatGPT-supported experimental group (n=21) versus control, and the review also notes positive attitudes among students and teachers, though with concerns about over-reliance and ethics.
finding.measure: Motivation, attitudes toward mathematics/AI, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review found that ChatGPT could reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, generating instructional materials, providing feedback, and automating or semi-automating assessment. In the hint-comparison study, 70% of ChatGPT hints passed manual quality checks, indicating practical utility, although human-authored hints still produced significantly larger learning gains; overall, the efficiency value was framed as immediate feedback and faster creation of plans/materials rather than fully reliable automation.
finding.measure: Lesson-plan generation quality, feedback generation, automated scoring, teacher time/workload implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper discussed broader institutional implications for AI adoption in mathematics education, including integrity, privacy, bias, and the need for human oversight in assessment. These are not measured effects but synthesized concerns and policy-relevant implications from the literature, including cautions that ChatGPT may amplify inequities or weaken assessment fairness without governance safeguards.
finding.measure: Ethical, governance, and assessment-policy implications

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT, and asks how these tools might transform teaching and learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors review existing literature on AI in education, summarize benefits and risks, and discuss ethical and practical considerations for educational use.

The article situates ChatGPT within the broader landscape of AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment, and educational chatbots. It does not report an empirical sample or a classroom experiment; instead, it draws on prior studies and examples across educational levels and functions to illustrate possible uses for students, teachers, and administrators.

The authors conclude that AI can support personalized learning, instant feedback, engagement, and teacher workload reduction, but that concerns about bias, privacy, accuracy, academic integrity, and overreliance must be addressed. They argue that successful adoption depends on ethical implementation, adequate teacher preparation, and alignment with pedagogical goals rather than technology use alone.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion article rather than an empirical study. It does not use a defined sample, comparison group, or analytic design to estimate effects, so it provides no direct causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that ChatGPT and chatbots may have broad educational potential, but it reports no measured impact. Because there are no study outcomes or effect sizes, the impact is speculative and cannot be rated as more than unclear/modest.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of ChatGPT and related chatbots as educational assistants for personalized learning, instant feedback, question answering, and student support in classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: Student Engagement and Achievement in American Secondary Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book examines why student disengagement is such a central problem in American secondary schools and argues that engagement is a prerequisite for meaningful academic achievement. Rather than focusing narrowly on test scores, the authors define engagement as students' psychological investment in learning and discuss why conventional indicators of achievement often fail to capture what schools should value. The introduction frames the book as a response to effective-schools research that had emphasized school variables but paid insufficient attention to the day-to-day problem of getting adolescents to participate seriously in academic work.

The book synthesizes findings from five projects conducted by the National Center on Effective Secondary Schools in 32 middle schools and 62 high schools across the United States. Across the chapters, it examines several routes to engagement: high-quality classroom discourse, intellectually demanding instruction, alternative programs for students at risk, organizational conditions that support teacher engagement, and the influence of family, peers, extracurricular activities, and part-time work. The work is primarily conceptual and explanatory, with empirical studies embedded in the broader argument.

Its main conclusion is that schools can promote engagement, but only if they create clear purposes, fairness, personal support, opportunities for success, and authentic intellectually challenging work. The authors argue that student engagement is shaped not just by individual motivation but also by school membership and the quality of academic tasks. They conclude that improving achievement requires deeper attention to how schools organize instruction and relationships, as well as broader social support for adolescents.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed scholarly book synthesizing multiple studies, but the excerpt is largely conceptual, qualitative, and correlational rather than a controlled evaluation. The paper does not provide a clear experimental or quasi-experimental design for the claims summarized here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The work has clear conceptual influence on engagement and school-restructuring debates, but the excerpt does not report medium or large causal effects on student outcomes. Its impact is mainly theoretical and institutional, with empirical effects described as modest or unspecified.

finding.finding_summary: This is a theory- and evidence-synthesis book chapter on student engagement, not a controlled intervention study. It argues that engagement is a psychological investment in learning and reports only modest statistical associations between survey-based engagement scales and achievement, with no effect size or CI provided; the authors note measurement limitations and conflicting patterns (e.g., some low-achieving students may be highly engaged).
finding.measure: Student engagement scales; student interviews and qualitative observations; achievement indicators discussed narratively

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that challenging students with higher-order thinking, authentic discourse, and meaningful academic work can increase engagement and deepen understanding. The empirical evidence described is qualitative and descriptive rather than experimental; no effect size is reported, but the chapter claims students reported more engagement in classes that challenged them to use their minds.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse quality, higher-order thinking opportunities, and student-reported engagement/understanding

finding.finding_summary: The volume synthesizes findings from five center projects across 32 middle schools and 62 high schools and argues that school membership, clarity of purpose, fairness, personal support, and authentic work are key institutional conditions for engagement. No single pooled effect size is provided; the evidence is primarily qualitative and correlational, with the impact framed as school restructuring and policy implications rather than a tested causal estimate.
finding.measure: School climate, organizational conditions, student engagement, and school restructuring themes
finding.study_size: 32 middle schools and 62 high schools (project-level studies); specific chapter samples not consistently reported

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Perspective paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), especially large language models and related generative systems, may reshape human learning. It asks what promises GenAI offers for education and learning, and what challenges must be addressed to use these tools responsibly and effectively. The paper is not an empirical study of a particular intervention; rather, it synthesizes ideas from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to frame a research and policy agenda.

The authors organize the discussion around GenAI’s potential roles in four areas: learning support, learning resource generation, feedback, and assessment. They argue that GenAI can provide scalable personalization, help create diverse and multimodal resources, deliver timely feedback, and enable more authentic and adaptive assessment. At the same time, they highlight technical and ethical risks, including hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, unequal access, and the possibility that GenAI could disrupt conventional assessment or weaken learners’ agency and critical thinking.

The paper concludes that realizing GenAI’s benefits will require AI literacy for learners and educators, evidence-based decision-making, and stronger methodological rigor in research on AI in education. It emphasizes that human-centred learning theories should guide the design and deployment of GenAI systems so that they augment rather than replace human cognition, creativity, and instruction. The paper is forward-looking and conceptual, proposing directions for future research, practice, and policy rather than reporting results from a specific population or intervention context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a Nature Human Behaviour perspective/theory article, not an empirical study. It synthesizes prior work and proposes a research agenda, but does not present a new evaluated intervention, sample, or causal design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention effect is measured in this paper, so there is no estimate of learner impact to classify. The article is conceptually important, but it does not demonstrate observable educational impact in the target population.

interventions.use_case: Perspective paper discussing generative AI tutors and chatbots such as ChatGPT and Khanmigo for personalized, dialogic learning support, including step-by-step math guidance, adaptive questioning, and conversational tutoring.

Perspective paper discussing GenAI systems that analyze student work and generate instant, personalized feedback for writing, programming, collaborative language tasks, and learning analytics dashboards.

Discussion of GenAI integrated into adaptive tutoring and personalized support systems that tailor content and prompts to learner needs, including AI-enabled tutoring within broader adaptive learning environments.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early stakeholder perspectives on the use of ChatGPT in mathematics education shortly after its public release. The authors ask two related questions: how students and educators perceive ChatGPT’s usefulness and risks for teaching and learning mathematics, and how well ChatGPT performs in a small set of math-teaching scenarios.

The study uses a qualitative instrumental case study design with two parts. First, it conducts content analysis of 30 interviews drawn from public blogs and online discussions involving people talking about ChatGPT in mathematics, including educators and students. Second, three experienced educators used ChatGPT for one week and evaluated its responses across several mathematics tasks, including solving equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry explanations. The context is mathematics education broadly, with some examples aligned to middle school geometry and algebraic reasoning.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is seen as promising for mathematics education because it can produce quick explanations, basic worked solutions, and accessible geometry instruction. However, the authors also find that ChatGPT can make elementary mathematical errors, misunderstand geometry, and give incorrect or overconfident answers without acknowledging uncertainty. The overall recommendation is cautious adoption: ChatGPT may support teaching and learning, but it should complement rather than replace human instruction, and more research is needed to ensure safe and responsible use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative instrumental case study with interview content analysis and small user-experience testing, not a controlled comparison. It provides useful descriptive evidence but has limited credibility for causal claims and no quantitative effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful usefulness for math support, but the evidence is mixed and largely anecdotal/qualitative, with several clear errors in problem solving. Any impact appears unclear and modest at best for general K-12 use.

interventions.use_case: Evaluates ChatGPT as a mathematics tutoring and explanation tool for solving algebra, calculus, limits, and geometry questions, including step-by-step responses and follow-up Q&A.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can sometimes provide clear, usable mathematics explanations, especially for basic geometry and simple problem solving, but it also makes notable errors in algebra, limits, derivatives, and geometry. In the user-experience scenarios, ChatGPT produced incorrect answers on several tasks (e.g., linear equation, cubic equation, limit, derivative, and Pythagorean theorem variants), with no formal effect size reported (n=3 educators for the user-experience stage; n=30 interviewees in the perception stage).
finding.measure: Accuracy and correctness of solutions/explanations to mathematics problems; qualitative user judgments of math teaching capability

finding.finding_summary: Participants and the authors describe ChatGPT as fast and convenient for generating explanations and solutions, often producing responses within seconds and reducing the time needed to draft worked examples or instructional text. The paper is qualitative and does not report a quantitative productivity effect size, but the central claim is that ChatGPT can speed up assistance and content generation for teachers and learners.
finding.measure: Perceived response speed, convenience, and ease of generating explanations/solutions

finding.finding_summary: Stakeholder reactions were generally enthusiastic about ChatGPT’s promise, but they were accompanied by caution about overreliance, misinformation, and reduced human interaction. The study reports positive public sentiment alongside concerns about trust and safe use, but no quantitative measure or effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Perceived enthusiasm, caution, and trust in ChatGPT for mathematics education

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could reshape mathematics education and calls for guidelines, responsible use, and further research before broad adoption. This is based on qualitative stakeholder perspectives and scenario testing rather than outcome measurement, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Perceived implications for safe integration, policy, and responsible educational use

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers think student-AI collaboration (SAC) should be designed and implemented in K-12 schooling. The authors note that AI is increasingly entering education, but there is limited guidance on how to structure curriculum, interactions, and environments when AI is treated as a collaborative learning agent rather than only a tool. To address this gap, the study uses a distributed cognition lens to organize a model of SAC across curriculum, student-AI interaction, learning environment, and how collaboration evolves over time.

The study is based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers involved in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools, SW leading schools, AI pilot schools, and AI convergence curriculum-oriented high schools. Teachers discussed desired learning goals (capacity building and subject-matter understanding), content (interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, creative tasks), and assessment (process-oriented and collaboration-performance assessment). They also identified supports for cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction, such as AI principles, data literacy, debugging, AI ethics, intuitive interfaces, and rich digital tools.

The main conclusions are that effective SAC requires more than introducing AI software into classrooms. Teachers emphasized the need for flexible spaces, strong digital infrastructure, systematic national policy, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and environments that allow safe experimentation and failure. They also anticipated SAC would evolve in stages: students first learn about AI, then learn from AI, and eventually learn together with AI in broader learning ecosystems. The paper is therefore primarily a conceptual and design-oriented contribution grounded in teacher perspectives rather than an evaluation of a specific AI tutoring intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study using thematic analysis with 10 teachers, so it provides rich contextual evidence but no causal identification or effect estimates. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but only one credibility criterion is met for causal claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable intervention effects, so there is no direct evidence of medium or large impact. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and design-oriented, offering plausible but unquantified implications for K-12 AIED practice.

interventions.use_case: Teacher interview study about student-AI collaboration in K-12 learning design, including AI as a collaborative learning agent, tutor, peer, and instructional scaffold rather than evaluating a specific product

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a qualitative interview study of 10 Korean leading teachers in AIED, so it does not estimate causal effects. It finds strong teacher consensus that successful student-AI collaboration depends on system-level conditions such as systematic AIED policy, teacher capacity building, flexible school structures, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on policy, governance, school systems, and culture

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified capacity building, particularly higher-order thinking, collaboration, communication, leadership, creativity, and computational thinking, as the central educational goals for student-AI collaboration. Because this is a qualitative study, no effect size was reported, but the paper argues that SAC should strengthen students' problem-solving, critical thinking, and collaborative competence.
finding.measure: Interview-derived themes on desired learning goals and competencies

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that SAC should improve subject-matter knowledge building through interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, and creative tasks. The study is qualitative and reports no statistical effect size; instead, it shows a perceived instructional value of AI-supported collaboration for deeper understanding and application of subject knowledge.
finding.measure: Interview themes on subject-matter knowledge building and task design

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized socio-emotional goals such as motivation, persistence, confidence, and willingness to try again, especially when AI is designed to support students through failure and gamified interaction. The study does not report effect sizes or test scores; findings are based on teacher perceptions from interviews.
finding.measure: Interview themes on engagement, persistence, confidence, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that AI systems should reduce repetitive teacher work via automated data collection, analysis, and integration with existing school systems, while also streamlining task execution through intuitive interfaces and cloud platforms. No quantitative productivity metrics were reported; the evidence is limited to perceived efficiency benefits from the interview data.
finding.measure: Interview themes on workflow, automation, and platform integration

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be used to evaluate how human tutors respond when students make math errors. The authors focus on a specific tutoring skill taught in the Reacting to Errors lesson, where tutors are encouraged to respond indirectly, supportively, and accurately rather than explicitly pointing out mistakes. The central question is whether GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can reliably score tutor responses on this skill and whether they can detect when a student has actually made an error.

To test this, the authors used two kinds of dialogue data. First, they generated 50 synthetic tutor-student dialogues with GPT-4 to help calibrate human grading and measure inter-rater reliability. Second, they evaluated 50 real tutoring dialogues from remote tutoring sessions. The corpus involved college-student tutors working with middle school students in online tutoring sessions. Human annotators coded each dialogue on five criteria: process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate, as well as whether a student error occurred.

The results suggest that both GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can assess several tutor moves reasonably well, especially immediate and accurate feedback, but both models struggle to determine whether a student made an error in the first place. GPT-4 performs slightly better overall and sometimes infers uncertainty as error, but the authors conclude that GPT-3.5-Turbo may be sufficient for scalable assessment given its lower cost. They caution that LLMs still have limitations for fully autonomous tutor evaluation and recommend larger datasets, improved prompts, and future analysis of learning transfer after tutor training.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop paper using a small observational corpus and model evaluation against human annotations, not an RCT or robust quasi-experiment. It provides useful methodological evidence, but credibility is limited by the small sample, synthetic calibration step, and lack of student learning outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising operational gains for automated tutor assessment, but it does not demonstrate direct student learning impact. The practical effect is therefore modest and mainly on tutor-evaluation workflow rather than educational outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 to score middle-school math tutoring dialogues for how tutors react to student errors, including identifying whether an error occurred and rating five response criteria (process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, accurate).

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can adequately automate scoring of tutor responses in real tutoring dialogues, suggesting potential for scalable tutor assessment. On 50 real-life tutoring transcripts, GPT-4 achieved higher F1 scores than GPT-3.5 on the five criteria (e.g., process-focused F1=0.64 vs 0.55; immediate F1=0.93 vs 0.80; accurate F1=0.95 vs 0.80), indicating utility for reducing human grading workload.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and F1 scores for LLM scoring of tutor-response criteria in tutoring transcripts

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how tutoring systems have evolved and what benefits, limitations, and ethical concerns characterize modern AI-enabled tutoring. The authors review the literature on Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), with special attention to adaptive learning, engagement, scalability, and responsible AI use. Their goal is to synthesize five decades of work, from early computer-assisted instruction to current systems using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and large language models such as ChatGPT.

The intervention/approach studied is not a single implementation but a systematic literature review following PRISMA. The authors screened 340 records and included 86 representative studies published from 1972 to 2024. They analyzed studies across dimensions of artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, affordances, and ethics, and also performed latent class analysis to group tutoring systems into computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal systems.

The review does not focus on one population or site, but it does note examples in elementary, middle school, secondary, and higher education contexts. A recurring example is middle school mathematics tutoring, and the paper also references robot-child tutoring and LLM-based tutoring in physics and language learning. The main conclusion is that software-based ITS generally offer stronger cognitive adaptability and scalability, while robot-based systems better support social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems combining both strengths may be most promising, but that ethical issues such as privacy, transparency, bias, and the risk of hallucinations remain important unresolved challenges.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review following PRISMA, so it has a clear methodology and broad synthesis value. However, it is not a meta-analysis or a primary experimental study, and the paper does not report pooled effect sizes or causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful benefits for learning, engagement, and scalability, but the evidence is synthesized qualitatively and no pooled effects are reported. The overall impact is therefore promising but still unclear in magnitude for K-12 practice.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of computer-based intelligent tutoring systems using adaptive algorithms such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and large language models to deliver personalized instruction, feedback, and real-time difficulty adjustment across educational contexts, including mathematics.

Systematic review of robot tutoring systems that use physical, semi-anthropomorphic, and fully anthropomorphic robots to provide verbal feedback, gestures, social presence, and embodied interaction for tutoring and engagement.
Review of generative AI and chatbot-enabled tutoring within tutoring systems, including ChatGPT-like models used for adaptive tutoring, natural language feedback, and conversational learning support.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature (86 studies), tutoring systems were reported to improve learning outcomes through personalized and adaptive instruction, with modern systems using BKT and LLMs to tailor content and feedback in real time. The paper does not provide a pooled effect size, but it repeatedly characterizes learning gains as significant and comparable in some cases to one-on-one tutoring; no single study-level estimate is synthesized in the review text.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes / academic achievement reported across included tutoring-system studies

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that robot-based and multimodal tutoring systems improve engagement, motivation, and social-emotional connection through verbal encouragement, gestures, eye contact, and human-like presence. These effects are described qualitatively across the included studies rather than pooled into a meta-analytic estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and social-emotional response indicators reported in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that software-based tutoring systems are relatively easy to deploy and scale because they rely on existing computer infrastructure and cloud-based delivery, whereas robot-based systems are more costly and complex. This is a conceptual synthesis rather than an effectiveness estimate, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Scalability/deployment feasibility and infrastructure requirements

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies important ethical and governance challenges—especially data privacy, transparency, algorithmic bias, and access inequities—while also describing mitigation strategies such as encryption, audits, access controls, and oversight committees. These institutional impacts are discussed as emerging risks and best-practice recommendations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Ethical concerns, governance practices, and responsible-AI safeguards in tutoring systems

paper_profiles.title: Educators’ Perceptions of Large Language Models as Tutors: Comparing Human and AI Tutors in a Blind Text-only Setting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language model (LLM) tutors compare with human tutors when both are evaluated in a blind, text-only setting. The authors focus not on learning gains, but on four perceived tutoring qualities: engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness. Their goal is to understand whether LLM-based tutors can match or exceed human tutors on these latent pedagogical factors that may influence learning.

The study compares dialog snippets from two sources: MathDial conversations, which were produced by human tutors interacting with simulated students, and MWPTutor conversations, which are LLM-generated tutoring dialogs with guardrails to maintain correctness. The materials are math word-problem tutoring conversations at the grade-school level, truncated to five turns and presented side-by-side in a blind pairwise evaluation. Human annotators with teaching experience, recruited through Prolific, judged which dialog was better on each metric; three frontier LLMs also performed the same comparisons.

The main finding is that both humans and LLM judges generally favored the LLM-based tutor, MWPTutor, across all four metrics, though the human judgments were less extreme and engagement was the only metric without a statistically significant advantage. The authors conclude that, in this constrained text-only tutoring context, LLMs can be perceived as at least as good as human tutors on several important dimensions, suggesting potential for delegating repetitive tutoring tasks to AI. They also note that LLM and human judgments are not perfectly aligned, and that the results are limited to a narrow math tutoring setting with simulated students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study, but it is a blind preference/annotation design rather than a causal student-learning experiment. The evidence is qualitative/correlational with substantial ecological limits (text-only, simulated student, one math dataset), so it does not meet strong RCT/QED criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest positive effects for tutoring quality and possible workload reduction, but it does not measure student achievement or real-world implementation impact. The findings are relevant to a priority K-12 domain, yet the practical effect on learners is indirect and uncertain.

interventions.use_case: Blind text-only comparison of a human tutor versus an LLM-based math word-problem tutor (MWPTutor/GPT-based with guardrails) using 5-turn tutoring snippets on grade-school mathematics.
Human tutoring conversations from MathDial are used as the comparator baseline against the LLM tutor in the head-to-head evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not measure student learning gains directly; instead, it evaluates tutoring quality in grade-school math word-problem dialogs. Human annotators with teaching experience preferred the LLM tutor (MWPTutor) over the human tutor on scaffolding and overall tutor quality in a blind text-only comparison, with significant advantages on scaffolding (t=3.16, p<0.001) and related tutor behaviors.
finding.measure: Human educator pairwise preference judgments on tutoring dialogs for math word problems, especially scaffolding quality

finding.finding_summary: Educator judges perceived the LLM tutor as more engaging and empathetic than the human tutor in this blind comparison, although engagement was not statistically significant while empathy was significant. Reported statistics include empathy mean score 0.65 with SD=2.81 and t=3.36 (p<0.001); engagement mean score 0.25 with SD=2.72 and t=1.32 (p=0.09), based on 210 paired dialog comparisons.
finding.measure: Human educator pairwise preference judgments on engagement and empathy in tutoring dialogs
