finding.effect_size: d=0.68 (engagement, subgroup analysis in Continue scenario); d=0.30 (engagement, Fresh scenario); other outcomes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The study uses scaffolding as a proxy for tutoring support that can promote independent problem solving, and the LLM tutor was judged better than the human tutor on this dimension. Human ratings favored MWPTutor on scaffolding with mean score 0.55, SD=2.19, and t=3.65 (p<0.001) across 210 dialog pairs.
finding.measure: Human educator pairwise preference judgments on scaffolding quality in math tutoring dialogs

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly argues that the LLM tutor was more concise than the human tutor, which is relevant to reducing conversational overhead and teacher workload. Human ratings significantly favored MWPTutor on conciseness (mean score 0.55, SD=2.19, t=3.65, p<0.001), and the authors interpret this as evidence that LLM tutoring could reduce the load on teachers.
finding.measure: Human educator pairwise preference judgments on conciseness of tutoring dialogs

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Provide Explanatory Feedback to Human Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of giving novice tutors timely, explanatory feedback while they practice responding to tutoring scenarios in an online lesson. The authors focus on whether large language models can help automatically identify useful versus less-desired elements in tutor-written responses and then use those identified elements to generate feedback.

The approach has two parts. First, the authors train a BERT-based binary classifier to label tutor responses in a lesson on giving effective praise as effort-based or outcome-based praise. Second, they adapt a named entity recognition (NER) pipeline to tag the relevant praise segments in tutor responses so that templated explanatory feedback can highlight exactly what in the response is aligned with the desired praise strategy. The data come from 65 volunteer tutors participating in an online training lesson; the full dataset contains 129 annotated tutor responses.

The work is framed as a work-in-progress and does not evaluate a deployed tutoring intervention with learners. The classifier performed reasonably well for effort-based praise but less well for outcome-based praise, and the NER model showed limited performance overall, reflecting sparse and imbalanced annotations. The authors conclude that LLM-facilitated labeling could support automatic corrective and explanatory feedback for tutor training, but that better data, improved evaluation metrics, and stronger modeling approaches are needed before practical use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop/work-in-progress study using a small annotated dataset and train/validation/test split, but it is not an RCT or QED and provides only model-development evidence rather than causal impact evidence. The methodology is clear, but evidence credibility is limited by low sample size and prototype status.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported model performance suggests potential for useful tutor feedback support, especially for effort-based praise, but the overall impact is unclear because the system has not been tested on learner outcomes or at deployment scale. NER performance is modest to low, so real-world instructional impact remains uncertain.

interventions.use_case: automatic explanatory feedback for novice tutors' constructed responses in a scenario-based lesson on giving effective praise, using BERT classification and LLM-facilitated named entity recognition to generate templated corrective feedback
large language model-facilitated named entity recognition and text classification to support real-time feedback generation for human tutors

finding.finding_summary: The system was evaluated on tutor responses in a 'Giving Effective Praise' lesson (n=129 responses from 65 volunteer tutors). BERT classified effort-based praise well (accuracy=0.731, F1=0.811), but outcome-based praise was much weaker (accuracy=0.596, F1=0.350, SD=0.235). The authors also report NER F1=0.202 (SD=0.039) for highlighting praise spans, indicating that the feedback system can support tutor learning on praise but remains uneven and low-performing for some categories.
finding.measure: BERT classification accuracy/F1 for praise type; NER F1 for praise-entity span detection

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues the method can automate real-time explanatory feedback for tutor training, reducing the need for human experts to manually diagnose responses. However, this is a prototype/work-in-progress paper and does not report a workload or time-saving effect size, only model performance metrics (e.g., Effort F1=0.811; Outcome F1=0.350; NER F1=0.202) that would enable automation.
finding.measure: Model performance as a proxy for automation capability

paper_profiles.title: Comparing Few-Shot Prompting of GPT-4 LLMs with BERT Classifiers for Open-Response Assessment in Tutor Equity Training
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI 2025 Workshop iRAISE (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether contemporary large language models can match or outperform a fine-tuned BERT classifier when grading nuanced open-ended learner responses in an educational training context. Specifically, the authors examine automated assessment of scenario-based, equity-focused tutoring lessons where responses are not simple right-or-wrong factual answers but depend on contextual judgment and explanation.

The study compares fine-tuned BERT with few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo on four binary prediction tasks drawn from two online tutor-training lessons: avoiding unconscious assumptions and helping students manage inequity. The data come from 291 completed responses written by 243 undergraduate tutors in the northeastern United States, all training to become middle school tutors in a remote tutoring organization. Human coders labeled responses, and the models were evaluated with stratified 5-fold cross-validation using accuracy, F1, and AUC where applicable.

The main finding is that BERT consistently outperformed both GPT-based approaches across the four tasks, with the clearest advantage in overall average performance. The authors conclude that for this kind of nuanced educational assessment, fine-tuning a task-specific smaller model is more effective and more resource-efficient than relying on few-shot prompting of commercial GPT models. They also note that GPT performance was less consistent and that these results suggest limitations of prompt-only approaches for ill-defined educational tasks requiring contextual reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop paper using a clear comparative cross-validation design, but it is not an RCT or QED and focuses on model benchmarking rather than learner outcomes. The evidence quality is therefore correlational/technical rather than causal in the K-12 sense.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong classifier performance differences, but these are not educational effect sizes on student learning or behavior. Its practical impact is promising for assessment infrastructure, yet the demonstrated impact on learners is indirect and untested.

interventions.use_case: automated open-response assessment of tutor equity-training answers using fine-tuned BERT and few-shot GPT classifiers to score responses as adequate or inadequate
few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo used as comparison models for judging open-ended tutor training responses in scenario-based equity lessons

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that fine-tuned BERT outperformed few-shot prompted GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo on automated scoring of open responses in tutor equity training, while also being more resource-efficient and offline deployable. Across tasks, average performance was BERT accuracy=0.837, GPT-4o=0.726, and GPT-4 Turbo=0.549; BERT also achieved AUC values around 0.794-0.953 on its binary classification tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy, F1, and AUC for automated open-response classification
finding.study_size: n=243 students; 291 lesson completions; 243 human-annotated responses (79 + 164 for the two lessons)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that offline fine-tuned BERT may be a more stable, cost-efficient institutional option than commercial GPT models for scalable assessment in tutor training. The authors argue this could support broader deployment of automated evaluation in educational organizations, though the paper does not test institutional outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Comparative model performance and resource-efficiency discussion for deployment feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether hints generated by ChatGPT can support algebra learning as effectively as human-authored hints already used in an adaptive tutoring system. The authors focus on two research questions: how often ChatGPT produces low-quality hints, and whether learning gains from ChatGPT-generated hints differ from those from human tutor hints.

The intervention was an A/B experiment in the Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor). For each algebra problem, ChatGPT was prompted to produce a worked-solution-style hint, and the outputs were manually quality-checked before use. The comparison condition used pre-authored human tutor hints from OATutor. The study included two algebra lessons: Elementary Algebra and Intermediate Algebra.

Participants were 77 Mechanical Turk workers with at least a high school degree and master status, randomly assigned to either ChatGPT or human-hint conditions and to one of the two lessons. Each session included a pre-test, five-item acquisition phase, and post-test. The main finding was that both conditions showed positive learning gains, but statistically significant gains occurred only in the human-hint condition. Human-authored hints outperformed ChatGPT hints in both lessons, and about 30% of ChatGPT hints were rejected during quality checking because they contained incorrect answers or incorrect solution steps. The authors conclude that ChatGPT-generated algebra hints are not yet a drop-in replacement for human-authored tutoring content and still require human supervision.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small randomized head-to-head experiment with random assignment to hint condition and lesson, but it is conducted with Mechanical Turk adults rather than the intended middle-school population and has only 77 participants. It is stronger than correlational evidence, yet there are notable concerns about external validity and a pre-test imbalance in Intermediate Algebra.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed learning effects are modest and mixed: both conditions improved, but ChatGPT underperformed human hints and was not statistically significant within-condition. Given the small sample and lack of clear positive advantage for the LLM, the practical impact is unclear to modest at best.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints for algebra tutoring problems in Open Adaptive Tutor, compared head-to-head against human-authored tutor hints in elementary and intermediate algebra lessons.
Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor) delivering algebra practice with pre-test, acquisition phase, post-test, and hint/scaffold support used as the experimental platform and human-hint baseline.

finding.finding_summary: Across 77 Mechanical Turk participants, both ChatGPT and human-hint conditions showed positive pre-post learning gains in algebra, but gains were statistically significant only for the human-hint condition. In Elementary Algebra, gain was 24.63% for control vs 11.14% for ChatGPT; in Intermediate Algebra, 23.65% vs 1.7%, with between-condition differences statistically significant at p=0.038 in both topic areas.
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test algebra accuracy / learning gain on repeated-item tests

finding.finding_summary: The human-authored hint condition produced statistically significant learning gains in both algebra topics, whereas the ChatGPT condition did not. In Elementary Algebra, average gain was 24.63% with pre-test 59.68% and post-test 84.32%; in Intermediate Algebra, average gain was 23.65% with pre-test 50.94% and post-test 74.59%.
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test algebra accuracy / learning gain on repeated-item tests

paper_profiles.title: Improving Assessment of Tutoring Practices using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models can be used to automatically assess the quality of tutoring practices, with a particular focus on social-emotional learning (SEL) strategies in math tutoring. The authors frame the problem as one of expensive and difficult human-expert assessment of novice tutors, especially when trying to evaluate whether tutors provide supportive, relationship-building instruction rather than only content help.

The approach studied compares four prompting strategies for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4: two zero-shot prompts, a Tree of Thoughts prompt, and a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) prompt. The prompts are designed to score tutoring transcripts and generate evidence-based explanations using rubric criteria drawn from five SEL-oriented tutoring principles: giving effective praise, supporting a growth mindset, reacting to errors, responding to negative self-talk, and using motivational strategies.

The data come from five real-world Zoom-based middle-school math tutoring transcripts from the United States, each about 30 minutes long, involving novice tutors working with grades 6-8 students in one-on-one breakout rooms. The tutors had previously completed some SEL-related lessons on a tutor-training platform. The paper reports that the RAG prompt generally produced the most accurate and least hallucinatory assessments, and it was also the most cost-effective option across both GPT models. The study concludes that RAG may be useful for scalable tutor assessment and for supporting personalized tutor training interventions, though the work is preliminary and intended as a proof of concept.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preliminary work-in-progress study using only five transcripts and a single human coder, with no experimental comparison on student outcomes. It is peer-reviewed conference proceedings, but the methodology is exploratory rather than rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential operational benefits for tutor assessment and training workflows, but it does not demonstrate measured learning gains or scalable real-world impact. The observed effect is about evaluation accuracy/cost, not direct educational impact.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with zero-shot, Tree of Thoughts, and retrieval-augmented generation prompts to automatically assess middle-school math tutors’ social-emotional tutoring competencies from dialogue transcripts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can automate tutor assessment more accurately and at lower cost than the other prompting strategies tested. Across five tutoring transcripts, RAG with GPT-3.5/GPT-4 produced more correct and less hallucinated evaluations, and GPT-4 was about 10x more expensive than GPT-3.5 for the same task; the authors report RAG as the most cost-effective approach.
finding.measure: Human-coded correctness and hallucination of GPT-generated tutor evaluations; API cost per lesson evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of scaling expert guidance for novice tutors in live K-12 mathematics tutoring. The authors argue that traditional professional development is expensive, slow to scale, and poorly matched to the real-time needs of tutors, especially in underserved settings. They ask whether a human-AI system can provide expert-like support during tutoring sessions and improve both tutor behavior and student learning.

The intervention, Tutor CoPilot, is a human-AI tool integrated into a virtual tutoring platform. When activated, it uses the ongoing chat context, lesson topic, and a chosen pedagogical strategy to generate suggestions for tutors in real time. The system is based on prior work that extracts expert decision-making from think-aloud protocols and adapts language models to produce pedagogically useful guidance. Tutors can edit, regenerate, or switch strategies, preserving human autonomy while providing immediate support.

The study is a randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students in historically underserved communities served by a large Southern U.S. school district and FEV Tutor. Students were in grades 3-8 and mostly Hispanic and economically disadvantaged. The authors find that access to Tutor CoPilot increases exit-ticket mastery by 4 percentage points overall, with larger gains for lower-rated and less-experienced tutors. NLP analysis of 550,000+ messages suggests treatment tutors used more high-quality instructional strategies, such as prompting explanation and asking guiding questions, and less often gave away answers. Tutor interviews were broadly positive, though some suggestions were not always grade-appropriate. The paper concludes that real-time AI support can improve tutoring quality at low cost and may help scale expert-like educational support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered randomized controlled trial with tutor-level random assignment, large sample sizes, balance checks, and pre-specified analyses. The paper reports causal evidence from a live educational setting, although there are some implementation nuances and the main outcome is proximal rather than standardized end-of-year achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a modest but meaningful improvement in proximal math mastery (+4 percentage points overall, with larger effects for lower-rated tutors). The impact is on a priority population of underserved K-12 students, but the measured gains are small-to-moderate and do not extend to a reported standardized end-of-year test effect.

interventions.use_case: human-AI tutoring support that uses a language model to generate real-time, expert-like pedagogical suggestions for live K-12 math tutors during sessions

finding.finding_summary: In a preregistered randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students (final analysis sample: 4,136 tutoring sessions), access to Tutor CoPilot increased the probability that students passed their exit tickets by 4 percentage points (62% to 66%, p<0.01). The benefit was larger for lower-rated tutors (+9 p.p.) and lower-experience tutors (+7 p.p.), suggesting the system especially helped weaker tutors improve proximal math mastery.
finding.measure: Exit ticket pass rate / topic mastery in live mathematics tutoring sessions
finding.study_size: n=1800 students; 900 tutors assigned; 4136 sessions analyzed
finding.effect_size: 4 percentage points increase in exit ticket pass rate; heterogeneous effects up to 9 percentage points

finding.finding_summary: Student survey measures of perceived tutor care, confidence in learning math, and session ratings did not show statistically significant changes from Tutor CoPilot access. Estimated treatment effects were small and mixed (e.g., -0.004 to 0.03 on 5-point scales), indicating no clear improvement in these attitudinal outcomes.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey items on tutor care, confidence, and session rating

finding.finding_summary: NLP-based analysis of 550,000+ tutor messages found that treatment tutors used more high-quality pedagogical strategies that foster understanding, such as prompting students to explain and asking guiding questions. These strategies were reported as approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent on the z-scored log-odds scale in treatment sessions, while low-quality answer-giving strategies were less frequent.
finding.measure: Classifier-based analysis of pedagogical strategy use in tutor chat messages
finding.effect_size: approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent on z-scored log-odds scale for key high-quality strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Tutor CoPilot could be delivered at very low cost, estimated at $20 per tutor annually based on observed usage during the study. Although not a labor-productivity trial, the system is presented as a scalable, low-cost way to provide real-time expertise that would otherwise require expensive human coaching or professional development.
finding.measure: Estimated annual cost per tutor

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Final Answers: Evaluating Large Language Models for Math Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs), including several ChatGPT models, can function as effective math tutors rather than merely as problem solvers. The authors argue that existing benchmarks emphasize final-answer accuracy and do not adequately assess whether models provide correct, pedagogically useful step-by-step tutoring support. To address this gap, they ask two questions: how accurately LLMs solve algebra problems drawn from an intelligent tutoring system, and how accurate and high-quality their interactive tutoring guidance is when humans engage them as if they were students.

The study uses two complementary evaluation approaches. First, the authors use the Apprentice Tutors platform, an intelligent tutoring system for college algebra, as a testbed: they generate 110 algebra problems across 22 problem types and ask GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview to solve them. Second, they conduct an interactive tutoring evaluation in which human evaluators prompt the same models for tutoring help on 30 problems, then rate the resulting dialogues for pedagogical quality and correctness using a rubric and independent review. The context is college algebra in an online tutoring setting, not a live classroom implementation with real learners.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can often produce reasonable final answers and generally supportive tutoring interactions, but they are not yet reliable enough to serve as standalone math tutors. In the tutor-based benchmark, models achieved 85.5% overall correctness on final answers, while in the interactive tutoring setting only 56.6% of dialogues were entirely correct, even though most were judged high quality in a pedagogical sense. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful for limited tutoring functions such as hint generation, alternative explanations, and positive reinforcement, but human oversight or additional correctness-checking mechanisms are still needed before direct instructional deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical evaluation with a clear methodology, but it is not an RCT or QED and does not measure student learning outcomes. The study is primarily qualitative/benchmark-based and compares model outputs against tutor solutions and reviewer judgments.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests important limitations for deploying LLM tutors in algebra, but it reports no direct learning gains or effect sizes on student outcomes. Its impact is therefore informative but still indirect and unclear for K-12 learners.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating ChatGPT-family models as math tutors for college algebra, including interactive step-by-step tutoring, hints, feedback, and final-answer generation.
Using the Apprentice Tutors college algebra system as a benchmark/testbed to generate problems and expert solutions for head-to-head evaluation of LLM math tutoring performance.

finding.finding_summary: Across 110 tutor-generated college algebra problems, LLMs produced correct final answers on 85.5% overall, with model-level accuracy ranging from 74.5% (GPT-4) to 97.3% (GPT-4o). In interactive tutoring with 150 dialogues, final-answer accuracy was 88.6% overall, but only 56.6% of dialogues were fully correct, indicating substantial error rates in stepwise mathematical support.
finding.measure: Final-answer correctness on algebra problems; correctness of complete tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: n=110 problem-answer pairs for tutor-based evaluation; n=150 interactive tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025: The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system data to support caregivers helping children with math homework. The central problem is that caregivers often want to help but lack the content knowledge and tutoring strategies needed to provide effective instructional support during homework, especially in modern middle school mathematics curricula.

The authors developed the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which is integrated into an equation-solving tutoring system called Lynnette. The tool uses the open-source Llama 3 8B Instruct model to generate personalized chat message recommendations for caregivers in real time. Prompts were iteratively engineered using tutoring best practices and live tutoring-system context such as current equation, hint use, accuracy, and suggested next steps. The system was evaluated through prompt-engineering trials and a qualitative prototyping study.

The user study involved ten middle school caregivers recruited through a university-affiliated summer program in the Northeastern United States and remote interviews. Caregivers interacted with the tool while supporting their children and then gave feedback about the generated recommendations. Findings suggest that caregivers preferred content-level guidance over motivational support, especially prompts that encouraged students to explain their thinking and revealed metacognitive processes. Participants also valued context-sensitive recommendations based on errors and hint use, though they found some messages too long and occasionally artificial in tone. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs can be made more useful for hybrid tutoring when grounded in tutoring-system intelligence and tutoring principles.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study/prototyping study with thematic analysis and prompt-engineering iterations, not a controlled experiment. It provides useful design evidence, but there is no randomized comparison or quantitative learning-outcome evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The work suggests potentially useful improvements to caregiver-supported math tutoring, but impact is based on qualitative perceptions rather than measured student gains. The study does not report effect sizes, so practical impact on learners remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated conversational recommendations for caregivers supporting middle school math homework inside a tutoring system, using prompt engineering and Llama 3 with tutoring-principle examples and real-time student context.
Middle school equation-solving tutoring system (Lynnette) providing adaptive hints, error-specific feedback, and solution-path context that is also used to condition caregiver support.

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers generally valued the tool’s supportive tone and motivational framing, but preferences were mixed: 3 of 7 caregivers found the tone inauthentic/artificial, while 4 of 7 described it as encouraging and positive. Six caregivers preferred content-level help over motivational support, suggesting that the motivational component was less compelling for this population, even though some still appreciated it.
finding.measure: Caregiver interviews and thematic feedback on message tone, motivational support, and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers preferred prompts that encouraged student metacognition and self-explanation, with 5 caregivers specifically valuing messages asking students to describe their thought process. This was interpreted as helping caregivers better understand where students were stuck and how to support reasoning, but the study was qualitative and did not report quantitative learning gains.
finding.measure: Caregiver interview themes about self-explanation / metacognitive prompting

finding.finding_summary: The LLM-generated recommendations were judged to be more contextually relevant and pedagogically fit for middle school equation solving when the prompt included ITS-derived problem-solving context (accuracy, hint use, and next steps). The paper reports qualitative improvement across prompt iterations, but no student achievement test or effect size was measured; caregivers particularly liked content-level math guidance and step-by-step support.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of generated math-help recommendations for equation solving
finding.study_size: n=10 caregivers; prompt experiments on ~50-80 generated examples per round

finding.finding_summary: The underlying ITS was central to generating the math support, supplying adaptive next-step solution paths, hints, and correctness feedback that made the recommendations more reliable and less hallucinatory. The paper qualitatively argues that the ITS context improved the math-specific quality of LLM recommendations, but it did not quantify student learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Generated recommendation quality in equation-solving context; caregiver judgments of context relevance
finding.study_size: n=10 caregivers; prompt experiments on ~50-80 generated examples per round

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to automatically identify and evaluate specific tutor behaviors in authentic tutoring transcripts. The authors frame this as a feasibility problem: can LLMs reliably detect when a tutor provides effective praise or responds appropriately to a student’s math error, and can they grade the quality of those responses in a way that aligns with human coders?

The study analyzes 50 randomly selected transcripts from remote math tutoring sessions. The tutoring interactions involved college-student tutors working with middle school students in mathematics, and the data came from audio-recorded and transcribed online sessions. The authors test several LLMs, including GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM, using prompt-engineering strategies such as zero-shot and few-shot prompting, rationale forcing, self-consistency, and prompt chaining. The models were asked first to detect whether a target situation was present and then to evaluate whether the tutor’s move met a best-practice criterion.

Results show that the LLMs performed well on both detection and evaluation tasks, with high agreement against human annotations. The models were especially strong at identifying tutor praise and student math errors, and they also achieved good accuracy in judging whether the praise was effort-focused or whether the error response guided the student toward self-correction. The authors conclude that LLMs can support scalable assessment of real tutoring dialogue, but they also note that performance depends on prompt design and that subtle distinctions in language remain challenging.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small feasibility study using 50 transcripts with human annotations and no experimental comparison of learner outcomes. The methodology is clear and systematic, but it is primarily a validation/coding study rather than a causal evaluation of an educational intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising accuracy for scaling tutor-move assessment, but it does not demonstrate downstream effects on student learning or tutoring quality at scale. Its impact is therefore operational and suggestive rather than directly educationally transformative.

interventions.use_case: Evaluating the feasibility of using LLMs to assess tutor moves in real-life middle school math tutoring transcripts, specifically detecting effective praise and appropriate responses to student math errors.

finding.finding_summary: LLMs were highly feasible for scalable assessment of tutor moves in authentic tutoring transcripts, with high agreement against human coders. Across 50 transcripts, models achieved 94-98% accuracy for praise detection and 82-88% for math-error detection, and 83-89% accuracy for grading praise quality and 73-77% for grading error responses.
finding.measure: Accuracy against human annotations for filter and evaluation prompts on tutor move classification
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported in the paper; specific CIs vary by model and prompt

paper_profiles.title: Examining the Influence of Varied Levels of Domain Knowledge Base Inclusion in GPT-based Intelligent Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adding a knowledge base (KB) to GPT-4-based intelligent tutoring systems can improve the quality and reliability of educational responses. The authors focus on a core concern with large language models in education: they can produce fluent but inaccurate answers, which may undermine their usefulness as tutors. The study compares three tutor configurations that differ only in how much curriculum information they can access: no KB access, partial KB access, and full KB access.

The intervention is a KB-integrated tutoring architecture that lets educators provide lesson content at different levels of granularity, from just the lesson subject to topic descriptions and full lecture material. The system uses GPT-4 to generate tutor responses, rank student answers, and produce feedback, while the full KB version also uses keyword generation and a Haystack-based retrieval pipeline to locate relevant lecture subtopics. The evaluated content was an artificial intelligence curriculum, specifically a lecture on the history of AI, with questions designed from that material.

The study involved four university students who had previously completed AI coursework and two professional AI curriculum experts. Students answered questions with intentionally varied accuracy, and then both the GPT-based tutors and the human experts assessed those answers. Students then judged which assessor response was more teacher-like, more understanding of the student, and more helpful. The authors report that KB access improved GPT-4 tutor accuracy relative to no KB access, and it also increased student preference for GPT-generated feedback on two pedagogical dimensions: speaking like a teacher and understanding the student. However, human experts still outperformed the tutors on overall accuracy and remained preferred for being helpful to students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small preliminary comparative study with asynchronous, manually collected responses and no random assignment of students to conditions. It is peer-reviewed conference paper-like work, but the design has major threats to internal validity and relies on a very small sample (n=4 students, n=2 experts).
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed gains from knowledge-base access are modest and context-specific, and no standardized learning outcome or robust effect size is reported. The study suggests possible improvement in tutor accuracy and perceived pedagogy, but the overall impact on student learning remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-based intelligent tutor that assesses student answers to AI curriculum questions, generates teacher-like feedback, and is tested with no, partial, and full knowledge-base access.

Knowledge-base augmentation / retrieval layer for the GPT-4 tutor, including lesson subject, topic description, and lecture transcript retrieval via Haystack and keyword generation to constrain tutor responses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that adding knowledge-base access improved the GPT-4 tutor’s answer accuracy on an AI-curriculum assessment. Accuracy increased from 67% with no KB access to 77% with partial KB access and 74% with full KB access, compared with 87% for human domain experts; agreement with expected answers was also higher for experts (63%) than for ITSs (43%).
finding.measure: Assessment accuracy and agreement on AI curriculum question answers
finding.study_size: n=4 students, n=2 domain experts, 3 GPT-4 tutor variants

finding.finding_summary: Student raters preferred KB-augmented GPT-4 responses more often on pedagogical dimensions than no-KB responses. Relative to the no-KB tutor, partial KB access increased preference for GPT-4 by 17.15% for 'talking like a teacher,' 10.00% for 'understanding the student,' and 12.86% for 'helpful to the student'; full KB access increased these by 11.43%, 10.00%, and 8.58%, respectively.
finding.measure: Student preference rankings of assessor replies on talking like a teacher, understanding the student, and helpfulness
finding.study_size: n=4 students providing rankings; 3 GPT-4 tutor variants

paper_profiles.title: AutoTutor meets Large Language Models: A Language Model Tutor with Rich Pedagogy and Guardrails
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can be used not just as free-form tutors, but as components in an AutoTutor-like intelligent tutoring system with stronger pedagogical control. The authors argue that direct use of GPT-4 as a tutor is hard to trust because it can reveal answers, drift from the intended tutoring strategy, and behave inconsistently. To address this, they propose a hybrid architecture in which learning scientists still design the tutoring pedagogy and state space, while an LLM fills in domain-specific tutoring utterances and solution steps.

The intervention is MWPTutor, a math word problem tutor built as a finite-state transducer with a structured solution-step space and a strategy space of pump, hint, prompt, and assertion moves. The system has two variants: a cached version that pre-generates utterances and a live version that queries GPT-4 during interaction. The paper evaluates MWPTutor against a single-prompt GPT-4 baseline on two math word problem datasets, MultiArith and MathDial, using AI-simulated student conversations. It also includes human evaluation of generated tutor utterances for grammaticality, non-revelation, relevance, specificity, and helpfulness.

The studied population is not real classroom learners, but math word problem scenarios drawn from middle-school-level datasets, especially GSM8K/MathDial problems described as appropriate for bright middle school students. The context is offline, AI-on-AI tutoring rather than deployment in schools, and the paper explicitly does not test with human students. Results show that the structured MWPTutor variants generally outperform or match the GPT-4 baseline on tutoring metrics, with the live GPT-4-backed version performing best overall in the harder dataset. However, manual inspection reveals remaining weaknesses such as false positives, redundant prompts, monotony, and occasional misdirection, leading the authors to conclude that the approach is promising but not yet ready for real students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference paper with a clear experimental setup, but the evidence is primarily an AI-on-AI simulation and human utterance evaluation rather than a student learning trial. It is methodologically informative yet does not meet stronger causal evidence criteria for learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The system shows promising improvements in tutoring behavior metrics, especially on harder math-dialog tasks, but the paper does not demonstrate direct student learning gains. The practical impact is therefore plausible but still unclear for real K-12 learners.

interventions.use_case: LLM-authored math word-problem tutoring dialogs with guardrails, including live GPT-4 tutoring and cached LLM-generated utterances within an AutoTutor-like finite state transducer (MWPTutor).

AutoTutor-style dialog-based tutoring architecture with finite state transducer state space, solution-step alignment, pump/hint/prompt/assertion pedagogy, and stepwise feedback for math word problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates tutoring performance on math word problems, using Success Rate, Telling Rate, Adjusted Success, and an overall Tutoring Score rather than student test gains. On MathDial (n=45 problems), MWPTutorcached GPT-4 achieved 0.91 success, 0.33 telling, 0.58 adjusted success, and 0.71 tutoring score; MWPTutorlive GPT-4 achieved 0.96 success, 0.11 telling, 0.84 adjusted success, and 0.90 tutoring score, while baseline GPT-4 reached 1.00 success but with 0.00 telling and 1.00 tutoring score in the authors' metric. On MultiArith (n=180), all models were near ceiling, with success 0.98-1.00 and tutoring scores 0.98-1.00, indicating strong performance on easier problems but weaker robustness on harder tutoring interactions.
finding.measure: Conversation-level tutoring metrics on math word problems: Success Rate, Telling Rate, Adjusted Success, Tutoring Score

finding.finding_summary: The paper's main contribution is a modular tutoring architecture intended to reduce expert authoring burden by having an LLM fill in the state space of a predefined pedagogical framework. The authors argue this shifts work away from domain experts and enables reusable, partially automated authoring, while still preserving controllable pedagogy; however, they do not report a quantitative efficiency effect size or a formal workload experiment.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of authoring/scaling burden and modularity of the tutoring architecture

paper_profiles.title: BIPED: Pedagogically Informed Tutoring System for ESL Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to build conversational intelligent tutoring systems (CITS) for English as a second language that are not just fluent, but pedagogically meaningful. The authors argue that existing LLM-based tutoring systems often focus on simple concepts or limited dialogue strategies, and therefore do not capture the richer instructional tactics used by human tutors.

To address this, they construct BIPED, a bilingual tutoring dataset derived from one-on-one human ESL tutoring sessions. The dataset is annotated with a detailed dialogue-act taxonomy containing 34 tutor acts and 9 student acts, designed in collaboration with ESL instructors and refined through pilot sessions. They then use BIPED to build two tutoring-system implementations: one based on GPT-4 prompting and another based on instruction tuning of SOLAR-KO 10.7B. Both follow a two-step framework in which the model first predicts an appropriate tutor act and then generates the corresponding response.

The study uses 112 bilingual tutoring sessions with 4 experienced ESL tutors and 60 students. Sessions focused on reading and understanding a real news article, along with vocabulary, grammar, and cultural context. The paper reports that the fine-tuned model performs better than prompted GPT variants on tutor-act prediction and utterance generation metrics, and better reflects diverse pedagogical strategies. The main conclusion is that pedagogically structured data and act-conditioned generation can improve LLM-based tutoring for ESL, though the work remains primarily a static evaluation and does not yet include a full interactive human study.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical systems paper with a real tutoring dataset and pre/post tests, but it is not a randomized controlled trial or causal comparison of learning outcomes across conditions. The evaluation is primarily descriptive/offline model benchmarking plus a single-group learning-gain report, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gain is modest (normalized gain=0.089), and the primary contributions are dataset and model-quality improvements rather than demonstrated large learner gains. The evidence suggests promise for ESL tutoring, but impact on broad educational outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: A bilingual conversational intelligent tutoring system for ESL education that uses GPT-4 prompting and fine-tuned SOLAR-KO to choose tutor dialogue acts and generate tutoring utterances for reading/vocabulary/grammar instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the tutoring sessions supported English proficiency gains and that the proposed LLM tutors produced human-like, pedagogically appropriate language. In the human tutoring dataset, the pre/post tutoring intervention yielded an average normalized learning gain of 0.089 (n=60 students; 112 sessions), and the fine-tuned model outperformed prompted GPT variants on utterance generation metrics including sBLEU=15.874 and BERTScore=0.716.
finding.measure: Pre/post English proficiency tests; generated utterance similarity to human tutor responses (sBLEU, BERTScore, embedding similarity); tutor act prediction accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed around reading an English news article with vocabulary and comprehension activities, and post-test items included reading comprehension, synonyms/antonyms, vocabulary, and phrasal verbs. The reported average normalized learning gain of 0.089 suggests modest improvement on literacy-related outcomes after tutoring, although the paper does not isolate which subskills improved most.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, vocabulary, synonyms/antonyms, and phrasal verb pre/post-test scores

paper_profiles.title: Interactive, Intelligent Tutoring for Auxiliary Constructions in Geometry Proofs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to teach students to discover auxiliary constructions in geometry proof problems, a notoriously difficult part of K-12 geometry reasoning. The authors argue that many existing geometry tutoring systems can help with standard proof steps but do not effectively teach the strategic skill of inventing helpful extra lines or points, especially in problems where construction is required.

To address this, they introduce AGPT (Advanced Geometry Proof Tutor), an interactive geometry tutoring system built on top of the automated prover iGeoTutor. AGPT accepts uploaded geometry figures, extracts the diagram and constraints, and then guides students through a template-matching process: students select a candidate construction template and then attempt to draw the missing auxiliary elements themselves. The tutor provides limited feedback first, then more explicit guidance if needed, while trying to keep students engaged in the problem-solving process rather than simply showing the answer. The system was evaluated with 78 ninth-grade students from a local high school, comparing three conditions: a human tutor, iGeoTutor alone, and AGPT.

The study found that AGPT produced learning gains comparable to a human tutor and superior to the non-interactive theorem prover alone. Students in the AGPT condition improved on post-tests, and when partial credit for incomplete proofs was considered, AGPT was significantly more effective than iGeoTutor in helping students learn auxiliary constructions. The authors conclude that interactive tutoring that exposes the reasoning of a strong solver can be pedagogically effective for geometry instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pilot study with a quasi-experimental group comparison, but students were not randomly assigned and the design has several credibility limitations. The sample is moderate, outcomes are narrow, and the paper reports limited statistical detail beyond t tests and ANOVA.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests a modest positive impact of AGPT on a priority population of high school geometry students, especially compared with a non-interactive geometry prover. The strongest reported evidence is statistically significant but small-to-moderate in scope, and the paper does not provide effect sizes large enough to justify a blue tier.

interventions.use_case: interactive geometry proof tutoring for auxiliary constructions, with template matching, hinting, backtracking, and guided construction practice for high school students

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students (n=26 per group), AGPT improved students’ ability to learn auxiliary constructions in geometry proof problems and performed significantly better than iGeoTutor. On the partial-credit improvement score, an ANOVA found a significant group difference, F(2,75)=3.23, p=0.045, with Tukey post hoc tests showing AGPT outperformed iGeoTutor while not differing significantly from the human tutor.
finding.measure: Geometry proof performance on pre-test/post-test problems, including solved-problem counts, correct constructions, and partial-credit improvement scores

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to train students’ problem-solving process, template matching, and independent discovery of constructions rather than only delivering solutions. The authors report that Group C students engaged in repeated attempts and redirections and that the interactive approach likely helped students develop thoughtful problem-solving skills, though no direct standardized durable-skill measure was reported.
finding.measure: Student interaction history, attempts, redirections, and qualitative observations of problem-solving behavior
finding.study_size: n=26 in AGPT group for interaction analysis

paper_profiles.title: Towards an Intelligent Tutor for Mathematical Proofs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to build an intelligent tutoring system for teaching textbook-style mathematical proofs, an area the authors describe as underdeveloped in existing e-learning systems. The focus is not on ordinary computation or problem solving, but on supporting students in constructing proofs at the level of individual proof steps, including handling underspecified, incomplete, and ambiguous student input.

The proposed approach adapts the Ωmega proof assistant into an intelligent tutor that can analyze student proof steps, judge their correctness, assess step granularity, and check relevance to the current proof goal. The system is designed around a Wizard-of-Oz study in which 37 students interacted with a mock natural-language proof tutor while four experienced tutors simulated the system. The corpus from these dialogs is used to motivate the design and to evaluate the reconstruction and hint-generation components.

The target population is final high-school students and undergraduate university students with domain knowledge in mathematics but not necessarily in formal logic. The paper argues for a model-tracing style tutoring architecture using assertion-level proof reconstruction and strategy-based hint generation. The authors conclude that their prototype can successfully reconstruct and assess many proof steps from the corpus and can generate hierarchical hints of increasing specificity, suggesting that the approach is feasible for proof tutoring in this domain.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systems paper with an empirical evaluation, but it is not a randomized or comparative educational effectiveness study. The evidence is primarily a small, domain-specific corpus evaluation and prototype validation rather than causal evidence of learning impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported performance is promising, but the measured outcome is system verification accuracy rather than student learning gains, and the study is confined to a narrow mathematical proof domain. There is no effect size on learner outcomes, so overall educational impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: rule-based intelligent tutoring system for mathematical proof construction, with step reconstruction, correctness checking, granularity analysis, relevance checking, and hierarchical hint generation for textbook-style proofs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the prototype ITS for mathematical proofs was successfully evaluated on a corpus of tutorial dialogs and achieved accurate step verification in its domain. Using 144 proof steps from a Wizard-of-Oz study, the system correctly verified or rejected nearly all steps at depth 4, with an overall accuracy of 98% (116 correct and 28 incorrect steps; 3 steps misverified or unverifiable).
finding.measure: proof-step verification accuracy on Wizard-of-Oz corpus of mathematical proof dialogs

paper_profiles.title: Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems Using Bayesian Approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) with a particular emphasis on Bayesian networks as a way to handle uncertainty in student modeling and system decision-making. It explains the basic architecture of ITSs—knowledge base, student model, teaching model, and control engine—and argues that Bayesian networks are useful because they can represent uncertain or incomplete information about a learner’s knowledge state and support probabilistic inference for diagnosis and instructional decisions.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention study. Instead, it surveys prior ITS examples such as Andes, ViSMod, and BITS to show how Bayesian networks have been used for selecting instructional strategies, predicting student actions, and tracking mastery over time. It also includes a small conceptual case study on graph concepts in data structures, illustrating how prerequisite relationships can be organized as a knowledge dependency graph.

Overall, the paper concludes that Bayesian networks are a strong formalism for intelligent tutoring because they combine knowledge representation with decision support and can adapt teaching to student performance. The paper positions Bayesian approaches as useful for student modeling, pedagogy selection, and adaptive feedback, but it is primarily a review and design-oriented discussion rather than a test of a specific tutoring system with learners.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review / conceptual paper rather than an empirical study with a defined design, comparison group, or reported analytic results. It discusses prior ITS examples and Bayesian-network approaches, but does not present original evaluative evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome effects are estimated in this paper, so there is no measurable intervention impact to classify. The paper is useful as background on ITS architecture and Bayesian student modeling, but it does not demonstrate student learning gains itself.

interventions.use_case: Review of classical intelligent tutoring systems using Bayesian networks for student modeling, adaptive decision-making, and feedback in domains such as physics, programming, algebra, and geometry.

paper_profiles.title: PATS: Personality-Aware Teaching Strategies with Large Language Model Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) tutors can adapt their teaching strategies to students’ personality traits, rather than simply answering questions or giving generic scaffolding. The authors argue that current LLM tutoring systems do not account for personality-personalized pedagogy, which may reduce engagement and effectiveness. To address this gap, they develop PATS (Personality-Aware Teaching Strategies), a framework that maps Big Five personality profiles to teaching strategies grounded in learning-science literature.

The approach has two parts: a student model that simulates personality-consistent learners and a teacher model that first selects a personality trait, then chooses a suitable teaching strategy, and finally generates a response implementing that strategy. The study uses a real-world classroom dataset from a language-learning deployment in which 110 high-school students used a GPT-based tutoring system for homework support. From these students, the authors analyze anonymized chat logs and personality survey results, then generate 1,920 simulated dialogs across two tasks (image description and storytelling) for comparison against two baselines: a simple prompt baseline and a personality-only baseline.

Evaluation combines automated LLM judgments and human ratings from expert teachers, with additional qualitative analysis of the classroom logs and strategy usage. The authors find that PATS consistently outperforms both baselines across multiple dimensions, including motivation/support, suitability to personality, proactivity, engagement, and empathy. They also report that PATS implements the intended strategies with high fidelity in simulated dialogs, and that teachers and LLM annotators prefer personality-aligned strategy use over generic tutoring. The paper concludes that LLM tutors should incorporate pedagogically grounded, personality-aware strategy selection, while noting that some recommended classroom strategies are difficult to realize in prompt-only settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical system paper with qualitative analysis plus pairwise preference evaluation, but not a controlled trial with student learning outcomes. The strongest evidence comes from simulated dialogs and expert/LLM judgments, so causal credibility is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear preference improvements for a personality-aware LLM tutor, but no measured learning gains or effect sizes on student achievement. The impact on actual learners is therefore plausible but unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Personality-aware GPT-based tutoring conversations that adapt teaching strategies (e.g., scaffolding, motivational support, role-play, direct instruction) for image description and storytelling tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Across simulated tutoring dialogs, expert teachers and LLM judges preferred PATS over both baselines on motivation/support, engagement, and empathy-related dimensions. In human ratings, PATS won 85-90% of the time for Motivation & Support versus the simple baseline and 75-85% for Suitability to Personality; it also outperformed the personality-aware baseline across all five rated dimensions.
finding.measure: Pairwise human and LLM preference judgments on Motivation & Support, Engagement, Empathy, and Suited to Personality
finding.study_size: n=40 human-rated dialogue pairs; 1920 simulated dialogs total

finding.finding_summary: PATS was designed to improve dialogue quality through more personality-aligned pedagogical strategies, and evaluators preferred it for proactive responses and engagement, both of which are durable-skill-adjacent tutoring processes. The paper does not report learning gains, but it does report strong preference gains in these interaction-quality dimensions relative to both baselines.
finding.measure: Pairwise dialogue quality judgments on Proactive Responses and Engagement
finding.study_size: n=40 human-rated dialogue pairs; 1920 simulated dialogs total

finding.finding_summary: The system was evaluated in language-learning tasks focused on describing images and writing children’s stories, with real-time feedback on grammar and argumentation. However, the paper reports preference judgments over dialogue quality rather than direct language-learning performance, so evidence is indirect and based on simulated interactions rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Quality of conversational support for image description and storytelling in a language-learning setting
finding.study_size: n=110 students in source classroom logs; 1920 simulated dialogs

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing students’ authentic mathematical problem-solving skills and confidence through error analysis of GPT-4 solutions
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether an error-analysis learning activity built around GPT-4-generated mathematical solutions can improve elementary students’ ability to solve authentic, real-life mathematics problems and increase their mathematical confidence. The authors focus on the challenge that authentic word problems are cognitively demanding for students, especially lower-achieving learners, and explore whether AI output can be transformed from a potential source of incorrect answers into a productive learning resource.

The intervention was a ten-week quasi-experimental classroom study with 59 fifth-grade students in a primary school in northern Taiwan. The experimental group worked in small heterogeneous groups to analyze GPT-4 solutions to authentic mathematics problems, mark errors, discuss corrections with peers, and present their reasoning to the class, while the control group received traditional instruction using the same materials. Outcomes were measured with pre/post authentic mathematical problem-solving tests, a TIMSS-based mathematical confidence scale, and semi-structured interviews with the experimental group.

Results showed that the experimental group improved significantly from pre- to post-test in authentic mathematical problem-solving and mathematical confidence. Between-group comparisons favored the experimental group, with statistically significant advantages for low-achieving students on problem-solving and for both high- and low-achieving students on confidence. Interview data suggested that GPT-4 explanations supported understanding, peer discussion, critical thinking, and metacognitive reflection. The authors conclude that GPT-4, when paired with structured error analysis and collaboration, can be an effective instructional support in elementary mathematics, particularly for helping lower-achieving students.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, but it is not randomized and uses purposive sampling from one school. The mixed quantitative/qualitative design supports credible inference, though selection bias and limited generalizability remain concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced statistically significant improvements in mathematical confidence and within-group gains in authentic math problem solving, with a notable subgroup benefit for low-achieving students. However, effect sizes are not reported, and the between-group overall achievement difference was only marginal, so the impact appears modest rather than large.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-generated worked solutions used by fifth-grade students for authentic mathematics problem solving, followed by error analysis of the AI’s solution steps in small-group discussion and class presentation

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group improved significantly on authentic mathematical problem-solving after 10 weeks of GPT-4 error-analysis activities (within-group Wilcoxon z=-4.318, p<.001; n=28). Between groups, post-test performance was higher for the experimental group overall, and the low-achieving subgroup showed a significant advantage over controls (U=48, p=.01), indicating stronger benefits for lower performers.
finding.measure: Authentic Mathematical Problem-Solving Test (AMPS) pre/post scores

finding.finding_summary: Mathematical confidence increased significantly in the experimental group after the intervention (within-group Wilcoxon z=-3.881, p<.001; n=28). Post-test confidence was also significantly higher than control overall (U=215, p=.001), with significant gains for both high-achieving (U=64, p=.045) and low-achieving students (U=43, p=.007).
finding.measure: TIMSS 2019 Mathematical Confidence Scale (9-item Likert scale)

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated improvements in understanding, collaborative problem-solving, critical thinking, mathematical creativity, and metacognitive knowledge after students worked with GPT-4 solutions and analyzed errors. The authors report that 93% of experimental-group students said GPT-4 improved understanding, 79% reported better collaboration, and 86% reported gains in metacognitive knowledge, but no standardized effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes and coded response proportions

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of Using MatGPT on Mathematical Proficiency among Undergraduate Students
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Information and Education Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using MatGPT, a MATLAB-integrated interface to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, improves undergraduate students’ mathematical proficiency when solving differential equations. The authors focus on a broader question relevant to AI in mathematics education: whether an AI-supported environment can improve not just overall performance but also specific strands of proficiency such as conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, strategic competence, and adaptive reasoning.

The intervention compared three instructional approaches for the same differential equations content: traditional paper-and-pen instruction, MATLAB without AI support, and MatGPT. The study was conducted with 94 undergraduate students enrolled in a Differential Equation course at a private Jordanian university, divided into one control group and two experimental groups. The treatment lasted three weeks, and teachers received a two-hour workshop before implementation on how to use MatGPT and score student work with the mathematical proficiency rubric.

Results showed that the MatGPT group outperformed the MATLAB and traditional groups on overall mathematical proficiency, with statistically significant gains especially in procedural fluency, strategic competence, and adaptive reasoning. Conceptual understanding did not differ significantly across groups in the adjusted analyses, which the authors interpret as reflecting students’ prior exposure to differential equation concepts before the intervention. The paper concludes that MatGPT may be a useful AI-supported tool for enhancing mathematical proficiency in university mathematics instruction, while also noting practical challenges such as teacher training and digital security needs.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental comparison with pretest adjustment (MANCOVA) and a clearly described intervention and outcome rubric, which supports moderate credibility. However, it is not randomized at the individual level and is limited to a single university course context, so it falls short of blue-tier rigor.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports a medium-to-large positive effect on overall mathematical proficiency (eta^2=0.36) and sizable gains on several subskills. Because the effects are substantial and directly relevant to mathematics learning, the paper merits a blue impact rating despite the nonrandomized design.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT embedded within MATLAB (MatGPT) to provide step-by-step conversational assistance, hints, immediate feedback, and solution verification for solving differential equations in a university mathematics course.
Traditional MATLAB-based computational instruction for solving and visualizing differential equations without the ChatGPT conversational layer.

finding.finding_summary: Using MatGPT improved overall mathematical proficiency for undergraduate students solving differential equations compared with MATLAB and traditional instruction. The adjusted mean overall proficiency was 59.03 for MatGPT versus 50.49 for MATLAB and 40.22 for traditional teaching; the treatment effect was statistically significant (F=16.65, p<=0.05, eta^2=0.36) in a quasi-experimental sample of n=94.
finding.measure: Mathematical proficiency test on five differential equations scored across conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, strategic competence, and adaptive reasoning

finding.finding_summary: MatGPT outperformed both MATLAB and traditional teaching on procedural fluency, strategic competence, and adaptive reasoning, while conceptual understanding showed no significant treatment effect in the omnibus model. Reported effect sizes were moderate-to-large for procedural fluency (eta^2=0.23), strategic competence (eta^2=0.26), and adaptive reasoning (eta^2=0.33), with adjusted means favoring MatGPT (63.76, 34.24, and 49.02, respectively).
finding.measure: Mathematical proficiency strand scores: procedural fluency, strategic competence, adaptive reasoning, and conceptual understanding

paper_profiles.title: To engage with AI or not: learning engagement among rural junior high school students in an AI-powered adaptive learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines what factors shape learning engagement when rural junior high school students use an AI-powered adaptive learning system (ALS). Grounded in self-determination theory, the technology acceptance model, and cognitive load theory, the authors ask how students’ basic psychological needs, technology acceptance, and cognitive load relate to behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement in mathematics learning.

The intervention/context is an AI-powered ALS delivered on tablets during after-school mathematics sessions. The system used diagnostic questions, personalized resource/path recommendations, precision learning, and precision practice, with feedback based on students’ errors and mastery patterns. The study was conducted in five rural junior high schools in southwest China, focusing on seventh-grade mathematics. Students received a week of training on the tablets and AI functions, and a technical staff member was present in classrooms during implementation.

Using a mixed-methods design, the researchers collected questionnaire data from 243 students and conducted interviews with 30 students and 5 mathematics teachers, along with classroom observations. Quantitative analysis showed that perceived competence and technology acceptance significantly predicted learning engagement, while perceived autonomy and relatedness influenced engagement indirectly through technology acceptance. Intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load did not significantly predict engagement in the final model. Qualitative findings supported the importance of usability, personalized feedback, and reducing extraneous load. The paper concludes that AI-powered ALS can support engagement in rural mathematics education, but its effectiveness depends on usability, supportive feedback, and careful instructional design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational study using survey data, SEM, and some qualitative interviews, but it is not an experiment or randomized design. It provides moderate internal validity for association testing, yet causal claims are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests engagement-relevant benefits in a priority rural middle-school population, but it does not report direct achievement effects or effect sizes meeting a modest-impact threshold. The observed findings are important for implementation, but the practical magnitude is unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-powered adaptive learning system on tablets for rural junior high mathematics, using diagnostic questions, knowledge graphs, personalized resource/path recommendations, precision learning, and precision practice with immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on grade 7 mathematics use of an AI-powered adaptive learning system, but it does not report direct math achievement gains for this sample. Instead, it focuses on engagement-related antecedents and notes that all participating students used the system for one academic year; prior studies cited in the paper reported higher math scores in ALS groups, but those are not the present paper's findings.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning engagement within AI-powered ALS; no direct achievement test reported in the study results presented here

finding.finding_summary: The core empirical result concerns learning engagement in the AI-powered ALS. Technology acceptance and perceived competence were significant positive predictors of engagement, while perceived autonomy and perceived relatedness were not significant in the revised model; extraneous and intrinsic cognitive load were also not supported as direct predictors. The paper reports SEM/path analysis with n=243, but does not provide standardized coefficients or confidence intervals for the final paths in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement) and its predictors

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing achievement and retention in circle geometry through digital storytelling for senior secondary learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether digital storytelling can improve senior secondary students’ achievement and retention in circle geometry, and whether effects differ by gender. The authors note persistent difficulties in mathematics learning, especially in abstract topics like geometry, and argue that digital storytelling may make concepts more engaging and easier to understand by combining narrative with multimedia elements.

The study used a pretest-posttest non-equivalent control group quasi-experimental design with 132 Senior Secondary School One students from four public schools in Nsukka Local Government Area, Enugu State, Nigeria. The experimental group was taught circle geometry through digital storytelling activities using tools such as Canva, Sway, GeoGebra, and Kahoot!, while the control group received conventional lecture-based instruction. Students completed a Geometry Achievement Test before instruction, after instruction, and again four weeks later for retention.

Results showed that students taught with digital storytelling outperformed those taught conventionally on both achievement and retention outcomes. The paper also found no significant gender differences and no significant interaction between instructional method and gender. The authors conclude that digital storytelling is an effective approach for teaching circle geometry in secondary mathematics classrooms and recommend its use by mathematics teachers.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest non-equivalent control group study with ANCOVA, a reasonable design for classroom intervention research but without random assignment. Internal validity is strengthened by pretesting, covariate adjustment, and reported reliability (KR-20=0.83), though selection bias remains a concern.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported achievement effect is very large (ηp²=0.843) and retention effect is also substantial (ηp²=0.380), indicating strong positive impact in a priority K-12 mathematics population. Even allowing for quasi-experimental limitations, the magnitude suggests meaningful educational benefit.

interventions.use_case: digital storytelling-supported mathematics instruction for senior secondary circle geometry, combining narrated multimedia stories, GeoGebra exploration, Kahoot quizzes, and student-created story presentations

finding.finding_summary: Digital storytelling produced substantially higher circle geometry achievement than conventional instruction for senior secondary learners (n=132). The experimental group’s posttest mean rose from 62.31 (SD=7.31) to 93.37 (SD=5.87), while the control group rose from 61.73 (SD=6.82) to 64.70 (SD=6.85); ANCOVA showed a significant group effect, F(1,127)=681.008, p<.05, ηp²=0.843.
finding.measure: Geometry Achievement Test (GAT) posttest scores on circle geometry
finding.std_deviation: experimental post SD=5.87; control post SD=6.85

finding.finding_summary: Retention in circle geometry was significantly higher for the digital storytelling group than for the conventional group. The paper reports a retention mean of 95.97 (SD=3.67) for the experimental group versus 64.08 (SD=6.73) for the control group, with ANCOVA indicating a significant group difference, F(1,127)=77.976, p<.05, ηp²=0.380.
finding.measure: Retention test scores on circle geometry four weeks after posttest
finding.std_deviation: experimental retention SD=3.67; control retention SD=6.73

finding.finding_summary: The study found no significant gender differences in achievement within the digital storytelling condition, suggesting the intervention benefited male and female learners similarly on performance outcomes. Gender was non-significant in ANCOVA, F(1,127)=0.113, p=.738, ηp²=0.001.
finding.measure: Achievement scores by gender on the GAT
finding.study_size: n=68 in digital storytelling group for gender comparison

finding.finding_summary: Gender did not significantly affect retention outcomes under digital storytelling, indicating no evidence of differential persistence of learning for male versus female learners. The paper reports a non-significant gender effect for retention in ANCOVA, though the exact F-statistic is not shown in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Retention scores by gender after digital storytelling instruction
finding.study_size: n=68 in digital storytelling group for gender comparison

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports no significant interaction between instructional method and gender on achievement, indicating the digital storytelling benefit was broadly similar across boys and girls. The interaction effect was small and non-significant, F(1,127)=1.127, p=.290, ηp²=0.009.
finding.measure: Interaction effect on achievement in circle geometry

paper_profiles.title: PISA 2022. Predictores del rendimiento en pensamiento computacional en Educación Secundaria en España
paper_profiles.venue: RED. Revista de Educación a Distancia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which student- and school-level predictors are associated with performance in computational thinking among Spanish secondary students who participated in PISA 2022. The study is framed around a broader educational question: why there are performance differences in computational thinking, including gender gaps and differences linked to socioeconomic background, digital competence, and access to ICT resources.

No intervention was implemented. Instead, the author analyzed existing PISA 2022 data using a multilevel multiple regression model. The student-level predictors included gender, socioeconomic and cultural status, digital competence, use of ICT for coding/algorithmic activities, and availability/use of ICT at home. School-level predictors included ICT availability at school, school ownership (public/private), and school location. The sample consisted of 30,800 Spanish secondary students from 966 schools.
