The results showed significant associations for most predictors: boys outperformed girls, higher socioeconomic status was associated with higher computational thinking scores, stronger digital competence predicted better performance, and more frequent ICT use for coding/algorithmic activities and greater ICT availability/use at home were also positive predictors. At the school level, greater ICT resources and private school ownership were associated with higher performance, while school location was not significant. The author concludes that strengthening students’ digital competence and improving ICT access in schools may help support computational thinking achievement, especially in public and disadvantaged schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multilevel regression study using a large, nationally representative PISA sample, but it is not an intervention study and cannot establish causality. Credibility is limited to observational associations and self-/school-reported predictors.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests sizable contextual associations, but it does not test a technology intervention or estimate an actionable treatment effect. Its relevance to the requested topic is indirect because it addresses predictors of computational thinking rather than ChatGPT or LLM use in middle school mathematics achievement.

finding.finding_summary: This PISA 2022 multilevel regression studied computational thinking performance in Spanish secondary students (n=30,800; 966 schools). The outcome is not a direct middle-school math achievement intervention effect, but a descriptive predictor model showing higher computational thinking scores for boys than girls and significant positive associations with socioeconomic status, digital competence, ICT use for coding/algorithm tasks, home ICT availability, school ICT resources, and private school attendance. The model explained 22% of student-level variance and 53% of school-level variance.
finding.measure: PISA 2022 computational thinking performance scale (mathematics assessment component)

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German-language tasks grounded in middle school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, rely heavily on multiple-choice formats, and do not adequately test whether models can combine visual reasoning with subject-specific background knowledge. To address this, they construct a new dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning nine school subjects, including mathematics, history, biology, geography, music, physics, religion, sports, and arts.

The benchmark draws from German school textbooks for grades 8–10 and includes some questions embedded directly in images, as well as intentionally adversarial questions that ask about objects or concepts not actually present in the image. The study evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs and uses a panel-of-LLMs scoring approach for open-ended responses. Results show that the benchmark is challenging: the best overall accuracy is below 45%, and performance is especially weak on math, music, and adversarial questions. Larger models generally do better, but scaling alone does not guarantee strong performance, and model rankings differ from those seen on public benchmarks such as MMMU.

The main conclusion is that middle-school-level German multimodal questions are a useful stress test for current VLMs and reveal important gaps in visual understanding, contextual reasoning, and the ability to refuse unanswerable questions. The paper is not an intervention study with human participants; instead, it introduces and evaluates a benchmark intended to support future research on model capabilities in educationally relevant settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clearly described methodology, but it is not a causal study and does not evaluate an educational intervention on learners. It provides observational model performance data rather than student outcome evidence, so it fits a lower internal-validity evidence tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact effect size because it benchmarks VLMs rather than testing classroom use or learner gains. Its relevance is indirect: it may inform future AI-in-education tools, but it does not demonstrate measurable impact on student achievement or school outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking and evaluating vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions using open-ended image-grounded tasks; not a student-facing tutoring or instructional intervention.

finding.finding_summary: Math is one of the weakest domains in the benchmark. The best model reaches only about 34% accuracy on math questions, and the paper reports that models struggle especially with counting, geometry, coordinate reading, and formulas that require integrating visual cues with background knowledge (e.g., calculating areas/circumferences from figures).
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle school math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: Physics performance is substantially limited, especially for questions requiring explanation rather than simple identification. The best models are around 32% to 46% on physics depending on model, and the paper notes frequent failures on causal explanations in diagrams and circuit reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math, non-science school subjects, performance varies widely by domain. Best accuracy is roughly 54% in history and religion, around the low 30s in music, and mid-to-high 40s in arts/geography/sports, indicating uneven subject-specific multimodal understanding rather than uniform competence.
finding.measure: Accuracy on arts, biology, geography, history, music, religion, and sports benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=1,532 questions across non-math/non-physics domains (arts 286, biology 169, geography 251, history 264, music 166, religion 206, sports 154)

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark suggests weak reasoning robustness, especially on adversarial questions that require rejecting misleading prompts or using contextual disambiguation. Performance on adversarial items is much lower than on the full set, with the best models only reaching about 29% to 33% overall and many smaller models far below that, indicating poor uncertainty handling and resistance to semantic traps.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial benchmark questions requiring refusal or disambiguation
finding.study_size: n=adversarial subset across domains; exact count not fully reported in text

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI-powered mobile app can proactively improve young adults’ well-being, rather than waiting to treat mental health problems after they emerge. The authors frame the work as a strengths-based alternative to deficit-oriented mental health tools, aiming to boost positive affect, resilience, belonging, mindfulness, and flourishing while buffering against declines in well-being.

The intervention was the Flourish app, an iOS/Android mobile application featuring an AI chatbot (“Sunnie”), brief check-ins, personalized recommendations for science-based well-being activities, and weekly summaries. The system used large language models to adapt its tone, content, and suggestions in real time, and included safety and escalation protocols for high-risk language. The study ran for six weeks in Fall 2024 across three U.S. institutions: Chapman University, the University of Washington, and Foothill College.

A total of 486 undergraduate students were randomly assigned to app access or a waitlist control. Outcomes were measured with repeated self-report surveys across four waves. The treatment group showed significant improvements in positive affect, calm, social well-being indicators such as loneliness and belonging, and overall well-being measures including resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing. Effects on negative affect, depression, anxiety, stress, and academic self-efficacy were not significant. The authors conclude that a purpose-built generative AI system can deliver scalable, preventive well-being support, though future studies should test active controls and longer-term effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered, multi-site randomized controlled trial with longitudinal follow-up and validated measures, which is strong causal evidence. Some concerns remain because the control was waitlist rather than active, and engagement/back-end usage data were self-reported rather than directly logged.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are statistically significant but modest in magnitude (e.g., positive affect d≈0.23 to 0.33; beta values around 0.03-0.05). The intervention shows promise for a college mental health population, but the impacts are small and focused on well-being rather than academic or clinical outcomes.

interventions.use_case: generative AI-powered mobile well-being app delivering brief check-ins, chatbot conversations, and science-based micro-activities with personalized recommendations and weekly insights

finding.finding_summary: In a 6-week multi-institutional RCT (n=486 undergraduates), access to the Flourish app improved several well-being indicators versus waitlist control. The strongest effects were on positive affect (Condition × Time b=0.22, p=.020; Week 6 d=0.33), resilience (b=0.11, p=.047), mindfulness (b=0.19, p=.045), and flourishing (b=0.19, p=.032), while negative affect showed no effect.
finding.measure: Positive affect, negative affect, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing scales
finding.effect_size: reported as d=0.23 at Week 4 and d=0.33 at Week 6 for positive affect; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved social well-being in the same RCT (n=486). Loneliness decreased more steeply in the treatment group than control (b=-0.05, p=.038), and belonging improved (b=0.06, p=.030), with a marginal increase in closeness to the university (b=0.04, p=.070).
finding.measure: UCLA 3-item loneliness, campus belonging, and closeness-to-school measures

paper_profiles.title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether reviewers in academic peer review anchor to their original scores when they are later shown new information that should objectively improve a paper. The authors focus on the rebuttal stage of conference peer review, where reviewers first score a paper, then receive additional information from authors, and are asked to revise their scores. The study asks whether revised scores remain artificially close to the initial scores because of anchoring bias.

To test this, the authors designed a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants who were PhD students or PhDs in computer science-related fields. Participants were assigned to either a control condition, where they viewed a paper with an animated GIF showing stronger evaluation results, or an experimental condition, where they initially saw a frozen frame of the GIF that made the paper appear weaker. After reviewing, experimental participants were told the GIF had failed to load and were then shown the correct animated version, after which they could revise their scores and comments. The task was framed as a mock conference review of an application-focused AI paper, and the setup was designed to isolate anchoring from other confounds.

The main finding is that the manipulation successfully created a perceived quality difference between the initial experimental paper and the control paper, especially on the Evaluation category. However, when comparing the experimental group’s revised scores to the control group’s scores, the authors found no significant evidence of anchoring in either the Overall score or the Evaluation category. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested possible differences by reviewer confidence and seniority, but these were not conclusive. Overall, the study concludes that reviewer anchoring was not detected in this peer-review setting, and that limited score change in rebuttal processes may reflect other factors besides anchoring.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a well-designed randomized controlled trial with preregistration, random assignment, and a clear experimental manipulation, which supports strong causal inference. However, it is a lab-style simulated peer-review setting rather than a real-world educational or schooling intervention, so relevance/generalizability constraints remain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper studies reviewer behavior in academic peer review, not an educational intervention affecting student outcomes. It finds no meaningful effect on the measured institutional process outcomes, so the practical impact as defined here is absent.

finding.finding_summary: This randomized controlled trial tested whether reviewers anchor to their initial scores in conference peer review after seeing corrected paper information. Across 108 participants, revised scores did not differ significantly from control scores for Overall review scores (Vargha-Delaney A=0.5048, adjusted p=0.6064) or Evaluation scores (A=0.4863, adjusted p=0.6064), providing no evidence of anchoring bias in this setting.
finding.measure: Reviewer Overall score and Evaluation category score in a simulated conference peer review task

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2023), PMLR 202
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the regulatory problem of how the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) should handle generative AI systems. The authors argue that the current DMA framework, which was designed for established digital platform services such as operating systems, web browsers, and social networking, does not explicitly cover generative AI even though such systems may become important gateways between business users and end users.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or empirical sample. Instead, it develops a legal and policy argument for treating certain generative AI services as “core platform services” under the DMA and for designating some AI developers as gatekeepers. It discusses how generative AI can function as a platform through products like ChatGPT and APIs, and it identifies sources of gatekeeping power such as computing resources, early-mover advantages, data resources, and integrated systems.

The authors conclude that the DMA should be amended or interpreted to prevent entrenched positions in generative AI markets and to support contestability, fairness, and diversity. The paper also sketches how specific DMA obligations could apply to generative AI providers, especially around data use, tying, and platform integration. No participant population, educational setting, or learning outcome is reported.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/policy position paper about the EU Digital Markets Act and generative AI market structure, not an empirical study of educational technology in schools. It contains no experimental, quasi-experimental, or observational evidence relevant to student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact and does not evaluate ChatGPT use in middle school mathematics achievement or any student learning outcome. Its contribution is regulatory/theoretical rather than intervention-effect evidence.

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how mixing different instruction-tuning datasets affects large language model (LLM) performance. The authors focus on an open question in instruction fine-tuning: how to combine general chat instructions, coding instructions, and NLP task instructions in a way that improves overall capabilities rather than optimizing one skill at the expense of another.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention with human participants, but a set of fine-tuning experiments on LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models using three instruction datasets: Alpaca for general chat, CodeAlpaca for code generation, and P3 for reformatted NLP downstream tasks. The models are trained under eight dataset-mixing configurations, with additional experiments varying the ratio and number of specialized instruction samples. Performance is evaluated on NLP benchmarks, HumanEval for coding, and FLASK/GPT-4-based alignment skill assessments.

The paper finds that specialized instruction datasets improve performance in their matching domains, but mixing all instruction types does not uniformly benefit all tasks. P3 improves NLP benchmark scores but harms alignment/chat abilities; CodeAlpaca improves coding and can also support chat alignment when combined with general instructions; and Alpaca is strongest for alignment overall. Larger models benefit more from diverse mixtures than smaller ones, and performance tends to plateau beyond roughly 10K examples per instruction type. Overall, the study argues that instruction mixture should be designed with target use cases and model scale in mind.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methods/benchmarking paper about instruction mixture for fine-tuning LLMs, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It does not evaluate educational outcomes with student participants or an instructional design in schooling, so the evidence framework is not applicable as an educational effectiveness study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct demonstrated impact on student learning or school outcomes. Its findings are technical and indirect, about how different instruction datasets affect LLM benchmark performance and alignment in general-purpose models.

paper_profiles.title: Search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos with the ATLAS experiment at the LHC
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a particle-physics search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos (R-hadrons) using the ATLAS detector at the LHC, not a study in education. The analysis asks whether slow-moving, long-lived, coloured supersymmetric particles can be detected in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV by combining measurements of ionisation energy loss in the pixel detector and time-of-flight in the tile calorimeter.

The approach uses 34 pb−1 of ATLAS collision data, together with Monte Carlo simulation and a data-driven background estimate, to reconstruct candidate masses and define signal regions for several mass hypotheses. The work examines multiple interaction models for R-hadrons in matter and studies systematic uncertainties from theory, detector response, and background estimation.

No evidence for signal is found. The paper sets 95% confidence-level lower mass limits for stable sbottoms, stops, and gluinos, with the most conservative limits reported as 294 GeV, 309 GeV, and 562 GeV respectively. Since the paper is entirely about high-energy physics and contains no education-related intervention, population, or user data, the education fields are not reported.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a high-energy physics paper about ATLAS searches for long-lived hadronising squarks and gluinos, not an education study. It does not evaluate any educational technology, AI intervention, or learner outcome relevant to the requested taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention or student outcome assessed, so there is no impact on middle school mathematics achievement or any K-12 education outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics tasks for students, and how that affects the quality, realism, and efficiency of the personalization process. The authors focus on the tension between broad personalization that a teacher can manage and the smaller-grain, more individualized personalization that students may prefer.

The intervention involved 7 middle school mathematics teachers using ChatGPT (with GPT-4o) to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so they better matched students’ popular-culture interests. Teachers first received a 2-hour training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then completed two personalization cycles: one for Unit 4 (Proportional Relationships and Percentages) and one for Unit 6 (Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities). They worked in Zoom sessions while their prompting and screen activity were recorded, and 521 seventh-grade students completed the resulting personalized assignments in ASSISTments. Students then provided closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests, plus open-ended feedback on what they liked and how the tasks could be improved.

The study finds that teachers used ChatGPT in iterative ways that reflected tradeoffs among grain size, depth, and ownership. Teachers often prompted the model to add specific pop-culture references, improve realism, adjust numbers and quantities, and tailor tasks to age, location, or names. Students, however, tended to respond more positively to specific, fine-grained references than to broad categories, while showing relatively little concern for deeper realism issues. In terms of efficiency, personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average and required about 3 prompts; performance was best when teachers used roughly 3–5 prompts. Teachers did not become faster over time—in fact, they used more prompts and took longer in Unit 6—though student ratings improved after teachers reflected on feedback and revised their approach. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports professional learning and can improve task quality, but it remains time-consuming and may not be able to deliver the fine-grained personalization students prefer.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative-plus-correlational study with teacher and student feedback, prompt logs, and mixed-effects models, but no randomized control group for learning outcomes. It provides useful descriptive evidence, yet it does not meet strong causal or RCT standards.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows modest-to-mixed impact on student interest ratings and no evidence of improved achievement, while teacher workload increased rather than decreased. The observed student-rating gains are small and mainly affect engagement-related outcomes, not general academic performance.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students’ interests, with iterative prompting to adjust context, realism, readability, and mathematical clarity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main academic outcome was students’ ratings of the personalized math problems, not achievement test scores. Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to students’ interests were significantly higher when teachers used 3–5 prompts to create a problem, with an estimated increase of about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student 1–5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to students’ interests

finding.finding_summary: Students often found the personalized problems interesting when the popular culture reference matched their preferences, but many disliked them when the reference did not match. Average ratings were modest overall (interestingness M=2.46, SD=1.24; closeness M=2.53, SD=1.28), and Unit 6 problems were rated higher than Unit 4 (interestingness B=0.33, SE=0.095, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback on whether the problem was interesting

finding.finding_summary: Teacher efficiency was not improved by using ChatGPT for personalization. Teachers took an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7) and 3.2 prompts per problem overall, with some teachers needing up to 6.6 prompts per problem and about 5.5 minutes per problem; time did not clearly decline over time, and in Unit 6 teachers actually used more prompts and more time than in Unit 4 (B=1.26 prompts, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Time spent creating each problem; number of prompts per problem

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Advanced Large Language Models with LLMSuite: A Free Comprehensive Recap of Techniques, Architectures, and Practical Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tutorial and обзор of advanced large language model (LLM) techniques rather than an empirical study of an educational intervention. It addresses limitations of systems such as ChatGPT and Gemini, including knowledge cutoffs, hallucinations, and weaknesses in mathematical reasoning, and explains approaches intended to improve reliability and capability. The main question is how current LLM applications can be made more useful through retrieval, external tools, prompt-based reasoning, and fine-tuning strategies.

The paper surveys several approaches: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), chain-of-thought prompting, Program-Aided Language Models (PAL), ReAct, and LangChain for building tool-using LLM applications. It also reviews transformer architecture, GPU memory scaling strategies such as DDP/FSDP and ZeRO, 1-bit LLMs, and fine-tuning methods including instruction tuning, multitask tuning, LoRA, prompt tuning, RLHF, and ReST. These are presented as general technical methods applicable across domains, not as a classroom study or student intervention.

No educational population, school setting, or learner outcome is studied. The paper does not test ChatGPT in middle school mathematics or report subgroup/moderator effects. Its main conclusion is that combining LLMs with external tools, better prompting, and parameter-efficient training can improve accuracy, efficiency, and reliability in a wide range of applications.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a tutorial/survey paper rather than an empirical study. It does not report a study design, comparison, or original outcome data, so it provides no direct evidence on student learning or subgroup effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper is conceptual and methodological, focusing on LLM architectures, prompting, RAG, RLHF, and fine-tuning strategies. It reports no measured educational impact and does not evaluate ChatGPT use in middle school mathematics achievement.

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Recommendations in EdTech: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether personalized content recommendations can improve engagement in an educational app, compared with the app’s existing editorial curation system. The authors focus on a recommendation problem in digital education: whether matching learning content to individual user preferences increases consumption of educational material, and whether those gains differ across user subgroups.

The intervention is a personalized recommendation system built from historical interaction data using matrix factorization. The system replaces manual/editorial ranking in one section of the Freadom app (“Recommended Story”) and is evaluated in a randomized controlled trial. Users with at least 60 prior story interactions were randomized to treatment or control. Treatment users saw personalized story recommendations while control users continued to receive editor-selected stories. The app is used by children ages 3 to 12 in India, mainly through smartphones, and the content consists of short illustrated English-reading stories with quizzes.

The study finds that personalization substantially increases engagement in the recommended section and also raises overall app usage. Specifically, the personalized section sees about a 60% increase in total story engagement, alongside higher story completion and reading time; overall app engagement rises by about 14%. The paper also reports heterogeneity: users with longer histories, heavier engagement, and niche preferences benefit more than light or mainstream users. The authors conclude that personalization can meaningfully improve engagement in educational apps, especially when sufficient historical data are available to support accurate recommendations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a clear treatment/control contrast and pre-specified outcomes, making it strong causal evidence. Internal validity is good, though the paper studies engagement rather than learning achievement, which limits direct relevance to academic impact questions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a modest-to-large increase in engagement outcomes, including a 14% rise in overall app usage and 60% higher engagement in the personalized section. However, because the study does not measure academic achievement, the educational impact is indirect and therefore best classified as green rather than blue.

interventions.use_case: Personalized content recommendations in a children's reading app, using matrix factorization to rank and re-rank stories for each user based on past engagement history.
App-based delivery of short illustrated reading stories and quizzes in the Freadom mobile/web learning platform.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure learning or reading achievement outcomes, so it cannot claim an effect on literacy achievement. The closest literacy-related outcome is reading-time/engagement with story content in the Freadom app, which increased under personalization, but this is only a proxy and not evidence of achievement gains.
finding.measure: Reading-time/engagement with story content; no direct literacy achievement measure reported
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; 3023 app launchers analyzed; 525 viewed at least one Recommended Story

finding.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations substantially increased user engagement with the educational app. In the main randomized controlled trial (n=7750 randomized; analysis on app launchers), Total Story Engagement in the Recommended Story section rose by 60% (SE 17%), completed stories by 78% (SE 26%), and reading time by 87% (SE 25%). Overall app usage also increased: Total Story Engagement across all sections rose by 14% (SE 7%).
finding.measure: Total Story Engagement, completed stories, and reading time in Recommended Story section and across all app sections
finding.effect_size: 60% increase in Recommended Story engagement; 14% increase in all-sections engagement

paper_profiles.title: ExpTrialMng: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical software problem in VR/AR/MR research: many researchers want to run user experiments in immersive environments, but existing tools can be too complex, too heavy, or too tied to specific workflows. The authors argue that these barriers are especially problematic for researchers who are not proficient in Unity programming, and that unexpected hardware issues such as tracking loss can interrupt experiments and cause data loss.

To address this, they propose ExpTrialMng, a Unity library for managing experimental trials. The library reads pre-generated CSV trial files, delivers trial settings to an experiment manager, saves results to a CSV file after each trial, and supports restarting the experiment from a specific trial number after an interruption. The approach is meant to be lightweight and general-purpose so it can be adapted to many VR/AR HCI or psychology experiments without needing extensive custom code.

The paper is not an empirical study with human participants; instead, it is a framework paper describing the design and functionality of the library. The main conclusion is that ExpTrialMng can lower the programming barrier for immersive-experiment researchers, reduce data loss from technical problems, and make experiment implementation more universal across VR/AR settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a tooling/preprint paper describing a software library, not an empirical study of learning or user outcomes. It does not present a controlled evaluation with participant outcomes or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational or achievement impact is measured. The contribution is infrastructural (experiment management) rather than an intervention with demonstrated outcome effects.

interventions.use_case: Unity-based trial management library for VR/AR/MR experiments that handles pre-generated trial sequencing, result saving, and resuming experiments after interruptions

paper_profiles.title: Digital learning and student outcomes: a mathematical synthesis from the last decade
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether digital learning improves students’ cognitive learning outcomes, and whether effects differ by intervention characteristics. The authors note conflicting prior findings and the need for a stronger quantitative synthesis of evidence before more recent AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, are widely integrated into education. To address this, they conducted a meta-analysis of randomized, pretest-posttest controlled studies published between 2013 and 2023.

The review included 17 studies with 1,896 participants across educational levels and subject areas. Interventions ranged from online quizzes and web-based e-learning to virtual reality, augmented reality, mobile learning apps, and learning platforms. Included studies covered primary, middle school, secondary, undergraduate, and graduate settings; outcomes were objective cognitive measures such as grades, knowledge tests, and skill assessments. The authors synthesized effects using a random-effects model and tested moderators including cognitive engagement mode, sample size, duration, setting, subject area, and tool usage environment.

Overall, digital learning showed a positive, moderate effect on cognitive outcomes compared with traditional instruction, and the publication-bias-adjusted estimate remained positive. Subgroup analyses suggested larger gains for active versus passive engagement and somewhat stronger effects in school settings, smaller samples, and shorter interventions, but none of these differences reached statistical significance. The authors conclude that digital learning can improve academic outcomes, yet the evidence base is highly heterogeneous and still too limited to support firm claims about which conditions produce the strongest effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of randomized controlled pretest-posttest studies with explicit inclusion criteria and quantitative synthesis. Although heterogeneity was high (I2=83%), the design and evidence synthesis quality are strong.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on cognitive outcomes was moderate and clearly positive (g=.62; adjusted g=.49), exceeding the threshold for medium impact. The review spans multiple subjects and levels, indicating meaningful general educational relevance rather than a niche effect.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analyzed digital learning and e-learning interventions delivered via software, online platforms, VR/AR apps, mobile apps, web-based courses, and other technology-supported instruction compared with traditional non-digital instruction; the paper treats these as technology-assisted learning conditions rather than a single specific product.

finding.finding_summary: Across 17 randomized pretest-posttest studies (n=1,896), digital learning interventions produced a positive moderate gain in cognitive learning outcomes versus traditional instruction. The pooled effect was Hedge’s g=.62 (95% CI .38 to .86, p<.01), and the trim-and-fill adjusted estimate remained positive at g=.49 (95% CI .40 to .59).
finding.measure: Objective cognitive learning outcomes / posttest academic achievement measures across subjects

paper_profiles.title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in the literature on whether AI-enabled personalized learning improves STEM outcomes for K-12 students, and which conditions or design features explain variation in effects. The authors note that prior work on AI in STEM education has often been descriptive or qualitative, with limited quantitative synthesis and limited attention to moderators such as school level, subject, and type of AI tool.

To answer these questions, the authors conducted a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published between January 2012 and October 2024. They synthesized 99 effect sizes from 32 journal articles focused on AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools. The included interventions covered several AI application types, including intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, augmented/virtual reality tools, and other AI technologies, and were coded by school level, subject, personalized learning model, observed outcome type, and generative-AI usage.

The analysis found an overall positive effect of AI-enabled personalized STEM education on student outcomes, with a small but statistically significant average effect. Moderator analyses suggested that effects were stronger in junior and senior high school than in kindergarten, were especially large for AR/VR-based interventions, and varied by personalized learning model and subject. The authors also found no significant difference between GAI-related and GAI-unrelated tools. Overall, they conclude that AI can support personalized STEM learning in K-12 settings, but its effectiveness depends heavily on pedagogical alignment and implementation context.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis synthesizing 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trials, with explicit effect-size computation, moderator analyses, and publication-bias checks. The design and evidence base are strong, though heterogeneity is high and some subgroup estimates are based on small numbers of studies.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The overall effect is statistically significant and above the medium-impact threshold, g=0.455, indicating meaningful positive effects on K-12 STEM learning. Several subgroups are also positive, including a very large effect for comprehensive courses and a moderate effect for knowledge/skills.

interventions.use_case: AI-enabled personalized STEM tutoring systems in K-12 schools, including classical intelligent tutoring systems that adapt instruction and feedback to student performance
AI-enabled personalized educational games used for STEM learning with adaptive tutoring and feedback
AI-enabled personalized learning platforms delivering adaptive content and pacing in K-12 STEM classrooms, including classroom-integrated and more automated models
AI-powered AR/VR or immersive embodied learning environments used for STEM instruction and practice
AI technologies in personalized STEM education that do not cleanly fit ITS, games, or AR/VR, such as other ICT or AI-supported classroom tools

finding.finding_summary: Across 99 independent datasets from 32 RCT articles, AI-enabled personalized STEM education showed a small but significant positive overall effect on learning outcomes, g=0.455, 95% CI [0.327, 0.583]. For mathematics specifically, the subgroup effect size was g=0.398 (p<0.001), indicating a small positive impact on math learning in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Mathematics/STEM learning outcomes and achievement measures reported in RCTs

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found a significant positive effect for science-related outcomes, though smaller than for math, with g=0.219 (p=0.002). This suggests AI-enabled personalized STEM tools modestly improved science learning and understanding in the included K-12 studies.
finding.measure: Science learning outcomes/achievement

finding.finding_summary: For comprehensive cross-disciplinary courses, AI-enabled personalized STEM education produced the largest subject-level effect, g=2.161 (p=0.004). This indicates a very large positive impact in integrated STEM or multi-subject courses, although only 5 studies contributed to this subgroup.
finding.measure: Comprehensive course learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review found small but significant improvements in affective outcomes when AI-enabled personalized STEM education measured perceptions/attitudes (g=0.264) and engagement (g=0.386). These results suggest the interventions modestly improved students’ interest, motivation, or engagement, but the effect was not as strong as for knowledge/skills outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions/attitudes; engagement surveys or similar affective measures
finding.study_size: n=24 studies for perceptions/attitudes; n=25 studies for engagement

finding.finding_summary: Knowledge/skills outcomes, which in this paper include competence-oriented learning results, showed a significant medium positive effect of g=0.603 (p<0.001). The paper also reports a non-significant comprehensive-ability subgroup (g=0.381, 95% CI [-0.065, 0.826]) based on only one study, so the evidence for higher-order durable skills is limited but generally favorable.
finding.measure: Knowledge/skills; comprehensive ability
finding.study_size: n=49 studies for knowledge/skills; n=1 study for comprehensive ability

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of the Effectiveness of Algebraic Teaching Interventions: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Synthesis
paper_profiles.venue: Nordic Journal of Systematic Reviews in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a protocol for a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-synthesis of algebra teaching interventions in K-12 education. The authors aim to identify which interventions improve algebra learning, for whom they are effective, and under what conditions. They also seek to understand which moderators—such as grade level, demographic characteristics, intervention type, delivery mode, and teacher training—explain variation in intervention effects.

The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it outlines a mixed-methods review process that will synthesize quantitative and qualitative evidence from U.S.-based studies published since 1980. The planned review includes randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies with baseline equivalence, and empirical qualitative studies, with outcomes focused on mathematics learning, thinking, and knowledge. The authors also propose an algebraic teaching framework grounded in learning progression theory to classify interventions by algebraic big ideas and thinking practices.

The population of interest is U.S. elementary and secondary students in grades K-12, with attention to diverse backgrounds and subgroup differences such as race/ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, and grade level. The context is classroom-based algebra, early algebra, and pre-algebra instruction across schools in the United States and its territories. The main contribution of the paper is methodological: it provides a detailed protocol for analyzing how algebra instruction works and which features are associated with stronger student outcomes, rather than reporting empirical results from an implemented intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review/meta-analysis protocol, not an empirical study reporting results. It outlines planned methods, search strategy, and moderators but provides no analyzed evidence or effect estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effects are reported because the paper is preparatory/protocol-only. As a result, there is no demonstrated impact on student outcomes in this paper itself.

paper_profiles.title: Can GenAI improve students’ mathematics learning outcomes effectively?—A meta-analysis of empirical research 2023-2025
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT and other large language models, improves students’ mathematics learning outcomes. It was written as a systematic review and meta-analysis of empirical studies published from 2023 to 2025, motivated by mixed prior findings and the lack of a mathematics-specific synthesis.

The review aggregates experimental and quasi-experimental studies comparing GenAI-supported mathematics instruction with traditional teaching. Outcomes were organized into cognitive skills and non-cognitive skills, with cognitive outcomes further split into higher-order and lower-order thinking. The analysis also examined moderators such as educational level, intervention duration, learning content, GenAI integration level, and sample size.

The included evidence covered primary school, middle school, high school, and undergraduate students. The review found an overall positive effect of GenAI on mathematics learning outcomes, with stronger effects for cognitive than non-cognitive outcomes. The most favorable effects appeared for higher-order cognition, elementary students, and interventions classified as creative transformation under the PIC-RAT framework. Smaller studies showed larger effects, while intervention duration and learning content were not significant moderators.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis with a clearly specified search window, inclusion criteria, quality appraisal (MERSQI), bias checks, and moderator analyses. Those features make it high-quality evidence despite being a protocol-style report rather than a completed journal meta-analysis article.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on mathematics learning outcomes is moderate and positive (g = 0.539), exceeding the threshold for medium impact. The strongest gains appear in priority K-12 subgroups, especially elementary students and creative-transformation use cases.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and other large language models used in mathematics instruction for personalized tutoring, step-by-step problem solving, conceptual explanations, interactive dialogue, and feedback generation.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of 22 empirical studies (46 effect sizes; N=5,132) found a moderate positive overall effect of GenAI on mathematics learning outcomes, with pooled Hedges' g = 0.539 (p < .005). The effect was stronger for cognitive outcomes (g = 0.596) than for non-cognitive outcomes (g = 0.320), and especially strong for higher-order cognitive skills (g = 0.740) compared with lower-order skills (g = 0.562).
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes; cognitive skill outcomes (higher-order and lower-order) and overall achievement/learning measures

finding.finding_summary: Across the non-cognitive outcome set, GenAI showed a positive but smaller pooled effect (g = 0.320) on motivational and affective variables such as anxiety, self-efficacy, engagement, and attitudes. The review reports these effects as favorable overall, but clearly weaker than the cognitive gains.
finding.measure: Math anxiety, self-efficacy, motivation, engagement, attitudes

finding.finding_summary: For cognitive skills that map to durable skills, GenAI had a stronger effect on higher-order thinking outcomes such as analysis, evaluation, creation, and complex problem-solving (g = 0.740) than on lower-order thinking (g = 0.562). This indicates a comparatively larger benefit for deeper reasoning and metacognitive-type performance in mathematics learning.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking / problem-solving / reasoning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Chatbots in Science Education: Meta-Analysis of Pedagogical Integration and Student Achievement
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Chemistry Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-powered chatbots improve student achievement in science education and which factors explain variation in effectiveness. The authors note that prior work has often focused on technical features or user satisfaction rather than instructional design, learner context, or learning outcomes, so they conduct a moderator-rich meta-analysis to address these gaps.

The intervention studied is chatbot-supported instruction, including tools such as ChatGPT, virtual teaching assistants, and other AI-powered conversational systems. The review synthesized 26 empirical studies published from 2020 to 2024 using a random-effects meta-analytic model and moderator analyses. The included studies covered science-related subjects such as biology, physics, medical/health sciences, computer science, programming, and mathematics, across primary, secondary, and higher education contexts in multiple countries.

Overall, chatbot use had a moderate positive effect on achievement, but effects varied substantially by context and design. The strongest outcomes appeared in lower-middle-income countries, in scaffolded and personalized learning environments, with longer interventions and with assessments targeting higher-order thinking or mixed outcomes. The review concludes that chatbots are not uniformly effective and should be integrated as context-sensitive pedagogical supports rather than one-size-fits-all tools, especially given weaker or mixed effects in mathematics and health-related subjects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis following PRISMA with a random-effects model, explicit risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity analysis, and publication-bias checks. The paper synthesizes 26 empirical studies with quantitative effect sizes, meeting the highest evidence-quality standard in this framework.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on achievement is moderate and clearly positive (g=0.610), exceeding the blue threshold for impact. The review also reports robust positive subgroup effects in several contexts, indicating meaningful practical impact rather than a trivial or ambiguous one.

interventions.use_case: AI-powered chatbots and conversational assistants (including ChatGPT-based tools) used for science education, often as scaffolded or personalized learning supports and sometimes as primary instructional agents.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis found a statistically significant moderate positive effect of AI-powered chatbots on student achievement in science education, pooled Hedges’ g=0.610 (95% CI 0.550–0.670, p<0.001) across 26 studies (n=3,287). The outcome was science learning achievement, with stronger effects when chatbots were used in scaffolded or personalized science learning contexts.
finding.measure: Science education achievement / learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Across the included studies, chatbots commonly improved engagement, motivation, and satisfaction. Moderator analyses showed positive effects on noncognitive outcomes such as satisfaction/perception (g=1.803) and engagement/motivation (g=0.761), though self-efficacy results were mixed.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, satisfaction, self-efficacy, perceptions
finding.effect_size: g=0.761 to 1.803 (subgroup effects); overall noncognitive ES=0.801
finding.confidence_interval: Overall noncognitive 95% CI 0.424–1.178; subgroup CIs vary

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that chatbot-supported instruction had stronger effects on higher-order thinking and mixed HOTS/LOTS assessments than on lower-order measures. Moderator results were positive for HOTS (g=0.974) and especially mixed assessments (g=1.778), suggesting gains in critical thinking, problem-solving, and conceptual transfer.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills, critical thinking, problem-solving, conceptual understanding

paper_profiles.title: Transforming Learning or Empty Promise? A Meta-Analysis of Generative AI in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI tools in education, including ChatGPT and related large language model systems, improve student academic achievement and under what conditions they are most effective. The authors synthesize evidence from experimental and quasi-experimental studies published from late 2022 through 2025, focusing on achievement outcomes such as test scores, grades, and GPA.

The intervention studied is broad GenAI-based instructional support, including uses such as tutoring, assessment and feedback, personalized recommendation, and mixed instructional applications. The meta-analysis includes 52 independent comparisons from 54 eligible studies across K–12 and higher education, with studies spanning STEM and non-STEM fields and multiple subject areas such as language education, computer science, art, engineering, and mathematics.

Overall, GenAI-based instruction showed a large positive effect on academic achievement (Hedges' g = 1.193), though heterogeneity was very high and publication bias was detected. Moderator analyses found that instructional role and subject area significantly influenced outcomes: GenAI was most effective when used for assessment/feedback and tutoring, and language education showed the strongest gains. Educational level, sample size, learning domain, and intervention duration were not statistically significant moderators, although descriptive patterns suggested larger effects in higher education and in longer interventions. The authors conclude that GenAI can substantially support learning when it is pedagogically aligned, but that effects vary considerably by context and implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis synthesizing 52 experimental and quasi-experimental studies, which is the strongest level of evidence in the framework. It includes formal effect-size estimation, heterogeneity analysis, moderator analyses, and publication-bias testing.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on academic achievement is large (g = 1.193), far exceeding the blue threshold of 0.20. Although the review notes substantial heterogeneity and possible publication bias, the average impact is clearly strong and positive.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of ChatGPT-like generative AI used to support learning through conversational tutoring, assessment/feedback, personalized guidance, and mixed instructional roles across K-12 and higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Across 52 independent comparisons from 54 eligible studies, GenAI-based instructional interventions produced a strong positive effect on academic achievement relative to conventional instruction. The pooled effect was Hedges' g = 1.193 (SE = 0.243, 95% CI [0.716, 1.669], p < .001), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 98.0%) indicating wide variation across contexts and implementations.
finding.measure: Academic achievement outcomes such as test scores, grades, and GPA
finding.study_size: n=52 comparisons (54 studies screened/eligible; 52 included in pooled analysis)

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German-language tasks grounded in middle school curriculum content. The authors address the problem that common VLM benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and may not reflect the kinds of visual reasoning and subject knowledge needed in real educational settings. Their goal is to create a more realistic and challenging testbed that combines image understanding with domain knowledge across school subjects.

The approach is a newly constructed dataset of 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions drawn from German school textbooks and other pupil-oriented materials across nine domains: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. Questions were created by German native speakers, and some items were intentionally adversarial or text-in-image based to test whether models can resist misleading cues or answer from visuals rather than text alone. The paper evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs using LLM-based judging with a panel of models.

The study is not a human learner intervention study; it is a benchmark evaluation focused on middle school-level content in Germany. The results show that even strong models perform poorly on these tasks, with best overall accuracy below 45% and particularly weak performance in domains such as math and music. Adversarial questions are much harder than ordinary questions, and larger models do not always scale proportionally. The authors conclude that current VLMs still struggle to combine visual evidence with domain knowledge, especially in German, and that this benchmark can support future research on multimodal reasoning in educational contexts.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmark/evaluation study with a clear, reproducible methodology and multiple model comparisons, but it is not an educational intervention study and does not use experimental or causal designs with learners. Evidence credibility is limited for K-12 learning effects because the outcomes are model benchmark accuracies rather than student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The work has clear relevance for educational AI evaluation, especially for middle school math and multimodal reasoning, but it does not demonstrate direct instructional impact on students. Its practical impact is therefore indirect and mainly useful for system selection, benchmarking, and future model development.

interventions.use_case: Benchmark evaluation of vision-language models on German middle school curriculum questions requiring visual understanding, subject knowledge, and open-ended response generation; includes adversarial questions and some prompts with text embedded in images.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that VLMs performed poorly on middle school math items, with best models reaching only about 34.09% accuracy on math and many models substantially lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors note that models were better at calculating than counting, but often misread shapes or coordinates, leading to incorrect answers on basic geometry and diagram-based calculation tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math benchmark questions involving geometry, counting, area, circumference, and diagram interpretation

finding.finding_summary: Across physics and biology, models showed limited performance on diagram-based reasoning and explanation questions. Best reported accuracy was 47.65% in physics (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and physics explanations were often incorrect even when the diagram type was recognized; biology questions also showed variable term-to-image matching and guessing behavior.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology questions requiring visual interpretation plus scientific explanation or terminology mapping
finding.study_size: n=234 physics questions; n=169 biology questions

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows low-to-moderate performance across non-math school subjects such as arts, history, music, religion, geography, and sports. Overall accuracy across domains stayed below 45% for the best model, with domain highs around 54% in history/religion and lows around 31% in music; this indicates that the models struggled to integrate visual cues with subject-specific background knowledge in middle school content.
finding.measure: Domain-specific accuracy on arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports questions
finding.study_size: n=486 images; n=2038 questions total across 9 domains

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly examines whether models can refrain from answering unanswerable or misleading items, treating this as a form of noncompliance and self-knowledge. On adversarial questions, even the best models reached only 32.83% overall accuracy, and many models gave confident but wrong answers instead of saying the question could not be answered from the image.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions designed to test refusal/recognition of unanswerable prompts
finding.study_size: adversarial subset of the 2038-question benchmark; exact adversarial n not reported

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT (two January 2023 versions) and GPT-4, focusing on whether these large language models can serve as useful assistants for mathematical work. Rather than studying classroom learning outcomes, the authors benchmark the models on a newly created dataset, GHOSTS, and a smaller subset, miniGHOSTS, designed to probe different dimensions of mathematical reasoning such as factual recall, proof completion, theorem proving, symbolic integration, olympiad-style problem solving, and search/definition retrieval.

The intervention studied is not an educational treatment but the use of ChatGPT/GPT-4 as a mathematical assistant. The paper uses prompts drawn from graduate- and undergraduate-level textbooks, math.stackexchange, the MATH dataset, and hand-crafted problems, and evaluates model outputs with manually assigned ratings, error codes, and warning codes. The paper’s context is advanced mathematics rather than school mathematics; the most relevant human populations are undergraduate and graduate-level mathematical users, not K-12 learners.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is most useful as a factual lookup or search-style assistant, but performs inconsistently on deeper mathematical reasoning and generally falls below the level needed for reliable graduate-level mathematics. GPT-4 improves performance substantially and can handle many undergraduate-level questions better than ChatGPT, but still struggles with graduate-level difficulty and proof-heavy tasks. The paper therefore positions these models as helpful support tools for mathematically proficient users, not as dependable solvers for advanced mathematical problems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style benchmark study with a clear manual evaluation protocol, but it is not an intervention study in K-12 education and does not use an experimental or causal design. The evidence is observational/analytical and focused on model capability assessment rather than learner outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no educational impact on student achievement in middle school mathematics; it evaluates LLM performance on advanced mathematics benchmarks and assistant utility for mathematicians. Any relevance to middle school math is indirect and the reported results suggest limited reliability for more complex tasks.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking ChatGPT versions and GPT-4 as mathematical assistants for advanced math tasks, including proof completion, theorem/fact retrieval, symbolic integration, and solving undergraduate/graduate-level exercises.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not study student learning; it benchmarks ChatGPT (9-Jan and 30-Jan 2023) and GPT-4 on natural-language mathematics tasks. Performance was mixed and generally below graduate level: 9-Jan ChatGPT averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) on GHOSTS, 30-Jan ChatGPT averaged 3.29/5 (SD=1.28), and GPT-4 averaged 4.15/5 (SD=1.12) on miniGHOSTS, with stronger results on fact retrieval than on proof-based or graduate-level tasks.
finding.measure: Human-rated correctness/performance on math benchmark prompts (rating 1-5), including GHOSTS and miniGHOSTS subdatasets
finding.study_size: n=709 prompts total in GHOSTS; n=170 prompts in miniGHOSTS for GPT-4

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be useful as a mathematical assistant for querying facts, acting as a search engine or knowledge-base interface, and speeding up lookup tasks in a mathematician’s workflow. This is a qualitative efficiency finding rather than a learning outcome, with no experimental effect size reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of usefulness for fact querying, definition retrieval, theorem naming, and proof-outline retrieval

paper_profiles.title: A multilevel Analysis of Saudi Arabian Student 8th Grade Mathematics Achievement TIMSS 2011
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines which student- and school-level factors are associated with mathematics achievement among Saudi Arabian 8th-grade students in TIMSS 2011. The authors use hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) to account for the nested structure of students within schools and to estimate how much variation in mathematics performance exists within and between schools.

The study does not evaluate an intervention; instead, it analyzes existing TIMSS survey and achievement data. At the student level, the model includes home educational resources, liking mathematics, self-confidence in mathematics, engagement in mathematics learning, and value placed on learning mathematics. At the school level, it includes academic emphasis, school discipline and safety, and instruction affected by mathematics resource shortages.

The population is Saudi Arabian 8th-grade students and their schools. The results indicate that all five student-level variables significantly predict mathematics achievement, with self-confidence in mathematics showing the strongest positive association. At the school level, academic emphasis is positively associated with achievement, while instruction affected by mathematics resource shortages is negatively associated. School discipline and safety is not statistically significant in the final model. The paper concludes that both student attitudes/beliefs and school context matter for mathematics performance, and that about 35% of the variance lies between schools in the unconditional model.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multilevel (HLM) analysis of TIMSS 2011 observational data, not an experiment. It has clear methodology and substantive modeling, but limited causal credibility and no random assignment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are informative but observational and context-specific to Saudi Arabian 8th-grade TIMSS data. The effects are statistically significant yet not directly evidence of an intervention impact on general or priority populations.

finding.finding_summary: This multilevel correlational study of Saudi Arabian TIMSS 2011 8th graders (n not reported in the excerpt) found that student and school factors significantly predicted mathematics achievement. Student confidence in mathematics was the strongest predictor (b=18.5 points per one-unit increase), while home educational resources, liking math, and valuing math were also positive predictors (b≈3.7-4.0), and student engagement was negative (b=-2.5 to -2.7). At the school level, emphasis on academic success was positive (b=7.9), resource shortages were negative (b=-4.0), and school discipline/safety was not significant (b=-1.4).
finding.measure: TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics achievement plausible values / scale score

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly modeled several affective/student attitude variables as predictors of mathematics achievement rather than as outcomes. Self-confidence in mathematics had a strong positive association with achievement (b=18.5), while liking learning mathematics and valuing mathematics were positive but smaller (b≈3.7-4.0), and engagement in mathematics learning was negative (b=-2.5 to -2.7).
finding.measure: TIMSS student attitude scales: self-confidence, liking math, engagement, value of learning math

finding.finding_summary: At the school level, the model found that emphasis on academic success positively predicted mathematics achievement (b=7.9, p<.001), whereas instruction affected by mathematics resource shortages negatively predicted achievement (b=-4.0, p<.05). School discipline and safety was not statistically significant (b=-1.4).
finding.measure: School-level TIMSS indices: emphasis on academic success, discipline/safety, and mathematics resource shortages

paper_profiles.title: A mathematical model for the bullying dynamics in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of bullying in schools and asks how bullying dynamics can be represented and controlled using a mathematical model. Rather than studying an educational technology intervention or an instructional program, the paper develops a compartmental framework that treats bullying as a contagion-like social process. The model is motivated by school-based bullying, peer conflict, teacher and parent intervention, and the possibility that bullying can escalate into more violent behavior.

The proposed approach divides individuals into four states: susceptible, bully, exposed to bullying, and violent. Transitions between states occur through social interaction and spontaneous recovery-like processes, with parameters representing recruitment into bullying, exposure to victimization, anti-bullying school control, family intervention, escalation to violence, and de-escalation. The model is analyzed both analytically, through differential equations and stability analysis, and numerically, including simulations on two-dimensional grids.

The paper’s main conclusion is that bullying-free and endemic regimes can both occur, depending mainly on the relative strength of bullying contagion versus school control. In particular, bullying disappears when the contagion parameter is below the control parameter, while sustained bullying persists when contagion is stronger. The results suggest that effective anti-bullying school programs and parental actions can reduce or eliminate bullying, and that stronger intervention decreases the endemic level of bullying and violence.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/mathematical modeling paper with no empirical design, no participant sample, and no intervention evaluation. It provides conceptual analysis rather than evidence meeting causal-inference criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not evaluate an actual educational technology or produce measurable student outcome impacts. Its implications for school bullying control are model-based and therefore not directly translatable into an effect size or impact estimate.

finding.finding_summary: This is a theoretical compartmental model of bullying dynamics in schools, not an intervention study. It does not report empirical effect sizes or a sample; instead, it analytically and numerically shows that bullying can either die out or persist depending on parameters, especially the recruitment/contagion rate α relative to the recovery/control rate γ (threshold at R0=α/γ=1).
finding.measure: Model-derived equilibrium densities and stability of bullying-related compartments (S, B, E, V)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that stronger school anti-bullying programs and parental intervention reduce the endemic level of bullying in the model, with the bullying-free equilibrium stable when α<γ and the endemic equilibrium stable when α>γ. However, these are simulation/analytic results from a stylized model rather than observed program impacts, so no empirical effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: Analytical stability analysis and numerical simulations of anti-bullying control in a school system model

paper_profiles.title: Role-Playing Simulation Games using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores how large language models, specifically ChatGPT, can be used to enrich teaching through role-playing simulation games. The authors frame the work as a way to move beyond passive lecture-based instruction and toward active learning, especially in digitally oriented higher education contexts.

The intervention described is a ChatGPT-enabled negotiation role-play in which students interact asynchronously with the chatbot as an interlocutor. A fixed prompt initiates the scenario, and students take on the role of advocating for and negotiating approval of a cloud migration project budget. The activity was implemented as a case study in the master's course "Impact of Cloud Computing on Organisations" within the "Cloud Computing Engineering" programme at the University of Applied Sciences Burgenland.

The paper argues that ChatGPT can be programmed to support realistic conversational simulations and that this can help students practice communication, negotiation, and decision-making skills in a flexible format that is not constrained by time or location. The authors present the work as an initial exploration rather than a conclusive evaluation, and they suggest future work involving additional prompts, scenarios, and master’s programmes to assess broader applicability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a brief practice-oriented case description in an ERCIM News article, not a controlled empirical study. It reports no analytic methodology, comparison group, or quantitative outcomes, so it does not meet evidence standards for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The article proposes a potentially useful classroom application of ChatGPT, but provides no measured effect sizes or robust outcome evidence. Impact is therefore unclear and modest at best, based on qualitative claims only.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a conversational role-play partner in an asynchronous simulation game for students to practice negotiation and decision-making in a cloud migration project scenario.
Role-playing simulation game design using ChatGPT to simulate real-life organizational negotiations and support active learning through practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that using ChatGPT in a role-playing simulation can support durable skills such as negotiation, decision-making, critical thinking, and problem solving, but it reports no quantitative effect estimate. The evidence is a single illustrative case study in a master’s course (n not reported), so the finding is qualitative and preliminary rather than causal.
finding.measure: Qualitative course case study of student role-play performance and reflective experiences; no standardized outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests the ChatGPT-based simulation may increase student interest and motivation by allowing learners to practice realistic scenarios independently. However, it provides no pre-post data, comparison group, or effect size, so the claim remains descriptive and speculative.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement/interest during the simulation; no formal scale reported

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses poor achievement in secondary school mathematics and asks whether an activity-based teaching method can improve students’ mathematics performance compared with the lecture method. The motivation is the persistent low performance of Nigerian students in mathematics and the need for more effective classroom pedagogy.

The study tested an activity-based instructional approach against a lecture-based approach in the topics of circle geometry and construction. It used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with intact classes, analyzing outcomes with ANCOVA to control for pretest scores. The intervention was delivered to Senior Secondary II students in two government-owned schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria.

A sample of 96 students participated, split evenly between the experimental and control groups. The main finding was that students taught with the activity-based method scored significantly higher on the posttest than those taught with the lecture method, even after controlling for pretest performance. The paper concludes that activity-based learning is more effective for improving mathematics achievement in this context and recommends training teachers to use it more widely.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with a comparison group and ANCOVA adjustment for pretest, which gives moderate credibility. However, it is not randomized at the individual level, uses intact classes from only two schools, and reports no confidence intervals.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported group effect is large (partial η²=0.261), exceeding the threshold for medium/large impact. The finding suggests a strong positive effect on mathematics achievement in a priority population, even though the intervention is pedagogical rather than technology-based.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with intact classes (n=96; 48 activity-based, 48 lecture), students taught with the activity-based method scored substantially higher on the mathematics posttest than those taught with lecture after controlling for pretest performance. The adjusted group effect was significant in ANCOVA, F(1,93)=114.461, p<0.001, with partial eta squared η²=0.261, indicating the activity-based approach explained 26.1% of posttest variance.
finding.measure: 20-item Mathematics Test (essay test) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest achievement scores

paper_profiles.title: Classifying German Language Proficiency Levels Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic German language proficiency classification using large language models (LLMs). The authors focus on CEFR-level prediction, asking whether prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and probing internal representations can improve classification of learner texts across the full A1–C2 scale.

The approach combines multiple German CEFR-annotated corpora (including Falko and MERLIN) with synthetic A1-level texts generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet to create a balanced dataset of 1,567 texts. The paper evaluates several LLM-based methods: English and German prompts (zero-shot and few-shot), supervised fine-tuning of LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct with LoRA, and a probing classifier trained on internal activations from LLaMA-3-8B. The work is methodological rather than classroom-based, aimed at language assessment tasks rather than an instructional intervention.
